108  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF ISIOLO   –   NO.11  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  254.   Inaccuracies in Transfers from County Revenue Fund  The statement of financial performance and Note 6 to the financial statements reflect  revenue   from   non - exchange   transactions   -   transfers   from   CRF   amount   of  Kshs.4,661,625,171. However, the County Revenue Fund (CRF) financial statements  reflected transfers to the County Executive amount of   Kshs.4,323,469,237   resulting in a  variance   of   Kshs.338,155,934.   F urther   included   in   the   transfers   from   CRF   are  development   and   special   purpose   transfers   amounts   of   Kshs.1,100,616,525   and  Kshs. 228,155,934 respectively . However, the CRF cashbook reflects transfer amounts of  Kshs.990,616,525   and   Kshs.338,155,934   to   the   dev elopment   and   special   purpose  accounts resulting in variances of Kshs.110,000,000 and Kshs.110,000,000 respectively.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of transfers from the CRF amount  of Ksh.4,661,625,171 could not be confirmed.  255.   Inaccuracies in Transfers to Other Government Entities  The statement of financial performance and Note 11 to the financial statements reflect  transfers   to   other   Government   entities   totalling   Kshs.885,484,501,   which   includes  transfers to self - reporting Pr oject - FLLoCA amounting to Kshs.133,555,181. However, the  statement of financial performance for the Financing Locally Led Climate Action (FLLoCA)  Program   -   County Government of Isiolo reflects transfers from the County Government  totalling Kshs.30,870,282.   This resulted in an unexplained variance of Kshs.102,684,899.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of transfers to self - reporting Project  -   FLLoCA amount of Kshs.133,555,181 could not be confirmed.  256.   Inaccuracies in Employee Costs  The   sta tement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs.2,003,131,850   as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial statements. Included in the  amount is basic salaries of permanent employees amounting to Kshs.1,453,191,674.  However, records from   the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) and  Human Resource Information System (HRIS) reflect total basic salary payments of  Kshs.930,322,388, resulting in an unexplained variance of Kshs.522,869,287. Further,  included in the employee costs are   payments totalling Kshs.1,860,000 in respect of basic  wages of temporary employees. However, the casual staff register, containing the bio -  data and employment details of the casual workers, was not maintained during the year  under review.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   employee   costs   of  Kshs.2,003,131,850 could not be confirmed.

109  257.   Unsupported Transfers to Dispensaries Centers  The statement of financial performance reflects transfers to other Government entities of  Kshs. 885,484,501, which as disclosed Note 11 to the financial statements includes  transfers to other County Government entities amount of Kshs.132,523,819. The amount  further includes transfers to fifty - two (52) dispensaries and vocational training centers  tota lling Kshs.12,271,145. However, no detailed breakdown, expenditure returns or  supporting documentation were provided to account for how the transferred funds were  utilized at each facility.  In the circumstances, the completeness and accuracy of the tran sfers to other county  Government entities of Kshs.12,271,145 could not be confirmed.  258.   Unsupported Payment of Stipend to Community Health Promoters  The statement of financial performance and Note 11 to the financial statements reflect  transfers to other Government entities amount of Kshs.885,484,501.   Included in the  amount are other current transfers, grants and subsidies totalling Kshs.36,635,000, o ut  of which an amount of Kshs.14,505,000 was made to the Department of Health for  payment of monthly stipend to Community Health Promoters (CHPs). However, transfers  of Kshs.9,825,000 made on 8 May, 2025, were not supported by acknowledgment  receipts   from   the   intended   beneficiaries,   payment   schedules   and   bank   transfer  documentation.  Further,   the   County   Government   reported   a   co - funding   arrangement   with   a   local  consortium for payment of the CHP stipends in four Wards of Kinna, Wabera, Bulapesa,  and Burat fo r the period from January, 2023 to December, 2024. However, contract  agreement and Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the two parties was not  provided for audit review.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of other current transfers,   grants  and subsidies amount of Kshs.14,505,000 could not be confirmed.  259.   Undisclosed Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance  The statement of financial position and Note 21 to the financial statements reflect cash  and cash equivalents balance of Kshs.318,040,60 1. Review of the records revealed that  the County Executive maintained a bank account in a local commercial bank which had  a balance of Kshs.193,411 as at 30 June, 2025. However, the account details and the  amount held at the bank were not disclosed in the   financial statements as required.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the cash and cash equivalents  balance of Kshs.318,040,601 could not be confirmed.  260.   Unsupported Expenditure on the Construction of County Fuel Station  The statement   of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect an  amount of Kshs.935,337,726 in respect of use of goods and services. During the year the  County Executive made a payment totalling Kshs.9,860,140 to a contractor towards  constructi on of a County fuel station in Isiolo Town. However, the Environmental Impact

110  Assessment (EIA), the needs assessment that justified the construction of the facility,  mechanical engineer’s drawings specifying materials and designs and proof of land  ownershi p or a duly executed lease agreement were not provided for audit review.  In   the   circumstances,   the   regularity   and   completeness   of   the   expenditure   of  Kshs.9,860,540 on the construction of the fuel station could not be confirmed.  261.   Unsupported Expenditure o n Governors Cup Tournament  The Department for Education, Youth and Sports, Gender, Culture and Social Services  paid an amount of Kshs.1,319,000 to facilitate a Governor’s cup tournament held in Isiolo  Town. However, no imprest warrant was issued   contrary to Regulation 93(1) of Publi c  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations ,   2015 which requires an  imprest to be issued for specific purpose.   Further, t he payment was not supported by  approved budget breakdown and   details of the participating teams and the venues were  not prov ided for review. In addition, a n amount of Kshs.532,000 was paid to nineteen (19)  individuals who were not County staff members at a rate of Ksh.28,000 per person. No  explanation was provided for paying non - staff individuals.  In the circumstances, the re gularity and completeness of the payment   amounting to  Kshs.1,319,000   could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  262.   Delayed Exchequer Disbursements  The statement of financial performance and Note 6 to the financial statements reflect  transfers from County Revenue Fund (CRF) amount of Kshs.4,661,625,171. However,  transfers amounting to Kshs.812,378,638 or 17% of the total transfers was received  during   the last week of June, 2025.  The late disbursement of funds may have disrupted the execution of planned projects and  activities, thereby negatively impacting service delivery to the public.  263.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison   of budget and actual amounts reflects final revenue budget  of Kshs.6,235,553,233 against the actual receipts of Kshs.4,843,949,289, resulting in an  under - funding of Kshs.1,391,603,944 or 22% of the approved budget. Further, the County  spent an amount of Ks hs.4,068,100,314 against actual receipts of Kshs.4,843,949,289,  resulting in under - utilization of Kshs.775,848,975 or 16% of the actual receipts.  This under - funding and underutilization affected the implementation of the County’s  planned programmes and m ay have impacted negatively on the delivery of essential  services to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of these matters.

111  Other Matter  264.   Unresolved Prior Year’s Matters  In the previous year’s audit report, several issues were raised under Report on Financial  Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources and  Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk   Management and Governance. Review of the  status during audit of the County Executive in 2024/2025 revealed that twenty (20)  matters remained unresolved as   listed at the end of this report .  Other Information  265.   There were no   material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  266.   Delay in Completion of Works in the Upgrade of Isiolo Abattoir  The statement of financial performance and Note 11 to the financial statement reflect  transfers to other Government entities amount of Kshs.885,484,501. Included in the  amount are transfers to other County Government entities of Kshs.132,523,819, out of  wh ich an amount of Kshs.12,289,655 was paid on 20 December, 2024 for the upgrading  of   Isiolo   Abattoir   to   International   Export   Standards.   The   project   with   a   cost   of  Kshs.169,746,482, began on 28 March, 2023, and was initially expected to be completed  on 10 Ju ne, 2023. Review of documents revealed that two (2) project extensions, the first  from 9 June, 2023 to 31 August, 2023 and the second from 29 August, 2023 to 30  November, 2023. However, physical inspection carried out on 14 August, 2025, six  hundred and th irteen (613) days after the upgrading works commenced, revealed that  construction works was still ongoing and project remain i n complete.  Further, the payment of Kshs.12,289,655 made in the year under review, includes an  amount of Kshs.1,441,164 withheld   as retention. However, review of the retention bank  account revealed that no retention amount was held.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Ksh.12,289,655 incurred  on the project could not be confirmed.  267.   Failure to Transfer Statutory Functions and Resources to Isiolo Municipality  The Isiolo   Municipality was granted a Municipal Charter effective 1 July, 2019, through  Gazette Notice dated 10 July, 2019, thereby transferring specified municipal functions  and operational authority from the County Government of Isiolo to the Municipality.  However , available information revealed that, more than seven (7) years after the Charter  came into effect, the County Executive had not fully operationalized the Municipality in  accordance with the Urban Areas and Cities Act, 2011 (Revised 2019), as follows:

112  (i)   Th e Municipality’s budget for the year under review was prepared and controlled  by the County Executive, and there was no evidence of budget approval or  appropriation by the Municipal Board as required under Sections 20 and 21 of the  Urban Areas and Cities A ct. Except for Municipal’s project account with joint  signatories, all expenditures were controlled by the County Treasury.  (ii)   The County Executive did not transfer approved allocations for the Municipality  for   the   financial   year   2024/2025   totalling   Kshs.14 5,579,859   comprising  administrative expenditure, capital transfers under Kenya Urban Support Program  –   Urban Institutional Grant (KUSP - UIG), and capital transfers under Kenya Urban  Support   Program   –   Urban   Development   Grant   (KUSP - UDG)   amounts   of  Kshs.46,918 ,661, Kshs.35,000,000 and Kshs.63,882,198 respectively.  (iii)   The County Executive did not demonstrate that human or physical resources were  transferred to enable the Municipality perform the functions assigned under the  Charter. This was contrary to Section   15(2)(a) and (c) of the Urban Areas and  Cities Act, 2011.  (iv)   Several functions legally transferred to the Municipality continued to be performed  by   the   County   Executive,   including   garbage   collection   and   solid   waste  management, storm drainage and flood contro l, street lighting, maintenance of  urban roads, market management, fire and disaster services, animal control, and  municipal planning and administration. This was contrary to the Municipal Charter  and Section 20(2) of the Act, which require municipalities   to independently  manage assigned services.  (v)   Isiolo Municipality’s financial statements revealed that the County Executive made  payments totalling   Kshs.31,567,374   on its behalf, rather than transferring funds  to the Municipality to execute its own mandated   functions.  In the circumstances, the County Executive was in breach of the law.  268.   Irr egular Payments to the Council of Governors  During the year under review, Management made payments totalling   Kshs.4,000,000 as  subscription fees to the Council of Governors. However, the expenditure is not provided  for in the approved County Executive’s budget. Further, no justification was provided by  Management for incurring expenditure on a function that cons titutionally falls under the  National Government. This was contrary to Section 37(b) of the Intergovernmental  Relations   Act,   2012,   which   requires   that   operational   expenses   of   the   Council   of  Governors be provided for in the annual estimates of revenue and e xpenditure of the  National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  269.   Irregular Splitting of Procurement of Motor Vehicle Insurance Services  Review of procurement records revealed that the County Executive entered into a  cont ract with an insurance company for the provision of motor vehicle insurance services

113  at a contract sum of Kshs.4,200,000. However, the procurement was irregularly split into  three separate quotation requests, each below the amount of Kshs.3,000,000 thresho ld,  in order to avoid the open tendering process. This was contrary to Section 91(1) of the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which provides that open tendering is  the preferred method of procurement for goods and services whose value exceed s the  prescribed threshold.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  270.   Non - Compliance with Procurement Disclosure and Reporting Requirements  Review of procurement processes for the year under review revealed that Management  did not publi sh all awarded contracts on the Public Procurement Information Portal (PPIP)  as required. This was contrary to Executive Order No. 2 of 2018 and Circular Ref. No.  OP/CAB 39/1A dated 28 June, 2018, which mandates all public entities to publish contract  awar ds in the prescribed format and manner.  Further, the County Executive did not provide the mandatory Biannual Reports to the  Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (PPRA) detailing contract awards to youth,  women, and persons with disabilities. This was c ontrary to Section 157(10), (12), and (13)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which require reporting,  disclosure, and certification of compliance with the preference and reservation framework.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  271.   Late Commitments of Goods, Works and Services  Review of Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) purchase order  data revealed that the County Executive awarded sixty - two (62) contracts totalling  Kshs .321,028,837 for the supply of goods and services after 31 May, 2025. This was  contrary to Regulation 50(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulations, 2015, which requires that all commitments for the supply of goods and  services be   made not later than 31 May of each financial year.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  272.   Irre gu larities in Human Resource Management  272.1.   Irregular Retention of Employees Beyond Mandatory Retirement Age  Review of the Human Resource Information System (HRIS) payroll for June, 2025  revealed that thirty - three (33) employees and four (4) County advisors were over sixty  (60) years of age, whic h is beyond the mandatory retirement age. This was contrary to  Section 80(10) (a) and (b) of the Public Service Commission Act, 2017 which requires an  officer to retire from the service with effect from the date of attaining age. The affected  employees col lectively earned a gross salary of Kshs.3,722,048 in the month of June,  2025.

114  Further, four (4) of the affected staff serving as directors in job group R, who were also  serving beyond the mandatory retirement age,   no documentary evidence was provided  to   define their roles, responsibilities and job description of their positions they occupy .  272.2.   Irregular Engagement of Advisors  Review of payroll and human resource records as at 30 June, 2025 revealed that the  County Executive had engaged thirteen (13) advi sors across various functions. This was  contrary   to   the   Salaries   and   Remuneration   Commission   (SRC)   Circular   Ref.  SRC/TS/CGOVT/3/16 dated 29 July, 2013, which limits the number of advisors to a  maximum of four (4). As previously reported, no documentary evi dence was provided to  demonstrate how the County Public Service Board established the additional nine (9)  advisor positions and there was no evidence that a proposal for their creation was  submitted to the County Assembly for approval through the County Ex ecutive Committee  Member responsible for the County Public Service, as required.  272.3.   Irregular   Payment of Leave Allowance  Review of the payroll for the year under review revealed that one hundred and three (103)  employees   were   paid   leave   allowance   above   the   maximum   leave   allowance   of  Kshs.10,000 resulting in payment of irregular leave allowance totalling Kshs.4,006,207.  This   was contrary to SRC Circular SRC/TS/TA/3/10 (86) that entitles a maximum leave  allowance amount of Ksh.10,000 to employees on job group P and above, contrary to  SRC Guidelines.  272.4.   Irregular Payment of Extraneous Allowance  Review   of   payroll   data   for   the   year   under   review   revealed   that   an   amount   of  Kshs.8,730,050 was paid as extraneous allowance which is not prescribed by any circular  or guidance by the Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC).  Further,   letters   of   assignment   or   deployment   indicating   th at   the   recipients   were  performing duties beyond their normal responsibilities were not   provided   for audit  verification. This was contrary to Article 230 of the Constitution of Kenya that gives the  SRC the power to set remuneration and benefits to National   and County Government’s  public officers.  272.5.   Irregular Recruitment of County Staff  During the year under review, the County Public Service Board (CPSB) recruited a total  of   eighty - six   (86)   staff   members   for   various   positions.   However,   key   supporting  docum ents   including   minutes   of   CPSB   meetings   approving   the   recruitments,   job  advertisements, shortlisting criteria, and evaluation or scoring records by the recruitment  committee were not provided for audit review.  Further, review of the County Annual Develop ment Plan (ADP) and approved budget for  the year revealed that there was no provision for recruitment activities, either in planning  or in financial allocation.

115  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  273.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Review of the payroll records provided for audit revealed that on different months, various  employees had deductions that were more than two - thirds of their basic pay. This was  contrary to the provis ions of Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which states that  the total amount of all deductions that may be made by an employer from the wages of  his employee at any one time shall not exceed two thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Manageme nt was in breach of the law.  274.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of June, 2025 payroll revealed that the County Executive had a total of one  thousand, seven hundred and six (1,706) employees out of whom seven hundred and  ninety - one (791) or approximately 46% were from one ethnic community. This was  contrary to Section 7(2) of the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008 that states  that no public establishment shall have more than one third of its staff from the same  ethnic c ommunity.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  275.   Stalled Projects  275.1.   Construction of Isiolo Municipal Stadium Phase I  As previously reported, the County Executive engaged a local contractor during the  2018/2019 financial year for the construction of Isiolo Municipal Stadium at a contract  sum of Kshs.345,998,315. The project commenced in May, 2019 with an expected  completi on date of December, 2020, for a period of twenty (20) months. However, as at  30   June,   2022,   the   project   had   stalled   following   its   suspension   to   pave   way   for  investigations. By time of suspension, the contractor had been paid an amount of  Kshs.231,622,838,   representing 66.9% of the contract amount. According to the Ministry  of Public Works, the physical completion of the project was estimated at 67%. Physical  inspection conducted on 11 August, 2025 confirmed that no construction activities were  ongoing at t he site, as the contractor was not on site. The project therefore remains  incomplete with no evidence of resumption of works.  275.2.   Proposed Construction of Isiolo County Headquarters  As previously reported, the National Government, through the State Department for  Public Works, in collaboration with the County Government of Isiolo, commenced the  construction of Isiolo County Headquarters on 4 March, 2019. The project was initially  valu ed   at   Kshs.870,700,000   but   was   subsequently   revised   downwards   to  Kshs.556,900,000   in accordance   with   applicable   Government guidelines.   However,  despite the lapse of approximately seventy - eight (78) months (or over six years) since the  project began, the pr oject remains incomplete and stalled. As at the time of audit in

116  August, 2025, only an amount of Kshs.180,400,000 had been paid, representing 32% of  the revised contract sum. Physical verification conducted on 11 August, 2025 revealed  that no construction   activities were ongoing and the contractor was not on site.  275.3.   Delayed Completion of Isiolo Municipality Market  As previously reported, the County Executive entered into a contract with a local  contractor on 25 June, 2018, for the construction of a modern   market, at a contract sum  of Kshs.545,211,810. A total amount of Kshs.366,626,237 or 67% of the contract sum,  had been paid to the contractor and a progress report indicated 80% completion level.  Physical inspection conducted on 11 August, 2025, which wa s more than seven (7) years  after the contract was signed and thirty - two (32) months after the lapse of the revised  project   completion   date   of   December,   2022,   revealed   that   the   project   remained  incomplete with no construction activities underway and the co ntractor was not on site.  No justification was provided by Management for the prolonged delays and failure to  complete the project. This was contrary to Section 149(1)(b) of the Public Finance  Management Act, 2012 that requires an Accounting Officer to be   accountable in ensuring  that the resources of the entity are used in a way that is effective and efficient.  In the circumstances,   the public may not receive value for money from funds already  spent on the projects.  276.   Irregularities in Imprest Management  276.1.   Irregular Issuance of Multiple Imprests  Review of the imprest   register maintained by the County Executive revealed that two (2)  officers that were issued with multiple imprests amounting to Kshs.8,410,300 issued to  one (1) officer totalling Kshs.1,134,200 and to another officer totalling Kshs.7,276,100.  This was con trary to Regulations 93(4)(b) of Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that the Accounting Officer should  ensure that the applicant has no outstanding imprests. No explanation was provided why  the officers were iss ued with multiple imprest before surrender of earlier imprests.  276.2.   Irregular Imprest Utilization for Garbatulla Land Adjudication Exercise  The County Executive paid an amount of Kshs.3,951,700 for facilitation of the Garbatulla  land adjudication exercise   and issuance of allotment letters by the National Land  Commission in Isiolo Township using temporary imprest. Review of the surrender  documents revealed that an amount of Kshs.3,310,750 was issued as imprest to various  County staff and National Government   land experts who participated in the exercise for  fourteen (14) days. However, no daily attendance sheets signed by the participants were  not provided to confirm their presence throughout the 14 days, making it difficult to verify  whether all individuals   were present and eligible for the facilitation allowances paid. An  additional amount of Kshs.372,650 was spent on the direct procurement of stationery  items which were not taken on charge, recorded in stores documents or supported with  records.

117  276.3.   Irregular   Issuance of Imprest and Direct Procurement for Peace Dialogue  Activities  Review of records revealed that an imprest   amounting to Kshs.1,200,000 was issued for  facilitation of the Inter - grazing Committee Peace Dialogues on resource sharing at Daaba  on 9 September, 2024. However, review of the surrender documents revealed that the  imprest was approved and paid on 18 Sept ember, 2024, which was nine (9) days after  the event had taken place. Despite the timing, the payment was processed as an imprest  instead of being recorded as a claim. The anomalies were not explained. Further, an  amount of Kshs.300,000 was paid to a local   supplier for the supply of tents and  refreshments. These services were procured directly without competitive tender process,  contrary to Section 91(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which  requires open tendering as the preferred m ethod of procurement for goods and services  above the prescribed threshold.  276.4.   Irregular Payment for Personnel and Payroll Data Cleaning  The County Executive issued an imprest totalling Kshs.3,124,800 to facilitate personnel  and payroll data cleaning for C ounty Government staff Mombasa, from 17 February, 2025  to 25 February, 2025. However, two (2) staff did not sign the attendance list on date 17  and 18 February, 2025 and the attendance lists for dates 23, 24, and 25 February, 2025  were not provided for aud it review.  Further, the County Executive paid per diem totalling Kshs.536,000 to three (3) facilitators  from a Government Institution based in Mombasa. Their specific role in the data cleaning  exercise was not defined, and no justification was provided f or paying them imprests while  at their duty station. This was contrary to SRC c ircular Ref.No.SCR/ADM/11/(156) dated  August 2023 on payment of daily subsistence allowance which states that payment of  daily subsistence allowance shall not be payable for a l ocation within a radius of 50km of  the affected duty station of the respective officers.  In the circumstances, the regularity of the payments totalling Kshs.16,881,850 could not  be confirmed.  277.   Undelivered Office Equipment and Computers  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statement reflect use  of goods and services amounting to Kshs.935,337,726. Included in the amount is other  operating   expenses   totalling   Kshs.89 ,441,968.   The   County   Executive   through   the  Department for Agriculture, Land, and Physical Planning, engaged a contractor through  a Request for Quotation (RFQ) to renovate and equip an office at Isiolo Fishery Farm at  contract sum of Kshs.1,999,654. Further , the Bills of Quantities included four (4) executive  high - back chairs costing Ksh.60,000, fifteen (15) visitors’ chairs at a total cost of  Ksh.15,000, four (4) three - drawer metallic filing cabinets at a total cost of Ksh.80,000, two  desktop computers valu ed at Kshs.102,000, and two laptops valued at Kshs.220,000 all  totalling Kshs.477,000. However, none of these items had been delivered as at the time  of the audit inspection on 7 August, 2025.

118  In the circumstances, the value for money on equipment and   computers expenditure of  Kshs.477,000 could not be confirmed.  278.   Unutilized Hatchery Equipment Project  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statement reflect use  of goods and services amounting to Kshs.935,337,726. Included   in the amount is other  operating expenses totalling to Kshs.89,441,968. The County Government, through the  Department   for   Fisheries   Development,   engaged   a   contractor   for   the   supply   and  installation of hatchery equipment and rehabilitation of the fisheries   pump at a contract  sum of Kshs.2,498,917. However, audit inspection carried out on 7 August, 2025 revealed  the hatchery was not operational. Further, Inspection and Acceptance report was not  provided to confirm that the goods and services delivered met the   required specifications.  In addition, Bill of Quantities required supply of one standby generator at a cost of  Kshs.50,000. However, the generator had not been delivered as at the time of the  verification.  In the circumstances, the value for money on   the expenditure of Kshs.2,498,917 included  in the project could not be confirmed.  279.   Delayed Upgrading of Ola Jarole Kachewa Road  The statement of financial position and Note 26 to the financial statements reflect  property, plant, and equipment balance of   Kshs.18,866,554,912, which includes Work in  Progress additions of Kshs.18,031,167. This amount was the first payment paid to a  company for the construction of Ola Jarole - Kachewa Road to bitumen standards. The  procurement was awarded on 12 May, 2025 with a   contract duration of nine (9) months  and contract sum of Kshs.180,311,676.   However, physical verification of the project on  7 August, 2025 approximately three (3) months, or 33% of project's duration revealed that  the estimated progress of works was only   about 10% an indication of significant delays in  project implementation. Review of the revised or supplementary budget further revealed  that   the   County   Executive   had   allocated   an   amount   of   Kshs.90,074,590   for   the  construction of bitumen standard roads during the year. The allocation is insufficient to  fully fund the nine months project valued at Kshs.180,311,676 resulting in a budget deficit  of Kshs.90,237,086.  In the   circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.18,031,167  incurred on the project could not be confirmed.  280.   Irregular Procurement of Ambulances  The statement of financial position and Note 26 to the financial statements reflect  property, p lant and equipment balance of Kshs.18,866,554,912, which include motor  vehicles balance of Kshs.400,752,524. Review of payment documents, cash book, and  bank statements revealed that during the financial year the County Executive incurred an  expenditure of   Kshs.32,000,000 on the purchase of three (3) ambulances. However,  examination of procurement records related to the supply and delivery of the ambulances  revealed that none of the bidders submitted the required two (2) copies of the tender

119  documents (orig inal and copy), yet the evaluation minutes indicated that all bidders  complied.  Further, no individual evaluation score sheets of evaluators were provided to support  the award decision. In addition, there was no signed contract agreement, cont rary to  Section 135 of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.32,000,000 on  motor vehicles acquisition could not be confirmed.  281.   Failure to Fully Implement e - P rocurement Processes  Review of procurement processes by the County Executive during the year under review  revealed instances of procurement activities being conducted outside the Integrated  Financial Information System (IFMIS) e - procurement module as requ ired. Specifically ,  the tender requisitions and advertisements, opening of tenders, tenders’ evaluation and  award of contracts were conducted manually. This was contrary to Regulation 49(2) of  the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, an d the Executive Order  No. 2 of 2018, which required full implementation and use of the e - procurement system  for all public procurement transactions.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  282.   Long Outstanding Trade and Other Payables Ba lance  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs.985,147,345   as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements. Out of this balance,  trade and other payables amounting to Kshs.364,159,486 or 36% have been outst anding  for over two (2) years. The payables were not paid as a first charge in the financial year  2024/2025. This was contrary to Regulation 41(2) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which states that debt service paymen ts shall  be a first charge on the County Revenue Fund and the Accounting Officer shall ensure  this is done to the extent possible that the county government does not default on debt  obligations.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  283.   Non - Remittance of Statutory Deductions  Review of records revealed that the County Executive did not remit statutory and pension  deductions amounting to Kshs.27,754,937, Kshs.10,462,150 and Kshs.39,725,361 to  LAPFUND, National Social Security Fund   (NSSF) and LAPTRUST, Pension Trust,  respectively. This was contrary to Section 19(1) and (6) of the Employment Act, 2007,  which requires employers to remit statutory deductions to the respective agencies within  the prescribed timelines. As a result, the Co unty Executive may incur additional and  avoidable costs of interest and penalties due to delay in settling the long outstanding  debts.

120  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  284.   Failure to Adhere to Rental Lease Agreement  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services amounting to Kshs.935,337,726. Included in the amount is an  expenditure on rental of produced assets totalling Kshs.49,621,250. During the year  under review, the County Government paid a total amount of Kshs.3,712,000 to a landlord  for rent of premises housing the Department for Youth, Sports and Talent at Desert Trail  Building, covering the period from October, 2024 to January, 2025. The payment  comprised of an amount of Kshs.1,856,000   fo r   two (2) office blocks and a warehouse ,  and Kshs.1,856,000   for   two (2) office blocks and a multipurpose   complex shed. However,  the lease agreement dated 4 April, 2022 provided for audit only makes reference to o ffice  space   and   a   warehouse.   No   amended   lease   agreement   addendum   or   formal  documentation was provided to support the expanded scope of leased premises.  In the above circumstances, the regularity and value for money of the additional rental  expenditure of   Kshs.1,856,000 could not be confirmed.  285.   Non - Compliance in Procurement and Asset Disposal Planning  Review of the Procurement Plan for the year under review revealed the following non -  compliance issues:  (i)   The Procurement Plan was not prepared in the prescri bed format provided in the  third Schedule of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020.  Descriptions of the goods being procured, procurement methods for items,  planned dates of execution and current status of items procured was not inclu ded  in the plan.  (ii)   The Procurement Plan was not signed by the Head of Procurement Unit and was  not   approved by the County Executive Committee Member for Finance as  required by the Third Schedule of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Regulations, 202 0.  (iii)   The Procurement Plan did not include and consider a minimum of 30% of the  annual   procurement   plan   being   reserved   for   women,   youth,   persons   with  disabilities and other disadvantaged groups. This was contrary to Regulation 149  of the Public Procurement a nd Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires  a procurement entity to allocate at least 30% of its annual procurement budget for  the purposes of procuring goods, works and services from enterprises owned by  youth, women and persons with disability.  (iv)   No evidence was provided to show there was stakeholder consultation during the  development of the plan. Further, no needs assessments, approvals, minutes and  justifications for the planned procurement were provided for review.

121  (v)   During the year under revie w a supplementary budget was passed and an  increment was approved for procurement of goods and services. However, the  procurement plan was not updated to reflect the changes in the County budget.  (vi)   There was no evidence provided to confirm that Chief Office rs of all departments  of the County Executive conducted quarterly reviews of the procurement plan and  reported on the implementation of the plan to the County Executive Member of  Finance. This was contrary to Regulation 40(6) of the Public Procurement and  Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires an Accounting Officer of a  procuring   entity   to   prepare   a   quarterly   report   on   the   implementation   of   a  procurement plan and submit it to the county executive committee member for  finance.  (vii)   The County did not ha ve an Asset Disposal Plan for the year under review.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  286.   Lack of Asset Management Unit  Review of asset management records revealed that the County Executive had not  established an Asset Management unit responsible for overseeing asset. Consequently,  there were no documented systems or designated officers accountable for planning,  acquisition , tracking, maintenance, storage, safeguarding of assets, disposal of obsolete  or unusable assets and, preparation and maintenance of comprehensive asset register.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over asset   management could  not be confirmed.  287.   Weaknesses in Internal Controls Related to Management of County Vehicles  A s   disclosed   in   Note   10   to   the   financial statements ,   the   County   Executive   spent  Kshs.9,591,989 on routine maintenance of vehicles and other trans port equipment.  Review of the County Executive’s vehicle fleet management revealed   that   the   County did  not have a fleet management system in place to support planning, coordination, and  monitoring of vehicle usage and movements , no   motor vehicle fleet stat us list indicating  the condition of each vehicle for the year under review was provided , and   motor vehicle  management was not centralized under the   T ransport   O fficer ,   resulting in gaps in  oversight and internal controls.  In   the   circumstances,   the   effecti veness   of   internal   controls   over   motor   vehicles  management   could not be confirmed.

122  288.   Inadequate Security and Safety Controls at the County Information and  Communication Technology Data Centre  Audit   inspection   of   the   County   Executive’s   ICT   Data   Centre   reve aled   significant  infrastructure   and   security   weaknesses,   including   lack   of   proper   network   cable  management, absence of fire suppression systems or fire extinguishers, and poor  ventilation, despite the room hosting critical County servers. Additionally, the   facility was  secured   with   a   basic,   easily   breakable   lock   and   lacked   adequate   access   control  mechanisms, making it susceptible to unauthorized access.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of IT internal controls could not be confirmed.  289.   Weaknesses   in   Drug   Inventory   Management   at   Isiolo   County   Referral  Hospital  Review of the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) payment  records for the year under review revealed that the Department for Health procured  medical   drugs   w orth   Kshs.150,496,019,   while   Kenya   Medical   Supplies   Authority  (KEMSA) records indicated that Isiolo County Referral Hospital received drugs worth  Kshs.18,712,036 during the year. The Hospital uses an automated management system  to manage pharmacy and store   operations. However, attempts to generate an annual  report from the system were unsuccessful due to system incompleteness, and the system  did not provide comprehensive records of drug receipts and issues for the year. This  limitation   hindered   reconciliati on   with   KEMSA   supply   data   compromising   audit  verification.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over drugs inventory records  could not be confirmed.  290.   Weaknesses in Management of Medical Insurance  During the year under review, the County Executive engaged an insurance company to  provide medical insurance cover at a contract sum of Kshs.120,508,279 and group life,  personal accident plus work injury bene fits covers at a contract sum of Kshs.14,965,831,  and a total of Ksh.104,408,646 was paid to the insurance company. However, review of  the procurement and contract records revealed that a schedule from the insurer detailing  the number of staff covered and   the applicable premium rate per category of staff was not  provided for audit, hence the basis on which the total contract sum was determined could  not be confirmed. Further, the County Government did not provide evidence that it had  verified the eligibilit y of the insurance company by obtaining a valid license from the  Insurance Regulatory Authority authorizing it to provide medical insurance cover. In  addition, details of the approved hospitals and medical facilities under the medical  scheme were not provi ded for audit.  The County Executive staff payrolls also indicated that the total number of staff was one  thousand, seven hundred and seven (1,707). However, only one thousand six hundred  and twenty - eight (1,628) were covered and Management did not provide   criteria on how  the covered staff members were identified and selected. Further, the County Executive

123  recruited eighty - six (86) additional employees during the year, but no evidence was  provided to confirm that the new staff were enrolled in the insurance   cover.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls relating to the management of  the medical insurance cover could not be confirmed.  291.   Ineffective Internal Audit Function  291.1.   Lack of Audit Committee  Review of the County’s governance structure revealed that the internal function unit  lacked functional independence due to lack of an Audit Committee. This was contrary to  Section 155(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2 015, which provides that the Head of Internal Audit shall report administratively to the  Accounting   Officer   and   functionally   to   the   Audit   Committee   to   ensure   operational  independence.  291.2.   Lack of an Audit Management System  The internal audit function was n ot supported by an audit management system or modern  analytical tool. The limitations significantly hindered its ability to conduct efficient, risk -  based audits and to offer independent and objective assurance on internal controls, risk  management and gove rnance.  291.3.   Lack of Access to Integrated Financial Management Information System  The internal audit function did not have access to the Integrated Financial Management  Information System (IFMIS) a core system in the processing of financial   transactions. This  restricted the unit’s ability to monitor and review financial transactions in real - time, thereby  compromising its oversight effectiveness.  291.4.   Lack of an Internal Audit Annual Review  There was no evidence that an annual review had been   conducted on the independence,  performance, and competence of the Internal Audit Function. This was contrary to  Regulation   159(2)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which requires the Audit Committee to undertake such r eviews and  provide commentary in its annual report.  291.5.   Lack of Implementation of Internal Audit Recommendations  Management did not demonstrate action on the findings and recommendations issued by  the Internal audit function. The absence of follow - up mecha nisms raises concerns about  the   effectiveness   and   impact   of   internal   audit   work   in   improving   governance   and  accountability.

124  291.6.   Understaffing of the Internal Audit Function  The County Executive’s Internal Audit function had only two (2) members of   staff, the  Head of Internal Audit and one Principal Internal Auditor. The limited human resources  constrained the unit’s ability to cover the broad range of County operations and to provide  timely assurance services.  In the circumstances, the effectivenes s of the internal audit function in delivering on its  mandate could not be confirmed.  292.   Lapse   of   Contract   for   the   County   Executive   Committee   Member   for  Education  Review of payroll and personal records revealed that the contract of the County Executive  Com mittee (CEC) Member for Education, Youth, Sports, Culture, and Social Services  lapsed on 9 October, 2024, and no evidence of renewal or extension was provided. As at  the time of audit in August, 2025, the position remained vacant.  In the circumstances, th e effectiveness of governance and decision - making in the  relevant Department could not be confirmed.  293.   Anomalies in Migration from Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database to  Human Resource Information System  The   County   Government   of   Isiolo   adopted   Human   Resource   Information   System  (HRIS - Ke) with effect from December, 2024. Comparison of IPPD data for November,  2024 HRIS - Ke December, 2024 data revealed the following inconsistencies:  293.1.   Job - Gr oup Changes  During   the   transition,   job   group   for   one   (1)   employee   disignated   as   Director   of  Administration was irregularly changed from job group Q to P. No explanation or  authorization for the change was provided for audit verification.  293.2.   Underpayment of Basic Salary  The total basic salary paid in November, 2024 was Kshs.80,88 3,049 while the amount  paid in December, 2024 was Kshs.75,628,397 reflecting an unexplained reduction of  Kshs.4,275,421. Further, a total of one thousand, five hundred and   seventy - two   (1,572)  employees   were underpaid their basic salaries despite maintain ing the same job groups  as in the previous month indicating inconsistencies in payroll processing during the  migration to HRIS - Ke.  293.3.   Variance in Payment of Health Workers’ Extraneous Allowance  Two hundred and fifty - one (251) employees were paid health wo rkers’ extraneous  allowance amounting to Kshs.6,208,000 in November, 2024. In December, 2024, the  same category of officers received only Kshs.3,620,000 resulting in a variance of  Kshs.2,588,000. No explanation or justification for the reduction was provid ed for audit  review.

125  293.4.   Inconsistencies in the Number of Employees in the New System  The total number of employees appearing in November, 2024 IPPD payroll was one  thousand, seven hundred and twelve (1,712) employees, while the December, 2024 HRIS  payroll   had one thousand, six hundred and ninety - eight (1,698) employees, resulting in  an unexplained variance of fourteen (14) employees.  293.5.   Unauthorized New Employees Added in the Payroll  Three (3) new employees comprising of an accountant, an enrolled   nurse and an  assistant game warden, who did not appear in the November, 2024 IPPD payroll were  included in the December, 2024 HRIS - Ke payroll. A total gross salary of Kshs.233,788  was paid to these employees. However, no explanation was provided to justify   their  inclusion in the payroll during the system transition.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on payroll management and  the actual status of staff composition and profiles for the County Executive could not be  confirmed.
