139  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF THARAKA - NITHI   –   NO.13  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  319.   Unsupported Property, Plant and Equipment  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.6,090,520,032   which   includes   motor   vehicles   and   land   balances   of  Kshs.368,260,755 and Kshs.56,548,329 respectively as disclosed in Note 19 to the  financial statements.   However, log books for one hundred and seventeen (117) motor  vehicles were not provided for audit review. In addition, tit le deeds or certificates of lease  documents for two thousand, six hundred and fifty - six (2,656) parcels of land) were not  provided for audit review. Further, there was no evidence that Management had carried  out physical inspection and verification of the   assets during the year under review.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and ownership of motor vehicles and land balances  of Kshs.368,260,755 and Kshs.56,548,329, respectively could not be confirmed.  320.   Unaccounted for   Contractors   Retention Money  As previously reported, the statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 15 to  the   financial   statements   reflects   retentions   account   payables   balance   of  Kshs.107,949,605.   However, the County Executive’s deposit bank account   reflected a  balance of Kshs.29,848,571, resulting to an unexplained and unreconciled variance  balance of Kshs.78,101,034. This was contrary to Regulation 210 (1) (g) of the Public  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides tha t a  public officer employed by a County Government or a County Government entity commits  an offence of financial misconduct if, without lawful authority, the officer fails to pay into a  government bank account any public money entrusted to the officer or r eceived by the  officer for or on behalf of that Government or that entity.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the retentions account payables  balance of Kshs.107,082,266 could not be confirmed.  321.   Unreconciled Variances in Trade Account   Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   account   payables   balance   of  Kshs.882,571,678 which includes Kshs.90,190,799 owed to the Kenya Medical Supplies  Authority (KEMSA) as disclosed in Note 16 to the financial statements. However, re cords  maintained at KEMSA reflected a balance of Kshs.152,014,693 as receivable from the  County Executive of Tharaka   -   Nithi resulting in a unexplained and unreconciled variance  of Kshs.61,823,894.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and   completeness of the trade account payables  balance of Kshs.882,571,678 could not be confirmed.

140  322.   Unexplained Voided Transactions  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   total   payments   amounting   to  Kshs.4,466,801,531. However, review of Integrated F inancial Management Information  System   (IFMIS)   records   revealed   that   five   hundred   and   forty - six   (546)   payment  transactions totalling Kshs.441,482,502 were processed and subsequently voided or  cancelled during the year ended 30 June, 2025. However, these vo ided transactions were  not supported by requests for voiding and no documentary evidence was provided to  confirming that the Controller of Budget was notified of the voiding of the payments to  facilitate the necessary adjustments.  In the   circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the voided transactions of  Kshs.44,482,502 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  323.   Budgetary   Control and   Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budg et  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   balances   of   Kshs.6,466,615,529   and  Kshs.4,955,540,851, respectively, resulting to an under - funding of Kshs. 1,511,074,678  or 23% of the budget. Similarly, the County Executive spent Kshs. 4,950,137,528   against  actual receip ts of Kshs. 4,955,540,851,   resulting to an under - utilization of Kshs. 5,403,323  of the actual receipts.  The under - funding affected the planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in res pect of this matter.  Other Matter  324.   Unresolved   Prior Year Matters  In the previous years’ audit reports, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial   Statements,   Report   on   Lawfulness   and   Effectiveness   in   Use   of   Public  Resources, and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance.   However, Management had not resolved the thirteen (13) matters listed  below as at 30 June, 2025 .  List of Unresolved Prior Year Matters  No.   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  1   Misclassification of Expenditure  2   Un - accounted for   Contractors   Retention Money  3   Variance in Acquisition of Assets

141  No.   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  4   Variance in Pending Bills Accounts Payables  5   Delayed   Upgrading of Kambandi - Cheera - Ruguti Road to Bitumen Standards  6   Delayed Upgrading of Karandini - Kithioroni Road to Bitumen Standards  8   Delayed Upgrading of Tunyai   -   Ntaara   Road to Bitumen Standards  8   Delayed Construction of Ndagani Market  9   Non - Compliance with the One Third Rule of Basic Salary  10   Non - Compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility Principle on Wage Bill  11   Non - Compliance   with   Fiscal   Responsibility   Principle   on   Development  Expenditure  12   Irregular Payment to Council of Governors  13   Voided Transactions  Other Information  325.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  326.   Irregular Payments to Council of Governors  Review of records revealed   that Management made a payment of Kshs.2,000,000 to the  Council of Governors during the year under review. However, Management did not  provide explanation for the payment to the Council which is an independent entity,  contrary to Section 37 of the Intergov ernmental Relations Act, 2012 which provides that  operational expenses for the structures and institutions established under the Act, shall  be provided for in the annual estimates of the revenue and expenditure of the National  Government.  In the circumst ances, Management was in breach of the law.  327.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility Principles on Wages  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employees’   cost   amount   of  Kshs.2,583,302,787 representing 56% of the total revenue of Ksh s.4,615,034,940. This  was   contrary   to   Regulation   25(1)(b)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires the County Executive to set a wage limit  which should not exceed 35% of the total revenue received.  In the ci rcumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

142  328.   Non - Compliance   with   the   Law   on   Fiscal   Responsibility   Principles   on  Development Expenditure  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects total expenditure  amount of   Kshs.4,950,137,528 comprising of recurrent and development expenditures of  Kshs.4,142,302,726 and Kshs.807,834,802 respectively. The development expenditure  accounted for 16% of the total expenditure which was below the 30% threshold stipulated  by   Regulati on   25(1)(g)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which provides that the County Government’s actual expenditure on  development shall be at least thirty percent 30% in conformity with the requirement under  Section 107(2)(a ) of the Act.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  329.   Non - Compliance with the Law on the One Third Rule on Basic Salary  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs.2,583,302,787 as disclosed in   Note 8 to the financial statements. Review of the  June, 2025 payroll revealed that seventy - six (76) employees received net salaries which  were less than a third (1/3) of their basic salaries. This was contrary to Section 19(3) of  the Employment Act, 2007 w hich provides that the total amount of all deductions may be  made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any one time, shall not exceed  two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  330.   Failure to Remit Payrol l Deductions  The statement of financial position reflects trade payables balance of Kshs.882,571,678  as disclosed in Note 16 to the financial statements, which further includes a balance of  Kshs.205,935,531 in respect to accrued salaries and wages. Revi ew of payables records  revealed that long outstanding remittances totalling Kshs.20,693,721 deducted from  employee salaries remained outstanding for more than twelve (12) months and had not  been remitted to the Local Authorities Pension Trust (LAPTRUST). T his was contrary to  Section 19(4)(5) of the Employment Act, 2007 which stipulates that an employer who  deducts an amount from an employee’s remuneration in accordance with Subsection  (1)(a), (f), (g) and (h) shall pay the amount so deducted in accordance w ith the time period  and other requirements specified in the law, agreement court order or arbitration as the  case may be.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  331.   Irregular Engagement of Road Marshals  Review of road marshals’ manual pa yrolls revealed that six hundred and forty - nine (649)  employees were engaged as casuals for more than twenty (20) months beyond the  allowed three (3) months period resulting in irregular payment of Kshs.17,314,500. This  was contrary to Section 9(1)(a) and   37(1)(b) of Employment Act, 2007 which requires a  written contract for employment that lasts for three months or more.

143  Further, it was observed that thirty - two (32) officers were engaged to replace officers who  had exited. However, the basis or criteria o f appointment was not supported by an  approval   from   County   Public   Service   Board   advertisements,   a   list   of   applicants,  shortlisting minutes interview minutes and final selection reports. This was contrary to  Section 65(2) of the County Governments Act, 2012   which provides for a fair and  transparent engagement of employees with merit and fair competition.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  332.   Irregular Payment of Special Salary to Staff  Review of employee records revealed that Management paid special salary amounting to  Kshs.1,346,760 to four (4) officers in addition to their basic salary they were entitled to  during the year. However, approval from the Salaries and Remuneration Commissio n  was not provided contrary the SRC circular SRC/TS/29(83), dated 22 August, 2023 on  Remuneration and Benefits for Public Officers in the County Governments for the third  remuneration Review Cycle 2021/2022   –   2024/2025, that lists all the earnings County  E xecutive Officers were entitled to and their respective appointment letters.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  333.   Non - Compliance with Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of payroll records revealed that out of the total employe es of three thousand and  sixty - six (3,066), two thousand and thirty - four (2,034) or 66% were from the dominant  community in the County.   Further , the recruitment conducted during the year did not  remedy the ethnic disparity. This was contrary to Section 7 (1 ) and   (2) of the National  Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, which stipulates that no public establishment should  employ more than one - third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  334.   Projects Implementation  334.1.   Delayed Upgrading of Karandini - Kithioroni Road  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 19 to the financial statements  reflects property, plant and equipment balance of Kshs.6,090,520,032 which includes  access   roads   balance   of   Kshs.374,263,966.   The   balance   includes   an   amount   of  Kshs .95,981,740 paid to a contractor for upgrading of Karandini - Kithioroni road to  bitumen standards. The contract was awarded on 10 December, 2020 for a period of  three (3) years and a contract completion date of 10 December, 2023 which was later  extended to   4 June, 2025 as per the approval dated 4 December, 2023. However,  physical inspection conducted in September, 2025 revealed 2.3 km of the road was yet  to be tarmacked but the contractor was on site.

144  Further, payment records reflected that out of a contra ct sum of Kshs.450,171,829, an  amount of Kshs.374,902,818 representing 83%, had been paid to the contractor.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure amount of Kshs.374,902,818  could not be confirmed.  334.2.   Delayed   Upgrading of Kambandi - Cheera - Ruguti Road  The   amount   of   Kshs.374,263,966   spent   on   access   roads   further   includes  Kshs.30,717,612 paid to a contractor for upgrading of Kambandi - Ch eera - Ruguti road to  bitumen standards. The contract was awarded on 21 November, 2018 for a period of  three (3) years and contract completion period of December, 2022 which was   later  extended   to 24 October, 2024 as per the approval dated 24 April, 2023. Payment records  showed total payments to date amounting to Kshs.293,415,939 representing 82% of the  contract sum of Kshs.356,261,151.  However, physical inspection conducted in September, 2025   revealed that the contractor  was not on site. No correspondences were provided on measures being taken to  complete the project.  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   for   the   expenditure   amount   totalling  Kshs.293,415,939 could not be confirmed.  334.3.   Delayed   Upgrading of Tunyai   -   Ntaara Road  As previously reported, tender for upgrading Tunyai - Ntaara road to bitumen standards  was awarded in November, 2018 to a contractor at a contract sum of Kshs.689,341,600.  The contract period was three (3) years from 25 Nov ember, 2018 to November, 2022 and  was   to cover twenty (20) Kilometres.   However, physical inspection conducted in  September, 2025, revealed that the project is yet to be completed and the project had  stalled with only four (4) Km of the road upgraded. Fur ther, the contractor had abandoned  the site after receiving payments totalling Kshs.179,265,569. The contract performance  period expired, with no valid contract as at the time of inspection.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure amount   of Kshs.179,265,569  could not be confirmed.  334.4.   Delayed Construction of Ndagani Market  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.6,090,520,032   which   includes   civil   works   and   infrastructure   balance   of  Kshs.2, 579,384,655 as disclosed in Note 19 to the financial statements.   The amount  includes Kshs.14,535,270 paid during the year under review, to a contractor towards  construction of Ndagani Market.   As previously reported, r eview of records showed that  the   cont ract for the construction of Ndagani Market was awarded to a contractor and  signed on 6 June, 2023 at a cost of Kshs.42,942,750 for a contract period of ten (10)  months. The order to commence works was immediately given and an amount of  Kshs.7,564,580   was   paid   towards   the   project.   Physical   inspection   carried   out   in  September, 2025 revealed that the project remained incomplete and the contractor was

145  not on site.   Total payments to the contractor amounted to Kshs.22,099,850 or 52% of  the contract sum.  In   the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure amount of Kshs.22,099,850  could not be confirmed.  334.5.   Stalled Construction of Igangara Bridge  The County Executive engaged a contractor for the construction of the Igangara Bridge  at a contract sum of Kshs.21,004,700 vide a contract signed on 8 May, 2023. The project  commenced on 8 May, 2023 and was scheduled for completion on 8 May, 2025 for a  pro ject period of twenty - four (24) months.  However, physical inspection carried out in September, 2025 revealed that the project  had   stalled.   The   contractor   was   not   on   site   and   had   been   paid   a   total   sum   of  Kshs.8,827,890 or 42% of the contract sum.  In the   circumstances, value for money on the amount paid totalling Kshs.8,827,890  towards the project could not be confirmed.  334.6.   Un - Occupied   Deputy Governor’s Residence  During the financial year 2018/2019, Management awarded a contract for construction of  Deputy   Governor’s residence at a contract sum of Kshs.30,279,440. An amount of  Kshs.26,742,335 or 89% of the contract price had been paid as at 30 June, 2023. Physical  inspection   conducted in   September, 2025 revealed   that   the   residence was   nearly  complete. Howe ver, there were   no ongoing works and the contractor was not on site. A  certificate of Practical Completion of the works was issued by the County Works Officer  on 23 May, 2025.  Further, the County Executive continues to pay rent for the Deputy Governor’s   resident,  yet the period for rent payment/leasing the Deputy Governor’s residence as provided for  in the Salaries and Remuneration Commission   Circular No.   SRC/TS/COG/6/61/48 VOL.II  (64) lap sed on 30 June, 2022.  In the circumstances, value for money on ex penditure amount of Kshs.26,742,335 for  construction of Deputy Governor’s residence   could not be confirmed .  335.   Non - Compliance with Kenya Quality Model for Health Policy Guidelines  Review of services offered and equipment in place and number of staff at   dispensaries in  the County revealed that during the year under review, the medical facilities did not meet  the requirements of Kenya Quality Model for Health Policy Guidelines due to staff deficits  and lack of essential machines/equipment as listed at the   end of this report.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of Universal Health Care Services could not be  confirmed.

146  336.   Non - Compliance with the Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy Order  Review of contracts records revealed that the County Executiv e entered into contracts  but no documentary evidence was provided for audit to confirm that the County Executive  complied with Paragraph 3(1) of the Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy, Order  2023 which states that there shall be paid a levy by a sup plier on all procurement  contracts signed between the supplier and a procuring entity, at the rate of point zero  three per centum (0.03%) of the value of the signed contract, exclusive of applicable  taxes. In addition, Public Procurement Regulatory Authori ty (PPRA) circular No. 01/2024  dated 30 August, 2024 also requires procurement entities to remit the levy to the Authority  through the e - Citizen payment platform by the 20 th   day of the subsequent month and also  file monthly returns.  Although Management ex plained that IFMIS was configured from January, 2025 to  automatically deduct the levy, no evidence was provided to confirm, that the required  deductions   and   remittances   were   made   for   the   period   between   September   and  December, 2024.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the Levy Order, 2023.  337.   Long Outstanding Trade and Other Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs.882,571,678 and as disclosed in Note 16 to the financial statements. Review of the  trade account payables balance revealed that payables balance of Kshs.150,504,534 had  been outstanding for more than four (4) years. Management did not provide explanation  why the long outstanding trade payables have not been settled in the year to which the  expenses were incurred or the subsequent financial years.   This was contrary to Sec tion  53 (8) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which states that an  Accounting Officer shall not commence any procurement proceedings until satisfied  that   sufficient funds to meet the obligations of the resulting contract(s) are reflect ed in  approved budget estimates.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  338.   Failure to Retain   Facilities Improvement Funds   at the Hospitals  Review of revenue records obtained from Level 5, Level 4 and Level 3 and other   lower -  level   health facilities in Tharaka   Nithi County revealed that during the year under review,  a total Kshs.293,274,998 was collected towards the Facilities Improvement Fund (FIF).  Out of the amount, a total of Kshs.235,535,466 was transferred to the County Revenue  Fund. However, the County T reasury did not reimburse any amount to the health facilities  resulting in a deficit of Kshs.235,535,466.  This was contrary to Section 5(1) of the Facilities Improvement Financing Act, 2023 which  requires that all monies raised or received by or on behal f of all public health facilities be  retained in the Hospital Facilities Improvement Financing account. In addition, failure to

147  reimburse the full amount transferred by the facilities impacted negatively on service  delivery by the health facilities.  In t he circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  339.   There were no material issues relating to effectiveness of internal controls, risk  management and g overnance.

148  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF EMBU   –   NO.14  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  340.   Unsupported   Retention Deposits  The statement of financial position   reflects refundable deposits and prepayments balance  of Kshs.18,340,626   as disclosed in Note 33 to the financial statements. Th e   balance is in  respect of retention money withheld by the County Executive, which is supposed to be  banked in a refundable depos its account.   Further, t he opening balance reflects a balance  of   Kshs.32,161,778   while   the   County   Executive   procured   capital   projects   totalling  Kshs.896,222,260 as reflected in the statement of comparison of budget and actual  amounts. However, the movement   of the deposits has not been disclosed in the Notes to  the financial statements.  Further, the bank account held at Central   B ank of Kenya revealed a closing balance of  Kshs.569,633   resulting in   an un explained and unreconciled variance of Kshs.17,770,993  but   Management did not provide deposit ledger/register .  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the   refundable   deposit s and  prepayments   balance   of   Kshs.18,340,626 could not be c onfirmed.  341.   Unsupported Expenditure on Legal Services  The statement of financial performance reflects an amount of Kshs.468,516,798 in  respect of the use of goods an d services, which includes   other operating   expenses  amount ing to   Kshs.90,698,285 .   As disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements, the  expenditure   includes   other   operating   expenses   of   Kshs.90,698,285   out   of   which  Kshs.2,287,351 was paid to an Advocate.   However, the files containing details of the work  done by the Advocate were not provided for audit review. Further, there was no approval  from the County Executive Committee regarding the outsourcing of legal services.  In the circumstances, the accuracy   and completeness of the legal expenditure amount ing  to   Kshs. 2,287,351   could not be confirmed.  342.   Unsupported Payments in Respect of County Industrial Aggregation Park  The   Embu   County   Revenue   Fund   financial   statements   reflect s   receipts   of  Kshs.186,000,000   from the   County Industrial Aggregation Park   Fund. Audit review of the  Embu   County Industrial Aggregation Park   Fund bank statements reflect s   payments and  transfers   amounting to   Kshs.219,554,655 during the year under review .   However, tender  documents, payment vouchers, project files, bid documents and the financing agreement  of the   Embu County Industrial and Aggregation Park Project were not provided for audit  review.   Management   indicated   that   the   tender   documents   had   been   burnt   during  demonstrations in Embu Town.

149  In the circumstances, the accuracy ,   completeness   and regularity of the expenditure could  not be confirmed.  343.   Undisclosed Account Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   current   liabilities   balance   of  Kshs.1,722,877,451. However, the balance   excludes   transfers from special purpose  account amount of Kshs.10,167,300 which was borrowed   but had not been   refunded back  to the account .   Further   all payables have been classified as current liabilities.  However , review of the payment plan   submitted   to Controller of Budget showed that  payables   balance   of   Kshs . 1,429,250,047   were scheduled to   be settled   over a period of  six (6) years   between 2026/2027   and   2032/2033   which   should have been classified as  non - current liabilities.  In the circumstances, the accuracy , classification   and completeness of current liabilities  balance of Kshs.1,722,877 ,451 could not be confirmed.  344.   Unreconciled Kenya Medical Supplies Authority Debt  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   current   liabilities   balance   of  Kshs.1,722,877,451.   The balance   includes supply of drugs and medical supplies   totalling  Kshs. 33,723,916   owed to Kenya Medical Supplies Authority .   However, the Authority’s  records   reflect   a balance of Kshs. 43,861,705   resulting in   a   variance of Kshs .10,137,789.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of current liabilities balance of  Kshs.1,722,877,451 could not be confirmed.  345.   Unsupported   Voided Transactions  Review of the County Executive’s system payments revealed that eight hundred and  sixty - two   (62)   transactions amounting to Kshs.313,720,244 were voided during the  financial year 2024/2025. However, Management did not provide the supporting   details,  approvals and justification for the voided transactions.  In the circumstances, regularity   and com pleteness   of the voided transactions amounting  to Kshs.313,720,244 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  346.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   of   Kshs. 6,534,262,282   and   Kshs.5,259,463,775  respectively, resulting   in   an under - funding of Kshs. 1,274,798,507   or 20% of the budget.  However,   the   County   Executive   spent   Kshs.5,093,307,106   against   actua l   receipts  amount   of   Kshs.Kshs.5,259,463,775   resulting   in   under - expenditure   amount   of  Kshs.166,156,669 of the actual receipts.

150  The under - funding affected the   planned activities and   may ha ve   impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  347.   Pending Accounts Payable s  Review of the budget revealed that an amount of Kshs.100,000,000 was allocated for the  settlement of pending bills, against a total outstanding balance of   Kshs.2,207,376,010   as  disclosed in the audited accounts for the year ended 30   June, 2024.   However, t he ageing  analysis schedule of pending bills revealed that the current year payables balance totalled  Kshs.1,560,148,304, while the outstanding payables bal ance for the last financial year  was   Kshs.1,521,621,076 ,   representing   an   increase   of   Kshs .38,527,228   (3%)   from  2023/ 2024 financial   yea r .  Further, review of the payables’ schedule revealed that as at the end of the third quarter  of   the   financial   year,   the   outstanding   balance   of   accounts   payable   was  Kshs.1,748,082,570. This indicate d   that the payables were not settled as a first charge  on the budget.  Failure to settle bills during the year in which they relate distorts the financial statements  and adversely affects the budgetary provisions for the subsequent year to which they  have to be charged.  My opinion is not modified in respect of these matters .  Other Matter  348.   Unresolved Prior Year   Audit   Matters  In the pr evious   year audit report, several issues were raised under the Report on Financial  Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources, and  Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance as   listed  at the en d of this report . However, review of the status during   the   audit revealed that the  matters   relating to the 2023/2024 financial year   revealed that the thirty - five (35) issues  remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025 .  Other In formation  349.   There were no material issues relating to   O ther   I nformation.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  350.   Irregular Extension of Revenue Collection and Managem ent Automation  System Contract  D uring the year   under review,   Management paid an amount of Kshs.3,000,000 to a local  company   for   an   extension   of   a   contract   for   the   supply,   delivery,   implementation,

151  customization, and commissioning of a revenue collection and management automation  system. The   original   contract expired   on 6 April, 2023 ,   but had not been   formally  extended.   Despite the lapse , Management   proceeded to   issue   two (2)   Local Purchase  Orders   intending to extend   the contract without a formal recommendation from the Tender  Evaluation Committee. This was contrary t o Section 139(1)(2) of the Public Procurement  and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which sets the contractual obligations to a contractor after  a procurement process is completed.  In addition , the County   Executive   was already in the process of acquiring a new re venue  system at a contract sum of Kshs.37,120,000 and an amount of Kshs.8,742,644 had  already been incurred towards acquiring the new revenue system.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  351.   Weaknesses in Management of County Vocationa l Training Centres  Review of the courses offered at   Vocational Technical Centres   ( VTC )   revealed that eight  (8) VTCs were offering eighteen (18) more courses than those formally approved by the  relevant accrediting bodies, such as the TVET Authority and the Curriculum Development  Assessment and Certification Council (CDACC). These additional   courses lacked official  accreditation   or   curriculum   approval,   thereby   constituting   non - compliance   with  established   academic regulatory   standards.   Mbonzuki   VTC,   was   operating   without  accreditation, licensing, or registration by the Technical and Vocational   Education and  Training Authority (TVETA), contrary to the requirements of   S ection 17 of the TVET  Act, 2023.  Further, the   Department   for   Vocational Training, offered appointment letters to twenty - six  (26) Station Managers to the Vocational Training   Centres across Embu County. However,  it   was   noted   that   proper   recruitment   procedures   was   not   followed   including  advertisements for the respective posts   and   interviews .  In addition,   at one   (1 )   VTC ,   one permanent and pensionable instructor, also served as  the Manager, responsible for training approximately eighty - three (83) enrolled students in  the financial year   under review .   The instructor was technically skilled in one technical  area, resulting in a competency gap for students   enrolled   in carpentry and   welding  courses.  In the circumstances, full optimization of the benefits from VTCs to the public could not  be confirmed.  352.   Failure to Establish Sub – County (Level 4) Hospital  As previously reported,   the   County   of Embu   has four (4) Sub - counties. However, the  County   Executive   Management has only established three (3) Sub   -   C ounty ( L evel 4)  Hospitals, and none had been established in Manyatta Sub   -   county. This was contrary  to Section 8 (1) of the Embu County Health Servic es Act, 2024 which states that there  shall be at least one County Hospital, at least one Sub - County hospital in each Sub -  County, and at least one   H ealth   C enter in each ward.

152  Further, the County Management   had not   established County Health Management Team,  Health Quality and Assurance Unit, Health Facility Improvement Board and policy on  transfer of unutiliz ed pharmaceutical and non – pharmaceuticals from one health facility to  another to ensure efficient stock manag ement. This was contrary to the requirements of  Sections 31, 35 and 45 of   the Embu County Health Services Act, 2024 .  In the cir cumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  353.   Stalled Construction of Gategi Health Centre  The County Executive awarded tender for the construction of Gategi Health Centre  (Upgrading from Level 3 to Level 4) through Negotiation No:1482228 at a contract sum  of Kshs.28,843,272 on 12 June, 2024. The   c onstruction was supposed to be completed  in twel ve (12) months from the date of the contract. The first payment for the contract  amounted to Kshs.13,305,153 for works done in the financial year 2023 - 2024 while the  second payment amount was Kshs.10,000,000 all totalling Kshs.23,305,153 paid to the  contra ctor.  Physical inspection   conducted on   the project revealed that the project had stalled and the  contractor was not on site despite a substantial amount of the contract sum having been  paid, and the completion date having expired on12   June, 2025.  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   on   the   project   expenditure   totalling  Kshs.23,305,153 could not be confirmed.  354.   Unutilized Health Facilities  Review   of payment records and supporting documents in respect of construction and civil  works   revealed   that   the   Cou nty   Executive   incurred   expenditure   amounting   to  Kshs. 11,474,068   in   respect   of   construction   of   Kiangungi   Dispensary,   Kangethia  Dispensary,   Gichera   Dispensary,   an   ablution   block   at   Gicheche   Dispensary,   and  renovation of an Isolation Ward at Kianjokoma Level 3 Hospital.   P hysical   inspection  carried   out on the projects   revealed   that   although   final   payments   had been   made , the  buildings had not been put   to   use.  Further,   at   Gichera   D ispensary ,   the   land was not fenced hence   the   risk   of   encroachment,  the buildings and toilets had been vandalized, and the   compound had   overgrown thickets  and bushe s .   In addition, at   Kiangungi dispensary, there was substandard fence, paving  of the compound was not don e, the buildings and toilets had been   vandalized   also   the  compound had   overgrown trees and bushes.  In the circumstances, value for money   on   the expenditure totalling Kshs.11,474,068   on  the three (3) projects   could not be confirmed.  355.   Stalled Twin Workshop at Siakago V ocational Training Centre  Construction of a twin workshop at Siakago   Vocational Training Centre , initiated by the  National Government in the financial year 2012 had stalled and remained incomplete   as  at 30 June, 2025 . Following devolution, no further works were undertaken, and there was

153  no documentation indicating whether the project was to be compl eted by the National  Government or handed over to the County Government. Physical inspection confirmed  that the contractor was not on site.   Further ,   the   female students occupied a dilapidated  wooden/prefab dormitory that was poorly ventilated, lacked natu ral light   during the day  and was on the verge of collapsing, thereby posing risk of loss of life.  In the circumstances, value for money for the stalled building could not be confirmed.  356.   Stalled Projects at Karaba and Kamweli Dispensaries  Physical inspe ction   conducted on   projects of unknown amount revealed that   construction  of   mortuary at Karaba dispensary and   a   M aternity   W ard at Kamweli dispensary, had  stalled, and the contractor was not on site. The Maternity Ward at Kamweli Dispensary  was initiated in   2009 .   However, Management had taken   no action to fast track its  completion as   at   July, 2025.  In the circumstances, value for money and benefits to be accrued from the dispensaries  could not be confirmed .  357.   Stalled   Construction of   Governor’s Official Residence  As previously reported, the County Executive entered into a contract for   the   construction  of   Governor’s   residence   with   a   firm   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.49,703,439   on  8 March, 2021. The contract period was for seventy - two (72) weeks with expected  completion date of 8 September, 2022. However, at the time of audit in Se ptember, 2025,  the   Governor’s official residence was not complete and the last certificate of work done  revealed that the project was 55% complete. Physical inspection confirmed that the  contractor was not on site.   Further, the building had deteriorated a nd the wooden  elements had begun to rot. Request for an engineer's opinion on status of the building  was not provided for audit review.   In addition,   n o evidence was provided to confirm  whether the contractor had sought   for   an   extension of   contract   period , or a default notice  issued to the contractor by the County Executive.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the SRC circular of 20 May, 2019  and   value for money from the stalled project   could not be confirmed.  358.   Failure to Establish   th e County   Alcoholic Drinks Board  Review   of   the   operations   from   the   Trade   and   Investment   Department,   where   the  Alcoholics' Drinks Board is domiciled, revealed that the County   Executive   does not have  in place an Alcoholic Control Board.   In stead, the functions of the Board were performed  by   an Ad hoc   Committee   contrary to Section 4 (1) of the Embu County Alcoholic Drinks  Control Act, 2021 which states that there   will be   established a Board to be known as  Embu County Alcoholic Control Board.   Further ,   the revenue   and rates charged   from the  liq uor licenses could not be confirmed.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

154  359.   Failure to Surrender Imprests  Review   of   t he   imprest   register   revealed   overdue   outstanding   imprest   balance   of  Kshs.21,768,240 issued between July, 2023 and 30 June, 2025 which had not been  surrendered or accounted for. This was contrary to Regulation 93 (5) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which stipulates that a holder   of  a temporary   i mprest shall account or surrender the Imprest within seven (7) working days  after returning to the duty station.   Further , some officers held multiple imprests contrary  to   Regulation   93(4)(b)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governme nts)  Regulations, 2015.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  360.   Irregular Engagement of Casual Employees  The review of the   County Executive recruited four hundred and forty - two (442) casual  employees for more than one month during th e financial year   under review . This was  contrary to   P aragraph (v) on the Basic Guidelines on Hiring of casual workers in the Embu  County Public Service of   March, 2024 which states that casual workers will not be  engaged for more than one (1) month on a con tinuous basis. Further, there was no  evidence of   recruitment of   the casual workers and the posting list of the casuals with the  respective responsibilities in each duty station provided for audit review.  In the circumstances, Management was in   breach of the law.  361.   Irregular Engagement of Staff Above Mandatory Retirement Age  Review   of payroll data revealed that   seventy - six   (76) officers who had attained the  mandatory retirement age of sixty (60) years were still in service as at 30 May, 2025. Th is  was   contrary   to   Regulation   70(1)(a)   and   (b)   of   the   Public   Service   Commission  Regulations , 2020   which states that the mandatory retirement age in the Public Sector  shall be sixty (60) years and sixty - five   (65)   for persons with disabilit ies .  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  362.   Non - Compliance with Law on One - Third   Rule on   Basic Salary  Review of Payroll data for the financial year under review revealed that the County  Executive had one thousand three hundred and   seventy - four (1,374) employees whose  net pay was below a 1/3 of their basic pay .   This was contrary to   Section   19(3) of the  Employment Act, 2007 which require that deductions made by an employer shall not  exceed two thirds of such wages.  In the circumstanc es, Management was in breach of the law.

155  363.   Non - Compliance with Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review the   payroll data revealed that a total of one thousand nine hundred and eighty -  nine   (1,989) employees were   from   the   dominant   ethnic community in   the   Coun ty  representing 55% of the total staff. This was contrary to the requirements of Section 7(1)  and (2) of the National Cohesion and Integration Act,   2008 which states that all Public  Establishments shall seek to represent the diversity of the people of Keny a in the  employment of staff and that no public establishment shall have more than one third of  its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  364.   Failure to Collect Revenue from Social Halls  The County   Executive   operated five (5) active   s ocial   h alls. During the year under review,  IEBC and Talent academy social halls   generated revenue   amoun ting   to   Kshs.120,000  and Kshs.206,000   respectively, totalling   Kshs.326,000 as reflected   in   the   financial  r ecords. However, revenue generated by the remaining three (3) social halls was not  banked   in   the County revenue account   but   was   instead   used by communities at source.  This was contrary to   Regulation 80(1) of the Public Finance Management (County  Government s) Regulations, 2015 which states that the County Treasury shall administer  the County Revenue Fund in accordance with the Constitutional provisions in Article s   207  and 209 (3) and (4) in controlling revenue receipts to ensure that all revenue receipts by  the County Government are paid into the County Exchequer Account, except   receipts  reasonably excluded by the Act, or any other Act of Parliament or an Act of County  Assembly.  Further, physical inspection   conducted on   one   of   the social halls revealed tha t, it was  constructed on a road reserve .   H owever,   there were no approvals from both the National  and County Government for   the   construction. In addition,   M anagement of the hall was  under   the   community   and   revenue   was   channe l ed   to   a   private   bank   account.  Management did not provide information on the other three   (3)   halls whose revenue  collection was neither disclosed nor accounted for.  In addition, the County   Executive   did not have any policy on handover of activities of halls  to the communities after construction. Therefore, the basis of communities   or   managing  and   collecting revenues from the halls could not be confirmed.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  365.   Irregular   Payment to   Subscriptions  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements reflects an amount of Kshs.468,516,798 in respect   of   the use of goods and  services, which includes an amount of Kshs.90,698,285 in respect   of   oth er operating  expenses . I nclude d in the expenditure is   an amount of Kshs.3,000,000   paid to   the Council  of Governors.   This was contrary to   Section 37 of Intergovernmental Relation s   Act, 2012  which provides that the operational expenses in respect of the stru ctures and institutions

156  established in this Act shall be provided for in the annual estimates of the revenue and  expenditure of the National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  366.   Failure to Deduct and Remit Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy  Review of   procurement   records revealed that the County Executive entered into contracts  but no evidence was provided to confirm that the County Executive complied with  P aragraph 3(1) o f the Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy, Order 2023 which  states that there shall be paid a levy by a supplier on all procurement contracts signed  between the supplier and a procuring entity, at the rate of point zero three per centum  (0.03%) of th e value of the signed contract, exclusive of applicable taxes.   Further , the  Public   Procurement   Regulatory   Authority   (PPRA)   circular   No.   01/2024   dated  30 August, 2024 require procurement entities to remit the levy to the Authority thr ough  the e - Citizen payment platform by the 20 day of the subsequent month and file monthly  returns.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the   law .  367.   Lack of   Annual Development Plan  The County Executive did not provide   evidence that   the   Annual Development Plan for the  financial year 2024 - 2025 was   submitted to the County Assembly. This was contrary to  Section 126(3) of the Public Finance Management   Act,   2012 which requires the County  Executive   Committee   member   responsibl e   for   planning   to   submit   the   county's  development plan to the county assembly for approval and also send copies to the  Commission on Revenue Allocation and The National Treasury.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of law.  368.   Non - Compliance with Law on the County Appropriation Act, 2024  Review of the County Revenue Fund bank statements revealed that withdrawals totalling  Kshs.606,491,986 and Kshs.290,384,401 between 01 July, 2024 and 14 July, 2024 were  made   by   the   County   Executive   for   the   recurrent   and   development   expenditures  respectively. However, approval from the County Assembly to the County Executive  Committee Membe r granting authority to withdraw from the County   R evenue   Fund was  not provided   for audit   as the County Appropriation Act, 2024 was   only   assented to on 15  July, 2024.   This was contrary to Section 8(1)(c) of the County Governments Act, 2012  which   requires C ounty Assembly’s approval before any expenditure of County funds.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of law.

157  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT,  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  369.   Failure to Activate   Exchequer Receipts Mod ule in the Integrated Financial  Management Information System  Comparison between the net exchequer issues by The National Treasury totalling  Kshs.5,797,242,036 to County Government against the MRR Receipts as captured in  Integrated   Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), revealed Nil amounts  resulting   in   an unexplained variance of Kshs.5,797,242,036. No explanation was provided  for failure to activate the Receipt Module in IFMIS.  In the circumstances, the   e ffectiveness of   i nternal   c ontrols,   r isk   m anagement and  g overnance   in   respect   of   complete   accountability modules   in   IFMIS   could   not   be  confirmed.  370.   Lack of Annual Recruitment Plan  The County   Executive   recruited six hundred and forty - one (641) officers during the year  under review. However, the   County   Departments did not have annual recruitment plans  to guide the recruitment   process .  In   the   circumstances,   the   effectiveness   of   internal   controls   over   hu man   resource  management could not be   confirmed .  371.   Weaknesses in   Information and Communication Technology   Governance  and Controls  Audit of the County   Executive’s   Information and Communication Technology (ICT)  environment revealed   several   critical weaknesses indicating inadequate ICT governance,  data protection, and systems control   as detailed below;  (i)   There   was   no   formally   approved   ICT   policy   to   guide   the   development,  deployment,   use,   and   management   of   ICT   resources   within   the   County  Execu tive;  (ii)   S taff were using personal email addresses for official communication, which  undermines data security and organizational accountability ;  (iii)   T he County   Executive   lacked a documented policy to ensure the collection,  handling, storage, and sharing of data that complied with legal and regulatory  data protection requirements ;  (iv)   C ore operational systems including the   B ursary   M anagement   S ystem,   H ospital  M anagement   S ystem ,   F inance   S ystem, and HR   S ystem were not integrated,  resulting in data silos, inefficiencies, and duplication of efforts ;

158  (v)   T here   were   no centralized and updated ICT asset s   register to track, manage, or  safeguard ICT infrastructure and equipment ;  (vi)   ICT funct ions were fragmented across departments, with no centralized oversight  or coordination, limiting strategic ICT planning and control ;  (vii)   T he County   Executive   had not developed a risk assessment framework to  identify, assess, and mitigate ICT - related risks ;  (viii)   T here was no formalized data backup process, exposing the County   Executive  to risk of data loss in the event of system failure, cyberattack, or accidental  deletion ;  (ix)   There was no   disaster recovery plan,   hence   the County   Executive   lacked the  capacity to   restore operations promptly following system disruptions or disasters ;  (x)   T here was no ICT steering committee to provide oversight, strategic guidance,  and decision - making on ICT investments and priorities .  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of ICT   gov ernance and system   controls   could not  be confirmed.  372.   Lack of   Updated   Fixed Assets Register  During the year under review,   Management did not maintain an updated fixed assets  r egister which could have provided critical information including location of the assets,  description, respective cost and serial numbers.   Further, t he   assets r egister   did   not  disclose values of various assets acquired by the County   Executive   such as land,  construction and refurbishment of buildings, motor vehicles and other assorted assets.  In addition , the County   Executive’s   twenty - six (26) Vocational Training Centres did not  provide updated and complete fixed assets registers, despite owning substantia l assets,  including buildings, furniture, and equipment.   Similarly , critical asset details such as  descriptions,   serial   numbers,   acquisition   dates,   values,   physical   locations,   and  operational   status   were   either   undocumented   or   unavailable,   thereby   hinderin g  verification of ownership, existence, and valuation.  In the circumstances, the existence of an effective measure for control and custody of  County Executiv e’s   assets could not be confirmed.  373.   Lack of Valuation Reports and Ownership Documents  Review of records   of twenty - six (26)   Vocational Training Centres (VTC) revealed   that,   five  (5) of the   centres   did not have title deeds for the parcels of land they occupied , and   no  valuation reports were   provided   for the assets.  Further, p hysical inspect ion carried out revealed that land of unknown size at   Kanja   and  Tenri VTCs had been encroached.   A p arcel of land at   Kanorori   VTC hosts two (2) National

159  Government entities' residential houses and offices, despite the   I nstitution lacking playing  grounds and adequate buildings for lecture halls and students’ hostels.  In addition,   twelve (12) Level 2 Hospitals had not secured title deeds for parcels of land  occupied and their valuation reports were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, the existence   of effective internal controls for safeguarding   the  property, plant and equipment could not be confirmed.  374.   Failure to Tag Fixed and Movable Assets  Phy sical inspection carried out on a sample of office desks, chairs, and desktops revealed  that the items lacked   asset   location ,   identifiers and asset tags. As a result, it was not  possible to verify whether these assets were owned by the County Executive. This was  contrary to Regulation 136 of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulations, 2015, which requires Cou nty Governments to maintain an up - to - date asset  register that accurately records all fixed and movable assets.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls   over   assets could not be  confirmed.  375.   Failure to Insure County   Executive’s   Buildings  Review   of   the   County   Executive   expenditure   revealed   that   an   amount   of  Kshs.189,117,557 was incurred   in   insurance costs. However, review of the insurance  contracts revealed that the buildings did not have ins urance cover. As a result, a section  of the County Governor ’ s building remained   unused in poor state   following extensive  damage caused   by riots in year 2024 . The lack of insurance   cover   hindered timely repairs  and refurbishments due to high associated cost s,   resulting in   the County Executive  incur ing   additional expenditure on leased premises to sustain operations.  In the circumstances,   the   existence of effective measures   for   safeguarding the assets  could not be confirmed.

161  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF   KITUI   –   NO.15  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  376.   Variances in   Trade and Other Payables  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflect trade and other payables   comparative balance   of Kshs.546,435,251 which differs  with the prior year audited financial statements balance of Kshs.835,868,265 ,   resulting   in  a   unexplained   variance of Kshs.289,433,014.  Further, the   trade and other   payables balance of Kshs.626,406,908 include s   payables  amounting to Kshs.89,848,440 which have been outstanding for more than two (2) years  with some dating back to th e year 2015. Management has not put   in place measures to  settle the debts.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of trade and other payables  balance of Kshs.626,406,908 could not be confirmed.  Other Matter  377.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the pr evious   year ’ s audit reports, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial Statements, Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources, and  Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance. Review of the  status during audit of the   County Executive in 2024/2025 revealed that   fourteen (14)  matters   detailed below   remained unresolved   as at 30 June, 2025 .  No.   Audit Issue s for   2023/2024  1   Storeyed   Maternity Ward at Kitui County Referral Hospital  2   Kabati Slaughterhouse  3   Proposed Completion of X - ray Building at Kauwi Hospital  4   Oxygen Plant Machine   -   Kitui County Referral Hospital  5   Construction of Livestock Office Block  6   Construction of a Snake Pit at Mutomo Reptile Park  7   Tyaa Sumpwell and Civil Works at Tyaa River  8   Water Projects -   Construction of sump well and pump house at Nzeeu river and  rehabilitation of Mukameni pipeline  9   Water Projects -   construction of elevated   steel water tank at Muuani,  10   Department of Health -   projects funded at approximately Kshs.573,553,514   were  incomplete.  11   Kitui Municipality (Kithomboani Modern Market)  12   Land Infrastructure and Urban Development (LIUD) Headquarters

162  No.   Audit Issue s for   2023/2024  13   Vandalized Completed Projects and Failure to Erect Signages  14   Non - Collection of Revenue Arrears -   property rates  O ther Information  378.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  379.   Failure to   Disclose   Provision s   for Contingent Liabilities  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services   amount of  Kshs.2,228,609,526 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements   which   include s  other operating expenses   amount of   Kshs.343,543,923. Included in the   expenditure is an  amount   Kshs. 14,369,803   in respect of   legal expenses. Review of   legal   records revealed  that   the   County   Executive   had   seventy - eight   (78)   ongoing   legal   cases .   However,  Management did not   make   provisions for contingent liabilities in   the financial statements.  This   wa s   contrary   to   Paragraph   22   of   the   International   Public   Sector   Accounting  Standards 19 which stipulates that   a provision should be recognized when: (a) an entity  has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event; (b) it is   probable  that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits or service potential will be  required to settle the obligation; and (c) a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of  the obligation.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of t he   law .  380.   Implementation of Projects  380.1.   Failure to   Operationaliz e Completed Projects  The County   Executive   awarded a contract   for procurement and   installation of equipment  for amenity ward at Mwingi Sub - County Hospital   on 20 January, 2025 at a contract sum  of   Kshs.2,497,395   for a contract period of one hundred and twenty (120) days.   However,  physical   inspection   revealed that the amenity ward was yet to be operationalized and the  procured equipment were lying idle in the   store.  Further, r eview of the Project Implementation Status Report (PIS) under the Department  for   Health   and Sanitation and verification of sampled completed projects during the  financial years 2023/2024 and 2024/2025 revealed that completed projects funded at a  cost of Kshs.51,019,671 were yet to be operationalized .  380.2.   Vandalization of Works at Ithookwe Sh owground  The County   Executive   awarded a contract on 23 July, 2024 for electrical repairs and  renovation works at Ithookwe   S howground at a contract sum of Kshs.2,991,205. The  payment was made on 15 January, 2025. However, physical inspection and verificati on  of   completed works   revealed that underground cables, power sub - mains, light fittings,

163  switches, bulbs, circuit breakers and other electrical works had been vandalized and  stolen. The County   Executive   failed to take the nece ssary security measures to saf e -  guard the electrical works, builders ’   works and all other works that had been carried out  as the place had been left unmanned   and unsecure , exposing the premises to   theft and  damage .  380.3.   Unsatisfactory Implementation of Projects  The County Executive awarded contracts   for the proposed construction of Sump Wells  and associated civil works which included piping and water distribution through kiosks.  However, documents provided for audit review and audit inspections conducted revealed  that the two (2) projects were implem ented, in accordance with the agreed scope and  contract specifica tions   as detailed below:  380.4.   Ngomano   -   Mwitika Market Sumpwell Water Supply  The County   Executive   awarded a contract for   the   construction of a solar pumping unit, a  guard house with a pit latrine, a rising mainline and an elevated steel tank at Ngomano   -  Mwitika   Market   in   Zombe/Mwitika   at a   contract sum of Kshs.43,038,259. Physical  verification conducted in May, 2025, revealed t hat the trenching deviated from the  specifications outlined in the Bill of Quantities (BQ) as sections of the pipelines were  observed to be shallowly   installed , not reaching the stipulated depth of 2 feet (60 cm).  The inadequate depth significantly expose s   the water   pipes to potential vandalism   and  breakages.  Further the p roject did not have   Environmental   Impact   Assessment license and   the water  permit from the Water Resources Authority (WRA)   which are   required to conduct the  water works .   This wa s contrary to Section 58 of the Environmental   Management and  Coordination Act, 1999   which stipulates that the proponent of any project specified in the  Second Schedule shall undertake a full environmental impac t   assessment study and  submit the   report to the Authority prior to being   issued wi th any license by the Authority.  Further , Section 36 of the Water Act, 2016, stipulates that   a permit is required for   any use  of water from a water resource . In addition, land   ownership   documents   were   not   provided  for   audit   review.  380.5.   Muvuko   -   Kyanyaa   -   Mwanianga Sumpwell Water Supply  The County   Executive   awarded a contract for   the   construction of a sump well, solar  pumping unit, guard house with pit latrine , rising mainline, bulk storage tank, distribution  lines, and water   kiosks   at a contract sum of Kshs.17,922,488 . Physical   inspection   conducted   in  May, 2025, revealed that the trenching deviated from   the specifications outlined in the Bill  of Quantities (BQ) as sections of the pipelines were observed to be shallowly   installed ,  not reaching the   required   depth of 2 feet (60 cm). The inadequate depth significantly  exposes the water   pipes to potential van dalism   and breakages   of the water pipes . In  addition, land   ownership   documents   were   not   provided   for   audit   review.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law   and   the   value for money   o n  the   expenditure incurred in the projects   could not be c onfirmed .

164  381.   Irregular Procurement of Water Projects  The County   Executive   awarded three (3) contracts   for   the   construction   of   sump wells and  associated civil works which included piping and water distribution through kiosks at   Tiva  -   Kilawani,   Tyaa   -   Wimbondo   -   Wikithuki and   Tiva   –   Kalala at a total contract sum of  Kshs.50,390,369 .   However,   the   projects   lacked   both   the   Environme ntal   Impact  Assessment (EIA) license from the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA)  and the water permit from the Water Resources Authority (WRA)   which are   required to  conduct   the   water   works.   This   was   contrary   to   Section   58   of   the   Environmental  Manage ment and Coordination Act, 1999   which stipulates that the proponent of any  project specified in   the Second Schedule shall undertake a full environmental impact  assessment study and submit report to the Authority prior to being issued with any licens e  by the Authority.   Further , Section 36 of the Water Act, 2016, stipulates that   a permit is  required for   any use of water from a water resource .  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  382.   Irregular Funding of National Government   Functions  The   County Executive   spent   an amount of   Kshs.76,727,758   i n the award of bursaries to  students in secondary schools, universities, tertiary   schools and special education  i nstitutions under the pro - poor program. This   was   contr ary to the   requirements of the  Fourth S chedule of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 ,   which   assigns   the functions of the  National   Government   to   include   univ ersities,   tertiary   educational   institutions,   other  i nstitutions of research and higher learning and primary, s econ dary and special education  i nstitutions.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  383.   Late Remittance of Statutory Deductions  Review of   payment   records revealed late remittance s   of statutory deductions totalling  Kshs.168,176,458 which wer e   due to Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), National Social  Security Fund (NSSF) and the Housing Levy.   T he County   Executive   risks incurring  additional   costs in form of penalties and interest on accrued amounts.   This   was   contrary  to Section 19(4) of the Employm ent Act, 2007 which stipulates that an employer who  deducts an amount from an employee’s remuneration shall pay the amount so deducted  in accordance with the time period and other requirements specified in law.  In the circumstances, Management was in   breach of the law .  384.   Non - Compliance with One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Review of payroll data both in the Human Resources Integrated System (HRIS) and  manual payroll revealed that s ixty - six (66) employees earned   net salary of less than one -  third of their basic salary. This   was   contrary   to   Section 19(3) of the Employment  Act, 2007 which require that deductions made by an employer from the wages of his  employee at an y one time shall not exceed two thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

165  385.   Non - Compliance with Law on   Staff   Ethnic   Composition  Review of the County   Executive ’s master roll and other staff records indicated that out of  five thousand five hundred   and forty - nine ( 5,549)   employees ,   five thousand and thirty -  seven ( 5,037)   or approximately 91% of the   employees   were from the dominant ethnic  community in the County.   This was contrary to Section 7(1) and (2) of the National  Cohesion and   Integration Act, 2008 ,   which stipulates that   all   public   establishments   shall  seek to represent the diversity of the people of Kenya in the employment of staff and that  no public establishment shall have more   than one - third of its staff from the same ethnic  community.  Further , review of personal files and recruitment documents revealed that during the year  under review, forty - three (43) employees were recruited out of which thirty - eight (38) or  approximately 88%   belonged to   the dominant ethnic community in   the County.   This   was  contrary to Section 65(1)(e) of the County Governments Act, 2012 which require s   that in  selecting candidates for appointment, the County Public Service Board shall ensure that  at least thirty percent (30%) of the vacant posts at entry   level are filled by candidates who  are not from the dominant ethnic community in the County. Although Management  indicated   that majority of the   County employees were   inherited   from   the National  Government and the d efunct Local Authorities   who were mainly   from the dominant ethnic  community, no   corrective   measures have been put in place to address the issue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  386.   Non - Compliance   with the Law on   Fiscal Responsibility   Principles on   Wage s  The   statements   of   financial   performance   and   as   disclosed   in   Note   9   to   the  financial   sta tements   reflect   employees’   costs   mounting   to   Kshs.5,536,786,270 ,  representing   approximately 48% of the total receipts of Kshs.11,607,623,868 .   This   was  contrary   to   the   provisions   of   Regulation   25(1)   (a)   and   (b)   of   the   Public   Finance  Management   (County   Gover nments)   Regulations,   2015   which   require   the   County  Executive Committee Member with the approval of the County Assembly to set a limit on  the County Government's expenditure on wages and benefits for its public officers which,  shall not exceed thirty - five p ercent (35 % ) of the County   Executive 's total revenue.  Although   Management   formed   a   taskforce   which   presented   their   findings   and  recommendations in February, 2023, as at time of the audit in October, 2025 the  recommendations had not been   implemented.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  387.   Irregular   Payment s   to Council of Governors  As previously reported, the statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and  services   amount   of Kshs.2,228,609,526 which, as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements ,   include s an amount of Kshs.343,543,923 in respect of   other operating  expenses. Included in the   operating expenses is an   amount is Kshs.2,000,000 ,   which  was paid to   the   Council of Governors . The payment was made   contrary to Section 37 of

166  the Inter - Governmental Relations Act, 2012, which states that the operational costs of t he  Council shall be funded from the allocation of the National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  388.   Failure to Submit Financial Statements for Kitui and Mwingi Municipalities  As previously reported, the County   Executive   of Kitui established Kitui and Mwingi  Municipalities   through   Charters   approved   on   29   June,   2018   and   9   June,   2020  respectively. However ,   both   Municipalities failed to submit financial statements for   six  financial years from   2019/2020   to   2024/2025   for audit. This was   contrary to provisions of  Sections 46(1) and (2) of the Urban Areas and Cities (Amendment) Act, 2019, which  require the Boar d or Town Committee to cause to be kept all proper books and records  of accounts of its income, expenditure, assets and liabilities and to submit the financial  statements to the County Executive Committee Member for   onward   transmission to the  Auditor - Gener al.  Further , Kitui and Mwingi Municipalities had total approved budget of Kshs.259,152,321  with expenditure totalling Kshs.218,755,330 reported under the County   Executive .  In addition , the Municipalities did not prepare and submit their   quarterly financial reports  to the County Treasury with a copy to the Office of the Auditor - General contrary to  Regulation 64(1) and (3) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which stipulates that the Acco unting Officer or Receiver of Revenue or  Collector of Revenue shall prepare a quarterly report not   later than the 15   day after the  end of the quarter and   submit them   to the County Treasury, with a copy to the Auditor -  General and to County Assembly.  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  389.   Failure to Dispose Unserviceable Assets  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.3,413,957,120   as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements . However,  physical   inspection   in October, 2025   revealed thirty - six (36) unserviceable vehicles had  not been disposed and remain unutilized. This   was contrary to   Section 164(1) of the  Public Procurement a nd Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which stipulates that the employee in -  charge of unserviceable, obsolete or surplus assets shall bring the matter to the attention  of the Disposal Committee through the Head of the Procurement Function.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  390.   Lack of Updated F ixed   Assets Register  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.3,413,957,120   as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements . However,

167  Management did not maintain a fixed assets register in the prescribed format. The register  in place lacked   key details such as identification   serial numbers, acquisition date,  description of   asset, location,   class   and   cost   of   acquisition.   This   was   contrary   to  Regulation   136(1)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which states that the Accounting Officer shall be responsible for  maintaining a register of assets under his or her control or possession as prescribed by  the rel evant laws.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on management of fixed  assets could not be confirmed.  391.   Use of Manual Payroll  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employees’   costs   amount   of  Kshs.5,536,786,270. Included   in the   expenditure is an amount of   Kshs.4,599,2 66 which  was   reported   through   manual   payroll   system.   Review   of   records   revealed   that  Management operated three   (3) payroll systems namely;   Manual (Excel   f ormat) Payroll  System ,   Integrated   Payroll   and   Personne l   Database   (IPPD)   System   and   Human  Resource Integrated System (HRIS - Ke). The use of the manual   payroll   system requires  manual calculations of deductions to arrive at a net monthly pay, and   frequent   updates  which makes it prone to human error and misuse lea ding to weak internal controls on  management of personnel emoluments.  In the circumstances,   the effectiveness of   internal controls   i n management of   payroll  system   could not be confirmed.

168  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF MACHAKOS   –   NO.16  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  392.   Un supported   Accumulated Surplus  The statement of changes in net assets reflects negative balance of Kshs.4,058,810,631  in respect of   accumulated surplus after adjusting for retention of Kshs.185,714,920,  opening accounts payables   –   salaries of Kshs.529,911,032, payments for prior year  budgets of Kshs.762,336,337, accounts trade payables of Kshs.2,809,360,187 and for  increase   in   accounts   payables   of   Kshs.1,207,474,034.   However,   the   supporting  schedules were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of negative accumulated surplus  balance of Kshs.4,058,810,631 could not be confirmed.  393.   Unsupported Intangib le Assets  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 27 of the financial statements  reflects intangible assets and goodwill balance of Kshs.93,279,600. However, the balance  was not supported by a list of software systems operated by the   County Executive   with  their corresponding costs.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the intangible assets and  goodwill balance of Kshs.93,279,600 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  394.   Budgetary Control and   Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   balances   of   Kshs.15,622,164,354   and  Kshs.13,340,945,013 respectively resulting in under - funding of Kshs.2,281,219,341 or  15% of the approved budget. Similarly, the County Executive spent an amount of  Kshs.10,617,940,332 against actual receipts amount of Kshs.13,340,945,013 resulting in  under - utilization of Kshs.2,723,004,681 or 20% of the actual receipts.  The under - funding   and under - utilization affected the planned activities and may have  impacted negatively on service delivery to the public.  395.   Long   Outstanding   Refundable Deposits and Prepayments  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 33 to the fin ancial statements  reflects refundable deposits and prepayments balance of Kshs.176,662,065. However,  review of the deposits register, cashbook, and bank statements revealed long outstanding  refundable   deposits   and   prepayments   totalling   Kshs.74,557,957   dati ng   back   to  March, 2015 and which had not been claimed as at 30 June, 2025.  My opinion is not modified in respect of these matters.

169  Other Matter  396.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the audit report of the previous year, several   issues were raised under the Report  on Financial Statements and Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public  Resources . Review of the status during the audit of financial year 2024/2025 revealed  that the following eleven (11) matters   remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025:  No.   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  1   Variances between Financial Statements and IFMIS Payment details  2   Other Grants and Transfers  3   Transfer to Other Government Units  4   Acquisition of Assets  5   Legal   Expenses  6   Non - Compliance with Law on Ethnicity  7   Lack of Approved Staff Establishment  8   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility  9   Payment of Salaries Outside the Integrated Payroll  10   Recruitment of Staff  11   Lack of Audit   Committee  Other Information  397.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  398.   Non - Compliance with Fiscal   Responsibility Principles   on Wages  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs.6,494,700,107 which is approximately 60% of the County Executive’s total receipts  amount of   Kshs.10,804,046,991 thus exceeding the set limit of thirty - five percent (35%)  by 25%. This was contrary to Regulation 25(1)(b) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015   which limits County Government spending on  personnel emol uments at   not more than 35% of the County Government’s total revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  399.   Non - Compliance   with   Fiscal   Responsibility   Principles   on   Development  Expenditure  The   statement   of   comparison   of   budget   and   actual   amounts   reflects   total   actual  expenditure of Kshs.10,617,940,332. The County Executive spent on development

170  expenditure   an   amount   of   K shs. 893,793,148   or   approximately   8 %   of   the   total  expenditure.   This was co ntrary to Regulation   25(1)(g) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that the County Governments  actual expenditure on development shall be at least thirty percent (30%) in conformity  with the requirement und er Section 107(2)(a) of the Act.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  400.   Outstanding   Payment of Medical Insurance Cover  As   previously   reported,   review   of   medical   insurance   cover   revealed   that   a s   at  30 June, 2025, the County Executive had an outstanding amount of Kshs.64,978,836  owed to an insurance company. This was contrary to Section 156(1) of the Insurance Act,  2023 which provides that no insurer shall assume risk i n Kenya in respect of insurance  business unless and until the premium payable thereon is received by the insurer.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  401.   Weaknesses in the Management of Imprests  Review of imprest   records revealed that imprest amounting to Kshs.104,685,474 were  issued to staff. However, overdue imprests balance of   Kshs.3,587,127 had   not been  surrendered as at 30 June, 2025.   This was contrary to Regulation 93(5) of the Public  Finance Management (Cou nty Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that a  holder of a temporary imprest shall account or surrender the imprest within seven (7)  working days after returning to duty station.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  402.
