Delay   in   Adoption of the County Fiscal Strategy Paper  Review   of   adoption   of   motion   by   the   County   Assembly   reference   number  MCA/SPK/08/VOL.XIII/06 dated 3   April, 2024, showed that the County Assembly adopted  the report of the   B udget and   A ppropriations   C ommittee on the County Fiscal Strategy  P aper (CFSP) for th e financial year 2024/2025   on   3   April, 2024. Th is   was contrary to  Section 117(6) of the Public Finance Management Act ,   2012, which set statutory deadline  for adopting the County Fiscal Strategy Paper not later than fourteen days   after submitting  the Paper   to the County Assembly by the 28 th   February   of each year   which should have  been not later than 13   March, 2024.  In the circumstances,   Management   was in breach of the law .  489.   Failure to Prepare Memorandum for Supplementary Budget by Accounting  Officers  The County Executive had an approved original budget   amount   of Kshs.9,619,521,511  which was   later   adjusted by   an amount   Kshs.258,314,740 through a supplementary  budget to a final   b udget   amount   of Kshs.9,877,836,251. However,   adjustments made in  t he   supplementary budget were not supported with memoranda from the Accounting  Officers confirming   that the changes had been requested and explanations   provided   for  either scaling down or   stopping   of planned development programmes. This was contrary  to   Regu lations   39(7)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations,   2015   which   provides   that,   the   C ounty   Government   entity   requesting  additional funds through a supplementary budget process shall submit a memorandum  to the County Treasury, on a date determined by   the   County Treasury.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of   the   law.  490.   Non - Pronouncement on Revenue Raising Measures  Review of financing records indicated that   CEC - Member for   F inance did not make  pronouncement on revenue - raising measures and no policy statement   was   submitted to  the County Assembly   to accompany   the County Finance   Bill.   This   was contrary to Section  132(2) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012.   Further, there was no evidence  that the County Assembly   considered and approved the Finance Bill with or without  amendments not later than ninety days after passing the   Appropriation Bill, contrary to  Section 133 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .

204  491.   Non - Compliance with   Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of employee records for   the   County Executive   revealed   that the dominant ethnic  community   had   four thousand, six hundred and seventy - nine   (4,679)   or 94%   out of the  total   workforce   of four thousand nine hundred and   fifty - four (4,994) employees. This was  contrary to   Section 7(1) and (2 ) of the   National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, which  provides that no public establishment shall have more than one third of its staff from the  same ethnic community.  Further,   review   of master data and payroll records and list of recruits for the year under  review revealed that the County Executive recruited eighty - six (86) new staff members.  However,   majority of the new recruits totalling   eighty ( 80 )   out of   eighty - six ( 86 )   or   93%  bel onged to the dominant ethnic community in the County .   This was contrary to Section  65(1) of the County Governments Act, 2012, which provides that in selecting candidates  for appointment, the County Public Service Board shall consider the need to ensure tha t  at least thirty percent (30%) of the vacant posts at entry level are filled by candidates who  are not from the dominant ethnic community in the county.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  492.   Non - Compliance with One - Third Rule on Ba sic Salary  Review of payroll data for   the   County Executive   revealed that a total of   one hundred and  fifteen   ( 115 )   employees were paid net salary less than a third (1/3) of their basic   salaries  in the month of March, 2025.   The excessive deductions resulted from Management  allowing the staff to incur loans and other liabilities whose repayment deduction put the  officer s at the risk of pecuniary embarrassment. Further, one   (1)   staff member had total  deductions that were more than the gross pay thus having a negative - net pay which puts  the County Executive ’s   resources at risk of   pecuniary embarrassment   by staff with  negat ive net pay.   This   wa s   contrary to Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which  provides that deductions made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any  one time shall not exceed two thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  493.   Unremitted Statutory and Pension Deductions  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects   a balance of   Kshs.3,228,256,308 in respect of trade and other payables,   out of  which   a balance of   Kshs.695,112,289   was   in respect of trade payables . R eview of the  universal pending bills report as at 30 June ,   2025 revealed that the County Executive had  total pending accounts payable of   balance of   Kshs.1,921,488,731, out of wh ich   an  amount of   Kshs.1,195,580,964 comprised recurrent pending bills relating to salary arrears  and statutory deductions.  Further,   i ncluded   in   this   balance   were   unremitted   statutory   deductions   of   NSSF  contributions   amount   of Kshs.39,250,914, due by the   9 th   of the subsequent month,   and  subject to   a 5% penalty for each month or part of a month that the amount remains unpaid,  as per Section 27(1) of the National Social Securit y   Fund Act, 2013.   Further, p ension

205  contributions   of   Kshs.187,903,354   Kshs.201,815,770 and Kshs.37,380,238   payable to  LAPFUND, LAPTRUST and the   Public Service Superannuation Scheme   respectively had  not been remitted .  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  494.   Irregular Payments   of Subscri ptions  The statement of financial performance reflects use of good and services amount of  Kshs.2,349,640,475 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements which includes  hospitality, supplies and services amount of Kshs.57,081,056.   Review of payments  relati ng to hospitality, supplies and services   indicates   that   an   amount of Kshs.1,000,000  was irregularly paid to the Council of Governors for devolution conference registration  expenses. This was contrary to Section 37 of   the   Intergovernmental Relations Act, 20 12  which provides that the operational expenses in respect of the structures and institutions  established in this Act shall be provided for in the annual estimates of the revenue and  expenditure of the National Government.  In the circumstances, Managemen t was in breach of the law.  495.   Long Outstanding   Accounts Payables  Review of   the universal pending bills ’   report   as at 30 June, 2025   revealed that as at  30 June ,   2025, the County Executive had outstanding   trade and other payables   from prior  years   totalling   Kshs.1 1,342,502,609 .   Review   of payments made during the year under  review indicated that   an amount of   Kshs.757,326,472 related to bills incurred in the year  202 3/2024.   Although the   County Executive   made efforts to settle pending bills during the  year, historical pending bills dating back to the year 2015 amounting to Kshs.448,144,407  remained unpaid and were not treated as a first charge on the budget. This   was   c ontrary  to   the   provisions   of   Section   94(1)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments)   Regulations,   2015.   No   justification   was   provided   for   failure   by  Management to prioritize the settlement of these long - outstanding obligations.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  496.   Non - Compliance with   Capacity Building Levy   Requirements  The statement of comparison of budget and actual   amounts reflects   an amount of  Kshs.8,243,969,936 in respect of actual total payments. However, no evidence was  provided to confirm that Management   deducted   Capacity Building Levy at the rate of  0.03% on all signed contracts and remitted it to the Public Pr ocurement   R egulatory  Authority (PPRA) through the eCitizen platform.  Further, there was no evidence to confirm whether Management filed monthly returns to  the Authority on all levy amounts deducted and remitted, by the 20 th   day of the subsequent  month, as required.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

206  497.   Non - Compliance with Law on Fiscal Responsibility Principles on Wages  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs. 4,216,302,622   as disclose d   in   Note 9 to the financial statements. Th e   amount  translates to 5 1 % of the County   Executive’s   total revenue   amount   of Kshs.8,269,978,762,  thereby exceeding the prescribed limit of 35% set out under Regulation 25(1)(b) of the  Public Finance   Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  498.   Delayed Exchequer Disbursements  The statement of financial performance reflect s   transfers from County Revenue Fund  (CRF)   amounting   to   Kshs.8,269,978,762   as   disclosed   in   Note   6   to   the   financial  statements.   However,   during   the   year   under   review,   E xchequer   disbursements  amounting   to   Kshs. 8,109,770,075   were   not received on time .  T he   E xchequer disbursement s   for the first quarter were done   eleven ( 11 )   days after the  deadline for disbursement.   Further, t he last   E xchequer disbursement for second quarter  and fourth quarter was done two   (2)   months after the disbursement deadline.   Further, t h e  last   E xchequer disbursement for second quarter was done one   (1)   month after the  disbursement deadline.  This was contrary to Section 17(6) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, which  provides   that   T he National Treasury shall, at the beginning of e very quarter, and in any  event not later than the fifteenth day from the commencement of the quarter, disburse  monies   to   county   governments.   Further,   Section   17(7)   of   the   Act   states   that   t he  disbursement referred to in subsection (6) shall be done in accor dance with a schedule  prepared by   T he National Treasury in consultation with the Intergovernmental Budget and  Economic Council, with the approval of the Senate, and published in the Gazette, as  approved, not later than the 30 May in every year.  In the cir cumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  499.   Pending Bills  Review of the universal pending bills’ report as at 30 June, 2025 revealed that the County  Executive had trade payables amounting to Kshs.1,921,488,730, out of which   a balance  of   Kshs.262,454,004 related to payables outstanding for 1 – 2 years, Kshs.53,925,158 for  2 - 3 years, and Kshs.434,902,965 had remained unpaid for over 3 years. It was no t clear  why Management did not adhere to the approved payment plan for clearing pending bills  developed at the start of the financial year, and why these long - outstanding bills were not  settled as the first charge in the subsequent financial year   as requir ed by   Regulation 41(2)  of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

207  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for   Conclusion  500.   Non - Alignment   of   Training Needs Assessment  The statement of financial performance reflect s an amount of   Kshs.2,349,640,475 in  respec ts   of use of goods and services as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements.  Th e   amount   includes training expenses tota l ling Kshs.53,681,693 .   Review of training  expenditure revealed that significant portion of the train ing conducted   was   not aligned  with   the approved Training Needs Assessment (TNA).   Several   trainings attended   by staff  did not correspond to the critical skill gaps   identified in the approved TNA for the year .  In the circumstances, the effective ness of   cap acity building towards achieving service  delivery goals   could not be confirmed.  501.   Ineffective   Internal Audit Function  Review of the Internal Audit function revealed that the   Internal Audit D epartment is  understaffed and inadequately resourced. Out of the approved establishment   of   twenty  (20) audit positions, only eight (8) positions   were   filled, and a number of the serving staff  do not possess the requisite professional qualifications or comp etencies in audit and risk  management.   T his undermines the independence and effectiveness of the internal audit  function. Further, during the year under review,   the internal audit function conducted   only  two   (2)   audit assignments .  In addition, the Depar tment did not have budget allocation.   This   wa s contrary to Standard  2030 of International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing that  requires that the Chief Audit Executive Officers must ensure that internal audit resources  are appro priate, sufficient, and effectively deployed to achieve the approved plan.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the internal audit function and its capacity to  strengthen the system of internal controls could not be confirmed.  502.   Unserviceable Motor V ehicles and Equipment  Review of the fleet of motor vehicles and motor cycle register, revealed that the County  Executive had a total of two hundred and seventy - eight (278) motor vehicles, out of which  one hundred and thirty - seven (137) were grounded, unserviceable   or   non - functi onal.  However, Management did not demonstrate measures put in place to dispose the assets  to prevent further loss. Further, Management did not   prepare   an Annual Disposal Plan  contrary   to   Regulation   176(1)   of   the   Public   Procurement   and   Asset   Disposal  Regu lations, 2020 which requires an Accounting Officer of a procuring entity to ensure  that an annual assets disposal plan is prepared of items declared as unserviceable,  surplus or obsolete, stores, asset or equipment.  In the circumstances,   the existence of   effective assets management mechanism could  not be confirmed.

208  503.   Lack of Risk Management Policy  Review   of   risk management   records revealed that the County Executive d id   not have an  approved Risk Management Policy.   Further ,   k ey risk management processes such as the  development of a risk register have not been implemented. In the absence of a risk  register Management’s ability to identify, assess, and   priori tize risks, as well as to  document mitigation strategies and assign res ponsibility for managing those risks   wa s  impaired. This   wa s contrary to good governance and public sector risk management  practices.  In the circumstances, financial losses due to unforeseen events such as fraud, loss of  information or data and theft   could not be confirmed .  504.   Inadequate Access Controls and Segregation of Duties  Review of   ICT system   records provided for audit revealed that the County Executive  operates critical application systems, including   Unstructured Supplementary Service Data  ( U S SD )   for Mobile Communications,   Revenue Management System,   Digital Health  Platform ( Afya KE )   and the Land Management System .   These systems fall under the  operational mandate of the County   Executive   ICT Department. However, it was noted  that   system   backups a re hosted on a cloud computing platform, with access   being  maintained by a single individual. Further, the existence of formally documented access  controls or an approved ICT organizational structure clearly defining the roles and  responsibilities of key p ersonnel, such as network administrators, information security  analysts,   database   managers,   system   programmers,   system   administrators   and  b ackup/disaster recovery officers with access rights to the cloud environment   could not  be confirmed .  In the circumstances,   the existence of an elaborate mechanism to mitigate against ICT  risks and other vulnerabilities could not be confirmed .

209  Unresolved Prior Years’ Matters  No   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  1  Variance Between the Statement of Receipts and Payments and Integrated  Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) Vote   B ook  2   Unreconciled Pending Bills Records  3   Unsupported Expenditure on Hospitality, Supplies and Services  4   Budgetary Control and   Performance  5   Pending Bills  6   Compensation of Employees  7   Failure to Comply with Staff Establishment  8   Non - Adherence to the Law on Staff Ethnic Diversity  9   Non - Adherence to the One - Third Basic Salary Rule  10   Failure to Comply with Fiscal   Responsibility Principles on Wage Bill  11  Failure to Adhere to Fiscal Responsibility Principles in Budget Allocation to  the County Assembly  12   Construction of a Septic Tank at Maragua Level 4 Hospital  13   Project Complete but Not in Use   -   Mabae Dispensary  14  Failure to Remit Balances from ASDSP II Accounts to National Programme  Account  15   Effectiveness in Implementation of Audit Recommendation  16   Lack of Asset Disposal Plan

210  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF   KIAMBU   –   NO.22  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  505.   Unconfirmed Employees Costs  The   statement   of   financial   performance   and   as   disclosed   in   Note   9   the   financial  s tatements ,   reflects employee costs amount of Kshs.7,993,839,174. Included in the  amount is Kshs .13,247,907 in respect of outstanding Public Service Superannuation  Fund. However, the supporting schedule indicating details of employee contributions was  not p rovided for audit.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the employee costs amounting  to Kshs.13,247,907 could not be confirmed.  506.   Cash and Cash Equivalents  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 21 to the   financial statements  reflects cash and cash equivalents balance of Kshs. 595,554,259. Review of records  provided revealed the following;  506.1.   Inaccuracies in Cash and Cash Equivalents  The cash and cash equivalents balance of Kshs. 595,554,259   includes County   Agriculture  Sector Development Support Programme ll Account with Nil balance. However, the trial  balance   reflects   a   balance   of   Kshs.15,936,995   resulting   in   an   unexplained   and  unreconciled   variance   amounting   to   Kshs.15,936,995.   Further,   the   cash   and   cash  equivalents balance includes Kiambu County Climate Change SPA account balance of  Kshs.158,632,515 which differs with the balance reflected in the Kiambu County Climate  Change   Fund   financial   statements   balance   of   Kshs.139,070,473   resulting   in   an  unexplained an unreconciled variance of Kshs.19,562,042.  In addition,   the statement of cash flows reflects cash and cash equivalents balance of  Kshs.596,064,527 which differs with the balance of Kshs.595,554,259 disclosed in the  statement   of financial position resulting in an unexplained and unreconciled variance of  Kshs.510,268.  506.2.   Irregular Operation of Commercial Bank Accounts  Review of the bank accounts register revealed that the County Executive operated two  hundred and eighty - eight   (288) bank accounts with various commercial banks. This was  contrary   to   Regulation   82(1)(b)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which require only imprest bank accounts for petty cash  and revenue collection bank account s to be maintained in commercial banks.  506.3.   Unsupported Account Balances  Included in Note 21 to the financial statements are three (3) bank accounts namely;   CBK  Kiambu   County   Special   Purpose   Agriculture,   Grant   Deposit   account   and   County

211  Agriculture Sector Development Support Programme ll with Nil balances . However, the  three (3) bank account with Nil balances were not supported with cashbooks, bank  reconciliation statements, bank statements and certificate of bank balances.  In the circum stances, the accuracy, existence and completeness of cash and cash  equivalents balance of Kshs.595,554,259 could not be confirmed.  507.   Misclassification of Expenditure  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 9 to the   financial  statements reflects employee costs amount of Kshs.7,993,839,174 which includes basic  salaries of   permanent   employees amounting   to   Kshs.6,833,199,629.   However, the  supporting ledger revealed that an amount of Kshs.20,460,631 in respect of payment   of  gratuity, bank commission to a local bank and insurance was incorrectly charged to basic  salaries of permanent employees.  Further,   balance   include s   employer contribution to compulsory National Social   Security  Scheme amount of Kshs.418,842,287. However,   the supporting ledger revealed that an  amount   of   Kshs . 33,986,864   relating   to   net   pay,   deductions,   gratuity to   contracted  employees, Pay - As - You - Earn income tax and taxes on gratuity   was incorrectly charged  to employer contribution to compulsory national so cial security schemes item.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness presentation and disclosure of the  employee costs amounting to Kshs.7,993,839,174 could not be confirmed.  508.   Trade and Other Payables  The statement of financial position and as   disclosed in Note 32(a) to the financial  statements reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.7,619,065,692 . However,  the following anomalies were noted;  508.1.   Failure to Reconcile Related Entities Balances  Included in the balance are   payables balanc e of Kshs.7,278,814 owed to The Kenya  Power and Lighting Company. However, records from the Company reflects receivables  balance of Kshs.81,034,362 as at 30 June, 2025 resulting in an unreconciled and  unexplained variance of Kshs.73,755,548.  Further, the trade and other payables balance reflects Nil balance payable to Kenya  Medical Supplies Authority (KEMSA). However, records at KEMSA reflect receivables  balance of Kshs.9,358,061 as at 30 June, 2025 resulting in an unreconciled and  unexplained   variance ledger of Kshs.9,358,061.  508.2.   Unsupported Trade and Other Payables  The supporting schedule provided for audit excluded supporting details such as contract  numbers, local purchase orders (LPOs), local service orders (LSOs) or invoice numbers  for trade and other payables totalling Kshs.351,101,026 and Kshs.682,277,894 under  recurrent   and   development   expenditure   respectively.   Further,   an   amount   of  Kshs.161,121,125 relating to legal fees was not supported by case numbers, advocate  names, payment voucher numbers and invoice numbers.

212  In the circumstances, the existence, accuracy , completeness and   occurrence   of   trade and  other payables balance of Kshs.7,619,065,692 could not be confirmed.  509.   Unsupported Use of Goods and Services  The statement of fin ancia l performance reflects use of goods and services expenditure of  Kshs.2,854,011,777 . Review of records revealed the following   unsatisfactory   issues:  509.1.   Unsupported Expenditure on Fuel, Oil and Lubricants  The balance includes an amount   of Kshs.342,504,719 spent on fuel, oil and lubricants as  disclosed in Note 10 to the f inancial statements. However,   the following issues were  noted;  (i)   Analysis of fuel records provided for audit revealed that general card 1 and card  2 were used for emergency   fueling , provision of lubricants and minor vehicle  service. During the year under review, an amount of Kshs.27,759,767 was  incurred as fuel and lubr icants cost while using the general cards. However, the  cards were not assigned to specific vehicles while, fuel statements provided did  not   specify   the   vehicle   registration   number.   Further,   the   County   Executive  maintained generators in various departments   which drew fuel amounting to  Kshs.20,160,982 during the year. However, the specific generators could not be  traced in the fuel cards statement as they lacked identification. In addition, the list  of generators and their capacity and records of fuel consum ption were not  provided for audit.  (ii)   Analysis of the fuel statement and the County Executive’s motor vehicles assets  register revealed that thirty - two (32) operational motor vehicles were not in the  fuel statement but were in the County   Executive’s asset register of motor vehicles,  casting doubt on whether they were operational or may be idle assets.  (iii)   Analysis of the fuel statement and the County Executive’s asset register revealed  that fifty - eight (58) vehicles with a status ‘not operati onal’ drew fuel amounting to  Kshs.67,530,512 .  (iv)   Analysis of the County Executive’s asset register revealed that two hundred and  forty (240) vehicles did not have County Executive registration numbers and  identification .  (v)   Analysis of the County Executive’s   assets register revealed that seventy - five (75)  motor vehicles and generators did not have their status updated in the asset  register. Therefore, it was not possible to confirm whether they were operational  or not.  (vi)   Review of County Executive’s assets and   log books provided for audit revealed  that twenty - five (25) generators did not have ownership documents and were not  tagged. Further, logbooks for two hundred and twenty - five (225) motor vehicles  were not provided for audit.

213  (vii)   Analysis of sampled work ticke ts and fuel statements provided revealed varying  fuel records. Further, the work tickets were not duly filled with fuel, oil and  lubricants details .  (viii)   Analysis of the County Executive’s fuel card transactions for two (2) consecutive  months, revealed   anomalies in Average Fuel Consumption (AFC). In particular,  ten (10) cards indicated positive AFC variance values exceeding +0.45, indicating  that fuel consumption was at least 45% or more above expected efficiency levels  based on mileage reported. Managem ent did not provide justification for the  excessive fuel usage.  (ix)   Review of fuel records revealed that a total of three hundred and two (302) fuel  cards were used to draw fuel from service stations without the corresponding  odometer readings being captured   at the point of fuelling. The value of fuel drawn  under these transactions amounted to Kshs.147,182,570. The lack of odometer  data limits the County Executive’s ability to monitor fuel consumption, assess  efficiency or verify vehicle usage, thereby weakeni ng internal controls over fuel  management. Further, review of the fuel statement for the period 1 July, 2024 to  31 May, 2025 provided for audit revealed that two hundred and sixty - three (263)  motor vehicles whose odometer readings were zero drew fuel amoun ting to  Ksh.98,623,348.  In the circumstances, the occurrence, accuracy and completeness of the fuel, oil and  lubricants expenditure totalling Kshs.361,257,179 could not be confirmed.  509.2.   Unsupported   Domestic Travel and Subsistence Payments  Included in use of goods and services expenditure is an amount of Kshs. 114,669,898  spent on   domestic travel   and subsistence   as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements. the expenditure   includes domestic travel and subsistence   allowances for  implementation of   various Financing Locally - Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) programmes  across different departments. However, review of sampled payment vouchers totalling  Kshs.3,971,920 revealed that the   vouchers were not supported with vehicle work tickets  or evidence of travel, invitation letters and programme of activities. This was contrary to  Regulation   104(1)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which requires all   receipts and payments vouchers of public moneys  to be properly supported with pre - numbered receipts, payment vouchers and appropriate  authority and documentation.  509.3.   Unsupported Insurance Costs   -   Payment of Staff Medical Insurance  The County Executive en tered into a contract with an Insurance Company for the  provision of Group Medical Insurance cover for four thousand four hundred and ninety -  six (4,496) staff for a duration of one (1) year starting 9 February, 2025 to 9 February,  2026 at a premium amount   of Kshs.375,497,753. The County Executive made payment  of Kshs.282,302,579. However, review of the records revealed the following anomalies;

214  (i)   Clause 3 of the renewal contract signed on 9 February, 2025 between the County  Executive and the   Insurance Company indicated that the scheme was intended to  cover four thousand four hundred and ninety - six (4,496) members of staff and their  dependents.   However,   Management   did   not   provide   a   detailed   list   of   the  beneficiaries or staff covered by the medi cal insurance plan, indicating their full  names, personal numbers, job groups and names of eligible dependents. This was  contrary   to   Regulations   104(1)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments)   Regulations,   2015   which   requires   all   receipts   and   payment  vouchers of public monies to be properly supported with pre numbered receipts  and   payment   vouchers   and   be   supported   with   appropriate   authority   and  documentation.  (ii)   Management paid a premium amount of Kshs.282,302,579 or 75% of contract sum  instead o f the contractual premium amount of Kshs.375,497,753 payable in  advance. This was contrary to provision of Clause 3.2 of the signed contract.  Further, Section 156(1) of the Insurance Act, 2020 requires that no insurer shall  assume a risk unless and until t he premium payable thereon is received by the  insurer. In addition, records indicated that renewal of the medical cover for the  County Executive was signed on 9 February, 2025 by the insurance company,  there was no prior notice in writing seeking for renew al of insurance cover before  contract agreement was entered into and signed.  (iii)   Review of the County Executive’s Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database  (IPPD) revealed that the total staff were six thousand, seven hundred and thirty -  two (6,732)   employees, however, four thousand four hundred and ninety - six  (4,496) or 67% were covered. Management did not provide evidence on how the  four thousand four hundred and ninety - six (4,496) staff were identified for medical  insurance.  (iv)   Clause 3 of the contra ct further states that, any additional employees will attract  additional premium as per the schedule of rates in the final renewal proposal and  the invoice provided in pro - rata basis settled in advance prior to on boarding of the  new entrants. However, the re was no evidence that three hundred and twenty - five  (325) newly recruited staff were insured or included in the premium payments.  (v)   Review of medical insurance records revealed that the County Executive paid  insurance premium of Kshs.8,685,023 for part pa yment for provision of group  medical insurance cover for newly recruited nurses. However, the expenditure was  not supported with documents which include appointment letters and human  resources recruitment records for the newly recruited nurses. Further, a   detailed  schedule showing how the part payment amount was arrived at was not provided  for audit review.

215  509.4.   Unsupported Motor Vehicle Insurance   Costs  509.4.1.   Unsupported Motor Vehicle Insurance Payment  Review of payment records revealed that an   insurance company was paid a premium  totalling Kshs.132,877,237 during the year under review for provision of comprehensive  insurance cover for the County Executive’s motor vehicles. However, Management did  not provide supporting documents in respect of i n spection and valuation reports for all the  County Executive’s vehicles and mechanical assessment report for vehicles over fifteen  (15) years.  509.4.2.   Irregular Contract Variation for Motor Vehicle Insurance Cover  Review of contract renewals for provision of comprehensive motor vehicle insurance  cover revealed an increase in the premium paid by the County Executive. For the contract  period from   12 March, 2024 to 11 March, 2025 , the County Executive paid a premium  am ount of   Kshs.32,258,018 . The subsequent renewal for the period   12 March, 2025 to  11 March, 2026   reflected a premium amount of   Kshs.50,177,300 , representing   56%  increase   in the contract price. However, the number of vehicles covered under both  contracts were   not specified   in the agreements and the justification for the increased cost.  Further, the significant variation in contract value was   not subjected to a separate  ten dering process   as required under Section 139(6) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015, which mandates fresh procurement for contract variations exceeding  25% of the original contract value.  509.4.3.   Comprehensive Motor Vehicle Insurance Payments   for Non - Operational  Vehicles  Review of motor vehicle insurance records revealed that the County Executive insured  eleven (11) motor vehicles at cost of   Kshs.34,870,000 , the vehicles which had not been in  operation for an unspecified period. This was   co ntrary to   Section 149(1) of the Public  Finance Management Act, 2012, which requires an Accounting Officer to be accountable  to the County Assembly for ensuring that the resources of the entity for which the officer  is designated are used in a way that is l awful and authorized, effective, efficient,  economical and transparent.  509.4.4.   Comprehensive Insurance Cover Paid for Motor Vehicles Without County  Executive Registration  The County Executive signed a contract for the provision of motor vehicles, plant and  equipment insurance services on   12 March, 2025   between the   County Executive   and   an  insurance company   at a total premium amounting to   Kshs.50,177,300 , covering the  period   from   12 March, 2025 to 11 March, 2026 . However,   twenty - three (23) motor  vehicles , that   did not bear the County Executive registration , were   included   in the  insurance cover under the same contract. The total insurance premium incurred for these  vehicles amo unted to   Kshs.114,910,000. Value for money on the expenditure could not  be verified.   In addition, out of the twenty - three (23) vehicles,   only twelve (12) vehicles’  l ogbooks were provided for audit review . As a result, the ownership of the remaining

216  eleven   (11) vehicles could not be confirmed. Management did not explain why the  vehicles had not been registered under the County Executive.  509.4.5.   Insurance Payments for Motor Vehicles with Unverified Status  Review of insurance records revealed that   twenty - five (25) motor vehicles   were insured  at a total cost of   Kshs.202,950,000 , as confirmed from the County Executive’s motor  vehicle list and cor responding insurance certificates. However, scrutiny of the list of  vehicles revealed that the vehicles were insured   without any indication of their current  operational status .  509.4.6.   Duplicate Payments for Motor Vehicle Insurance Cover  Review of certifica te of insurance provided for audit revealed that among the insured  motor vehicles, there were seventeen (17) motor vehicles bearing duplicate registration  numbers   which   were   insured   as separate   assets,   resulting   in an   irregular   double  insurance premium pai d of Kshs.113,230,000.  509.5.   Unsupported Renewal of Personal Accidents and Insurance Contracts  Review of insurance expenditure incurred under the   Personal Accident and Work Injury  Benefits Act (WIBA) , revealed that the   County Executive   paid a premium amount of  Kshs.51,149,478   for renewal of insurance coverage for six thousand seven hundred and  thirty - four ( 6,734) staff   for the period   12 March, 2025 to 11 March, 2026 . However, the  expenditure was   not supported with   detailed list of covere d employees, including their  personal numbers , a ccident notifications   sent to the   Director of Occupational Safety and  Health Services (DOSHS), notices of accidents   submitted by the affected employees,  m edical reports   of injured staff, c ompleted claim forms   for   all the   affected employees,  a cknowledgment letters and reference numbers   issued by the insurance provider for each  claim,   c orrespondence   with   DOSHS/WIBA   Director   and   the   insurance   company,  including   WIBA files and a list of unresolved or pending claim s   yet to be resolved or  settled.  509.6.   Insurance Premium Payment for Non - Existing Staff  The County Executive paid an insurance premium amount of   Kshs.51,149,478   under  policy number   745/23/11/HO   to cover six thousand seven hundred and thirty - four ( 6,734)  staff   for the period from 12 March, 2025 to 11 March, 2026 .   However, review of the official  staff registers as at   June, 2025   revealed that only six thousand, four hundred and forty -  two   ( 6,442) emp loyees were actively   on the County Executive’s payroll resulting in an  unexplained variance of two hundred and ninety - two ( 292) staff. This   indicates that the  County Executive may have paid insurance premium for individuals   who are not bona fide  employees .  In the circumstances, the   occurrence , accuracy and completeness of the insurance costs  could not be confirmed.

217  510.   Unsupported Authority to Incur Expenditure  The County Executive incurred an expenditure totalling Kshs.20,049,772 in respect of  Authority t o Incur Expenditures (AIEs) issued to Sub - County offices for facilitation of  revenue   enhancement   activities,   Huduma   Mashinani   and   quarterly   operating  expenditure. However, supporting documents   such   as expenditure returns from the Sub -  Counties indicating th e AIEs issued and whether they were spent as per the approved  budget were not provided for audit.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy,   com p leteness   of   the   AIEs   amounting   to  Kshs.20,049,772 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  511.   Budgetary   Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   amounts   of   Kshs.22,111,444,560   and  Kshs.17,586,323,328   respectively,   resulting   in   an   under - funding   amount   of  Ksh s.4,525,121,232 or approximately 20% of the budget. Similarly, the County Executive  spent an amount of Kshs.17,410,829,925 against actual receipts of Kshs.17,586,323,328  resulting in under - expenditure amount of Kshs.175,493,403 of the actual receipts.  The under - funding   affected the planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  512.   Contingent Liabilities  Note 44 to the financial statements reflects contingent liabilities relating to Court cases  against   the   County   Ex ecutive   totalling   Kshs.1,657,375,047.   However,   the   balance  includes contingent liability relating to Civil Suit No.785 of 2017 between the Postal  Corporation of Kenya (PCK) and County Executive in respect to a Court order issued on  13 July, 2018 directing   the County Executive to remove the alleged bus stage on the  Corporation suit property and to desist from charging the Matatu operators who are using  the   property as   a   bus   stage   or   terminus until   the   suit   is   heard   and   determined.  Subsequently, on 7 October,   2025, the Court issued a further order directing the County  Executive to pay the Corporation all monies arising from the operation of the bus stage  and any other development erected by the County Executive on the property.  The County Executive may be ex posed to huge cash outflow which may affect its ability  to meet its obligations as and when they fall due, thus impacting on service delivery   in the  event that those contingent liabilities crystalizing.  513.   Long Outstanding Refundable Deposits and Prepayment s  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 33 to the financial statements  reflects refundable deposits and prepayments balance of Kshs.434,129,226. Included in  the balance is an amount of Kshs.144,337,720 in respect of retention money   held by the  County Executive for a period of more than three (3) years. However, no justification for  failure to repay the amount was provided for audit.

218  The County Executive may be exposed to escalation of cost in form of interest and  penaltion should t he creditors move to court to recover their dues.  My opinion is not modified in respect of these matters  Other Matter  514.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the   prior year’s audit report, several issues were raised under the Report on Financial  Statements, Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources and Effectiveness  of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance. Review of the status during audi t  of the   County Executive   in 2024/2025 revealed that the twenty - five (25)   matters as listed  at the end of the report remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  Other Information  515.   There were no material issues   relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  516.   Irregularities in Procurement for Construction   of   Project s  516.1.   Failure   to   Report   Reserved   Procurements   to   the   Public   Procurement  Regularity Authority  Review of the status report for Early Childhood Development and Education (ECDE)  Centres projects revealed that the Department for Education procured contractors for  construction works of two hundred and eleven (211) ECD E classrooms   and centres at a  total contract sum of Kshs.722,272,380. Analysis of the categories of   contract award  revealed that forty - eight (48) contracts for construction of the ECDE classrooms and  centres works at a total contract sum of Kshs.106,903,26 9 were awarded to categories  of youth, women and persons with disabilities. However, the contracts were not reported  to Public Procurement Regulatory Authority as required by Section 158(3) of the Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requi res all procurement awards by  procuring entities where a preference or reservation scheme was applied to be reported  with disaggregated data to the Authority on a quarterly basis.  516.2.   Anomalies in Construction of   Early Childhood Development and Education  Cen tres  Review of payments and procurement records in respect to construction of seven (7)  Early Childhood Development and Education (ECDE) centres with an office and ablution  block at a total cost of Kshs.29,018,313 revealed that the inspection minutes prepared b y  the Inspection and Acceptance Committee did not provide specific details regarding  compliance with the terms and specifications of the contract and whether the works met  the technical standards defined in the contract.

219  Further, certificates of completi on for contracts awarded were issued, however, progress  reports and minutes by the Inspection and Acceptance Committee were not provided for  audit. Therefore, it was not possible to confirm whether the works done met the required  specifications.  In   addition, the tender evaluation report revealed that the successful bidder did not  provide evidence of financial capability but was recommended for award on the basis of  financial evaluation as the lowest evaluated bidder. Therefore, the bidder did not mee t  the evaluation criteria. This was contrary to Section 80(2) of the Public Procurement and  Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requires the evaluation and comparison to be done using  the procedures and criteria set out in the tender documents.  516.3.   Irregularities   in Implementation of Proposed Construction of Model   Early  Childhood Development and Education   Centres  Physical inspection of the ECDE projects revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   The construction of Kianjau ECDE Centre in Thika Town Ward with offices and  ablution block at a contract sum of Kshs.2,228,212 was complete but not in use  despite the project being officially launched on 25 April, 2025.  (ii)   Physical inspection of ECDE Centre with offices and an ablution block at Limuru  Mission Primary school construc ted at a contract sum of Kshs.3,670,360 revealed  that the corridor ceiling board was deteriorating due to water leakage from the  gutters. The contractor dug a pit latrine instead of an   Asian   step toilet complete  with wall hang cistern including flush pipe   and a pan connector as specified in the  Bill of Quantities. Further, 1,000 litres plastic storage tank was not installed and  the ceiling board finishes were not done.  (iii)   The construction of ECDE Centre at Kawaida in Cianda Ward was completed,  however, the co ntractor dug a pit latrine instead of   an   Asian   step toilet complete  with wall hang cistern including flush pipe and a pan connector as specified in the  Bill of Quantities. Further, 1,000 litres plastic storage tank was not installed and  ceiling board fini shes were done.  (iv)   Physical inspection of Model ECDE Centre with offices and toilet block at Athena  in Thika Town Ward revealed leaking roof inside the classroom and the veranda,  the walls had visible cracks, an indication of poor workmanship. Further, the h and  wash area had no delay press action pillar taps as specified in the Bill of Quantities.  In addition, although the ECDE Center was officially commissioned on 25   April,  2025, as at the time of audit, the Center was not in use.  In the circumstances, valu e for money incurred on the above projects could not be  confirmed   and Management was in breach of the law.

220  517.   Irregularities in Procurement for Construction of Stadiums  517.1.   Implementation for the Phase II Construction of Thika Stadium  The County Executive awarded construction of phase II of Thika Stadium consisting of a  basketball pitch, stalls, swimming pool, changing rooms, steel bleachers and borehole on  21 June, 2024   at a contract sum of Kshs.165,669,432 for a period of twenty - four (24)  months. However, review of the procurement records revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Budget allocation for sports during the financial year 2023/2024 amounted to  Kshs.140,000,000 while   the procurement plan allocation for stadium construction  works was Kshs.136,071,184 against the contract sum of Kshs.165,669,432.  Management explained that the project was multi - year. Although a breakdown of  expected payments relating to the annual portio n of the multi - year contract and  delivery schedule was not provided for review. This was contrary to   Regulation  50(4) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2015 which requires the   procurement plan to include proper descriptions   of the  procuring items, unit cost, the estimated contract value and the procurement  method   relating   to   the   annual portion   of   a   multi - year   contract   and   delivery  schedule.  (ii)   Review of bid document for evaluation of experience in similar works revealed that  t he bidder, was awarded the contract for renovation and alterations at Thika  Stadium on 7 June, 2023 had not been   completed the   works as at the time of audit.  However, the same contractor was awarded another contract for the   same  stadium.  (iii)   Site   handing over report and minutes were not provided for audit despite the  progress report of 5 December, 2024 indicating that the works commenced on 12  August, 2024 while review of the progress report of the contract implementation  team of 17 May, 2024 revea led that works started on 12 August, 2024 while the  contract was executed on 21 June, 2024.  (iv)   Review of the latest progress report by the contract implementation team dated 5  December, 2024 revealed that 29% of works had been done while payment  amounting to Kshs.52,689,237 or approximately 32% of the contract price was  made instead of an amount of Kshs.48,044,135 resulting in an overpayment of  Kshs.4,645,102 for Certificate Number 1.  (v)   Review of the statement for payment on account for certificate   number 1 revealed  that the basketball pitch had a cost of Kshs.3,982,280 while the Bill of Quantities  reflected   a   cost   of   Kshs.2,193,600   resulting   in   overpayment   amounting   to  Kshs.1,788,680.

221  517.2.   Implementation of Chain - Link Fence and Finishing of Footba ll Pitch at  Thigio Primary School  The County Executive awarded a contract for erection of a chain - link fence and finishing  of the football pitch at Thigio Primary School on 24 April, 2024 at a contract sum of  Kshs.26,785,500 for a period of six (6) months . However, the procurement records  revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   The County Executive implemented works in the primary school which is a  National Government entity, therefore carrying out the function of the National  Government.  (ii)   Review of the bid doc ument of the successful bidder in respect of work  experience of the project manager, foreman, site agent, surveyor and mason  revealed that appointment letters for the company staff were not attached as  required under the technical evaluation criteria.  (iii)   Review of the report of contract implementation committee dated 5 March,  2025 in respect of approval for payment certificate number 2 revealed that the  works were incomplete. This was ten (10) months from the contract execution  date of 24 April, 2024 and t he contract duration had lapsed in September, 2024.  Further, there was no evidence of request for extension by the contractor for  approval.  517.3.   Implementation of Upgrading of Kanjeru Stadium  The County Executive awarded a contract for upgrading of Kanjeru St adium on 20  February, 2024 for a period of two (2) years at a contract sum of Kshs.163,875,850.  However, review of the procurement records revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Budget allocation for sports during the financial year ended 30 June, 2024  amounte d to Kshs.136,071,184 against contract sum of Kshs.163,875,850.  Management   explained   that   the   project   was   multi - year,   however   the  explanation was not supported with a breakdown of expected payments  relating to the annual portion of the multi - year contract   and delivery schedule.  This was contrary to   Regulation 50(4) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires the procurement plan  to include proper descriptions of the procuring items, unit cost, the estimated  contrac t value and the procurement method relating to the annual portion of a  multi - year contract and delivery schedule.  (ii)   Review of the tender opening committee minutes revealed that four (4) bids  were received and opened by the committee, however, only three (3)   bids were  subjected to evaluation without explanation for dropping one bid.

222  (iii)   Progress report by the implementation committee was not provided despite  approval for payment of Kshs.37,081,475 for certificate No. 1 while works were  estimated to be only 23%   complete despite time lapse of fifteen (15) months  casting doubt on whether the works would be completed within the contract  period.  517.4.   Proposed Fencing of Githunguri Stadium  Review of contract records in respect of proposed fencing of Githunguri Stadium at a  contract sum of Kshs.5,935,450 revealed that minutes of the contract implementation  team meeting held on 16 May, 2024 at Githunguri Stadium site indicated that the project  was completed as per the Bill of Quantities and proposed payment for the works.  According to the minutes, the first month of the contract period had already lapsed.  However, the implementation team was appointed on 16 May, 2024. Therefore, it was not  poss ible   to   confirm   how   the   team   executed   its   functions   within   the   same   day   of  appointment.  Further, minutes of the contract implementation team did not specify whether the  materials used met the required standards and whether the works included   fencing and  chain link. In addition, there was no evidence of a completion certificate issued to the  contractor.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law and value for money  obtained from the projects could not be confirmed.  518.   Irregulariti es in Repair and Maintenance of Motor Vehicles  518.1.   Use of Imprest for   Procurement of Services  Review of payment records revealed that an amount of Kshs.4,901,785 was paid to  various officers as standing imprest for procurement of repair and maintenance serv ices  instead of using other appropriate procurement methods to acquire the services. This was  contrary to the requirements of Section   107(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015 on   use of low - value procurement procedure which provides up   to a  m aximum   level   of   Kshs.50,000   and   Kshs.100,000   to   procure goods   and   services  respectively per financial year.  518.2.   Irregular   Procurement   of   Repair   and   Maintenance   of   Motor   Vehicles  Services  Review of payment vouchers totalling Kshs.4,855,158 and procurem ent records for award  of contracts for routine maintenance of motor vehicles revealed that, whereas the post  inspection reports of various motor vehicles were provided, the reports did not clearly  indicate the works done as per the pre - inspection report, q uoted prices and assessment  of whether the repairs done met the expected standards. This was contrary to Section  48(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requires the  inspection and acceptance committee to immediately after the de livery of the goods,

223  works or services, inspect and where necessary, test the goods received, inspect and  review the goods, works or services in order to ensure compliance with the terms and  specifications of the contract and accept or reject on behalf of   the procuring entity, the  delivered goods, works or services.  Further, a firm was awarded a contract of Kshs.2,720,000 for the supply and delivery of  tyres   for Fire Engines and Grader. The quotations were issued on 31 December, 2024 to  various suppliers. However, bid document for the winning bidder was not provided for  audit review.  518.3.   Lack of Equitable Rotation of Suppliers  Review of payments for the year   revealed that a total amount of Kshs.166,723,123 was  incurred   as   expenditure   on   routine   maintenance   of   vehicles   and   other   transport  equipment. The County Executive had a pre - qualified list of suppliers under the category  of provision of motor vehicle gara ges and suppliers of spare parts for vehicles, plant and  machinery, however, However, sampled payment vouchers revealed that Management  did not ensure fair and equitable rotation of suppliers. It was not explained why only few  suppliers were awarded most o f works and quotations. This was contrary to Regulation  91(5) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires an  Accounting Officer to ensure fair and equitable rotation among the persons on the list  under Sections 57, 71 and   106 of the Act and Regulations.  In the circumstances, value for money on the repair and maintenance of motor vehicles  expenditure could not be confirmed and Management was in breach of the law.  519.   Human Resource Management  519.1.   Irregular Expenses for Hire   of Security Officers  The County Executive incurred an amount of Kshs.5,688,561 on security officers attached  to   the   County   Executive   offices .   However,   the   payments   were   irregular   as   the  Administration Police are already compensated by the Ministry of Interior Services, and  their allowances were inappropriately directed to their personal accounts rather than The  National Treasury as provided in Section 104(3) of the Natio nal Police Service Act, 2011  which stipulates that the monies paid for the private use of the police as specified in  subsection (1) shall be paid to the Treasury.  Further, the police officers were paid monthly, casting doubt   on the regularity of the  month ly payment, as the officers are considered full time employees and are therefore  paid their full salaries by the National Police Service Commission.  519.2.   Irregular Payment of Wages  Review of memos and supporting documents for payment three (3) vouchers am ounting  to Kshs.714,000 in respect of reimbursement of standing imprest revealed that the  standing imprest was used to pay security officers guarding the dumpsites. However,  Management did not explain how the security officers were engaged, including appro vals  to engage them.

224  519.3.   Failure to Recognise Agreement with Workers Union  The   County Executive failed to formulate and sign   recognition agreement   with   Kenya  National Union of Medical Laboratory Workers (KNUMLW)   despite being granted   30 days  by the Conciliator on 29 September, 2024 to review the proposed recognition agreement,  propose amendments and finalize the signing process. As at the time of audit, no  agreement had been executed, leading to unresolved labor   relations issues.  519.4.   Lack of a Substantive County Secretary  The County Executive appointed the County Secretary on acting capacity with effect from  2023 for a period of six (6) months. Upon expiry of the six (6) months, the Officer’s acting  capacity wa s extended. However, review of documents and personal files revealed that  at the time of audit, the County Secretary’s office was still vacant without a substantive  office holder.  519.5.   Irregular Engagement of Casual Workers  During the year under review, County Executive engaged   one thousand, one hundred  and eighty (1,180) casual workers for period exceeding more than three (3) months. The  total amount paid to the workers amounted to Kshs.335,704,654.   However, the County  Execu tive did not ensure that casual workers who served   continuously for two (2) months  or more from the date of employment as a casual employee enjoyed the terms and  condition of services as full employees of the County Executive.  This was contrary to Sectio n 37(1)(b) of the Employment Act, 2017 which states that,   an  employee   who   works   continuously   for   two   (2)   months   or   more   from   the   date   of  employment as a casual employee shall be entitled to such terms and conditions of  service as he would have been entitle d to under this Act had he not initially been  employed as a casual employee.  Further, the Human Resource Directorate did not maintain personal records for the casual  workers including documentation on their recruitment and onboarding processes. This  was c ontrary to Section 66, 67 and 68 of the County Governments Act, 2012 which  requires all appointment or assignment of any duty in a County Public Service to be in  writing and the County Public Service Board to maintain a record of all applications  received   in   response   to   advertisements   inviting   applications.   Further,   competitive  engagement of casuals by the Departments could not be confirmed as the recruitment  process documents were not provided for audit.  519.6.   Failure to Align Human Resource Policy Instruments   to County Staff  Establishment  Review of the County Executive’s Scheme of Service revealed that the scheme was  prepared and developed by the National Government for use by its officers long before  the County Governments were established. Therefore, the scheme of service, in its  current   state, does not include all the cadres of staff employed by the County Executive

225  or incorporate the changes that have occurred within the County Executive’s staff  establishment over the years. It was not possible to confirm whether the County Executive  had   an optimal staffing level.  Further, the County Executive did not provide an annual recruitment plan as required in  Paragraph C.1.0 (2) of the County Human Resource Policy and Manual, 2019 which  requires all Departments to develop a recruitment plan and f orward to the County Public  Service Board at the beginning of each financial year.  519.7.   Irregularities in Disciplinary Process  Review of human resource documents revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Five (5) officers were interdicted in 2019 for gross   misconduct. It was not clear why  their disciplinary cases remained unresolved for more than five (5) years while the  staff affected continued to receive half (½) salary plus house allowance and  enjoyed medical insurance cover, This was c ontrary to Paragrap h 7 of the Public  Service Commission Human Resources and Procedures Manual, 2016 which  states that except for disciplinary cases that are subject to Court proceedings, all  other disciplinary cases should be dealt with promptly and finalized within a perio d  of six (6) months and where it is found impracticable to do so, the Authorized  Officer shall report individual cases to the Public Service Commission explaining  the reason for the delay.   Untimely resolution   of administrative actions leads to  unfair labou r practices;  (ii)   Further, the Board through minute dated 4 February, 2025 authorized summary  dismissal from service for the (5) five officers recommending that the officers forfeit  half of their salaries from the date of interdiction and the recovered amount s be  used to offset the misappropriated funds. However, review of the February, March  and April payroll revealed that four (4) officers were still in the payroll and earned  salary, even after the Board recommended for summary dismissal. In addition,  review   of their personal files revealed that the Board had not communicated to the  officers of their dismissal through a dismissal notice or letter;  The   County Executive did not halt the salary of staff absent from duty within a  period of ten (10) days contrary   to the provision of County Executive   Human  Resource Policy, 2019 which required that where a public officer is absent from  duty without leave or reasonable or lawful cause for a period exceeding twenty -  four (24) hours, and is not traced within a period o f ten (10) days from the  commencement of such absence, the officer’s salary shall be stopped and action  to dismiss the officer initiated The County Executive paid two (2) staff a total  amount of Kshs.349,455 after stoppage of salary and before the discipli nary  process was completed;  (iii)   Payment of salary for the month of January of Kshs.413,079 was made to a  dismissed staff. It was established that the staff was dismissed with effect from 8  January, 2025. However, review of the payroll revealed that the officer was paid  the full salary fo r the month of January, 2025. This was contrary to Section 18(4)

226  of Employment Act, 2007 which requires that, where an employee is summarily  dismissed for lawful cause, the employee shall, on dismissal be paid all moneys,  allowances and benefits due to him   up to the date of his   dismissal .  (iv)   Review of human resource records revealed that there were unresolved cases for  two (2) officers that resulted in unjust salary stoppages and prolonged staff  grievances. The salary for one (1) officer was stopped in 2018 d ue to alleged non -  compliance with headcount requirements. However, the officer’s case remains  pending without resolution, denying them rightful remuneration for years. In  addition, the salary for another officer was stopped in December, 2015, and the  case   remained unresolved until the officer retired without redress, potentially  depriving them of terminal benefits.  In the circumstances, value for money on salaries paid to interdicted and dismissed  employees could not be confirmed and Management was in br each of the law.  519.8.   Irregular Recruitment of Employees  Review of human resource documents on recruitment revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   The recruitments for the year under review were not supported with an approved  recruitment plan.  (ii)   One   officer was appointed as a Deputy Director but had not served for a minimum of  eight (8) years with relevant experience.  (iii)   Review of the recruitment documents and personal file at least revealed that the  officer appointed as Deputy Director Litigation and   Prosecution had not attached her  current practicing certificates during the application yet, this was a mandatory  requirement and the same was not in the personal file. Further, the officer lacked a  strategic leadership development course not lasting at l east six (6) weeks from a  recognized institution. In addition, the personal file did not have evidence of post  admission experiences of seven (7) years with minimum of five (5) years’ experience  in litigation as no recommendation or expense letters from th e previous employers  were provided. As at the time of audit, the officer had also not been assigned personal  number.  (iv)   Another officer appointed as Director for Legal Services lacked strategic leadership  development course not lasting less than six (6) week s from a recognized institution  and a master’s degree in law or any other relevant social science from a recognized  university as required in the Scheme of Service.  (v)   The officer appointed as Director for Legislative Drafting had not served in the grade  of   Chief Legal Officer (JG P) or in a comparable and relevant position in service for a  minimum period of three (3) years. Rather the officer had served as a Legal Officer  under job group I for only twenty (20) months. Further, the officer lacked a strategic  leadership development course not lasting at least six (6) weeks from a recognized

227  institution and a master’s degree in law or any other relevant social science from a  recognized University.  (vi)   The officer appointed as Director of Communication and Public Re lations had not  served in the grade of Assistant Director of Public Communication and above or its  equivalent in the wider public service for a minimum period of three (3) years and had  not been in continuous service for a period not less than ten (10) yea rs. It was  established that the officer had served as Deputy Director of Communication for one  (1) year ten (10) months and had been in continuous service in public service for nine  (9) years and four (4) months.  (vii)   The staff appointed as Director of   Veterinary Services lacked a master’s degree in  any of the relevant disciplines of Agricultural, Veterinary or Animal Science. Instead,  her records indicated that she was still pursuing her master’s degree at the time of  appointment.  (viii)   Another staff persona l file had only a letter of appointment as the Acting County Chief  Officer Public   Health, without   any evidence of academic credentials.  In the circumstances, the regularity of the recruitment process and promotions could not  be confirmed.  519.9.   Failure to Construct Governor and Deputy Governor’s Residence  Review of fixed assets records revealed that the Governor and Deputy Governor’s  residence had not been constructed. This was contrary to the Salaries and Remuneration  Commission (SRC) Circular   dated 20 May, 2017 which gave guidelines on housing  benefits   for   Governors,   Deputy   Governors   and   County   Assembly   Speakers.   The  Commission gave a deadline of 30 June, 2022 for the completion and commissioning of  the Governor’s and Speaker’s residence.  In   the circumstances, Management was in breach of the SRC’s guidelines.  519.10.   Long Outstanding Leave Days  Analysis of outstanding leave days for Department for Finance and Economic Planning  revealed that some staff had accumulated more than one hundred and   fifty (150) leave  days despite the human resource polices directive of thirty (30) days leave to be utilized  within a financial year and carrying forward of fifteen (15) days. This implies that the staff  worked throughout the year on normal hours, which wa s contrary to Chief of Staff Circular  which states that all staff with outstanding leave should ensure that all leave days are  utilized. Further, the other County Executive Departments did not provide the leave  roasters for audit.

228  519.11.   Irregular Engagemen t of Community Health Workers  The County Executive engaged the services of three thousand and sixty - eight (3068)  community health promoters each earning a monthly stipend of Kshs.2,500. However,  review of human resources records and data provided   revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Community Health Policy (CHP) was not provided for audit and therefore, there  was no evidence of the scope of duties and management controls of the  activities of the CHPs hence the likelihood of not achieving the intended  objective.  (ii)   The   Department   of   Health   engaged   one   hundred   and   twenty - two   (122)  Community   Health   Promoters   (CHP)   out   of   the   total   community   health  promoters with effect from 1 January, 2025 for a period of one (1) year hence  incurring an amount of Kshs.1,52 5,000 in the year under review. However, it  was not clear how the CHP were engaged and whether the County Executive  adhered to Section 9(1) and (2) of the Primary Health Care Act, 2023 on  engagement.   No   support   documents   were   provided   for   audit   on   the  enga gement of the Community Health Promoters. Review of the payment  voucher revealed that the payment was not supported with reports from the  field on achievements of the workers by the community health officer and  therefore it was not clear whether the work w as done as required. Further,  Management explained that the County Executive pays Kshs.2,500 and the  National Government pays the same amount, however, the signed service level  agreement between the parties was also not provided for audit.  (iii)   Review of the   Community Health Promoter register provided revealed that four  hundred and eight nine (489) CHP were above the mandatory retirement age,  the oldest being eighty - six (86) years, contrary to Section 9(2) of the Primary  Health Care Act, 2023 which states that   a person qualifies for selection and  appointment as a community health promoter under subsection (1) if the  persons are not disqualified for appointment to office by the above criteria or  by any other law.  In the circumstances, the regularity of the recr uitment process and promotions could not  be confirmed and Management was in breach of the law.  520.   Anomalies in Payroll Management  520.1.   Delay in Remittance of Statutory Deductions  Analysis of the manual payroll data revealed that the County Executive deducted and  delayed in remitting PAYE, NSSF, housing levy and NHIF/SHIF statutory dues for the  month of January, 2025 totalling Kshs.761,519.   Delay in remitting statutory deductions  co ntravenes Section 19(4) of   the Employment   Act, 2007   which   stipulates that an  employer who deducts an amount from an employee’s remuneration shall pay the amount

229  so deducted in accordance with the time period and other requirements specified in the  law.  520.2.   Lack of Human Resource and Recruitment Plans  The County Executive recruited four hundred and six (406) officers, out of which sixty (60)  officers were traced in the main IPPD/HRIS - Ke payroll, one hundred and sixty - one (161)  in the manual payroll, and one   hundred and eighty - five (185) in the casuals’ payrolls.  However, the human resource department did not prepare annual recruitment plans  backed   by   evidence   of   budgetary   allocation   to   guide   the   recruitments.   Further,  Management did not prepare human resourc e plan to support achievement of goals and  objectives outlined in the Strategic Plan as required under Section C.1.0 of the County  Human Resource Management Policy and Manual, 2019.  In addition, a total of forty - one (41) officers were identified in both   the manual and  IPPD/HRIS - Ke payroll systems as having joined and exited the County Executive during  the year under review. Thirty - seven (37) officers, who were not engaged as casuals,  remained in the payroll for less than two (2) months and were paid a cum ulative amount  of Kshs.3,470,625.  520.3.   Weaknesses in Management of Casual Workers  Review of casual employees’ records from the departments revealed   non - adherence to  labour laws on employee rest days.   In the year ended 30 June, 2025, eight hundred and  seventy - seven (877) casual employees were recorded as having worked every day for a  cumulative period ranging between twenty - eight (28) to thirty - one (31) consecutive days  without any rest days.  520.4.   Process ing   of   Salaries   Outside   the   Integrated   Payroll   and   Personnel  Database (IPPD) System  Clause 6.3 of the Kiambu County Financial Accounting and Reporting Manual, requires  salaries, allowances, and/or arrears of the County Executive staff to be paid through t he  IPPD/HRIS - Ke System. However, during the year under review, the County Executive  paid a total amount of Kshs. 283,609,248   to five thousand, eight hundred and ninety  (5,890) staff through the manual payroll.   T he use of manual payroll systems for salary  pr ocessing is susceptible to manipulation and fraud, potentially resulting to unauthorized  payments.  520.5.   Duplicate Payment to Casual Workers  Review of banking records revealed that in the month of April, 2025, a worker was paid  an amount of   Kshs.24,696 as a garbage collector in WENRECC Department and was  also paid an amount of Kshs.27,783 as a caretaker assistant in the Administration  Department .   Further, the bank account received funds in May, 2025 of Kshs.46,617 as  payment to administrator   -   liaison and an additional amount of Kshs.45,063 as payment  to administrator   -   casual worker in the Administration Department, resulting in duplication  of payments .   In addition,   review of the Manual payroll revealed that five (5) bank  accounts,   were   share d   by   ten   (10)   different   officers,   who   received   a   total   of  Kshs.1,633,184 during the year under review.

230  520.6.   Overpayment of Allowances Above Rates in Manual Payroll  Review of manual payroll records revealed that forty - four (44) officers in the manual  payr oll were paid basic salaries above the approved rates, resulting to overpayment  amounting   to   Kshs.2,484,816 .   Further,   twenty - one   (21)   officers   were   paid   house  allowance totalling Kshs.328,397 above their entitlement in the respective job groups.  while twen ty - four (24) officers were paid commuter allowance totalling Kshs.265,491  above their approved job group rate. The overpayments were not supported with  approvals and no recovery for the overpayment had been initiated by the County  Executive.  520.7.   Irregular Payment of Hardship Allowance  Three (3) officers were paid hardship allowance totalling Kshs.91,905, despite not being  stationed in non - hardship areas contrary to Circular No. 7 of 2023 of the Salaries and  Renumeration Commission, which ou tlines gazetted hardship zones.   According to the  circular, Kiambu County is not designated as a hardship area.  520.8.   Irregular Payment of   Both Rental and Special House Allowances  Review of payroll records revealed that one hundred and forty - seven (147) of ficers were  paid   both   rental   and   special   house   allowances   totalling   Kshs.23,777,100   and  Kshs.7,826,305 respectively. Further, one hundred and thirty - four (134) officers were paid  above   the   approved   rates,   resulting   in   irregular   expenditure   amounting   to  Ksh s.2,081,000.  520.9.   Irregular Payment of Health Risk Allowances  Review of payroll records revealed that eighty - nine (89) officers were irregularly paid  health risk allowances totalling Kshs.925,452, despite not meeting the eligibility criteria  outlined in the SRC Circular dated 14 September, 2015, which stipulates and   lists the  health risk allowance payable to health workers and specifies health workers categories  entitled   to receive such allowances. Further, the manual payroll revealed that four (4)  officers were paid health service allowance above the approved rates,   resulting   in  overpayment   amount of Kshs.91,617  520.10.   Overpayment of Nursing Allowances  Review of the manual payroll revealed that two (2) officers on the manual payroll were  paid nursing allowances amounting to Kshs.80,000 each while onaother one was paid  Kshs.40,000, instead of the approved rate amount of Kshs.20,000 each resulting to  overp ayment amounting to Kshs.140,000 per month.  520.11.   Irregular and Frequent Payment of Salary Arrears  Review of salary records revealed that forty - four (44) employees were paid salary arrears  covering a period of between three (3) and seven (7) months, totalling   Kshs.6,046,477

231  during the year under review. T he County Executive made frequent arrears payments for  the same officers within short   intervals, indicating ineffective controls in in payroll  adjustment. This was contrary to standard practice where arrears a re expected to be  computed and paid once upon issuance of a valid Pay Change Advice   (PCA).  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law and the regularity and value  for money on incurred expenditure could not be confirmed.  521.   Non - Compliance with Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Analysis of employees in the IPPD System revealed that 85% of the staff were from the  dominant ethnic community in the County contrary to the requirements of Section 7(2) of  the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008   which states that, all public   offi ces shall  seek to represent the diversity of the people of Kenya in the employment of staff and that  no public institution shall have more than one - third of its staff establishment from the  same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in br each of the law  522.   Non - Compliance with One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Review of the staff payroll for the year under audit revealed that two hundred and eighty -  seven (287) employees were paid net salaries that were less than one - third of their basic  salari es contrary to   Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which requires that  deductions made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any overtime shall  not exceed two thirds of such wages .  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .  523.   Irregularities in Procurement for Construction of Hospitals  523.1.   Delay in Completion of Thogoto Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for completion of Thogoto   Hospital in Kikuyu  on 31 August, 2023 at a contract sum of Kshs.157,304,215 for a period of eighteen (18)  months.
