However,   review   of   the   contract   implementation   team   minutes   dated  19 February, 2025 revealed that a contract variation o f Kshs.38,952,492 or approximately  25% was recommended for additional works and was approved by the Accounting Officer  on 10 March, 2025. However, the variation was not supported with the Evaluation  Committee appraisal report, recommendation from the procu rement function and the bill  of quantities for the variation.  Further, the works remained incomplete despite lapse of contract duration and there was  no evidence of any request for or extension of contract period.  523.2.   Delay in Construction of a Medical Ward   Block at Karuri Level 4 Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a medical ward block   -  ground, first and second floor at Karuri Level 4 Hospital on 8 September, 2023 at a  contract sum of Kshs.180,734,625 for a period of e ighteen (18) months. However, review

232  of minutes of the contract implementation team dated 4 February, 2025 indicated a time  lapse of seventy (70) weeks translating to approximately 97% of the time allocated  against works done measured at 69% and amount cer tified of Kshs.129,573,860 or  approximately 72% resulting in pending works of 28% as at the time of audit, an indication  that the project was behind schedule.  Further,   review   of   contract   minutes   revealed   that   a   contract   sum   variation   of  Kshs.43,917,340 or   approximately 24% was recommended for additional works and  approved by the Accounting Officer on 24 February, 2025. However, the variation was  not supported with the user appraisal report, recommendation from the procurement  function and the bill of quant ities for the variation. This was contrary to Regulation 132(2)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires any  variation request to be reviewed by the contract implementation or an Evaluation  Committee, before they are su bmitted through the head of a procurement function to the  Accounting Officer for approval.  In addition, approval for extension of contract duration period by twenty - six (26) weeks  with effect from 4 April, 2025 was issued on 28 March, 2025 by the Chief Of ficer Health  Services. However, the approval was not supported with recommendation from the  evaluation committee before it was submitted through the head of a procurement function  to the Accounting Officer for approval.  523.3.   Irregular Procurement of Completion   Works at Bibirioni Level 4 Hospital  Block  The County Executive awarded a contract for completion works at Bibirioni Level 4  Hospital Block on 26 March, 2025 for a contract period of ninety - six (96) months and a  contract sum of Kshs.224,608,050. However,   review of procurement records revealed  that the available funds in the Vote Book amounted to Kshs.17,773,755. Although  management explained that the project was multi - year, the breakdown of expected  payments relating to the annual portion of the multi - year   contract and delivery schedule  was not provided for audit. This was contrary   to   Regulation 50(4) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires the procurement  plan to   include proper descriptions of the   procuring items, unit cost, the estimated contract  value and the procurement method relating to the annual portion of a multi - year contract  and delivery schedule.  523.4.   Delay in Construction of a Level 3 Health Facility at Wangunyu  The contract for construction of a Level 3 Health Facility at Wangunyu   -   Ruaka was  awarded on 8 September, 2023 at a contract sum of Kshs.44,112,284 for a period of  twelve (12) months. Howeve r, review of the contract implementation team minutes dated  21 January, 2025 revealed a contract period of fifty - four (54) weeks translating to  approximately 112% of the time had lapsed while the works done was at approximately  90% despite lapse of contrac t duration period in September, 2024.

233  Further, the Committee report on progress reflected works done estimated at 90% against  amount of works certified of Kshs.42,633,965 or approximately 97% resulting in an  unexplained overpayment of works by Kshs.2,932 ,908.  In   addition,   variation   of   the   contract   sum   by   an   amount   of   Kshs.10,490,112   or  approximately 24% was approved by the Accounting Officer on 24 February, 2025 yet the  contract period lapsed on 8 September, 2024. Therefore, the variation was done outsid e  the contract period. In addition, no evidence was provided confirming that review of the  variation was conducted by the procurement function and evaluation committee contrary  to Regulation 132(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations,   2020  which requires any variation request to be reviewed by the contract implementation team  or an evaluation committee before they are submitted through the head of a procurement  function to the Accounting Officer for approval.  It was also noted that the   contractor requested for extension of time for the execution of  works on 02 December, 2024. This request was made after the lapse of contract period.  The Accounting Officer approved time extension on 3 December, 2024 for a period of four  (4) months withou t evidence of review by contract implementation team.  523.5.   Irregular Implementation of Contract for Construction of Kiambu Level 3  Hospital at Ndumberi  The contract for the construction of Kiambu Level 3 Hospital at Ndumberi was awarded  on 25 October, 2023 a t a contract sum of Kshs.41,913,760 for a contract period of ninety -  six (96) weeks. However, the performance guarantee expired on 9 May, 2025 and the  contractor had not renewed the performance guarantee at the time of audit.  Further, Management paid an amount of Kshs.8,299,384 but that there was no evidence  of any progress of works since 27 November, 2024. Management explained that the site  was no longer active and the contractor had been served with notice of default due to  n on - performance. However, contract termination letter was not provided for audit. In the  absence of a performance guarantee, the County Executive is not likely to receive any  liquidated damages from the contractor. This was contrary to Regulation 133(1) of   the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires that any  ascertained liquidated damages shall be deducted from the amount of approved invoices  due for payment or the performance security.  523.6.   Irregular Implementation of Contract for   Construction of Inpatient Wing  at Ndeiya Health Facility  The contract for the construction of in - patient wing at Ndeiya Health Facility was awarded  on 16 May, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.42,965,100 for a contract period of ninety - six  (96) weeks. Howe ver, review of progress report dated 7 February, 2025 indicated works  done equivaent to 78% against an amount of Kshs.37,526,150 paid for certified works,  translating to 87% and resulting to an overpayment of Kshs.4,726,161. Therefore, the  amount certified   was not directly proportional with the works that had been completed.

234  523.7.   Irregular Procurement of Construction of Level 3 Health Facility at Gitaru  The County Executive awarded a contract for construction of Level 3 Health Facility at  Gitaru on 22 April, 2025 at a contract sum of Kshs.64,279,468 for a period of twelve (12)  months. However, review of the vote book for availability of funds for the work s revealed  that only an amount of   Kshs.17,773,755 was   available at   the time   of   requisition.  Management explained that the project was multi - year, however, this was not supported  with a breakdown of expected payments relating to the annual portion of the mu lti - year  contract and delivery schedule.  This was contrary to   Regulation 50(4) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires the   procurement plan to   include proper  descriptions of the procuring items, unit cost, t he estimated contract value and the  procurement method relating to the annual portion of a multi - year contract and delivery  schedule.  Further, the CR12 records for the lowest evaluated bidder revealed encumbrances  charge of Kshs.16,000,000 made on 20 Apri l, 2022. Therefore, the successful bidder did  not meet the mandatory and technical evaluation requirement under No.12 on financial  capabilities that required the tenderer to demonstrate that they had unencumbered real  assets despite having been evaluated a s responsive.  523.8.   Irregular Procurement for Construction of Ndururumo   -   Ndarasha Level 3  Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for construction of Ndururumo   -   Ndarasha  Level 3 Hospital on 22 April, 2025 at a contract sum of Kshs.68,835,000 for a p eriod of  ninety - six (96) weeks. Confirmation of the vote book for availability of funds for the works  revealed that only an amount Kshs.17,773,755 was available at the time of requisition.  Management explained that the project was multi - year. However, this   was not supported  with a breakdown of expected payments relating to the annual portion of the multi - year  contract and delivery schedule. This was contrary to   Regulation 50(4) of the Public  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which re quires the  procurement plan to include proper descriptions of the procuring items, unit cost, the  estimated contract value, and the procurement method relating to the annual portion of a  multi - year contract and delivery schedule.  523.9.   Irregular Implementation   of Contract for Construction of Inpatient Wing  at Uthiru Health Facility  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a Level 3 Hospital in  Uthiru   on 19 April, 2024 for a contract period of twenty - four (24) months at a contract sum  of   Kshs.64,640,607.   However,   review   of   the   progress   report   of   the   contract  implementation team dated 12 November, 2024 revealed that site handing over was done  on 22 July , 2024 while the contract agreement was signed on 19 April, 2024, three (3)  months later with no explanation for the delay. Further, the progress report revealed that  works were at approximately 5% against time lapse of three (3) months and payment of  Kshs .19,087,064 made translating to approximately 29%, hence resulting in overpayment  of Kshs.15,855,033.

235  In addition, Management did not provide progress report on works and certificate of  completion or certified works since 12 November, 2024. Therefore, the   audit could not  establish the extent of works and whether the contract implementation team adequately  monitoring the progress of works. This was contrary to Regulation 33(3)(u) of the Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires   the procurement  function to monitor contract management to ensure implementation of contracts in  accordance with the terms and conditions of the contracts and to report any significant  departures from the terms and conditions of the contract to the head of   the procuring  entity or Accounting Officer.  523.10.   Irregular Implementation of Construction of Level 3 Health Facility at  Kahawa Sukari  The County Executive entered into a contract on 8 September, 2023 for the proposed  construction of Level 3 Health Facility in Kahawa Sukari. However, the site was handed  over on 17 November, 2023 seventy (70) days after signing of the contract. This was  co ntrary to Article 4 of the contract which required the contract to commence upon  execution of contract and not later than fourteen (14) days after handing over of the site  for works to the contractor.  The contract duration was for eighteen (18) months fro m commencement of the contract.  However, physical inspection carried out revealed that the works were not complete. This  was one (1) year, eight (8) months (20 months) from commencement date of the contract.  There was no evidence of project extension in pl ace yet mechanical works, electricity  connections and wiring, doors, windows, floor and painting in theatre had not been  completed.  Further, physical inspection revealed that the contractor had not installed doors as per  the specifications stipulated in t he bill of quantities which required installation of cultured  hardwood frames amounting to Kshs.2,203,700. Instead, the contractor installed light  flash doors.  523.11.   Delay in Handing Over the Gatundu Level 5 Funeral Home  The County Executive entered into a c ontract on 5 January, 2024 for the completion of  works at Gatundu Level 5 Funeral Home in Gatundu South Sub Location at a contract  sum of Kshs.57,327,900 for a period of twenty (20) weeks. According to the contract  implementation meeting minutes dated 18 D ecember, 2024 the project was completed  on 9 June, 2024. However, physical inspection carried out in July, 2025 revealed that  even a year later, the facility was still not in use and the County Executive had not handed  over the project to Gatundu Level 5 H ospital.  523.12.   Irregularities in the Renovation Works at Gachege Health Centre  The County Executive entered into a contract on 8 July, 2024 for the proposed renovation  works at Gachege Health Centre in Gatundu North at a contract sum of Kshs.4,140,132  for a   period   of   twelve   (12) weeks. Review of documents and physical inspection

236  conducted in July, 2025 revealed that the proposed renovation works at the facility was  certified as complete.  However,   physical inspection revealed poor workmanship in the ceiling   renovation, with  some sections already falling off. Further, in some arears including   the antenatal clinic,  laboratory,   store   for   non - drugs,   registry   and   observation   room,   injection   room,  consultation room, and pharmacy, the old tiles were not replaced with new ones as stated  in the bill of quantities.  In addition, despite the completion   of renovations, the maternity wing remained unutilized.  This was contrary to Section 160(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act,  2015 which requires an Accounting Officer of a procuring entity to manage its inventory,  assets and stores for the   purpose of preventing wastage and loss and continuing  utilization of supplies.  The bill of quantities provided also included a sum of Kshs.100,000 for facelifting   the  service   charter   within the facility. However, the board was in place but did not display the  standard services offered by the facility.  In the circumstances, regularity and value on money on the construction of hospitals could  not be confirmed and Management was in brea ch of the law.  524.   Construction and Civil Works  524.1.   Irregular Implementation of Municipal Offices  Review of procurement records and award of contract for the construction of Municipal  Offices   at Red Nova   revealed that   the project was   awarded   to the Contractor   on  29 May, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.51,670,660 for a period of twelve (12) months.  The progress report of the Contract Implementation Committee dated 4 December, 2024  indicated commencement date of 13 June, 2024 and   completion date of 13 June, 2025  for the works. However, physical inspection of the site revealed that the project had stalled  and the contractor was not on site despite lapse of contract duration period.  Further,   the   performance   security   issued   on   6   Jun e,   2024   for   an   amount   of  Kshs.2,583,533 revealed that the validity period lapsed on 6 December, 2024 and had  not been renewed, therefore casting doubt on performance of works to completion.  524.2.   Irregular Implementation of Construction of Wendani Bridge  The   County Executive awarded construction of Wendani Bridge on 25 September, 2023  at a contract sum of Kshs.17,094,468 and completion date of November, 2023. Review  of   the   implementation   records   provided   for   the   audit   revealed   that   the   expected  completion dat e for the works was November, 2023. However, as at the time of audit  certificate of completion had not been issued due to incomplete works, yet the contract  duration period had already lapsed.  Further, the progress report of the contract implementation te am dated 7 November, 2024  indicated that certified works done was approximately 93% complete. Subsequently, to  this, the implementation team did not monitor the progress of the remaining works

237  contrary to Regulation 110(h) of the Public Procurement and Ass et Disposal Regulations,  2020 which requires the team to monitor the implementation of the project and report to  the Accounting Officer of the procuring entity.  524.3.   Irregular Implementation of Construction of Mariguiti   -   Gituamba   Single  Cell Box Calvert  The County Executive awarded the construction of Mariguiti - Gituamba   single cell box  culvert on 23 May, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.6,348,390. However, review of the  implementation report revealed that the validity of the performance security issued on  20 June, 2024 lapsed on 20 December, 2024 and had not been renewe d, therefore  casting doubt on performance of works to completion.  Further, the work delivery report by the contractor dated 13 February, 2025 revealed that  75% of work had been completed. However, as at the time of audit the works remained  incomplete with out a clear completion date.  524.4.   Irregular Implementation of Upgrading of Bus Parks  Review of procurement records revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Contract for the construction and upgrading of the bus parks to cabro standard  at Kwambira and Githiga was   awarded on 5 April, 2024 at a contract sum of  Kshs.51,229,384. Review of the implementation records revealed that the   works  were to be completed on 5 July, 2024, three (3) months after the contract signing  date. However, as at the time of audit the projec t was not complete and no  extension request had been lodged by the contractor.   Further, site handing over  minutes to the contractor were not provided for audit.  (ii)   The County Executive entered into a contract on 28 February, 2024 for the  proposed fabrication   and installation of steel sheds and steel modern kiosks at  Makongeni Bus Park at a contract sum of Kshs.4,968,136 for a period of one  (1) month. Review of documents and physical inspection revealed that work was  completed   and the twelve   (12) steel modern   kiosks   constructed   were all  occupied. Review of revenue records and interview with the tenants revealed  that the County Executive was not charging any fee for the occupancy.  (iii)   The County Executive entered into a contract on 14 May, 2025 for proposed  constr uction of one hundred and six (106) modern kiosks in Kiambu Bus   -   Park  at a contract sum of Kshs.24,367,800. However, review of documents and  physical inspection conducted in July, 2025 revealed that the contract did not  specify the contract period contrar y to Section 129(2) of the Public Procurement  and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requires the contract to be in writing and  set out either the maximum amount of money that can be paid under the contract  or the maximum amount of time that can be paid for un der the contract. Physical  inspection of the kiosks revealed that only twenty - eight (28) out of one hundred  and six (106) kiosks or 26% were completed even though some had already  been   vandalized while four (4) kiosks were occupied and in use.

238  524.5.   Irregular P rocurement of Drilling Services   for Gatuanabu Borehole at  Muguga  The County Executive awarded a contract for drilling services for Gatuanabu borehole in  Muguga   Ward on 15 March, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.2,598,640. However, review  of the evaluation committee minutes revealed that the winning bidder was evaluated as  responsive under the technical evaluation criteria requiring demonstration of financial  capac ity and which required the bidder to have unencumbered real assets yet the CR12  of   the   winning   bidder   dated   1   September,   2023   reflected   encumbrances   of  Kshs.132,000,000 for debt instrument dated 21 June, 2021. This was contrary to  Regulation 30(a) of the P ublic Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which  stipulates   that   the   evaluation   committee   shall   conduct   the   technical   and   financial  evaluation of the tenders in strict adherence to the compliance and evaluation criteria set  out in the tender do cuments.  Further, the ownership documents, authority and license from the Water Resource  Authority to drill the borehole was not provided for audit.  524.6.   Irregular Procurement of Drilling Services for Njiku Borehole at Karuri  The County Executive awarded a contract for drilling of Njiku Borehole in Karuri Ward on  12   February, 2024 at   a   contract   sum of Kshs.2,431,279. However, review of the  evaluation   committee   minutes   revealed   that   the   winning   bidder was   evaluated   as  responsive   under the technical evaluation criteria requiring demonstration of financial  capacity and which required the bidder to have unencumbered real assets yet the CR12  of the winning bidder dated 1 September, 2023 reflected encumbrances amounting to  Kshs.132,00 0,000 for debt instrument dated 21 June, 2021. This was contrary to  Regulation 30(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which  stipulates   that   the   evaluation   committee   shall   conduct   the   technical   and   financial  evaluation of the t enders in strict adherence to the compliance and evaluation criteria set  out in the tender documents  524.7.   Irregular   Requisition,   Supply   and   Installation   of   Booster   Pump,   Steel  Towers and Tanks at Marengeta Community Water Supply  The County Executive awarded   a contract for the supply and installation of a booster  pump, construction of 18M high elevated steel tower and installation of two (2) 10M 3  plastic tanks and installation of assorted pipes at Marengeta Community Water Supplies  in Nachu on 30 January, 2024   at a contract sum of Kshs.4,594,974. However, review of  the requisition and implementation records revealed that the request for the works by  Marengeta   Community   Water   Supplies,   who   are   the   users   as well   as   the   needs  assessment report was not provided for   review.  Further, the Memorandum of Understanding between the Marengeta Community Water  Supplies and County Executive regarding the land on which the construction and  installation was to take place was not provided for audit.

239  524.8.   Irregular Procurement of C onstruction of Tower and Installation of Plastic  Tanks at Lari  The County Executive awarded a contract for construction of an 18M high steel tower and  installation of four (4) 10 cubic metres plastic tanks at Lari DCC Borehole at a contract  sum of Kshs.3 ,425,310 on 22 April, 2024. Confirmation of the vote book for the availability  of funds revealed that only an amount of Kshs.687,194 was available at the time of  requisition. However, Management awarded a tender amounting to Kshs.3,425,310  contrary to the   provisions of Section 45(3)(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015 which requires that all procurement processes to be within the  approved budget of the procuring entity and shall be planned by the procuring entity  concerned through an a nnual procurement plan.  524.9.   Delayed   Completion   of   Construction   of   County   Aggregation   and  Industrial Park  Review of supporting documents in respect of an award of contract for construction of  County Aggregation and Industrial Park at Waruhiu Centre signed on 31 October, 2023  revealed that the initial completion period was 31 October, 2024. However, an applicat ion  for extension was made on 3 April, 2025. This was five (5) months after the lapse of the  contract period. The contractor cited increased scope of works and delayed approval. The  project scope was revised to include additional excavation, extra warehous e roofing, side  paneling sheets and enlarged design and quantities for ablution block.  Further, there was no evidence that the contract implementation team reviewed the  request for extension of contract period. The project was ongoing and the contractor   was  still on site but no approval for the extension of the contract period from the head of  procurement function was provided for audit. This was contrary to Section 139(2A) of the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requires an Accountin g Officer  of a procuring entity, on the recommendation of an evaluation committee, to approve the  request for the variations, which request shall be accompanied by a certificate from the  tenderer making a justification for extension of contract period and   reimbursable costs.  524.10.   Irregular Procurement of Cabro - Making Machine  The County Executive procured two (2) cabro - making machines at a total cost of  Kshs.13,110,000. The machines were delivered, inspected and accepted on 11 October,  2024. Physical inspecti on revealed that one (1) cabro machine was not in use and has  been stationed in the Governor’s headquarter office for the past eight (8) months.  Further, review of the procurement records revealed that the contract signed between the  County Executive and   the Contractor on 8 November, 2023 and provided for audit did not  outline the terms, specific and general conditions including timelines.  In addition, t he County Executive requested for a pre delivery inspection of two (2) cabro  making machines on 8 Nov ember, 2023, from the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure.  The status inspection report was carried out by the Ministry on 10 and 17 November,  2023 while the delivery of the machines was done on 11 October, 2024, eleven (11)

240  months later, despite the   machines having a twelve (12) months warranty and the  inspection report confirming the machines were in good condition.  In the circumstances, value for money on the above projects could not be confirmed and  Management was in breach of the law.  525.   Irregularities in Construction of Markets  525.1.   Irregular Procurement for Construction of Markets  Review of procurement records revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   A contract was awarded on 28 June, 2024 for the proposed construction of  Ndeiya Market Complex   at a contract sum of Kshs.21,016,620 and a contract  duration of fifty - two (52) weeks. Review of procurement documents revealed  that, the requisition from the user department specified ground floor and first  floor, modern ablution block, parking area, wate r tank tower or underground  water tank and two rows of storeyed modern kiosks along the market boundary.  However, the tender invitation specifications only considered the ground floor  and preliminary scope of work. It was not clear how the other specificat ions  requisitioned were to be delivered and whether the resulting complex would  meet the needs of the users. Further, there was no evidence of completion of  works despite lapse of contract duration period.  (ii)   A contract was awarded on 10 May, 2024 for the pr oposed construction of Kinoo  Market Complex at a contract sum of Kshs.48,098,013 and a contract duration  of fifty - two (52) weeks. Review of procurement documents revealed that at the  preliminary evaluation, the winning bidder did not fill the confidential   business  questionnaire form. The bidder was also required to give a list and type of  relevant equipment owned or provide evidence of ownership by way of lease.  However, the document was not traced in the bidder’s documents, thereby  casting doubt on the bid der’s eligibility. This was contrary to Regulation 30(a) of  the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which stipulates  that   the   evaluation   committee   shall   conduct   the   technical   and   financial  evaluation of the tenders in strict adherence t o the compliance and evaluation  criteria set out in the tender documents.  (iii)   Further, the validity of performance security amounting   to Kshs .2,404,900  issued by the contractor and dated 7 June, 2024 had already lapsed at the time  of audit and there was no   evidence of renewal.  525.2.   Initiation of Procurement for Construction of Markets without Sufficient  Funds  Review of procurement and budget records revealed that the user - department initiated  construction of Lusigetti Market, Kimbo Matangini Market Complex, Dagorreti Market and  Kinoo   Market   during   the   financial   year   2023/2024   at   an   estimated   cost   of  Kshs.168,94 6,933. However, the available budget was amount of Kshs.92,926,122 under  Vote D4081 could only have accommodated construction of two (2) markets, resulting in

241  an unbudgeted expenditure amount of Kshs.76,020,811. Management explained that the  projects were   multi - year, however, this was not supported with a breakdown of expected  payments relating to the annual portion of the multi - year contracts and delivery schedule  contrary to   Regulation 50(4) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulation s, 2015 which requires the procurement plan to include proper descriptions of  the procuring items, unit cost, the estimated contract value and the procurement method  relating to the annual portion of a multi - year contract and delivery schedule.  525.3.   Irregula r Procurement for Proposed Kiandutu Market  Review of procurement records provided for audit revealed that a contractor was paid an  amount of Kshs.4,985,325 in respect of ground preparation and ablution block at Kiandutu  market Thika Township Ward. Furthe r, it was established that the   County Executive  awarded and paid another contractor an amount of Kshs.4,993,980 for   construction of  masonry perimeter wall for the proposed Kiandutu Market. Both contracts were signed on  22 March, 2024. However, no explanati on was provided why the works were not   tendered  as a single tender, given that the County Executive had proposed to construct the market.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the projects could not be confirmed and  Mana gement was in breach of   the law.  526.   Anomalies in Procurement of Motor Vehicles  526.1.   Irregular Procurement of Motor Vehicles  The County Executive through the State Department for Public Works   –   Supplies Branch,  procured three (3) motor vehicle at a cost of Kshs.28,482,179 using a con tract signed  between the State Department for Public Works and a supplier dated 22 November, 2023.  However, the following anomalies were observed:  (i)   Requisition from the user department did not provide details regarding the  specifications of the required m otor vehicle and needs assessment report.  (ii)   Pre - delivery   inspection   reports   were   not   provided   for   audit   to   confirm  compliance with required specifications.  (iii)   There was no report from the Mechanical Engineer (Department of Roads,  Public Works, and   Infrastructure) to verify that the delivered vehicle conformed  to the required specifications.  This was contrary to Regulation 104(1) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulation, 2015, which requires all receipts and payments vouchers of  public moneys to be properly supported with pre - numbered receipts, payment vouchers  and appr opriate authority and documentation.  526.2.   Lack of   Ownership Documents   of an Ambulance  Review of payment voucher in respect of payables for supply and delivery of a hospital  ambulance amount of Kshs.9,778,001 revealed that the supplier wrote a demand letter  f or payment of the outstanding amount within fourteen (14) days on 2   May, 2019 and

242  subsequently withheld the original logbook for five (5) Hospital ambulances until the debt  was cleared.   This was contrary to Section 53(8) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal   Act,   2015   which   requires   the   Accounting   Officer   not   to   commence   any  procurement proceeding until satisfied that sufficient funds to meet the obligations of the  resulting contract are reflected in its approved budget estimates. The County  Executi ve is also exposed to loss of assets.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  527.   Irregular Supply and Delivery of Agricultural Products  527.1.   Irregular Procurement of Certified Seeds  The County Executive directly procured certified maize seeds from Kenya National  Trading   Corporation   in   the   year under review totalling   Kshs.44,249,700.   However,  Management did not provide evidence of reporting the direct procurement to the Public  Procurem ent Regulatory Authority within fourteen (14) days after notification of award of  contract contrary to Regulation 90(1)(c) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Regulations, 2020.  Further, the professional opinion by the head of supply chain management required a 5%  performance guarantee of the value of total bid price to be submitted before signing the  contract, however, there was no evidence to indicate that the supplier provided   the same.  In   addition,   one   of   the   requirements   under   technical   evaluation   was   a   dealer’s  authorization from Kenya Plant Inspectorate Services (KEPHIS). The license provided by  the supplier expired on 31 December, 2024, one and a half months before the clos ing  date of the bid on 14 February, 2025. This was contrary to   Section   18(5) of the   Seeds and  Plant Varieties Act, Revised 2012 which states   that no person shall sell seeds unless he holds a  valid license issued under the regulation. The supplier was there fore not legally allowed  to supply the maize seeds which risks the impact on food security or farmers livelihoods.  527.2.   Irregular Supply and Delivery of Two - Month - Old Piglets  The County Executive entered into a framework contract on 14 February, 2025 for su pply  and delivery of two (2) months old piglets at a total cost of Kshs.2,499,150.   However, the  County Executive issued three (3) local purchase orders on 23 March, 2025, however the  piglets were delivered on 4 April, 2025 to various Wards. This was twelve   (12) days from  issuance of the Local Purchase Orders (LPO’s) contrary to the contract agreement terms  that required the supplier to supply and deliver the piglets within seven (7) days from the  date of issuance of an LPO. Further, Paragraph 4.3 of the con tract required that  communication be done in writing in the event of any delays. There was no evidence that  a request for extension was lodged by the supplier.  Further, r equisition was raised from the user department, however, it was not supported  with a   sustainability report of the project prior to procuring of the piglets in order to  determine whether farmers had the capacity to rear the piglets. Management explained  that there was demand for breeding stock by the farmers during public participation for  development of the current County Integrated Development Program.

243  527.3.   Irregular Advance Payment for Supply and Delivery of Seedlings and  Cuttings  The County Executive entered into a contract with JKUAT Enterprises Limited on 5 May,  2025 for supply and   delivery of grafted has avocado, mangoes, oranges, pawpaw  seedlings and cassava cuttings at a cost of Kshs.11,400,000. Review of the procurement  file and payment voucher revealed that an advance payment was made on 27 May, 2025  equivalent   to   the   full   contr act   amount   with   no   evidence   of   delivery.   Management  explained that the supplier stored the goods and delivered them on a need basis upon  request from the County Executive. This was contrary to Article 5.2 of the contract signed  on 5 May, 2025 between JKUAT   Enterprise Ltd and the County Executive of Kiambu  which required that the contract price, less any tax that may be required to be remitted  through the County Executive shall be payable upon receipt of the seedlings, inspection  and issuance of an acceptanc e certificate by the inspection and acceptance committee  of the County Executive.  The County Executive was in breach of the contract terms and Regulation 98(2) of the  Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which states that  no ad vance payment shall be paid to suppliers of goods and services unless provided for  in the contractual terms and conditions contained in a valid contract signed between the  procuring entity and the supplier.  Further, there was no evidence that Management r eported to the Public Procurement  Regulatory Authority (PPRA)the direct procurement within fourteen (14) days after the  notification of the award of contracts exceeding Kshs.500,000 as prescribed in Regulation  90(1)(c) of the Public Procurement and Asset D isposal Regulations, 2020.  527.4.   Supply and Delivery of One Month Old Local Chicks Using an Expired  Contract  The County Executive entered into a framework contract on 24 October, 2023 for supply  and delivery of one (1) month old improved Local Chicks.   Review of the payment voucher  and   procurement   records   revealed   that   the   supplier   was   paid   an   amount   of  Kshs.2,400,000 for supply and delivery of the chicks based on a contract that had expired  on 24 October, 2024. The requisition from the user department w as approved on  21 March, 2025, for procurement of eight thousand (8000) one month old chicks through  the already expired framework contract. The County Executive paid for the goods using  an expired contract.  527.5.   Non - Rotation of Suppliers und er Framework Contracting  During the year under review, the County Executive entered into a framework contract  with four (4) suppliers for supply and delivery of two - months old piglets for two (2) years.  However, review of payment documents provided by the   Department for Agriculture  amounting to Kshs.6,038,650 for supply and delivery of the piglets revealed the County  Executive awarded the suppliers an order amounting to Kshs.3,901,350 which translates  to 64% of the total expenditure, while one supplier in   the framework contract was not  engaged in any supply orders as at the time of audit. This was contrary to Regulation

244  91(5) of Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 that requires the  Accounting Officer to ensure a fair and equitable rotati on amongst the persons on the list  under Sections 57, 71 and 106 of the Act and the Regulations.  527.6.   Irregular Direct Procurement for Supply of Fertilizer  Review of payment records revealed that an amount of Kshs.100,000,000 was paid to  National Cereals a nd Produce Board through five (5) payments vouchers amount of  Kshs.20,000,000   dated   23   October,   2024,   amount   of   Kshs.20,000,000   dated  18 December, 2024, amount of Kshs.20,000,000 dated 17 February, 2025, amount of  Kshs.20,000,000 an d Kshs.20,000,000 dated 5 May, 2025 respectively for supply of  fertilizer. However, review of the procurement records revealed that the Accounting  Officer did not issue tender documents to the supplier as a basis of negotiation, ad hoc  evaluation committee   minutes for evaluation of the tender and recommendation and  contract agreement for the supply of fertilizers were not provided for audit.  Further, delivery and receipt of eight thousand (8,000) bags of fertilizer was done on 8  May, 2025 while payment was   made on 29 April, 2025 without contract document to justify  advance payment. This was contrary to Section 146 of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015 which requires that no works, goods or services contract shall be paid  for before they are   executed or delivered and accepted by the Accounting Officer   of a  procuring   entity   except   where   so   specified   in   the   tender documents   and   contract  agreement. Such an advance payment shall not be paid before the contract is signed.  In the circumstances, le gality and value for money for the above projects could not be  confirmed and Management was in breach of the law.  528.   Irregularities in Use of Goods and Services  528.1.   Irregular   Procurement   for   Printing,   Advertisement   and   Information  Supplies  Review   of   procurement   processes   and   payment   records   revealed   the   following  anomalies;  (i)   The County Executive procured assorted accountable documents from the  Government Printer at a total amount of Kshs.875,162.   However, review of  records revealed that the procured d ocuments were not supported with delivery  notes   or   taken   on   charge   through   S.13   forms.   Further,   inspection   and  acceptance certificates were not provided to confirm the   items’ suitability and  conformity.  (ii)   The County Executive procured services for printing   and branding of billboards  for waiver on land rates from two (2) firms at a total cost of Kshs.8,600,889. The  billboards were to be erected in the twelve (12) Kiambu Sub - Counties. However,  review of the documents revealed that the contracts between the sup pliers and  the County Executive did not include the dates of contract expiry or completion  or how long the billboards were to remain displayed. Further, the reports of the  inspection and acceptance committee provided did not provide proof of work  done by b oth firms. In addition, the County Executive procured services for

245  printing and branding of billboards for change of USSD codes from two (2) firms  at a total cost of Kshs.5,733,926, however, Management did not provide proof  of work done by both companies.  (iii)   The County Executive procured advertising, awareness and publicity services  at total cost of Kshs.16,915,530 from various media entities. However, review  of the procurement records revealed that the procurement processes were not  initiated through user re quisitions and the user needs of the procured services  was   not   assessed.   This   was   contrary   to   Regulation   71(1)   of   the   Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which states that needs of  the user department shall include the procurement proce ss through requisition  as per the approved procurement plan.  528.2.   Irregular Procurement of Supply and Delivery of Assorted Items  Review of payment voucher for supply and delivery of assorted items amounting to  Kshs.1,081,200 revealed that two (2) local purc hase orders were issued on 5 August,  2024. However, the following anomalies were observed;  (i)   The County Executive issued Local Purchase Orders on 5 August, 2024 with  validity period of thirty (30) days while the goods were delivered by the supplier  on 12 S eptember, 2024 which was thirty - six (36) days after local purchase order  was issued contrary to Section 52(1) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which directs that a local purchase  order or local service order shall be   valid for a period of thirty days from the date  of issue.  (ii)   There was no evidence of regret letters sent to unresponsive bidders citing  reasons   for not being awarded.  (iii)   The professional opinion stated that the tender was advertised in the Public  Procurement Information Portal (PPIP) on 8 May, 2024 and opened on 13 May,  2024. This period did not meet the minimum period of seven (7) days prescribed  in Section 132(3) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.  528.3.   Direct Procurement Using Im prest  Review of sampled payment vouchers in respect of hospitality supplies and services  expenditure   revealed   that   Management   issued   standing   imprests   totalling  Kshs.1,063,555 to officers in various departments for procurement of toners and printing  mate rials.  Further, review of surrender documents revealed that the imprest holders did not maintain  detailed memorandum cash book and the receipts were not supported with electronic tax  register receipts. This was contrary to Regulation 93(2) of the Public   Procurement and  Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires a ny procurement under paragraph (1)  to be supported by the original Kenya Revenue Authority Electronic Tax Receipt (KRA  ETR Receipt) duly signed by the person undertaking the low value procure ment of goods,  works or services.

246  528.4.   Irregular Claims under Domestic Travel and Subsistence  Review of payment records and surrender vouchers provided for audit revealed that the  County Executive staff undertook activities through daily subsistence allowances totalling  Kshs.3,997,800   while   away   from   their   duty   stations   which   were   later   claimed   for  reimbursements. However, the claim forms were not supported with prior approvals or  authority for staff to incur the expenses and to be reimbursed later, attendance registers  and programme or itinerary for the conferences attended. This was contrary to Re gulation  93(4) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which  requires that before issuing temporary imprests, the Accounting Officer shall ensure that  the main objective of the journey cannot be achieved by other cheaper mea ns and that  adequate funds are available against the relevant items of expenditure to meet the  proposed expenditure.  528.5.   Irregular   Payment of Overtime Allowance  Review of surrender vouchers revealed that overtime allowance totalling Kshs.2,910,700  was paid to drivers and other staff. However, the following anomalies were identified;  (i)   Requests for overtime and approvals for drivers by the Head of Department was  no t provided for audit.  (ii)   There were no records of the exact overtime hours covered by each driver.  (iii)   Payments were not supported with daily duty roasters or approved timesheets  indicating time in and out for the drivers. In addition, the nature of overtime wo rk  being paid for was not indicated. This was contrary to Section 149(1) of the  Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which requires an Accounting Officer for  a County Government entity to be accountable for ensuring that the resources  of the entity for whic h he or she is the Accounting Officer are used in a way that  is lawful and authorized, effective, efficient, economical and transparent.  528.6.   Irregular Cash Purchases of Airtime  Review   of surrender vouchers provided for audit revealed that the County   Executive  incurred an expenditure of Kshs.3,405,000 on purchase of airtime and data bundles for  various departments. However, the purchases were not supported with electronic tax  register receipts from the vendors, policy guiding provision of airtime and p ayment rate  per job group. Further, the airtime purchased exceeded the threshold for cash purchases  on low value procurement set at a maximum of Kshs.50,000. This was contrary to Section  107(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which s tates that a  procuring entity may use a low - value procurement procedure if the entity is procuring low -  value items which are not procured on a regular or frequent basis and are not covered in  framework agreement. The Second Schedule to the Regulations also   sets the maximum  level of expenditure under this method at Kshs.50,000 and Kshs.100,000 for goods and  services respectively per financial year.

247  528.7.   Payments of Stationeries and Tonners without Electronic Tax Invoices  Review of supplier’s invoices for suppl y of office stationeries and tonners totalling  Kshs.1,330,106   paid by the County Executive were not supported with electronic tax  invoices. This was contrary to Regulation 6(1) of Value Added Tax (Electronic Tax  Invoices) Regulations, 2020 which requires e ach sale to be recorded with the use of the  register and an electronic tax invoice is generated in respect of each sale.  528.8.   Irregular Supply and Delivery of Motor Vehicle Tyres  Review of payment vouchers in respect of supply and delivery of motor vehicle tyres at a  contract sum amounting to Kshs.2,980,000 and local purchase order revealed that the  u ser department requisition dated 20 August, 2024 was issued in respect of request   for  tyres for nine (9) vehicles. The records included tyres size 265/70R16 for five (5) vehicles  and size 245/70R16 for four (4) vehicles all totalling thirty - six (36) tyres. However, the  sixty - four (64) tyres were received for different sizes specificatio ns.  The procured items did not meet the requirements, number and specifications provided  in the user requisition. Further, preliminary evaluation criteria required provision of a valid  trading license/business permit. However, review of the bid document   revealed that the  awarded supplier’s single business permit had expired on 26   November, 2024 before the  opening of the tender on 19   December, 2024 and therefore should have been evaluated  as non - responsive at the preliminary stage. This was contrary to Reg ulation 30(a) of the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which stipulates that the  evaluation committee shall conduct the technical and financial evaluation of the tenders  in strict adherence to the compliance and evaluation criteria se t out in the tender  documents.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of law and the value for money could  not be confirmed.  529.   Irregular Payments of Subscriptions  Review of payment records revealed payments for intergovernmental contributions and  legal fees support to the Council of Governors totalling Kshs.3,000,000. However,  Management did not provide an explanation for the payments made to the Council, which  is a n independent entity. This was contrary to Section 37 of the Intergovernmental  Relations Act, 2012 which provides that operational expenses for the structures and  institutions established under the Act shall be provided from the annual estimates of the  rev enue and expenditures of the National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of law  530.   Irregular Procurement of Computers   Equipment and Furniture and   Fittings  Review of procurement and payment records revealed the following   anomalies;  (i)   Procurement records for supply and delivery of office stationeries, HP printers,  scanner and all in one desktop amount of Kshs.2,484,195 revealed that the

248  goods were delivered after the expiry of validity period for local purchase orders.  The r ecords indicated that the goods were delivered on 22 November, 2024 as  per two (2) delivery notes. This was more   than thirty   (30) days contrary to  Regulation   52   of   the Public Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which requires that a l ocal purchase order or local service  order shall be valid for a period of thirty days from the date of issue. Further, the  user requisition did not include estimated value and specifications for the  desktops, laptops and printers among other items to be pr ocured. The review  could not establish whether the items delivered met user department’s needs.  (ii)   Review of procurement records for supply and delivery of Governor’s protocol  security equipment at a cost of Kshs.2,077,560 revealed that the tender opening  m inutes were signed and dated 9 April, 2024. However, the minutes were not  supported with a tender register for the received quotations.  (iii)   Review of procurement records for supply and delivery of tonners at a total cost  of Kshs.2,960,505 revealed that the us er department requisitioned for items  which differed with what was delivered as highlighted below;  User Department  Requisition  Units  Required   Goods Delivered  Unit  Delivered  Hp Tonners (Black and  White) 59A  40pcs   Kyocera 1k53507,  1k53507m,   1k53507c,  1k53507k  30pcs  Hp Tonners (Black,  Magneta Cynan Yellow)  207A set  15 sets   Laser jet proM 404dn 59A   25sets  As a result, it was not possible to confirm whether the items delivered met the user’s  specifications and needs.  (iv)   Review of   payment vouchers in respect of supply and delivery of an audio - visual  and production equipment at a total cost of Kshs.16,493,494 revealed that,  according to IFMIS payment details, the contractor was paid an amount of  Kshs.9,000,000   while   the   payment   vouch er   reflected   an   amount   of  Kshs.16,493,494 resulting in an unexplained variance of Kshs.7,493,494. In  addition, the market survey report was not provided for audit contrary to  Regulation 33( 3 )(a)   of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations,  202 0 which requires the procurement function to carry out market surveys to  inform the placing of orders or adjudication by the relevant awarding authority.  (v)   The County Executive awarded a contract for development of an Integrated  Bursary   Management   System   (IBS)   meant   to   simplify   students’   bursary  applications at a contract sum of Kshs.2,958,000. However, the contract signed  did not clearly outline the obligati ons and responsibilities of both parties and

249  further, there was no evidence of a service level agreement between the  supplier and the County Executive as a measure for contract monitoring.  Further, the payment was not supported with any evidence of testing   or  commissioning of the system and inspection and acceptance by the inspection  and   acceptance   committee   to   confirm   that   the   system   met   the   user  requirements.  In addition, the supplier was paid in full on 2 September, 2024, however, as at the time of  aud it in July, 2025, the System was not in use. This was contrary to Section 149(1) of the  Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which requires an Accounting Officer to be  accountable to the County Assembly for ensuring that the resources of the entity for whic h  the officer is designated are used in a way that is lawful and authorized, effective, efficient,  economical and transparent .  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure could not be confirmed and  Management was in breach of the law.  531.   Irregular Splitting of Tender  The County Executive made seven (7) different requests for quotation for purchase of  computers, printers and other IT equipment from different suppliers, incurring expenditure  amounting to Kshs.19,184,784. However, review of   procurement files revealed that the  requests for quotations (RFQs) were issued within the same period for the same items,  at varying prices. Management did not explain why the items were not procured through  an open tender procurement method. Using severa l RFQs for similar items led the County  Executive to incur more costs as a result of varying prices of similar items from suppliers.  Therefore, the Management may have structured procurements for the purpose of  avoiding use of open tender procurement metho d. This was contrary to   Regulation 43(1)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which   directs that a  procuring entity shall not split or structure its contracts for the purpose of avoiding the use  of a procurement procedure as provi ded for under Section 54(1) of the Act except where  unbundling of categories is allowed under preference and reservation schemes in the Act  and Regulation 154.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.19,184,784 could not  be confir med and Management was in breach of the law.  532.   Legal Costs  532.1.   Unsupported Legal Payables  (i)   Review of legal records revealed that the County Executive reported an amount  of Kshs.9,818,587 as litigation services fee due to an Advocate. However, the  payment voucher provided for audit was not examined and authorized by the  Accounting Officer. Furthe r, the supporting document attached to the voucher  related to payment voucher of an amount of Kshs.14,016,000 in respect of legal  services fee due to the Advocates that was stamped paid on 30 June, 2021 and  all the supporting documents including the invoic es and Court rulings and

250  petitions were all stamped paid. In addition, the amount was not traced in the  schedule of accounts payables.  (ii)   Review of legal records revealed that the County Executive reported an amount  of Kshs.13,531,472 as legal services fee d ue to another Advocate for litigating  Court case number Kiambu HCC No 18 of 2019   -   Export Consolidated Services  Vs Kiambu County Executive. However, the amount was not disclosed in the list  of outstanding legal fee provided by the Office of the County Atto rney.  (iii)   Review of legal records revealed that the County Executive reported an amount  of Kshs.7,788,259 as legal services fee due to an additional Advocate for ELRC  Nairobi Case number 1068 of 2015.   However, this amount was not disclosed  in the list of ou tstanding legal fee provided by the Office of the County Attorney.  Further, according to the status of the case, it was noted that on 30 October,  2024 the file was marked closed after the claimant’s counsel confirmed to the  Court that the respondent had pa id up the decretal amount. In addition, the  payment voucher was not examined, approved by AIE holder and authorized by  the Accounting Officer.  (iv)   An amount of Kshs.19,720,000 in respect of legal fees was paid in respect of  case number Kiambu HCJR 007 of 2025   Sauti Business Community vs County  Executive of Kiambu and 4 others and HCCHR PET 031 of 2025 & 18 others vs  County Executive. The County Executive engaged the services of external  advocates to represent the County Executive in the two legal matters despi te  the County Executive having a fully established Office of the County Attorney  tasked with representing it in Court or in any legal proceedings.  (v)   Further, no evidence of approval by the County Executive Committee to engage  external advocates was provide d for audit contrary to Section 16(1) of the Office  of the County Attorney Act, 2020 which requires a department or public entity  established within a County Executive not to engage the services of a consultant  or render any legal services relating to the   functions of the County Attorney  without the approval of the County Executive Committee.  532.2.   Avoidable Legal Expenses  Review of records from the County Executive Legal Department revealed that an amount  of Kshs.403,437,444 was payables in respect of conte mpt of Court orders and failure to  settle decretal sum on time leading to accrued interest payable to the advocates. The  expenditure could have been avoided if the County Executive had honoured the claims  in respect of the Court rulings.  In the circumstan ces, value for money on expenditure amounting to. Kshs.403,437,444,  could not be confirmed.

251  533.   Non - Compliance with the Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy Order,  2023  During the year under review, the County Executive planned to procure goods, work and  services as per the procurement plan. However, review of procurement contracts of  goods, works and services revealed that Local Purchase Orders (LPOs) and Local  Service O rders (LSOs) issued after 1 September, 2024 did not include the mandatory  0.03% Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy as a separate line item and therefore  the levy was not deducted for all contract awards, contrary to Section 3(1) of the Public  Procur ement Capacity Building Levy Order, 2023,   which requires that there shall be paid  a levy by a supplier on all procurement contracts signed between the supplier and a  procuring entity, at the rate of point zero three per centum (0.03%) of the value of the  s igned contract, exclusive of applicable taxes.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the levy orders.  534.   Failure to Report Termination of Procurement Proceedings  Review   of   procurement   files   revealed   that   the   Accounting   Officer   terminated   the  procurement   proceedings   of   eight   (8)   tenders   namely   tender   number  CGK/FWA/001/2024/2025 to CGK/FWA/008/2024/2025 due to lack of feasibility study.  However, the termination of the procurement proceedings was not reported to the Public  Procurement Regulator y Authority within 14 days stating the reason for termination  contrary to Section 63(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which  state   that   an   accounting   officer   who   terminates   procurement   or   asset   disposal  proceedings shall give the Au thority a written report on the termination within fourteen  days.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  535.   Accounts Payables  535.1.   Ineligible Pending Bills  Review of payables records revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   Review of   payment voucher for networking and installation of CCTVs for the  new Kiambu Sub - County Offices at Red Nova at a total cost of Kshs.15,593,717  revealed that the payment voucher was not supported with the supplier invoice,  delivery notes for the items deliv ered and requisite procurement documents  which include   tender opening minutes and register, tender evaluation committee  reports, appointment letters for the opening, tender evaluation and inspection  and acceptance committee and evidence of regret letters s ent to unsuccessful  bidders.   This was contrary to Section 44(2)(d) of the Public Procurement and  Assets Disposal Act,   2015 which   stipulates that an accounting officer of a public  entity shall ensure that proper documentation of procurement proceedings and  safe custody of all procurement records.  (ii)   The Payables balance of Kshs.14,574,056 in respect of payables for conversion  of meeting hall to banking hall was not supported with requisite procurement

252  documents including tender opening minutes and register, te nder evaluation  committee reports, appointment letters for the opening, tender evaluation and  inspection and acceptance committee and evidence of regret letters sent to  unsuccessful bidders.  (iii)   Review of payables balance of Kshs.10,783,000 in respect of pay ables for  supply and delivery of uji flour (pure wimbi porridge) revealed that the notification  of award to the supplier was issued on 24 June, 2020 and the contract entered  into on the same day. This was contrary to Section 135(3) of the Public  Procuremen t and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which provides for fourteen (14)  days window period after notification of award. Further, the goods were received  under delivery notes dated 1 and 2 January, 2020 while the contract was signed  on 24 June, 2020.   In addition,   the payment voucher was not supported with  requisite procurement documents which includes tender opening minutes and  register,   tender   evaluation   committee   reports,   appointment   letters   for   the  opening, tender evaluation and inspection and acceptance committ ee and  evidence of regret letters sent to unsuccessful bidders.  (iv)   Review of payables balance   of Kshs .8,150,000 for supply and delivery of one  Ford Everest with a capacity of 2.2lXTL 4*4 revealed that the payment voucher  was   not   supported   with   requisition   fr om   the   user   department   giving   the  specification   of   the   required   vehicle,   delivery   note   and   inspection   and  acceptance reports.  (v)   Review of payment voucher and supporting documents for an amount of  Kshs.6,829,005 in respect of administrative costs for revenu e collected between  1 January, 2020 to 31 March, 2020 revealed that the County Executive, a  contractor   and   a   local   commercial   bank   entered   into   a   contract   on  7 November, 2014 for two (2) years with an expiry date of 6 November, 2017.  Therefore,   the   administrative   costs   for   revenue   collected   between  1 January, 2020 to   31 March, 2020 was irregular since the contract period had  lapsed.  (vi)   Review of payment voucher for an amount of Kshs.5,510,000 for provision of  Office 365 and official emails revealed that the County Executive entered into a  contract with a company for provision of Microsoft 365 on 15 June, 2016 for a  period of fifteen (1 5) weeks at a contract price of Kshs.34,800,000. However, on  1 November, 2016 an addendum to the contract was entered into stating that  due to the nature of implementation of the service, the contract be restructured  and the payments to be aligned to the p rovision of the service level agreement  signed and be part of the contract. The addendum varied the contract price to  Kshs.24,000,000 and service level agreement expiry period to two (2) years.  This variation was irregular since it was contrary to Section   139(3) of Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which states that no contract price  shall be varied within twelve (12) months from the date of the signing of the  contract. Further, the contract indicated that payment would be made upon  certificat ion by the inspection and acceptance committee. However, there were  no evidence of inspection and acceptance committee reports.

253  (vii)   Review of payables balance of Kshs.4,636,950 in respect of construction of  Karinde to Njiku Access Road in Kikuyu Sub - County re vealed that the payment  voucher was not examined or signed by the AIE holder or authorized by the  Accounting Officer. Further, the professional opinion dated 11 December, 2020  was not approved by the Accounting Officer. In addition, appointment letters of  inspection and acceptance committee were not provided for audit.  (viii)   Review of payables balance of Kshs.180,000,000 due to a contractor for  administrative costs of 7% for revenue collected revealed that the payment  vouchers were not supported with requisite p rocurement documents which  include tender opening minutes and register, tender evaluation committee  reports, letters appointing opening, evaluation and inspection and acceptance  committees and evidence of regret letters sent to the unsuccessful bidders. In  addition, the signed contract was not provided for audit.  535.2.   Accumulation of Pending Accounts Payables  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.7,619,065,692. The balance includes  an amount of Kshs.3,887,624,177 representing 51% of the total trade payables t hat was  outstanding for more than ten (10) years and which did not form a first charge on the  County Revenue Fund. This was contrary to Regulation 41(2) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires debt service  pay ments to be a first charge on the County Revenue Fund and that the Accounting  Officer shall ensure this is done to the extent possible that the County Executive does not  default on debt obligations.  The County Executive risks incurring additional losses   in form of interest and penalties  arising from continued delay in the settlement of the bills. In addition, failure to settle bills  during the year in which they relate to distorts the financial statements and adversely  affects the budgetary provisions for   the subsequent year. Further, the payment plans,  payables reports and detailed ageing analysis reports were not provided for audit.  535.3.   Long Outstanding Staff Payables  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial state ments  reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.7,619,065,692. Review of payables  listing provided for audit revealed that a balance of Kshs.99,419,754 related to domestic  and subsistence allowances and other allowances due to County staff which fu rther  included   payables   totalling   Kshs.12,616,451   relating   to   domestic   and   subsistence  allowances and other allowances that were outstanding for more than a year and did not  form first charge. This was contrary to Regulation 93(4)(d) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which stipulates that before  issuing temporary imprests, the Accounting Officer shall ensure that adequate funds are  available against the relevant items of expenditure to meet the proposed expenditure.

254  In   addition,   review   of   the   staff   payables   list   revealed   that   payables   balance   of  Kshs.72,553,390 lacked staff details such as staff personal numbers, job group, date  when the request was approved and reference number.  535.4.   Non - Compliance with Debt Fiscal Respo nsibility Principles on Payables  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of   Kshs.7,619,065,692 .   The balance represents  43% of the total receipts of Kshs. 17,916,386,160 which is   23% over and above the  maximum allowed limit. This was contrary to Regulation 25(1)(d) of Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires that   the County  public debt shall never exceed twenty (20%) percent of the County Government total  revenue at any one time. In addition, the County Executive did not have a debt  management policy.  535.5.   Failure to Circularize Accounts Payables  The statement of f inancial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of   Kshs.7,619,065,692. However, the County  Executive   did   not   undertake   supplier   circularization   and   reconciliation   exercise   as  directed   by   T he   National   Treasury.   In   the   absence   of   supplier   confirmations,  reconciliations, and supporting documentation, the opening and closing balances could  not be confirmed.  In   the   circumstances,   the   regularity   of   the   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs.7,619,065,692 could not be confirmed and the Management was in breach of the  law.  536.   Lack of an Annual Assets Disposal Plan  The County Executive did not prepare an annual disposal plan for items declared  obsolete. Further, the Accounting Officer did no t establish a disposal committee. This was  contrary to Regulation 176(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations,  2020 which requires an Accounting Officer of a procuring entity to ensure that an annual  assets disposal plan is prepared of   items declared as unserviceable or obsolete stores,  asset or equipment as set out under Section 53(4) of the Act.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  537.   Irregular   Hire   of   Heavy   Equipment,   Plant   and   Machinery   at   Kang’oki  Dumpsite  An expenditure of Kshs.4,500,000 was incurred in respect of provision of clearing of  garbage at tipping sites at Kang’oki dump site. However, the following anomalies were  noted:  (i)   Records of trips provided for audit revealed that the billing wa s based on daily  hour readings of the machines for sixty - three (63) days with daily shifts of eight  hours each. From the records or   trips made   it was established that these

255  machines worked non - stop per shift, casting doubt on the validity of the records,  g iven that there were no downtimes recorded for   fueling   or even the drivers  taking a break at any point.  (ii)   There was no evidence of needs assessment done at the Kang’oki Dumpsite to  determine   the   number   of   heavy   machineries   needed   daily   at   the   site   to  supple ment those already running and owned by the County Executive. This  would inform the additional number of heavy equipment required at any point in  order to meet the existing gap.   In addition, there was no record of quantity of  garbage dumped daily to justif y the   need for the hire of the machines.  (iii)   There was no corroborative evidence provided to indicate that the machines  worked for the hours paid. The start time and finish time measurement and  records were susceptible to manipulation. Therefore, the Cou nty Executive  should have included records of fuel consumption per day per machine.  (iv)   The supporting schedule and time sheet lacked crucial information such as  registration number for the plant/machinery equipment, clock in time, odometer  reading, fuel   consumed and any downtime duration casting doubt on the  authenticity of the time sheets provided.  (v)   Call order for tender number KCG/WEENR/005/2019/2020(29 - 07) required the  supplier   to   provide   evidence   of   plant,   machinery,   equipment   registration  numbers and   credentials of the supervisor of the fleet and plant operator.  However, there was no evidence that the documents were prepared.  This was   contrary to Regulation   100 of   the   Public Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires Ac counting Officers to maintain such  books and registers as may be necessary for the proper maintenance and production of  the accounts of the Vote for which he or she is responsible.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  538.   Irregular Suppl y and Delivery of Integrated Solar Street Lighting  The County Executive awarded a contract for supply and delivery of four thousand (4000)  integrated solar street lighting under negotiation number 1465808 - 2023 - 2024 on 17   April,  2024 at a contract price o f Kshs.337,650,253. However, review of the procurement  records provided revealed that Part K of the price schedule indicated that the supplier  should allow for prior inspection before and during manufacturing and loading at a cost of  Kshs.2,700,000. Howeve r, the prior inspection was not conducted.  According to two (2) S11 dated 19 August, 2024, four thousand (4000) solar lamps and  brackets were issued from the stores. However, review of integrated solar street lighting  (ISSL) issuance and distribution lis t to different wards in the County revealed that only  three thousand, eight hundred and sixty (3860) integrated solar street lighting were issued  and distributed to different wards resulting to one hundred and forty (140) street lighting  valued at Kshs.8,6 83,616 that were unaccounted for. This was contrary to Section 149(1)  of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which requires an Accounting Officer for a

256  County Government entity to be accountable to the County Assembly for ensuring that  the resources of   the entity for which the Officer is designated are used in a way that is  lawful authorised, effective, efficient, economical and transparent. Further, inspection and  acceptance certificate did not specify the serial numbers of the integrated street lighti ng  lamps. Therefore, it was not possible to track the items received.  In the circumstances, the regularity and value for money on the expenditure could not be  confirmed.  539.   Irregular Installation, Testing and Commissioning of Solar Street Lighting  The County Executive awarded a contract for installation, testing and   commissioning of  three thousand, six hundred and eighty five (3,685) solar street lighting in sixty (60) wards  bundled into two lots as follows; installation, testing and commissioning of one thousand,  seven hundred and eighty (1,780)   solar street lightin g in twenty - nine (29) wards at a  contract price of Kshs.95,016,586 and installation testing and commissioning of one  thousand nine hundred and five (1,905) solar street lighting in Thirty - one (31) wards at a  contract price of Kshs.103,361,978. However, rev iew of the procurement file revealed the  following anomalies;  (i)   Review of integrated solar street lighting (ISSL) issuance and distribution list to  different Wards in the County revealed that three thousand, eight hundred and  sixty (3,860) integrated solar   street lighting were issued and distributed to  different wards. However, the supplier was awarded a contract to install three  thousand, six hundred and eighty - five (3,685) solar street lighting resulting in an  unexplained variance of one hundred and sevent y - five (175) ISSL valued at  Kshs.10,854,520.  (ii)   Review of the procurement files for installation, testing and commissioning of  three thousand, six hundred and eighty - five (3,685) solar street lighting in sixty  (60) wards at a contract price totalling Kshs.19 8,378,564 revealed that the price  schedule included various concrete poles valued at a total of Kshs.119,831,594.  However, there was no inspection and acceptance report on the delivery of the  poles. It was also not clear why the concrete poles were include d in what  seemed to be a labour - based contract.  (iii)   The price schedule included HP laptops, desktops core   i7 and printers totalling  Kshs.1,233,600. However, the counter receipt voucher and inspection and  acceptance   certificate did   not   indicate   the serial numb ers of   the   devices  delivered. Therefore, it was not possible to confirm whether the specification of  items procured met the requisition requirements.  This was contrary to Section 149(1) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which  requires an Account ing Officer for a County Government entity to be accountable to the  County Assembly for ensuring that the resources of the entity for which the Officer is  designated are used in a way that is lawful authorised, effective, efficient, economical and  transpar ent.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

257  540.   Irregular Procurement of Culverts  The County Executive awarded a contract for supply and delivery of assorted culverts  and   other   materials   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.116,083,008.   However,   review   of  procurement   records revealed that one of the technical criteria required the bidders to  demonstrate profitability of at least Kshs.20,000,000 per year. However, the winning  bidder did not attach the statement of financi al performance to demonstrate profitability.  Instead,   the bid document contained statement of financial position and statement of cash  flows only and was awarded full marks. The evaluation was not conducted in strict  adherence to the compliance and evaluat ion criteria set out in the tender documents.  Further, the form of tender provided in the bid document for the successful bidder did not  indicate the total tender sum, representing the sum of all individual bid items, instead,  summaries of the cost of cul verts for each ward was indicated.   Therefore, it was not  possible to confirm the total price of tender read out during tender opening as per the  bidder’s application. This was contrary to Section 78(6) of the Public Procurement and  Asset Disposal Act, 201 5 which states that as each tender is opened, the following shall  be read loud and recorded in a document to be called the tender opening register; (a) the  name of the person submitting the tender; (b) the total price, where applicable including  any modifi cations or discounts received before the deadline for submitting tenders except  as may be prescribed; and (c) if applicable, what has been given as tender security.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  541.   Low Absorption of Development   Expenditure  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects acquisition of assets  actual amount of Kshs.3,139,551,144 which reflects actual development expenditure of  18% of the total expenditure for the year. This was contrary to   Regulation 25(1)(g) of the  Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires  the County Executive to spend at least 30% of the actual expenditure on development  projects.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the   law.  542.
