Preparedness for Transition to Accrual Basis of Accounting  Management did not appoint an Asset Management Officer to support the transition to  accrual   accounting   for   assets   as   provided   for   in   The   National   Treasury   Circular  No.03/2025 of 14 April, 20 25.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of The National Treasury’s Circular.

258  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  543.   Failure to Establish a Functional Audit Committee  The County Executive appointed four (4) Audit Committee Members in August, 2021  through Kenya Gazette notice for a three - year term which ended in the month of   August,  2024. However, the County Executive did not appoint new members of the Audit  Committee . Further, the audit committee held only one (1) meeting in August, 2024 during  the   year   under   review   and   did   not   prepare   an   annual   report   on   independence,  performance and competence of the internal audit unit. This was contrary to Regulation  159(2) of the   Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015  which stipulates that   each   year the Audit Committee shall carry out annual review of the  independence, performance and competency of the internal audit unit and comment on  their effectivenes s in the annual report.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the   internal controls, governance and risk  management systems at the County Executive could not be confirmed.  544.   Weakness in Internal Audit Function  Review of internal audit records provide d for audit revealed that whereas the Internal  Audit reports and workplan were provided for audit, it was noted that they were all in draft  status as there was no audit committee to approve them for further action. Further, there  was no evidence to confirm   that recommendations made by the Internal Audit were  implemented by the respective departments. In addition, mechanism for follow up of  implementation of recommendations was not put in place. Similarly, the Department  lacked   operational and   functional   ind ependence   due   to   lack   of   a   functional   Audit  Committee.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the   internal control systems in the County  Executive could not be confirmed.  545.   Lack of a Risk Management Policy  The County Executive did not have a Risk Man agement Policy in place to provide a  framework of addressing risks including risk identification, assessment, prevention and  mitigation to contingency planning and give clarity on who is responsible for identifying,  assessing and managing specific risks.   I n the absence of a Risk Management Policy, it  was not possible to confirm how Management identified and controlled threats and  vulnerabilities that could negatively impact its operations.  In the circumstances, effectiveness of the   internal   controls and risk management systems  could not be confirmed.

259  546.   Lack of Approved Information and Communication Technology Policy and  Steering Committee  The County Executive did not have an approved ICT Policy to provide a f ramework for  effective implementation of ICT, including standards, guidelines, and procedures.   In  addition,   there was no functional Information Technology Steering Committee in place to  provide strategic guidance and oversight. This was contrary to Regulat ion 110 of Public  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires the  Accounting Officer for a County Government entity to institute appropriate access controls  needed to minimize breaches of information confidentiality, data integ rity and loss of  business continuity. This represents a significant gap in ICT governance and poses risks  to strategic alignment, compliance and operational effectiveness.  In the circumstances, effectiveness of the internal controls on ICT management coul d not  be confirmed.  547.   Failure to Implement E - Procurement System  Review of County Executive Procurement system revealed that contracts and tenders  awarded to the various suppliers were not processed through the e - procurement. All  ongoing contracts entered in to, and to which finalization of expected works, supplies or  services pending completion and final payment were not in the e - procurement system  contrary to Executive order No. 6 of 2016 and No. 2 of 2018.  In the circumstances, transparent and   efficient management of procurement process  could not be confirmed.  548.   Discrepanc ies   in Insurance   and Legal   Register s  Review of the certificates of insurance and the motor vehicle register provided during the  audit revealed discrepancies in the record of in sured motor vehicles. Specifically, thirty -  seven (37) motor vehicles valued at Kshs.223,747,859 were not insured but were not  listed in the County Motor Vehicle Register.  Further, review of the register of legal cases provided for audit revealed that five hundred  and twenty - three (523) cases lacked updated status while some had remained open for  more than ten (10) years. Therefore, it was not possible to confirm the financi al implication  of the cases. The register was also found incomplete as some cases lacked critical  information, such as claim amount, case number, advocate involved, and other parties to  the case.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal contro ls on management of legal  matters could not be confirmed.  549.   Weaknesses in Inventory Management  Physical inspection and review of controls and documentation in management of stores  revealed that the County Executive did not have an inventory management and control  software to assist in meeting the objectives of sound supply chain management. Instead,

260  manual records were maintained of goods received and issued to the user department.  Further, the County Executive had two (2) motor cycles and two (2) car washing machines  that had been in the store for more than two (2 ) years and had not been put to use.   In  addition, physical inspection of the Headquarter Offices revealed that ninety - one ( 91)  waste bins   and window glass panes were left exposed to direct sunlight resulting to  material degradation. These items could not be traced in the stock take reports p rovided.  Physical inspection of medical stores revealed that several medical equipment   were  defective   and had been held for repair for unspecified duration. The items were not traced  in the repair management system, while the equipment repair requisition   form, medical  equipment repair register and defective equipment transfer records were not provided for  audit. Further,   t he medical store had obsolete items which included twelve (12) 13kg gas  cylinders that had been in the store for more than two (2) years   and the items could not  be accounted for as per stock take reports.  In addition, the County Executive had one (1) motor cycle that had been kept in the store  since December, 2024 and had not been put into use. However, the motor cycle was not  listed in t he County Executive’s fleet records.   Similarly, the Central Medical Store located  within Thika Level 5 Hospital, revealed that the storage facility had a leaking roof,  exposing medical equipment and supplies to potential damage and resulting in non -  complia nce with the Public Health Act on proper medical storage, dry, clean and secure  environment.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls in management of stores could  not be confirmed.  550.   Failure to Close Dormant Bank Accounts  Review of the list of bank accounts operated by the County Executive during the year  revealed two hundred and eighty - eight (288) bank accounts out of which five (5) bank  accounts listed below remained dormant;  Account Name   Type   Purpose  Balance  (Kshs)  Lari Level 4   Recurrent   NHIF Revenue   1  Thika Level 5   Recurrent   Grant   1  Thika Level 5   Recurrent   Grant   1  Kiambu County UNICEF Account   Recurrent   UNICEF   Account  Operation  1  Veterinary Services Development Fund   Recurrent   Operations   0  In the   circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on cash management could  not be confirmed.

261  551.   Weaknesses of Assets Management  551.1.   Lack of Fuel Management Policy  Review of payment vouchers and support documents for fuel and lubricants revealed that  there was no policy guiding on requisition of fuel, approval, top up period and top up  quantities for each card. Further, requisition of cards for newly acquired motor v ehicles  and appointment of the card holders was not provided for audit. In the absence of Fuel  Management Policy, the effectiveness of internal controls on fuel management could not  be confirmed. This was contrary to Regulation 158 of the Public Finance Ma nagement  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires the Accounting Officer to  ensure that the County Government entity develops risk management strategies, which  include fraud prevention mechanism, a system of risk management and internal contro ls  that builds robust business operations.  551.2.   Unserviceable Motor Vehicles  Analysis of the County Executive’s assets register revealed that the County Executive  had in its possession, two hundred and fifteen (215) unserviceable motor vehicles.  However, ther e was no evidence to indicate that Management had initiated their disposal.  This was contrary to Section 163(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act,  2015 which requires an Accounting Officer to establish a disposal committee as and when  prescr ibed for the purpose of disposal of unserviceable, obsolete, obsolescent, or surplus  stores, equipment or assets.  551.3.   Failure to Insure County Buildings  The County Executive incurred medical and motor vehicle insurance costs amounting to  Kshs.339,009,879 i n the year under review. However, review of insurance details as at  May, 2025 revealed that the County Executive buildings did not have insurance cover to  mitigate against losses in case of a disaster contrary to Section 79(2)(c) of the Public  Finance Mana gement Act, 2012 which requires a public officer within his area of  responsibility to ensure that adequate arrangements are made for the proper use,  custody, safeguarding and maintenance of public property including application of best  office to prevent an y damage from being done to the financial interest of the County  Executive.  Failure to secure insurance covers for County Executive buildings exposed the County  Executive to potential losses and undermines the financial protection measures intended  by the   legislation.  551.4.   Inadequate Insurance Coverage of County Executive Assets  During the year under review, the County Executive paid an amount of   Kshs.132,877,237  to   an insurance company   for the provision of comprehensive insurance cover for its fleet  of motor vehicles and motorcycles. However, review of the insurance documents provided  for audit which include insurance certificates, policy documents, and the County fleet  register reveale d that n inety - nine (99) motor vehicles   and ten ( 10) motorcycles   belonging

262  to the County Executive were not insured .   Further, t wenty - four (24) generators   distributed  across various sub - county offices and health facilities were not covered by any insurance  p olicy .   In addition,   o ne hundred and forty - nine (149) accident vehicles , grounded at  various locations, remain uninsured.  In addition, seventeen (17) vehicles were held in external garages, and there was no  documentation to show an existing salvage or paym ent plan for their recovery or repair  by the insurer. This was contrary to Section 153(1)(b) of the Public Finance Management  Act, 2012 which requires the Accounting Officer for a County Government entity to  manage these assets in such a way as to ensure t hat the County Government entity  achieves value for money in acquiring, using or disposing of those assets.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of risk management and internal controls put in  place to safeguard assets could not be confirmed.

264  COUNTY EXECUTIVE   OF TURKANA   –   NO.23  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  552.   Inaccuracies in Comparative Balances  The   statement   of   financial position   reflects   comparative   trade   and   other payables  (pending bills) of Nil balance. However, review of the prior year audited financial  statements revealed pending bills balance of Kshs.801,687,224. The resultant variance  was   not explained.  Further, the opening statement of financial position is not balanced as it reflects net assets  of Kshs.896,700,712 against accumulated surplus balance of Kshs.244,112,385 resulting  in an unexplained variance of Kshs.652,588,327.  In the ci rcumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the opening Nil balance of trade  and other payables and net assets balance of Kshs.896,700,712 could not be confirmed.  553.   Unsupported Property, Plant and Equipment Balance  The statement of financial position and   as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements  reflect property, plant and equipment balance of Kshs.2,663,174,395. Included in this  amount are additions in respect of land amount of Kshs.9,550,000, buildings amount of  Kshs.7,326,334   and   water   infras tructure   of   Kshs. 217,006,374   all   totalling  Kshs.233,882,708 .   However,   title   deeds   for   land   purchased,   interim   certificates,  completion certificates and handover certificates were not provided to support the  capitalization of assets in relation to land, bui ldings and water infrastructure.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, existence, rights and obligations and completeness  of property, plant and equipment balance of Kshs. 233,882,708   could not be confirmed.  554.   Unsupported Legal Fees Expenses  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services expenses  amount of Kshs.5,975,887,689 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. The  amount includes specialized materials and services amount of Kshs.3,531,377,240 out  of   which an amount of Kshs.22,844,620 was incurred in respect of legal expenses.  However, Management did   not provide itemized fee notes and invoices to show how the  fees was computed and whether the charges were in line with Advocates Remuneration  Order.  Fu rther,   review of legal files and documents revealed that four (4) law firms were paid  without approval from the Executive Committee regarding outsourcing of legal services  as required under Section 16 of the Office of the County Attorney Act, 2020. In addi tion,  Management did not provide justification for outsourcing of costly legal services instead  of using inhouse legal personnel contrary to Section 5(b) of the County Attorney Act, 2020

265  which provides that a County Legal Counsel shall handle   matters without undue delay,  risk or unnecessary expense to the county government which may expose the County  Executive to costly damages and compensation claims.  In the circumstances, the occurrence, accuracy and completeness of legal expenses  amounting   to Kshs.22,844,620 could not be confirmed.  555.   Non - Disclosure of Contingent Liabilities  Review of   Note 43 to the financial statements reflects Nil balance in respect of contingent  liabilities. However, review of legal documents submitted for audit verificati on revealed  various pending legal cases yet to be determined. Non - disclosure of contingency liabilities  may lead to the County Executive facing sudden huge expenses or liabilities impacting  on its financial operations.  In the circumstances, the presentati on and disclosure could not be confirmed  556.   Unsupported Payment of Salary Arrears  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial  statements reflects employee costs totalling Kshs.5,659,171,913. Review of the payroll  recor ds for the year under review revealed that the County Executive paid salary arrears  amounting to Kshs.261,488,315 to one thousand, two hundred and fifty - two (1,252)  employees.   However,   no   documentary   evidence   such   as   approved   computation  schedules, authori zation by the relevant County Public Service Board, or communication  from the Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) was provided to support or justify  the payments.  In the circumstances, the regularity, accuracy and completeness of the employee cost s  amounting to Kshs.5,659,171,913 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  557.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and actual on comparable basis of Kshs. 15,758,953,939   and Kshs. 12,712,800,011  respectively   resulting   in   an   under - funding   amounting   to   Kshs. 3,046,153,928   or  approximately 19% of the budget. However, the County Executive spent an amount of  Kshs. 15,332,641,532 against actual receipts of Kshs.12,71 2,800,011   resulting in an over  expenditure amounting   to Kshs.2,619,841,520   or approximately 20% of the   actual  receipts.  The under - funding and over - expenditure affected the planned activities and may have  impacted negatively on service delivery to the pub lic.  My opinion is not modified in respect of these matters.

266  Other Matter  558.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the prior year audit report, several issues were raised under the Report on Financial  Statements, Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of Public Resources, and Effectiveness  of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance. Review of the status durin g audit  of the   County Executive   in 2024/2025 revealed that the nineteen (19) matters remained  unresolved as listed at the end of this report remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  Other Information  559.   There were no   material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  560.   Non -   Compliance with Law on Fiscal Responsibility Principles on   Wages  During   the year under review, the   County Executive’s total revenue   amounted   to  Kshs.12,712,800,011. Based on the revenue, the County Executive was expected to  spend a maximum of Kshs.4,449,480,004 or 35% of total revenue on employees ’   costs.  However, the actual expenditure during the year was Kshs.5,659,171,913 equivalent to  45% of total revenue   which was exceeded by an amount of Kshs.143,538,035.   The  overspending was contrary to Regulation 25 of the Public Finance Management (County  G overnments) Regulations, 2015 that caps personnel expenditures at thirty - five (35)  percent of the county government's total revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  561.   Non - Compliance with One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Examina tion and analysis of the staff payroll for the year under review revealed that four  thousand, eight hundred and thirty (4,830) employees were paid net salaries below one -  third of their basic salaries. This was attributed to excessive deductions arising fro m loans,  advances, and other third - party commitments processed through the payroll system. This  was contrary to Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which requires that the total  amount of all deductions that may be made by an employer from the wages   of his  employee at any one time not to exceed two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  562.   Un - Confirmed Remittance of Statutory Deductions to Respective   Agencies  Review of the payroll revealed that statutory deductions for PAYE, NHIF, NSSF and  provident fund amounting to Kshs.859,836,652, Kshs.115,148,964, Kshs.42,511,880 and  Kshs.259,347,835, respectively were deducted from employees’ salaries during the year.

267  How ever, Management did not provide evidence by way of bank remittance or deposit  slips to show that the statutory deductions were remitted to the relevant agencies in full,  inclusive of employer contributions, or whether the remittances were made within the  statutory deadlines.  This was contrary to   Section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act which requires an employer  paying emoluments to an employee to deduct therefrom, and account for tax thereon;  Section 20(1) of the National Social Security Fund Act, 2013 requir es employers to make  payments deducted from employees’ earnings together with employer amounts to NSSF;  Section 15(4) of the National Health Insurance Fund Act, 2022 (now repealed) provides  contributions are due on the ninth day of each month or on such la ter date as the Board,  in consultation with the Cabinet Secretary, may prescribe and Section 19(4) of the  Employment Act, 2007 requires an employer who deducts an amount from an employee’s  remuneration to pay the amount so deducted in accordance with the t ime period and other  requirements specified in the law.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  563.   Non - Compliance with Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  During the year under review, out of the County Executive’s four thousand, nine   hundred  and thirty - two (4,932) members of staff in payroll, four thousand, two hundred and twenty -  two (4,222) or 86% hailed from one (1) dominant ethnic community. This was contrary to  Section 7(1) of National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, which prov ides that all public  establishments shall seek to represent the diversity of the people of Kenya in the  employment of staff and Section 7(2) also provides that no public establishment shall  have more than one third of its staff from the same ethnic communi ty.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  564.   Non - Compliance with Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025  Review of the master staff register revealed that out of a total of four thousand, seven  hundred and forty - five (4,745) employees, only   one hundred and fifty (150) employees,  representing three percent (3%), were persons with disabilities. This representation falls  two (2%) percentage below the statutory minimum threshold of five percent (5%).   This  was contrary to Section 5(1)(e) of   the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025 which states  that every county government shall promote the inclusion of persons with disabilities in  the county public service by putting in place measures to ensure that at least five per  centum of the employment p ositions are filled by persons with disabilities.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  565.   Failure to Charge and Remit the Public Procurement Capacity Building   Levy  The County Executive incurred expenditure on use of goods and services a mounting to  Kshs.5,975,887,689 and acquired assets under property, plant and equipment totalling  Kshs. 2,728,488,287.   However, Management did not provide evidence to confirm that

268  public procurement capacity building levy amounting to Kshs. 2,591,719   was dedu cted  and remitted on procurement contracts signed and paid. This was contrary to Paragraph  3(1) of the Public Procurement Capacity Building Levy Order, 2023 which requires that  there shall be paid a levy by a supplier on all procurement contracts signed be tween the  supplier and a procuring entity, at the rate of point zero three per centum (0.03%) of the  value of the signed contract, exclusive of applicable taxes.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  566.   Failure to Settle Long Outstanding   Trade and Other Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs.3,304,644,604 as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements. Review of the  ageing analysis revealed tha t trade payables balance of Kshs.2,314,029,373 had been  outstanding for between one (1) and three (3) years. Further, failure to settle pending bills  during the year to which they relate affects the implementation of subsequent year’s  budget programs as th e accounts payable form a first charge on that year’s budget  provision. This was contrary to The National Treasury Circular Ref AG3/101/75 which  requires Accounting Officers to establish effective financial controls and maintain financial  discipline in ord er to achieve efficient utilization of resources and ensure adherence to  financial regulations and procedures to prevent accumulation of accounts payables.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of Government policy.  567.   Stalled   Construction of Projects  Review   of   available   documents   and   project   verifications   revealed   the   following  procurement and contract management weaknesses:  567.1.   Lokiriama Revenue Centre Phase II  The County Executive awarded a contract for the proposed Lokiriama Revenue Centre  Phase II, at a contract sum of Kshs.38,195,895. Audit revealed that a payment of  Kshs.15,019,430 (Invoice dated 13 June, 2024) was made, yet the project remained  incomplete a nd stalled by September, 2025. Further, the payment was made without  supporting inspection or progress reports and certificates of measured works to confirm  actual work completed.  In   addition,   there   were   no   documented   appointment   letters   for   the   contract  implementation team and the progress reports.  567.2.   Rehabilitation of the Main Slaughter House in Lodwar Town  The County Executive awarded a contract for the proposed rehabilitation of the main  slaughter   house   in   Lodwar   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.2,999,255.   The   contract  agreement was signed on 3 April, 2024 and the works were to commence on the same  day of signing the contract with an expected completion date of 3 July, 2024. However,  project verification done in July, 2025 revealed that, the project had stal led while works  certified and paid amounted to 37% of the total sum and the contractor was not on site.

269  567.3.   Equipping of Agricultural Mechanization Station  Review of tender for the proposed equipping of Agriculture Mechanization Station in  Naotin awarded to a local supplier at a contract sum of Kshs.7,879,200 revealed that a  contract agreement was signed on 19 February, 2024 with expected end date of  19 July, 2024. The goods were delivered on 14 June, 2024 as evidenced by the delivery  note, inspection and acceptance report and S13. However, physical inspection done  revealed that the items procured were not at the mechanization station   and were stored  at the Department main store and not in use. Further, the mechanization station which  was constructed in the financial year 2021/2022 consisting of classrooms, an outside  training station and a fence was not in use. In addition, vandalizati on of the buildings was  evident from missing window panes, fallen gate and the roof of the training station had  been blown off by wind hence exposing the floor   slab to rain water and other elements of  the weather, affecting the structure’s overall integrit y.  567.4.   Completion of Kataboi Eco Lodge  As previously reported, the County Executive initiated the construction of Kataboi Eco  Lodge in the financial year 2014/2015 to promote tourism in Lake Zone Ward at an initial  contract sum of   Kshs.66,389,746.   A contract   variation of   Kshs.9,958,464   was approved  in October, 2018 increasing the contract sum to   Kshs.76,348,210 .   In February, 2019 the  County Executive and the contractor mutually agreed to terminate the contract.  A new contract for completion of the project w as entered into in February, 2021 at a  contract   sum   of   Kshs.60,016,621   with   an   expected   completion   date   of  1   November,   2022.   Payments   amounting   to   Kshs.33,121,200   were   made   to   the  contractor as at March, 202 5. The project was at   72%   of completion level in March, 2025.  The remaining project works includes drilling and equipping of the borehole and purchase  and installation of a generator. Physical inspec tion revealed that the project was being  vandalized and t his may lead to additional rehabilitation costs.  567.5.   Construction of Plastic Re - Use Facility  As previously reported, the County Executive initiated contract for the construction of a  plastic re - use facility on 13 January, 2017 for twelve (12) weeks with a lo cal contractor at  contract sum of Kshs.13,626,320. However, the project had stalled with total payments  amounting to Kshs.8,983,516. Further, physical inspection conducted   on the project  revealed that the contractor was not on site.  567.6.   Delay in   Completion of Turkana County Headquarters Building  As previously reported, the construction of the County Executive/HQ Offices was awarded  to a local contractor at a contract price of Kshs.695,854,432 on 23 October, 2014 to take  120 weeks (two and half ye ars) with expected completion date of 22 May, 2017. The  following anomalies were noted:

270  (i)   As   at   the   time   of   audit   cost   variations   amounted   to   Kshs.172,827,489  (comprising contract variation of Kshs.16,264,551 (IPC14) and contractor’s  claims of Kshs.156,562, 939).  (ii)   Contract extensions were granted to 30 June, 2017 which was extended to  30 June, 2019 then further extension to 31 December, 2020, resulting in a total  duration delay of four (4) years by 30 June, 2025.  (iii)   Total   payments   to   the   contractor   as   at   30   June,   2025   amounted   to  Kshs.740,724,014.  (iv)   During the audit in November, 2025 the main contractor was on site completing  works within the thirty (30) days given by the Senate Devolution Committee to  hand over the project to the County Ex ecutive. However, no contract period  extension letter was provided.  (v)   During interviews, the contractor attributed the project delays directly to the  County Executive failure to pay various certified progress certificates. Despite  being compelled to hand o ver the site following Senate Committee intervention,  the contractor indicated unresolved pending payments and intended to pursue  legal action for recovery. Management provided no explanation for the non -  payment of these certified works, an omission that e xposed the County to  significant risk of litigation costs, penalties, and further financial liabilities.  (vi)   Electrical work was at initial stages with the base for generator and delivery of  two distribution boards done and nothing else was observed to be ong oing. No  satisfactory explanation was provided for slow work progress which may result  in cost escalation.  (vii)   Progress payment certificates, certificates of practical completion and handover  certificates were not provided to professionals for assessment of w orks and  extent of completion.  (viii)   The contract sum of Kshs.695,854,432 included a provisional contingency  amount of Kshs.73,400,000 in respect of the purchase and installation of lifts,  air   conditioning,   plumbing,   builders   work   connection,   electrical   works   and  project managers expenses and project managers stationary. However, all  these were later contracted by the County Executive yet they were part of the  original contract. Management explained that the subcontracts lapsed before  full   perf ormance   necessitating   re - contracting.   However,   the   original   bill   of  quantities of the main contract and certificate of measured works for the main  contract   and   revised   Bill   of   Quantities   in   support   of   additional   works   of  Kshs.17,490,292 were not provided f or audit.  567.7.   Stalled   Construction   of Governor’s Residence  As previously reported, a   new contract was awarded to a contactor on 24 April, 2019 for  proposed completion of Governor’s residence at a contract sum of Kshs.90,563,900 for  a period of fifty - two (52)   weeks with expected completion of 24 May, 2020. The last  contract   extension   was   granted   on   3   April,   2020   for   fifty - two   (52)   weeks   ending

271  31 October, 2021. The works certified as at the time of audit was Kshs.17,917,599 with  total paymen ts totalling Kshs.14,559,620 being   the first and the second interim payment  certificates of Kshs.2,327,540 and Kshs.12,186,620,   respectively. The project was stalled  at 25% level of completion as at June, 2025 having delayed for five (5) years based on  the   revised contract.   Physical inspection undertaken in June, 2025 revealed that the  contractor was on site but no works were on - going and interview with the contractor  revealed the reason for stalled work was non - payment of various progress certificates  rais ed under the project and was considering legal action against the County Executive.  Management did not provide satisfactory explanation on why payments for certified works  had not been made which may result into penalties and litigation costs.  567.8.   Stalled Construction of Modern Business Centre  As previously reported, the County Executive awarded a local contractor a contract   for  the construction of Modern Business Centre at a contract sum of Kshs.132,390,490.   The  contract was to run for a period of   five (5) years beginning 23 May, 2016 with an expected  completion date of 20 June, 2020. The County Executive had so far paid an amount of  Kshs.61,913,081   towards the contract. The project stalled and the contractor disputed the  termination and sued the C ounty Executive. The case was on - going in Court .  In the circumstances, value for money of the funds spent on the above projects could not  be confirmed .  567.9.   Construction of Kalokol Resource Centre  As reported in the previous year, tender for construction of Kalokol Resource Centre at  Kalokol was awarded to a local contractor at a contract sum of Kshs.25,104,510. The  contract agreement was signed on 12 January, 2021 and works expected to be completed  within sixteen (16) weeks commencing 27 January, 2021. The contractor was paid an  amount of Kshs.11,678,590 by 28   June, 2021. However,   physical inspection on the  project revealed that the project was complete but not in use. The verandah’s ceiling  board wa s almost falling due to leakages in the roof. Further, fixtures such as taps and  window panes were vandalized due to lack of security at the center.  In the circumstances, value for money of the funds spent on the project could not be  confirmed .  568.   Projects   Implementation Status for the Financial Year 2024 - 2025  Review of the projects implementation status (PIS) report as at 30 June, 2025 revealed  that the County Executive had planned to implement three hundred and seventy - four  (374) projects during the year   under review valued at Kshs.2,026,900,776 with total  cumulative payments of Kshs.271,831,731. However, the projects were at various stages  of implementation as summarized below;

272  Project Status   No  Total Contract Sum  (Kshs.)  Cumulative Payments  (Kshs.)  Completed   176   883,491,307   201,663,178  Ongoing   109   701,808,101   70,168,553  Not Started   83   372,484,418   -  Stalled   6   69,116,950   -  374   2,026,900,776   271,831,731  Non - completion of projects in time was an indication of inadequacy in project   planning,  control and monitoring to ensure efficient absorption of available funds.  In the circumstances, value for money in respect of the projects that were set to be  implemented could not be   confirmed .  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RI SK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  569.   Lack of a Risk Management Policy  Review   of   the   internal   controls   of   the   County   Executive   revealed   that   the   Risk  Management Policy was not in place. Further, no documented formal risk   assessments  were provided for audit for the period under review. This was contrary to Regulation  158(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015  which requires that an entity develops risk management strategies, which include   fraud  prevention mechanism and a system of risk management and internal control that builds  robust business operations.  In the circumstances, mechanisms to mitigate risks could not be confirmed.
