274  COUNTY   EXECUTIVE   OF   WEST POKOT   –   NO.24  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  570.   Unsupported Property, Plant and Equipment  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   property,   plant   and   equipment   balance  of   Kshs.1,407,398,580 as disclosed in Note 14 to the financial statements . The balance  represents only the value of assets acquired during the financial years 2023/2024 and  2024/2025 financial years. However, detailed assets register in support of the balance  was not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, the existence, a ccuracy and completeness of property, plant and  equipment   balance of   Kshs.1,407,398,580   could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  571.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final   receipts budget  and actual amount of Kshs.7,204,252,695 and Kshs.6,552,285,097 respectively resulting  in an under - funding of Kshs.651,967,598 or 9% of the budget.   However, the County  Executive spent an amount of Kshs.6,443,896,242 against actual receipts o f Kshs.  6,552,285,097 , resulting to under - utilization of Kshs.108,388,855 or about 2% of the  actual receipts.  The under - funding affected the planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified   in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  572.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the audit report of the previous year, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial   Statements,   Report   on   Lawfulness   and   Effectiveness   in   Use   of   Public  Resources and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance. Review of the status during the audit revealed that the following eight (8)  issues remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  No.   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  1   Inaccuracies in own source Revenue

275  No.   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  2   Pending Accounts Payables  3   Stalled completion of Pkopoch Tourist Hotel and Hospitality Development Centre  4   Stalled completion of Education Administration Office Block in Kapenguria  5   Delay in completion of cons truction of Governor’s Office Complex  6   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  7   Non - Compliance with Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  8   Lack of Enforcement of Internal Audit Recommendations  Other Information  573.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  574.   Undelivered Library Equipment to Schools  Review of procurement documents reve aled that the   Department for Education awarded  a contract for supply and delivery of library equipment to Early Childhood Development  Education (ECDE) Schools at a cost of Kshs.1,999,500 which was paid in full on  29 May, 2025. However, the list of the i ntended beneficiary schools and distribution list to  confirm that the equipment were actually delivered to the schools were not provided for  audit.  In the circumstances, the value for money of the expenditure on the equipments could  not be confirmed.  575.   Lack of Rotation of Evaluation Committee Members  Review of nineteen (19) contracts awarded by the Department for Liv estock, Fisheries  and Veterinary Services, with a cumulative value of Kshs.45,172,970, revealed that the  contracts were evaluated by an ad - hoc committees composed of the same members,  rather than by committees formed on a rotational basis. This was contrar y to Section  46(4)(b) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which requires that  evaluation committees to be appointed rotationally and to comprise the head of the user  Department and representatives from two (2) other Departments.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  576.   Irregular   Payments of Subscriptions  Review of payment records revealed that an amount of Kshs.2,600,000 was paid to the  Council of Governors as a contribution towards Devolution Conference. This was contrary  to Section 37 of the Intergovernmental Relations Act, 2012, which provides that the

276  operational expenses in respect of the structures and institutions established in the Act  shall be provided for in the annual estimates of the revenue and expenditure of the  National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  577.   Irregular Annual Salary Increments  Review of payroll data revealed that four hundred and forty - eight (448) officers received  more   than   one   (1)   annual   salary   increment   during   the   year   resulting   in   multiple  unauthorized changes to their basic pay. This was contrary to Paragraph C.3 of the  Human Resource Policies and Procedures Manual for the Public Service, 2016, which  stipulates that an officer is entitled to o nly one (1) annual increment, effective from the  first of the month of their appointment.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .  578.   Non - Compliance with   Salaries and   Renumeration Commission Allowances  Guidelines  Review   of   payroll   data   revealed   irregularities   in   payment   of   allowances,   including  overpayment of basic salary to forty (40) employees amounting to Kshs.7,030,402,  overpayments of house allowances amounting t o Kshs.4,999,255 and irregular payments  of   extraneous   and   emergency   call   allowances   amounting   to   Kshs.3,349,839   and  Kshs.15,450,000 respectively.  Further,   eight   (8)   members   of   staff   were   irregularly   paid   a   total   of   Kshs.551,060  simultaneous   disbursement   of   basic   salary   and   an   unexplained   "special   salary  allowance." This was contrary to the SRC Circular SRC/TS/29(81) dated 10 August, 2023,  which provides an exhaustive list of all permissible earnings for county executive officers,  and no such special salar y allowance is provided for within the legal framework.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .  579.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Review   of   the   staff   payroll   revealed   that   five   thousand   and   fifty - two   ( 5,052)  employees   received net pay below the legal threshold, indicating that the cumulative  statutory and third - party deductions exceeded the two - thirds limit of their basic salaries.  This was contrary to Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which req uire that  deductions made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any one time shall  not exceed two thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  580.   Non - Remittance   of Statutory Deductions  580.1.   Under - Deduction of Social Health Insurance Fund  Review of the payroll revealed Social Health Insurance Fund under - deductions from two  thousand eight hundred and eighty (2,880) employees amounting to Kshs.7,105,325. This

277  was contrary to   Regulation 16(1)   of the Social Health Insurance (General) Regulations,  2024 which requires income derived from salaried employment be subjected to a monthly  deduction at a rate of 2.75% of gross salary by ninth day of each month.  580.2.   Non - Deduction of National Social Secur ity Fund  Review of the payroll and other accounting records revealed that under National Social  Security Fund, contributions were either under - deducted or not deducted from five  thousand one hundred and sixty - four (5,164) employees amounting to Kshs.83,9 39,040.  This was contrary to   Section 20(1) of the National Social Security Fund Act , 2013 which  obligates employers to deduct the required contributions from employees' earnings and  remit them, together with the employer's portion to the Fund by the ninth   day of each  month.  580.3.   Non - Deduction of Pay - As - You - Earn (PAYE) Tax  Review of payroll and other accounting records revealed non - compliance with tax  regulations, specifically the non - deduction of PAYE from ninety - one (91) employees  earning above the taxable   threshold amounting to Kshs.2,422,386 and under - deduction  from   two   thousand   two   hundred   and   ninety - two   (2,292)   employees   amounting   to  Kshs.9,766,955.   This   was   contrary   to   Section   37(1)   of   the   Income   Tax   Act  (Cap.470)   which   requires   an   employer   to   deduct   th e   correct   amount   of   tax   from  emoluments and remit it to the Commissioner of KRA by the tenth day of the following  month.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  581.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility Principles on Wages  Review of the payroll revealed that the County Executive had a budgeted wage bill of  Kshs.3,014,039,183   representing   41%   of   the   budgeted   total   revenue   of  Kshs.7,342,973,958. The actual financial performance further reflects staff emoluments  amount of Kshs. 3,011,654,291 which was 46% of the actual revenue collected amounting  to Kshs.6,552,285,097. This was contrary Regulation 25(1)(b) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires that expenditure  on wages and benefit s shall not exceed thirty - five percent of total county revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  582.   Lack of Annual Recruitment Plans  Review of human resource documents revealed that County Executive did not have an  annual recruit ment plan for the year under review, despite payroll analysis confirming that  five hundred and forty - three (543) new officers were employed at a total cost of  Kshs.168,656,112. This was contrary to Section 59(1)(g) of the County Governments Act,  2012, and   Regulation 119(2) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulations, 2015 which require the development of a coherent human resource plan

278  and a detailed human capital plan, respectively, to form the basis for personnel budgeting  and recruit ment.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  583.   Un - Authorized Opening of Bank Accounts  Review of the County Executive's bank accounts revealed that out of two hundred and  seventeen (217) bank accounts operated by the County   Executive, two hundred and  fifteen (215) accounts lacked evidence of authorization from the County Treasury. This  was contrary to Regulation 82(4) and (5) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires prior County T reasury authorization for  opening   any   bank   account   and   requires   that   such   authorization   be   formally  communicated to both the Controller of Budget and the Auditor - General.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  584.   Lack   of Project   Co - ordination Committee   for the   Transition to Accrual  Accounting  Review   of   accounting   records   and   transition   processes   revealed   that   the   County  Executive had not formed a Project Coordination Committee. There was no evidence of  the committee's   formation, including terms of reference, membership lists or minutes of  meetings. Further, there was no coordinated structure in place to drive the activities  outlined in the transition roadmap, such as asset verification, system evaluation, staff  training , and the development of opening balance sheets for a structured and successful  transition to accrual accounting. This was contrary to Section 1.5 (iii) of the   Guidelines on  Transition from cash to accrual accounting by ministries and County Governments in  Kenya.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  585.   Non -   Compliance with Provisions of Facility Improvement Financing Act  Review of bank statements for four (4) Level   -   4 hospitals in the County revealed that the  hospitals deposited an am ount of Kshs.43,669,982 into   the West Pokot County Health  FIF account. Subsequently, an amount of Kshs.38,212,580 was returned to the Hospitals’  Faculty   Improvement   Financing   (FIF)   operations   accounts   while   the   balance   of  Kshs.5,457,402 was withheld at the   County Executive level.   This was contrary to   Section  5 of the Facility Improvement Financing Act, 2023, which requires all facility funds to be  retained   in   designated   FIF   accounts   and   prohibits   their   transfers   to   unauthorized  accounts.  In the circumstanc es, Management was in breach of the law.  586.   Irregular Issuance of Bursaries to Secondary Schools  The County Executive allocated an amount of Kshs.150,000,000 from the West Pokot  Bursary   Education   and   Development   Infrastructure   Fund   for   capital   infrastructure

279  development   in   secondary   schools.   The   expenditure   constitutes   an   unauthorized  payment, as the   development, management, and infrastructure funding of secondary  education falls exclusively under the functional mandate of the National Government. This  was contrary to   Part 2, Paragraph 9 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya  (2010) , which   limits the mandate of County Governments to pre - primary education, village  polytechnics, homecraft centers, and childcare facilities.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  587.   Stalled Completion of Education Administration Office Block  Review of procurement records revealed that a local contractor was awarded a contract  for   the   construction   of   an   education   administration   office   block   in   Kapenguria   to  completion in May, 2015 at a contract sum of Kshs.52,457,964 for a period of three (3)  years. However, the contract was terminated in September, 2020 on the grounds that the  contract period had lapsed yet the pr oject was not complete. At the time of contract  termination, the contractor had been paid an amount of Kshs. 35,842,107.  In May, 2021, another contractor was awarded a contract to do some works which  included door and window fixing, stone pitching, plaster ing, painting and staircase and  ramp linkage at a contract sum of Kshs.4,999,960 for a period of three (3) months where  works   valued   at   Kshs.4,094,417   were   completed.   Physical   inspection,   conducted  approximately ten (10) years after commencement, confirmed   the project was still  incomplete and no contractor was on site.  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   on   the   expenditure   incurred   on   the  delayed   construction of an education administration office block could not be confirmed.  588.   Irregularities in the Drilling of Boreholes Projects  The Department for Water, Environment and Natural Resources utilized the force account  procurement   method   for   drilling   of   fourteen   (14)   boreholes   at   a   total   cost   of  Kshs.25,500,000 without adhering to the   mandatory legal safeguards governing this  procedure. Review of the project documentation revealed that the Department failed to  prepare essential technical documents, including bills of quantities, cost estimates,  technical drawings and water chemical ana lysis. This was contrary to Section 109 of the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 and Regulation 95 of the Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, which provides conditions and  required documentation for the lawful use of the   force account method of procurement.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  589.   Stalled Completion of Pkopoch Tourist Hotel and Hospitality Development  Centre  Review of procurement documents revealed that Management awarded a local contractor  tender to construct Pkopoch Tourist Hotel and Hospitality Development Centre at a  contract sum of Kshs.352,123,565 on 15 May, 2015. The works stalled at first floor

280  superst ructure and another contract was awarded to the same contractor at a contract  sum of Kshs.19,691,777 to carry out protection works at the project site with no contract  period stated in the contract agreement. However, no documentation in support of the  ter mination process were presented for audit even though a second contract was  awarded on the same project. The total amount paid as at the time of audit was an amount  of Kshs.84,740,392 which included an amount of Kshs.17,722,599 paid for the second  contract . Physical inspection conducted revealed that the project had stalled at first floor  sub - structure and the contractor was not on site.  In the   circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.84,740,392  incurred on the project could not be confirmed.  590.   Irregularities in Implementation of Roads Projects  Review of ward - specific road construction projects under the Department for Roads  revealed systemic failur es in project planning, execution, and monitoring. Ten (10)  projects with a total cost of Kshs.14,895,834, remained incomplete due to inadequate  funding and poor budgetary planning. Further, several road constructions demonstrated  significant regulatory an d quality control failures, with roads being opened through private  properties   without   proper   land   acquisition   approvals   and   there   was   evidence   of  substandard workmanship compromising the integrity of the works.  In the circumstances, the value for money   on the expenditure of Kshs.14,895,834  incurred on the road projects could not be confirmed.  591.   Irregularities i n Implementation of Water Projects  Physical   inspection   of   water   projects   implemented   by   the   Department   for   Water,  Environment, Natural Resources and Climate Change, with a total contract cost of  Kshs.15,498,820 revealed systemic failures in project execu tion and quality control,  resulting in non - functional or sub - optimally performing assets. Key deficiencies included:  multiple completed boreholes that were not equipped, projects with unreliable water  supply   due   to   technical   failures   and   systems   operating   at   low pressure,   severely  restricting water access for the intended beneficiaries, including primary schools and  community.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of   Kshs.15,498,820  incurred on the water projects could not be   confirmed.  592.   Delayed Completion of Construction of a Modern Mortuary at Kapenguria  Referral Hospital  Review of contract documents revealed that the Department for Health and Sanitation  awarded a contract, for the construction of a modern mortuary at Kapenguria Referral  Hospital at a contract sum of Kshs.14,356,156 on 4 April, 2024 with a one hundred and  e ighty (180) - day completion period, from 4 April, 2024 to 5 October, 2024. However,  physical inspection conducted revealed that the project was incomplete at about 99%  completion level. The contractor had been paid an amount of Kshs.6,855,607 while a

281  second   payment certificate amounting to Kshs.7,348,166 remained unpaid. Further,  critical components were omitted from the original contract such as a walkway linking the  mortuary to the Hospital wards and landscaping due to the site's topography for safe and  ac cessible use.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure incurred on the project  could not be confirmed.  593.   Unused Elevated Tank and Plumbing at Paraywa Dispensary in Siyoi Ward  Review   of   procurement   documents   revealed   that   the   Departmen t   for   Health   and  Sanitation awarded a contract for the construction of a septic tank, elevated tank and  plumbing system at Paraywa Dispensary at a contract sum of Kshs.2,499,591 which was  fully paid by 30 December, 2024. However, physical inspection conduc ted in June, 2025  revealed that the completed facility was non - operational because it lacked a water source.  Further, the Department had not budgeted for this essential component.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of   Kshs.2,499, 591   incurred  on the   project could not be confirmed.  594.   Un - Utilized Kruru Dispensary in Riwo Ward  Review of contract documents revealed that the   Department for Health and Sanitation  awarded   a   contract   for   the   construction   of   Kruru   Dispensary   at   a   total   cost   of  Kshs.5,999,137, with the final payment made in February, 2025. Physical inspection  conducted confirmed that the building was constructed as   per the bill of quantities.  However, the dispensary remained non - operational as the project failed to provide for  essential utilities and resources including water, electricity, medical equipment and staff.  In the circumstances, the value for money on t he expenditure of   Kshs.5,999,137   incurred  on the   project   could not be confirmed.  595.   Delayed Operationalization o f Nasukuta Export Abattoir Project  Review of procurement records revealed that Nasukuta   Export Abattoir project was  initiated in the year 2018 with a total project cost of Kshs.214,400,000 and a completion  date of March, 2022. However, the project remained incomplete as at 30 June, 2025 with  the contract for the supply and installation of ex port processing equipment remaining  outstanding. Lack of the equipment renders the entire abattoir facility non - operational,  despite   the   substantial   investment   comprising   an   amount   of   Kshs.110,000,000   of  European   Union   grant   and   an   amount   of   Kshs.62,000,00 0   in   County   Executive  counterpart funding.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure incurred and completion of  the project could not be confirmed.  596.   Delay in   the   Construction of Governor’s Office  Review of contract records revealed that   t he County Executive awarded two (2) contracts  for construction of a Governor's Office Complex to the same local contractor: Phase I was

282  awarded on 4 June, 2019 at a contract sum of Kshs.198,475,572 while Phase II was  awarded on 12 April, 2024 at a contrac t sum of Kshs.20,000,000.  Physical inspection carried out on the project and review of original bill of quantities  revealed that, the County Executive changed the office complex floors design from the  initial six (6) story building to a four (4) story bui lding. However, the revised architectural  design and plan, revised Bill of Quantities (BQs), Project Implementation Committee  minutes and recommendations and accounting officers’ approvals for the changes were  not provided for audit. The project was incomp lete and had stalled while the contractor  was not on site.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure incurred on the project could  not be confirmed.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  597.   Inadequate Facilitation of the Internal Audi t Department  The Internal Audit Function was under - resourced with only two (2) staff members,  severely constraining its capacity to execute the approved annual work   plan. Further, the  budget lacked provision for essential operational requirements with no dedicated motor  vehicle and fuel allocations, fundamentally impeding its field audit capabilities. This was  contrary to   Regulation 167(8) of the Public Finance Manage ment (County Governments)  Regulations,   2015 ,   which   mandates   that   accounting   officers   to   ensure   the   audit  committee and internal audit function are adequately funded and supported.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the internal audit function in   ensuring existence  of internal controls could not be confirmed.  598.   Lack of Updated Project Implementation Status Report  Review of projects records   revealed that Management failed to prepare the mandatory  Monthly   Progress   Reports   on   all   procurement   contracts.   Further   the   Project  Implementation Status Report lacked critical details including the contract description,  number, value, commencement date, c urrent status, amount paid, and the expected  completion date. This was contrary to Regulation 140(1) of the Public Procurement and  Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, which requires the Head of the Procurement Function  to prepare and submit such detailed mon thly reports to the Accounting Officer.  In   the   circumstances,   the   effectiveness   in   monitoring   and   control   of   projects  implementation could not be confirmed.  599.   Failure to Update the Bank Account Register  Review of the bank records register revealed that the County Executive maintained two  hundred and seventeen (217) bank accounts. However, the register lack ed mandatory

283  data elements required by law including bank account types, authorized signatories,  account opening dates, specific account purposes, annual account balances and official  Treasury approval references. This was contrary to Regulation 87(3) of t he Public  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires an  Accounting Officer to maintain complete, current and approved records of all bank  accounts with specified details.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the contro l and safeguarding of the County  Executive’s bank accounts could not be confirmed.

284  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF SAMBURU   –   NO.25  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  600.   Unsupported and Long Outstanding Trade and Other Payables  The statement of financial position and Note 32 to the financial statements reflect trade  and other payables balance of Ksh s.431,831,736 comprising of trade payables of  Kshs.343,574,482   and   third - party   payables   of   Kshs.88,257,254.   However,   trade  payables amounting to Kshs.176,378,605 were not supported by local service/ purchase  orders, invoices, signed contracts, or delivery   notes to confirm delivery of goods, provision  of services, or execution of works.  Further, payables totalling Kshs.28,555,160 had been outstanding for over three (3) years  and were not paid as first charge on the County revenue. In addition, the third - pa rty  payables include salary deductions amount of Kshs.27,467,566 due to Savings and  Credit Cooperative Organizations (SACCOs) that had not been remitted for more than  five (5) years.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the trade and ot her payables  balance of Kshs.431,831,736 could not be confirmed.  601.   Inaccuracies in Refundable Deposits and Prepayments  The statement of financial position and Note   33 to the financial statements reflects  refundable deposits and prepayments balance of Kshs.94,726,058 relating to the County  Deposit Account.   However, review of   bank reconciliation   statements   revealed that  receipts in the cashbook amounting to Kshs.82,190 ,366 dated between June, 2024 and  May, 2017, were not reflected in the bank statements.  Further,   the   County   Executive   had   borrowed   deposit and   retention   funds   totalling  Kshs.75,310,761 over the years, which had not been refunded back to the deposits and  retentions account. The borrowings were not supported by evidence of approval by the  County Assembly, utilization details, the specific budget lines funded, or the reasons for  the continued non - refund of the monies.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and   completeness of the refundable deposits and  prepayments balance of Kshs.94,726,058 could not be confirmed.  602.   Inaccuracies in the Property, Plant and Equipment  The statement of financial position and Note 26 to the financial statements reflect  property, plant and equipment balance of Kshs.1,067,261,831. However, audit review  revealed that expenditure totalling Kshs.18,495,800 was incurred on the procurement of

285  f our (4) computer   software   during the year under review but   were erroneously reflected  as computers and ICT equipment assets under property, plant and equipment instead  of intangible assets.  Further, the procurement was not linked to the County Integrated   Development Program  (CIDP) .  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   property,   plant   and  equipment balance of Kshs.1,067,261,831 could not be confirmed.  603.   Unaccounted for Transfers to Other Government Entities  603.1.   Transfers to Self - Reporting Projects  The statement of financial performance and Note 11 to the financial statements reflect  transfers to other Government entities amount of Kshs.541,736,919, which includes an  amount of Kshs.326,609,787 in respect of tr ansfer to self - reporting projects. Included in  the amount are transfers to health centers and dispensaries amount of Kshs.14,341,738  which were not supported by the facilities’ cash books and bank statements, payments to  County   officers   amount   of   Kshs.33,3 29,560   which   were   not   supported   by   imprest  warrants and surrender vouchers, and an amount of Kshs.9,413,000 transferred to  community   health   promoters   which   was   not   supported   with   schedules   and  acknowledgements from the beneficiaries.  Further,   review   of   t he   disbursement   of   conditional   allocation   from   the   National  Government share of revenue for the financial year 2024/2025 revealed that the County  Executive received an amount of Kshs.46,140,000 for community health promoters  resulting in a variance amounti ng to Kshs.36,727,000 which was not transferred to the  intended beneficiaries.  603.2.   Transfers to Other County Government Entities  The statement of financial performance and Note 11 to the financial statements reflect  transfer to other Government entities amount of Kshs.541,736,919 which includes an  amount of Kshs.215,127,132 in relation to transfers to other County Government entitie s.  Included in the amount is a balance of Kshs.10,000,000 transferred to Nomotio Livestock  Improvement Centre which was not supported with an acknowledgement note from the  Institution. Further, the purpose for the expenditure was not explained.  In   the   cir cumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   transfers   to   other  Government to other entities could not be confirmed.  604.   Non - Disclosure of Transfers to Kenya Devolution Support Program Funds  The statement of financial performance and Note 6 to the financ ial statements reflect  transfer from the County Revenue Fund (CRF) amount of Kshs.5,883,453,597. However,  review of the disbursement of conditional allocation to the County Executive from the  National Government share of Revenue for the financial year 2024 /2025 revealed that

286  the County Executive received an amount of Kshs.37,500,000 for transfers to IDA (WB)  KDSP II which were not disclosed in the financial statements or accounted for.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of transfers from C RF amounting  to Kshs.5,883,453,597 could not be confirmed.  605.   Variances in Other Grants and Subsidies Amount  The statement of financial performance and Note 13 to the financial statements reflect  other grants and subsidies amount of Kshs.98,758,637, which i ncludes   scholarships and  other educational benefits in respect of transfers to Samburu County Bursary Fund  amounting to Kshs.68,758,637. However, the statement of cash flows of the Samburu  County   Bursary   Fund   reflects   transfers   from   the   County   Executive   am ount   of  Kshs.13,096,800,   resulting   in   an   unexplained   and   unreconciled   variance   of  Kshs.55,661,837.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   scholarships   and   other  educational benefits amounting to Kshs.68,758,637 could not be   confirmed.  606.   Unsupported Medical Insurance Expenditure  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services totalling Kshs.1,782,133,252, which includes insurance costs  amount of Kshs.23,292,664 i n relation to various insurance covers.  Further, the statement of financial position and Note 30A to the financial statements  reflects pre - payments on medical insurance amount of Kshs.137,771,033. However, the  medical insurance contracts, cover payments   for the previous financial year, the details  of the persons covered under the scheme and details of payments made to Social Health  Authority (SHA) in respect of the medical cover were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and   completeness of insurance costs amounting to  Kshs.161,062,697 could not be confirmed.  607.   Voided Transactions  Review of Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) records for the  year ended 30 June, 2025 revealed that one thousand, nine hundr ed and fifty - five (1,955)  transactions totalling Kshs.1,574,202,029 were processed and later voided or canceled  during the year. However, no documentation was provided to support the authorization,  justification, or approval for voiding these transactions,   despite having been presented to  and approved by the Controller of Budget (CoB).  Further, there was no evidence that the CoB   was notified of the reversals or that the  requisite adjustments were made to accurately reflect the voided amounts.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the transaction reversal could  not be confirmed.

287  Emphasis of Matter  608.   Budgetary Co ntrol and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   amounts   of   Kshs.7,382,117,765   and  Kshs.5,935,052,203 respectively, resulting   to under - funding of Kshs.1,447,065,56 2, or  20% of the approved budget. However, the County Executive spent an amount of  Kshs.5,689,501,085 against actual receipts of Kshs.5,935,052,203, resulting to under -  utilization of Kshs.245,551,119 or 4% of the actual receipts.  The under - funding affecte d planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  609.   Unresolved Prior Year’s Audit Matters  In the previous year’s audit report, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial   Statements,   Report   on   Lawfulness   and   Effectiveness   in   Use   of   Public  Resources, and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Cont rols, Risk Management and  Governance. Review of the status revealed that thirty - seven (37) matters as listed at the  end of this report remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  Other Information  610.   There were no material issu es relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  611.   Non - Compliance with   the   Law on Fiscal Responsibility   Principles   on  Wage s  The   employee   costs   amount   of   Kshs.2, 695,047,761   represents   about   46%   of   the  County’s total revenue of Kshs.5, 883,453,597.   This was contrary to Regulation 25(1)(a)  and (b) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015  which provides that the County Executive expendit ure on wages and benefits for public  officers should not exceed thirty - five per cent (35%) of the total County revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  612.   Failure to Deduct and Remit   Taxes  Review of the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) for the year under  review revealed that the County Executive did not deduct Pay As You Earn (PAYE) of

288  approximately Kshs. 2,707,946   from forty - seven (47) employees, and did not remit the  applica ble taxes to the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA). This was contrary to Section 5  of the Income Tax Act (Cap 470) requiring that all income earned in Kenya to be subject  to income tax.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  613.   Irregula r   Tax   Deductions from Employees with Disabilities  Review   of the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) for the period between  December, 2024 to June, 2025 revealed that the County Executive deducted Pay As You  Earn (PAYE) from the salaries of nineteen (19) employees with disabilities amounting to  Kshs . 2,707,946 . However, records provided indicated that these employees were duly  registered as persons with disabilities and therefore eligible for tax exemption under  Section 12(3) of the Persons with Disabilities Act (Cap. 133), which provides that   a n  empl oyee with disabilities shall be entitled to exemption from tax on all income accruing  from his employment.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  614.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Review   of the payroll records revealed that eighty - one (81) employees received net pay  which was below one - third of their basic salaries. This was contrary to Section 1 9(3) of  the Employment Act, 2007, which provides that the total amount of deduction of the wages  of an employee shall not exceed two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  615.   Irregular Payment of   Allowances  Review   of   special   house   allowance   records   revealed   that   an   amount   of  Kshs.2,879,328   was   paid during the year under review to ten (10)   employees. The staff  wer e employed on various dates after 10   December, 2014, when the terms and conditions  of service in the Public Service had been determined by the Salaries and Remuneration  Commission and which did not permit the payment of the special house allowance. No  expl anation was provided to justify the payments.  Further, an   amount of Kshs.10,188,000 was paid to ninety - one (91) employees as  extraneous duty allowances during the year under review. However, no documentation  was provided for audit to support how the payment rates were determined and the basis  for the allowances   was not explained.  In addition,   an   amount of Kshs.6,474,217 was irregularly paid to thirty (30) employees as  special salary. The affected staff were not eligible for such payments and no justification  or documented basis for determining the rates was prov ided for audit. Further, the  payment of the special salaries had not been approved by the Salaries and Remuneration  Commission.

289  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  616.   Salaries Paid Outside Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database System  Review of the payroll revealed that   an   amount of Kshs.59,395,509 was paid as salaries  to staff members outside the Integrated Pay roll and Personnel Database (IPPD) Payroll  system. This was contrary to Section 1.5.1 of The National Treasury Financial Accounting  Recording and Reporting Manual which requires salaries, allowances or arrears of  County   Government   employees   to   be   processed   through   Integrated   Payroll   and  Personnel Database (IPPD).  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  617.   Irregular Recruitment   of Staff  Review of human resource documents revealed that an amount of Kshs.27,601,612 was  paid to twenty - nine (29) staff members under the Governors Delivery Unit for the months  between July, 2024 to November, 2024, when the Unit was dissolved. As previously  reported, the Unit was not provided for in the approved organization structure and the  duties and responsibilities of the members were not defined. Further, the approval from  County Public Service Board (CPSB), advertisement, applications, shortlisting, interviews  and selection of successful candidates were not provided for audit. This was contrary to  Section 68 of the County Governments Act, 2012 which provide that subject to   the  relevant legislation, the County Public Service Board shall, for a specified period, maintain  a record of all applications received in response to advertisements inviting applications  and such record may be inspected by any person.  In the circumstanc es, Management was in breach of the law.  618.   Irregular   Retention of Officers Beyond Mandatory Retirement Age  Review of the County Executive’s IPPD payroll revealed that two (2) employees had  exceeded the mandatory retirement age for public officers of sixty   (60) years and  Management did not provide any explanation for the anomaly. This was contrary to The  National Treasury Circular No. 18 of 2010, which set the retirement age at 60 years.  619.   Non - Compliance   with the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025  The County Executive had a total of three thousand and sixty - one (3,061) employees, out  of whom twenty - eight (28) were person s with disabilities, representing about 0.009%. This  was contrary to Section 5(1)(e) of the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025 which states  that every County Government shall promote the inclusion of persons with disabilities in  the county public service   by putting in place measures to ensure that at least five per  centum of the employment positions are filled by persons with disabilities.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

290  620.   Non - Compliance with the Law on   Staff   Ethnic Composition  Review of the County Executive’s payroll for June, 2025 revealed that the County  Executive had a total workforce of three thousand and sixty - one (3,061) employees, out  of whom two thousand five hundr ed and eight (2,508) employees, representing 82%,  belonged to the dominant ethnic community in the County. This exceeded the threshold  set under Section 7(1) and (2) of the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, which  stipulates that no   single ethnic   community should constitute more than one - third of the  employees of a   public body.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  621.   Irregularities in the Procurement Processes  621.1.   Construction of Access Roads, Buildings and Other Road   Works  Review of Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) payment details  revealed   payments   totalling   Kshs.578,559,157   paid   to   sixty - five   (65)   suppliers   for  construction of access roads, buildings and other road works. Payment analysis re vealed  that twenty - two (22) suppliers received an amount of Kshs.399,941,637, representing  69%   of   the   total   payments,   with   individual   payments   ranging   from   amount   of  Kshs.51,716,221 to Kshs.10,466,518. This concentration of payments indicates potential  unf airness and lack of equitable distribution in the award of contracts.  In the circumstances, the value for money and regularity of procurement amounting to  Kshs.578,559,157 could not be confirmed.  621.2.   Procurement and Distribution of Food and Ration  The sta tement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services amount of Kshs.1,782,133,252, which includes specialized  materials and services amounting to Kshs.348,010,691, out of which an amount of  Kshs.104,320, 550 was incurred on food and ration. However, analysis of the food  procured per type, distribution list of the beneficiaries and deliveries, the basis used on  beneficiaries’ identification/selection and the acknowledgement/confirmation of receipt of  the fo od and rations by the beneficiaries were not provided for audit.  Further, included in the amount is a balance of Kshs.4,450,000 paid to two (2) local  suppliers under framework agreements for the supply and delivery of cooking oil.  However, review of payme nt records revealed that a payment of Kshs.1,925,000 for the  supply and delivery of cooking oil was indicated as a pending bill for financial year  2023/2024. However, while the delivery of the cooking oil was recorded as made on  22 April, 2024, th e Local Purchase Order (LPO) was dated 24 May, 2024, while the  purchase requisition was prepared on 2 May, 2024 and the acceptance certificate was  dated 17 May, 2024, which was after the date of the delivery. The inconsistencies in the  sequence of the proc urement process were not explained.

291  In addition, the awarded contractor was non - responsive at the preliminary evaluation  stage by failing to attach the tax compliance certificate, but was awarded the contract at  a   sum   of   Kshs.2,525,000.   The   inspection   and   acceptance   certificate   was   dated  8 January, 2025 while the delivery was made on 10 January, 2025. No explanation was  provided for the inconsistency.  In the circumstances, the value for money for the expenditure of Kshs.104,320,550 could  not be confirmed.  622.   Irregul ar Procurement of   Motor Vehicle Insurance Services  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services expenditure amount of Kshs.1,782,133,252, which include  insurance costs amounting to Kshs.23 ,292,664, out of which a tender of a contract sum  of Kshs.2,077,800 was awarded to an insurance agency on 22 November, 2024.  However,   review of the Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA)   R egister , 2024   indicated  that the awarded   a gency was not   licensed . This was   contrary to Section 19 of the  Insurance Act, (Cap 487) which prohibits unlicensed entities from conducting insurance  business.   Further,   the   bid   evaluation   documents,   the   list   of   the   insured   County  Executive’s vehicles submitted to the ag ency and documents, including motor vehicle  valuation   reports   and   the   signed   insurance   contract   indicating   vehicles   under  comprehensive or third - party cover, were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  623.   Irregular Expenditure on Foreign Travel  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services expenditure amounting to Kshs.1,782,133,252, which inclu des  an amount of Kshs.25,460,220 on foreign travel and subsistence. Included in the amount  is a balance of   Kshs.1,710,120 paid to an officer on 8 April, 2025 to facilitate participation  in a Leadership and Change Management training course in Dubai. Howeve r, there was  no evidence that a Training Needs Assessment was conducted to justify the officer’s  nomination, contrary to the Human Resource Policy.  Further, while the training was scheduled to take place from   17 February, 2025 to 28  February, 2025, the o fficer travelled on 20 February, hence   missing three (3) days of  training and returned on 6 March, 2025 which was six (6) days after the end of the training.  No explanation or justification was provided for the delayed arrival and the extended stay.  In add ition,   an amount of Kshs.297,735 was paid for tuition, but due to the officer’s three  (3) - days absence, the fee was therefore not fully utilized and the officer did not submit a  back - to - office report to demonstrate knowledge gained or application for the t raining.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.1,710,120 incurred on  foreign travel could not be confirmed.

292  624.   Other Operating Expenses  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services expenditure amount of Kshs.1,782,133,252, which includes an  amount   of   Kshs.336,177,045   in   respect   of   other   operating   expenses.   Review   of  docume nts in relation to this expenditure revealed the following anomalies:  624.1.   Doubtful Consultative Meeting Expenditure   –   Maa Culture Day Preparation  Included in the other operating expenditure is an amount of Kshs.3,136,000 paid to  various staff who   attended a consultative meeting held from 11 to 13 October, 2024 in  preparation for the Maa Culture Day. However, the user department did not provide  justification for the meeting, including a clear statement of objectives, details of activities  undertaken , or evidence of prior approval from the Accounting Officer. Further, review of  accountability   documents,   including   payment   schedules   and   back - to - office   reports,  revealed that they were not dated and therefore it was not possible to confirm when funds  were   disbursed or whether they were accounted for within the required timelines.  624.2.   Doubtful Expenditure on Tobong’u Lore Festival  Included in the other operating expenditure is an amount of Kshs.2,765,000 paid to staff  who attended the Tobong’u Lore Festi val, 2024 held from 22 to 26 October, 2024 at  Ekalees Centre. However, the daily attendance registers signed by the participants and  the   details   of   activities   undertaken   were   not   provided   for   audit.   Further, payment  schedules   indicated   that one hundred and   twenty - eight (128) community members were  paid accommodation allowance at a rate of Kshs.3,000 per day for five (5) days. The  basis for this rate was not provided, considering that Government guidelines do not  prescribe accommodation rates for members of   the public.  624.3.   Basketball   Team   Facilitation   Kenya   Youth   Inter - Counties   Sports  Association Games  Included in the other operating expenditure is an amount of Kshs.2,447,270 which was  paid to an individual as facilitation for the Samburu County basketball teams participating  in the Kenya Youth Inter - Counties Sports Association (KYISA) Games held from 13   to 19  April, 2025. Review of the payment schedules revealed that the team members and  officials were paid amounts totalling Kshs.1,836,400 for the eight (8) days, at a rate of  Kshs.2,500 per day. However, no policy guideline or approval was provided to su pport  the basis of this rate or justification for payments of this nature to members of the public.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.8,348,270 could  not be confirmed.  625.   Projects Implementation  The statement of financial position and Note 26 to the financial statements reflects a  balance of Kshs.1,067,261,831 in respect of property, plant and equipment which  includes   infr as t r u cture   additions   balance   of   Kshs.587,130,407.   Review   of   the  procurement   documents and contracts revealed the following anomalies:

293  625.1.   Stalled Project   -   Construction of Holding Pen at Nomotio Abattoir  Infrastructure balance includes an amount of Kshs.4,968,300 paid to a local contractor  for the construction of holding pens at Nomotio Abattoir. However,   the Bills of Quantities  (BQs)   and   other   payment   records   to   show   the   cumulative   payments   since  commence ment, the percentage of completion, or the contract period were not provided  for audit .   Further, physical inspection conducted in July, 2025 revealed that the project  had stalled and the contractor was not on site.  625.2.   Defective Floodlights  The infrastructure asset additions include a contract sum of Kshs.13,002,000 for the  proposed installation of Maralal floodlights paid to a local contractor. However, review of  the pay ment vouchers, other tender documents and physical inspection carried out in  July, 2025 revealed that four (4) solar lamps (200W) were non - functional at the time of  physical inspection and electrical cables and wiring systems were exposed, increasing  vulne rability to theft and vandalism.  Further,   the   balance   of   infrastructure   assets   additions   includes   an   amount   of  Kshs.3,300,000 for the contract for on installation of floodlights at Livestock   Market paid  to a local contractor. However, physical inspection   carried out in July, 2025 revealed that  two solar lamps of 200W were not functioning and electrical cables and wiring system on  the floodlights were exposed, increasing the risk of theft and vandalism.  In addition, the balance of infrastructure assets in cludes an amount of Kshs.3,285,000 for  the contract on installation of floodlights at Kirisia Area. However, review of the payment  vouchers and other tender document, and physical inspection carried out in July, 2025  revealed that   two (2) solar lamps of 20 0W were not functioning, the electrical cables and  wiring system on the floodlights were exposed, increasing the risk of theft and vandalism .  Also, the project was not branded with a sign board hence, it was not possible to confirm  whether the project was   funded by County Executive.  625.3.   Incomplete Works on Construction of Resim Dispensary, Staff House, Pit  Latrine and Fence Works  The contract for the construction of Resim Dispensary, staff house, pit latrine, and fence  works   were   awarded to a local company at a contract sum of Kshs.6,998,674, as per the  agreement dated 4 December, 2024. As at 30 June, 2025 the contractor had been p aid  in full. However, physical inspection conducted on 9 July, 2025 revealed that, contrary to  the Inspection and Acceptance Certificate dated 25 February, 2025, which indicated that  all works were complete and executed to specification; several works were   incomplete.  The dispensary block with a cost of Kshs.2,897,077, was approximately 50% complete  with all finishing works outstanding, the staff house block with a cost of Kshs.2,100,147,  was approximately 50% complete with all finishing works outstanding w hile the pit latrine  and fencing work at a cost of Kshs.415,250 and Kshs.1,286,200 respectively, had not  commenced.

294  625.4.   Delayed Construction of Fourteen ECDE Kitchens  T he County Executive, through the Department for Education, entered into a contract on  18 December, 2024 for the construction of fourteen (14) Early Childhood   Development  and   Education (ECDE) kitchens at a contract sum of Kshs.8,952,160. However, physical  i nspection conducted on 8 July, 2025 revealed that several key works had not been  completed, including ceiling works internal and external finishes such as floor tiles, wall  tiling, and concrete worktops, rainwater disposal systems, and kitchen extraction s ystems  valued at Kshs.481,320, Kshs.1,017,800, Kshs.179,200 and Kshs.182,000 respectively.  Further, there was evidence of poor workmanship, including poorly fitted doors and  windows.  625.5.   Irregularities in the Contract for Improvement of Naisiicho - Loruko Roa d  The County Executive awarded a contract for the improvement of the Loruko – Naisiicho  Road, at a cost of Kshs.3,992,500, procured through request for quotations method.  However, review of the payment and procurement documents revealed that the contract  agreement did not specify the contract duration or the implementation period. Further,  physical inspection carried out on 8 July, 2025 revealed that the contractor did not  construct a site - house structure and erect a publicity signboard.  .  625.6.   Irregularities in the Construction of Kangibalae - Kamoiti Road at Nachola  Ward  The County Executive awarded a con tract for the construction of the Kangibalae – Kamoiti  Road, at a cost of Kshs.6,997,300, procured through open tender advertised on 13  February, 2025. However, individual tender evaluation score sheets were not provided  for audit. This was contrary to Regul ation 31(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Regulations, 2020, which requires that they be retained as procurement records.  Further,   the   contract   agreement   did   not   indicate   the   contract   duration   or   the  implementation period, and it was signed   by the Head of Procurement Unit without  evidence of written delegation by the Accounting Officer. In addition, the professional  opinion dated 28 February, 2025 indicated that due diligence was conducted, but no due  diligence report was provided, contrary t o Section 83(1) of the Public Procurement and  Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which requires that such verification be documented in writing.  625.7.   Irregularities in the Improvement of Lmisigiyoi - Rangau - Lolgese Road  The County Executive awarded a contract for the improvement of the Lmisiyoi – Rangau –  Lolgese Road at a   contract sum of Kshs.3,995,000 to a local contractor. However, the  procurement documents, including the required three (3) quotations, tender evaluation  report, and regret letters to unsuccessful bidders, were not provided for audit. Further,  physical insp ection carried out on 10 April, 2025 revealed that although the contractor  was to undertake grading works valued at Kshs.2,016,000, cambering and drainage were  poorly executed, causing flooding during rainy seasons and leaving sections of the road  cut off   by the rains and the signboard had not been erected.

295  625.8.   Irregularities in the Improvement of Lolmolog - Kitobor Road  The County Executive entered into a contract with a local contractor for the opening of  the Lolmolog – Lesua – Kitobor Road at a contract sum of Kshs.3,995,000. However, only  one (1) quotation from the winnin g bidder was provided for audit, while the tender  evaluation report and regret letters to unsuccessful bidders were not provided, raising  doubt whether the mandatory minimum of three (3) quotations was sought as provided  by Section 106(2)(b) of the Public   Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which  requires at least three quotations to ensure effective competition.  Further, physical inspection carried out on 10 April, 2025 established that cambering and  drainage works were poorly executed, causing flo oding and sections of the road being  cut off during rainy seasons and signboard had not been erected.  625.9.   Irregularities in the Upgrading to Bitumen Standards to Marala l Law Court  –   Nuclear Roundabout Road  Review of the procurement and implementation of the road upgrading project awarded to  a local company at a contract sum of Kshs.18,890,669 revealed that the interim payment  documents lacked inspection and acceptance ce rtificates. This was contrary to Section  48(3)(b)   of   the   Public   Procurement   and   Asset   Disposal Act, 2015   which   requires  inspection of works immediately after their completion in order to ensure compliance with  the terms and specifications of the contract.  Further,   physical   inspection carried out on 11 July ,   2025 revealed depressions and  potholes, and key components including wingwalls, aprons, toe   walls and drop inlets,  s everal drainage structures, including headwalls and slab - on - drain works, all provided f or  in the Bills of Quantities and paid for were not constructed.   In addition, poor - quality sand  was used for drainage and roadside works and the poor sand - cement mix resulted in  erosion and depressions after rains, indicating substandard workmanship.  625.10.   Irregularities in the Procurement for Construction of Mbukiwa Footbridge  The   County   Executive   entered   into   a   contract   with   a   local   company   on  6 February, 2025 for the construction of the Mbukiwa Footbridge at a contract sum of  Kshs.9,399,700. Audit review of procurement documents revealed that the project was  awarded to the second - highest bidder, despite the lowest bidder quotin g an amount of  Kshs.8,732,800. The financial evaluation ranked the lowest bidder third with eighty - six  (86) points, while the winning bidder scored ninety - seven (97) points, yet no justification  was provided for the inconsistent ranking, even though all th ree (3) responsive bidders  passed the technical evaluation. Further, individual evaluation score sheets were not  provided, contrary to Regulation 31(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Regulations, 2020, which requires independent scoring by ea ch evaluation committee  member. In addition, although the contract period lapsed on 7 May, 2025, there was no  evidence that the contractor requested or was granted an extension. Physical inspection  carried out on 10 July, 2025 confirmed that construction h ad not commenced and the  implementing department did not provide an explanation or a completion plan.

296  625.11.   Poor Workmanship in the Construction of Gabions in Lesirkan Centre  The County Executive entered into a contract with a local company for the construction  of   gabions   at   Lesirkan   Centre   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.4,973,500.   However,  procurement   and   payment   documents,   including   the   payment   voucher,   supplier  quotations, requis ition documents, appointment letters, opening and evaluation minutes,  evaluation report, professional opinion, notification of award, regret letters, acceptance of  award, purchase order and the signed contract, were not provided for audit. Physical  inspect ion carried out on 9 July, 2025 revealed that while   the contractor was to construct  one hundred and fifty (150) gabion boxes valued at Kshs.4,020,000, only one hundred  and nineteen (119) boxes had been completed, leaving incomplete works of thirty - one  (31)   boxes costing Kshs.830,800 and the grouting applied to exposed gabion sections  exhibited poor workmanship, with cracks and weak finishes raising concerns on the  structural integrity and durability of the installations.  625.12.   Unsupported Provisional Prime Co st on Construction of Roads  Review   of   road   construction   contract   documents   revealed   that   an   amount   of  Kshs.1,350,000 was provided as a provisional prime sum for technic al supervision during  the implementation of eight (8) road construction contracts in the County. However, the  utilization   of   this   amount   was   not   supported   with   detailed   payment   schedules   or  supporting documents. Further, there was no evidence that the use   of the provisional sum  was requested and approved by the evaluation committee as required under Section  139(2)(e) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which mandates  written justification and formal approval before utilizing provisional   sums.  625.13.   Short Deliveries in the Contract for   Leirr Borehole Solarization  The County Executive awarded the Leirr Borehole Solarization Project to a local company  at a contract sum of Kshs.4,900,333 during the year under review. Physical inspection  carried out on 9 July, 2025 revealed that the supplier delivered ten (10) 550W pan els  instead of the specified twenty - six (26) 330W panels, and the camera inspection report  and the water chemical analysis and borehole reports were not provided for audit.  625.14.   Irregularities in the Contract for Improvement of Nairimirimo - Milgis Road  The County Executive entered into a contract with a local company for the improvement  of the Nairimirimo – Milgis Road at a contract sum of Kshs.3,998,320. However, review of  th e procurement documents revealed that the tender evaluation report was not signed by  the chairperson of the evaluation committee. This was contrary to Section 80(7) of the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which requires all committee member s  to   sign   the   report.   Further,   the   contract   agreement   did   not   indicate   the   contract  commencement and completion dates. In addition, physical inspection conducted on 10  July, 2025 revealed that although the contractor was to undertake grading works valued  a t Kshs.2,217,600, cambering was poorly executed, resulting in water stagnation, erosion  and depressions in several road sections.

297  625.15.   Undisclosed Project in the   County Integrated Development Plan  The statement of financial position and Note 26 to the   financial statements reflect an  amount of Kshs.1,067,261,831 in respect of property, plant and equipment. Included in  this amount is a balance of Kshs.587,130,907 relating to infrastructure assets out of which  an amount of Kshs.227,669,542 relates to payme nt for access roads.  Review of the County Integrated Development Plan (CIDP) revealed that the County  Executive in its third year was to construct and rehabilitate various roads and bridges.  However, the kilometers of constructed roads, graveled   and graded   roads, number of  drifts,   culverts,   gabions,   footbridges,   major   bridges   and   concrete   slabs   that   were  constructed or ought to have   been   constructed were not indicated in the County  Integrated   Development Plan, Annual Development Plan, approved budget for the year  2024/2025 and the procurement plan for 2024/2025.  In the circumstances, value for money on the expenditure totalling Kshs.330,667,998  could not be confirmed.  626.   Late Commitments of Good s , Works and Services  Review of procurement records revealed that expenditure commitments for various  supplies   of   goods   and   services   amounting   to   Kshs.227,303,314   were   made   after  31 May, 2025 without the written approval of the Acc ounting Officer. This was contrary to  Regulation 50(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2015 which provides that all commitments for the supply of goods or services shall be  done not later than the 31 May each year, except   with the express approval of the  Accounting Officer in writing.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  627.   Un - Utilized Cooking Appliances  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflects  use of goods and services expenditure of Kshs.1,782,133,252, which includes specialized  materials and services amoun t of Kshs.348,010,691. This amount includes a balance of  Kshs.5,304,000 for the purchase of thirty (30) cooking appliances for selected Early  Childhood Development and Education (ECDE) centres from a local supplier at a unit  cost   of   Kshs.176,800.   Review   of   procurement   documents   and   physical   inspection  conducted in July, 2025 revealed that no market survey was provided to justify the pricing.  This was contrary to Regulation 33(3)(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Regulations, 2020, which requir es procuring entities to conduct market surveys to inform  cost estimates. Further, inspection of seven (7) sampled ECDE centres established that  only one (1) appliance was in use, with headteachers reporting that the appliances lacked  adequate capacity for   their pupil populations, rendering them unsuitable for the intended  purpose.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.5,304,000 could  not be confirmed.

298  628.   Procurement of Live Animals  628.1.   Irregularities in the Purchase and Distri bution of Breeding Stock  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services expenditure totalling Kshs.1,782,133,252, which includes an  amount of Kshs.253,531,662 in respect to purchase of certified seeds, breeding stoc k  and live animals. Review of the procurement and payment documents revealed that an  expenditure amounting to Kshs.206,119,046 on purchase of live animals levealed the  following anomalies:  (i)   The approved list of animal suppliers, showing the type of animals   from each  supplier,   County   Integrated   Development   Plan   (CIDP)   to   show   the   animal  purchase plan, distribution list per Sub - County, individual beneficiaries’ list, the  basis of selection of beneficiaries and acknowledgement of receipt of the livestock  by th e beneficiaries, were not provided for audit.  (ii)   No market survey, price comparisons, or analysis was conducted to confirm that  the prices paid reflected prevailing market rates.  (iii)   The County Executive did not carry out pre - award farm inspections to verify th e  suppliers’ breeding capacity and herd health status to certify that the certification  of animals supplied were free from diseases, vaccination records and quarantine  requirements.  (iv)   There was no approved policy or framework for   beneficiaries’ selection and  distribution. The County Executive relied on community barazas and Member of  the County Assembly (MCA) lists, with many distribution forms lacking contact  details and containing unverifiable fingerprint acknowledgments.  (v)   The Co unty Executive did not provide Monitoring and Evaluation reports to assess  program performance, beneficiary satisfaction, or the impact of the breeding stock  distribution.  628.2.   Irregularities in the Purchase of Camels  The Department for Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries procured five hundred and  twenty - four (524) camels through open tendering at a contract sum of Kshs.42,320,000,  awarded to a local company.   However, review of tender opening minutes and evaluation  reports revealed that they were not signed or initialed by all committee members. This  was contrary to Sections 78(11) and 80(7) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Act, 2015. Further, a bid der with a lower offer amount of Kshs.41,796,000 was disqualified  on grounds of failing to submit a tender security amount of Kshs.890,800, despite  evidence that the security had been submitted. In addition, the winning bidder was  awarded   full   marks   for   fi nancial   capacity   despite   failing   to   provide   certified   bank  statements for the previous two (2) years as required, and the bidder lacked technical  experience, with no due diligence carried out as required under Section 83(1) of the Public  Procurement and As set Disposal Act, 2015.

299  Although the contract signed on 11 October, 2024 required delivery within twenty - one  (21)   days,   only   two   hundred   and   twenty - four   (224)   camels   were   delivered   on  12 March, 2025, five (5) months late and as at 30   June, 2025, three hundred (300) camels  remained undelivered despite the supplier having received an advance payment of  Kshs.18,090,992 which was not supported by an invoice, delivery note, or inspection and  acceptance report.  In the circumstances, the va lue for money on the expenditure live animals could not be  confirmed.  629.   Payment for Consultancy Services for Undelivered Valuation Roll  Review   of   payment   documents   revealed   that   the   County   Executive,   through   the  Department for Lands, Housing and Urban Planning, contracted a local consultancy firm  to prepare a valuation roll for the Maralal Municipality at a cost of Kshs.8,120,000, under  a   contract signed on 6 June, 2023, and full payment made on 25 September, 2024.  However, physical inspection in July, 2025 revealed that the final valuation roll had not  been submitted to the County Executive for use in revenue collection, an indication that  full payment was made without delivery of the contracted service.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure of Kshs.8,120,000 for  preparation of a valuation roll for the Maralal Municipality could not be confirmed.  630.   Long Outstanding Imprests  The statement of financial position and Note 23 to the financial statements reflect  receivables from non - exchange transactions balance of Kshs.1,303,300 in respect to  imprests which had not bee n surrendered long after their due dates and Management  had not initiated their recoveries. This was contrary to Regulation 93(6) of the Public  Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that in  the event of the imprest holder   failing to account for or surrender the imprest on the due  date, the Accounting Officer shall take immediate action to recover the full amount from  the salary of the defaulting officer with an interest at the prevailing Central Bank Rate.  In the circumst ances, Management was in breach of the law.  631.   Doubtful Training Payment on Fire Eradication  The statement of financial performance, and Note 10 to the financial statements, reflects  use of goods and services expenditure amount of Kshs.1,782,133,252. Included in the  balance is domestic travel and subsistence amount of Kshs.293,801,226, out of whic h an  amount of Kshs.1,189,000 was paid on 20 September, 2024 for the facilitation of a ten  (10) day firefighting training exercise. However, the attendance records of the one  hundred and seventy - four (174) trainees,   the course program, trainees’ travel evi dence  such as work tickets or bus fare receipts, documents supporting venue expenses and  participants selection criteria were not documented.

300  Further, the cash acknowledgement list accounting for the expenditure amounting to  Kshs.1,184,000 contained inco nsistencies, including missing Identity Card (ID) numbers,  signatures or thumbprints, lack of contact details and the payment voucher and cash  acknowledgement list were not dated. In addition, discrepancy between the payment  voucher which indicated trainin g on building materials and the imprest warrant which  indicated firefighting training was not explained.  In the circumstances, the value for money of the expenditure totalling Kshs.1,189,000  could not be confirmed.  632.   Lack of Framework Agreements in the Pro vision of Legal Services  The statement of financial performance and Note 10 to the financial statements reflect  use of goods and services expenditure of Kshs.1,782,133,252. Included in the amount is  other operating expenses balance of Kshs.336,177,045 out   of which an amount of  Kshs . 17,223,480   was   paid   to   four   (4)   private   legal firms representing   the   County  Executive   in   various   legal   cases   through   framework   agreements.   However,   the  framework agreements were not provided for audit review. Thi s was contrary to Section  114(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which limits framework  agreements to a maximum of three (3) years and requires annual value - for - money  assessments for agreements exceeding one (1) year.  In the circum stances, Management was in breach of the law.  633.   Failure to Transfer Resources to Maralal Municipality  The statement of financial performance and Note 11   to the financial statements   reflect  transfers to other Gov ernment entities amounting to Kshs.541,736,919. However, review  of transfers documents revealed that the County Executive did not transfer financial  resources to the Maralal Municipality, despite an approved budgetary allocation for the  year under review c omprising of current and capital transfers to Government agencies of  Kshs.35,000,000   and   Kshs.25,375,442   respectively.   No   evidence   was   provided   to  confirm that these funds were disbursed to the Municipality during the year under review.  This was contrary t o Section 20(1) of the Urban Areas and Cities Act, 2011 (amended  2019), which requires that all municipal functions specified in the First Schedule be  transferred upon establishment, and Section 2.3 of the Maralal Municipal Charter, (2018)  which outlines t he key functions under the Municipality’s operational mandate.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  634.   Non - Submission of Financial Statements for County Emergency Fund  The statement of financial performance and Note 13 to the financi al statements reflect  other grants and subsidies amount of Kshs.98,758,637, out of which an amount of  Kshs.30,000,000 relates to Emergency Relief and Refugee Assistance. However, the  County Executive did not prepare and submit financial statements for the   Emergency  Fund to the Auditor - General. This was contrary to Section 115(1) of the Public Finance  Management Act, 2012 which requires the County Treasury to prepare and submit to the

301  Auditor - General, financial statements in respect of the Emergency Fund for   that year not  later than three months after the end of each financial year.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  635.   Non - Compliance with the Facilities Improvement Financing Requirements  The statement of financial   performance and Note 11 to the financial statements of the  County   Revenue Fund   reflects own source   revenue amount of Kshs.262,226,498.  Included in the amount is hospital fees of Kshs.9,410,585 in respect to transfers to County  Revenue Fund (CRF) by Samburu   County Teaching and Referral Hospital which were  not transferred back to the health facility. This was contrary to Section 5(1) of the Facilities  Improvement Financing Act, 2023 which requires that all monies raised or received by or  on behalf of all publ ic health facilities be retained in the Hospital Facilities Improvement  Financing account. In addition, there were no Authority - to - Incur Expenditure (AIEs)  issued to the Hospital by the Chief Officer - Health before utilization of the funds.  In the circumst ances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AN D GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  636.   Lack of Effectiveness in Internal Audit Function  Review of the Internal Audit Function revealed weaknesses, including lack of functional  independence due to the absence of a dedicated budget, non - adherence to The National  Treasury’s Internal Audit Guidelines (March, 2016) as audit reports were prepared  a nnually instead of quarterly, and a limited audit scope that covered only two (2) rather  than all departments.  Further, the Internal Audit Committee met only twice during the year under review instead  of the required quarterly meetings, and Management di d not respond to or implement  recommendations issued by the Internal Audit Function.  In the circumstances, the independence and effectiveness of the internal audit function  could not be confirmed.  637.   L ack of Risk Management Policy  Review of policy documents revealed that Management did not provide evidence of an  approved Risk Management Policy to guide on risk identification, assessment and  mitigation during the year under review.  In   the   circumstances,   the   effectiveness   of   risk   ma nagement   and   internal   control  processes could not be confirmed.

302  638.   Integrity of Data Maintained in Integrated Payroll Personnel Database and  Manual Payrolls  Review of both the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) and manual  payrolls for the year under review revealed that two (2) employees shared the same  national identification number but appeared under two (2) different payroll numbers. No  explan ation was provided to justify how one identity card could have multiple payroll  entries. Further, eighty - three (83) employees had no recorded job designations, the  absence   of   assigned   roles   and   responsibilities   raises   concerns   regarding   proper  deployment,   supervision, and accountability for staff.  In addition, key employee bio data including NSSF numbers, NHIF numbers, ID numbers,  dates of birth, appointment dates, KRA PINs, and bank account details, was not recorded  for all employees. The reliability of p ayroll processing was in doubt and increased the risk  of paying non - existent or irregular employees.  In the circumstances, the existence and effectiveness of internal controls over payroll  management could not be confirmed.  639.   Lack of an Annual Recruitment P lan  The County Executive recruited seven hundred and forty - eight (748)   employees during  the year under review.   However, the County Public Service Board did not have in p lace  the annual recruitment plan to guide on the recruitments. Further, no evidence was  provided as proof that budgetary allocation was sought before recruitment.  In   the   circumstances,   the   effectiveness   of   internal   controls   in   human   resource  management c ould not be confirmed.
