343  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF ELGEYO/MARAKWET   –   NO.28  REPORT ON   THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for   Qualified   Opinion  713.   Inaccuracies in Property, Plant and Equipment Balance  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balan ce of  Kshs.8,676,298,839   which   differs   with   the   corresponding   Note   26   to   the   financial  statements balance of Kshs.8,656,393,383 resulting in an unexplained variance of  Kshs.19,905,456. Included in property, plant and equipment balance are assets from the  D efunct Local Authorities   balance of   Kshs.568,889,166 which were not valued.  In the circumstances, the accuracy of the biological assets could not be confirmed.  714.   Inaccuracies in Biological Assets  The statement of financial position reflects   biological assets balance of Kshs.274,642,715  as disclosed in Note 30 to the financial statements. However, the recognition of biological  assets failed to account for the change in fair value in biological assets arising from growth  and valuation.  In the   circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of   property, plant and equipment  balance of Kshs.8,676,298,839   could not be confirmed.  715.   Misstatements in the Statement of Cash Flows  The statement of cash flows reflects cash flows from investing activities of   NIL balance.  However, casting of the statement of cash flows balances revealed cash out flows from  investing activities balance of Kshs.7,727,881. In addition, the statement of cash flows  reflects net increase in cash and cash equivalents of Kshs.256,614,8 59. However, casting  of the statement cash flows disclosed net decrease in cash and cash equivalents of  Kshs.240,188,338 resulting in a variance of Kshs.496,803,197.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the statement of cash flows  could not be confirmed.  716.   Non - Disclosure of Returns of Unutilized Funds to County Revenue Fund  The statement of financial performance of the County Executive did not disclose returns  to County Revenue Fund. However, the statement of performance of the County Revenue  Fund and Note 9 to the financial statements reflect returns from County Executive ba lance  of Kshs .17,775,994.  In the circumstances,   the accuracy and completeness of the financial statements could  not be confirmed.

344  Emphasis of Matter  717.   Budgetary   Control   and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects an approved final  budgeted receipts of Kshs.6,043,895,538 against actual receipts of Kshs.5,013,283,841  resulting in under - funding of Kshs.1,030,611,607 or 17% of the budget. However, the  Co unty Executive spent an amount of Kshs.4,748,941,101 against actual receipts of  Kshs.5,013,283,841, resulting in an under - utilization of Kshs.264,342,740 or 5% of the  actual receipts.  The under - funding of funds affected the planned activities and may have   impacted  negatively on service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  718.   Unresolved Prior Year Audit Matters  In the audit report of the previous year, several issues were raised under report on  Financial Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in the use of Public  Resources and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance. However, review of their status during the audit indicated that twenty - two  (22) i ssues remained unresolved   as listed at the end of this report.  Other Information  719.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  720.   Failure to Establish a County Budget and Economic Forum  As previously reported, the County Executive has not established a County Budget and  Economic Forum. This contravenes Section 137 of the Public Finance and Management  Act, 2012   which provides that a County Government shall establish a forum to be known  as the Elgeyo/Marakwet County Budget and Economic Forum.  This forum is to provide a means for consultation by the County Government on  preparation of County Plans, the County Fisc al Strategy Paper and the Budget Review  and Outlook Paper for the County and matters relating to budgeting, the economy and  financial management at the County level.

345  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  721.   Excessive Budget   Allocation to the County Assembly  Review of budget documents revealed that the County Assembly of Elgeyo/Marakwet  was allocated an amount of Kshs.619,407,879 which is eq uivalent to 12% of the County  Government’s total revenue of Kshs.5,013,283,841. The approved allocation exceeded  the statutory limit, as allocation should have amounted to Kshs.350,929,869 or 7% of the  total county revenue. The excess allocation of 5% or K shs.268,478,010 was contrary to  the   provisions   of   Regulation   25(1)(f)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that the approved expenditure of a  County Assembly shall not exceed seven percent (7%) of the total   revenue of the County  Government or twice the personnel emoluments of that County Assembly, whichever is  lower.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  722.   Inadequate Planning for Transition from Cash Basis to Accrual Reporting  The   County Executive did not plan adequately to transition from cash basis of reporting  to accrual reporting in accordance with The National Treasury’s Circular No.3/2025   dated  14 April, 2025 which provides guidelines for the migration to accrual accounting in   the  Public Sector. The County Executive did not appoint a Steering Committee and a Project  Manager to guide the transition process as required.  Further, transition roadmap, work plan or implementation framework were not developed  to facilitate structured   and timely migration to accrual reporting.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  723.   Acting Appointments Beyond the Stipulated Period  Review of the payroll and payment schedules revealed that seven (7) Senior County  Executive officials have been in acting position beyond the stipulated six (6) months  period. Two (2) officers; Director of Human Resources and Director of Alcoholic Drinks  C ontrol Fund, were in acting positions without official appointment letters to the acting  positions. The Director of Supply Chain Management had been acting since 9 February,  2022   through   an   appointment   letter   dated   10   March,   2022,   from   the   County  Secretary /Head of County Public Service .  Further   County Public Service Board did not provide any evidence to show efforts to  recruit   substantive   holders   of   the   above   positions   despite   the   prolonged   acting  appointments. This was contrary to Section   34(5)(b) of the Public Service Commission  Act, 2017 (Revised 2023) which states that an officer may be appointed in an acting  capacity for a period of at least thirty (30) days but not exceeding a period of six (6)  months.

346  In the circumstances, Management   was in breach of the law.  724.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Casual Employment  Review of the payroll revealed that the County Public Service Board   engaged ninety - five  (95) employees at   the   Department   for Lands and   thirteen   (13) employees at   the  Governor’s   Office on temporary basis on a three (3) months’ renewable contract on  1 July, 2016. However, they have served continuously since then. The   employees’   terms  of employment were not converted to permanent basis contrary to Section 37 of the  Employment Act, 2007 which provides for conversion of the casual employment to regular  employment terms for employees who have worked in an entity continuously for mor e  than two (2) months.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  725.   Lack   of Annual Recruitment Plans  Review of records revealed that the County Executive recruited fifteen (15) employees  during the year.   However, there was no recruitment plans to guide the recruitment  process.  Further, no evidence was provided for review to prove that the recruitment was budgeted  for. In addition,   twelve (12)   employees in the IPPD system were not in the employee list  pro vided by Chief Officers, and were paid salaries amounting to Kshs.3,993,880   during  the year under review.   This was   contrary to Section 59(1)(g) of the County Governments  Act, 2012 which requires the County Public Service Board to facilitate the developmen t  of   a   coherent,   integrated   human   resource   planning   and   budgeting   for   personnel  emoluments in counties.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  726.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on   Basic Salary  Review of the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) and Human Resources  Information Systems (HRIS) for the County Government revealed several employees  earned net salaries which were less than a third of their basic pay during the year as  tabula ted below;  Month   Jul   Aug   Sep   Oct   Nov   Dec   Jan   Feb   Mar   Apr   May   Jun  No. of Officers  below a Third  163   154   146   371   260   2   98   12 3   135   120   142   19  This was contrary to Section (19)(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which provides that  without   prejudice to any right of recovery of any debt due, and notwithstanding the  provisions of any other written law, the total amount of all deductions which may be made  by an employer from the wages of his employee at any one time shall not exceed two -  thirds   of such wages.

347  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  727.   Audit of the Payroll  727.1.   Irregular Budgeting of Employee Costs  A Special Audit established that the ratio of the budgeted compensation of employees to  budgeted revenue   exceeded 35% in the three (3) financial years which were reviewed  and reported (2022   -   38%, 2023   -   43% and 2024   -   43%) .   This was   contrary to Regulation  25(1)(b) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015  which limits the County   Governments’ expenditure on wages and benefits to a maximum  of 35% of total revenue for the year.  In addition, comparison of actual   c ompensation of   e mployee   with actual revenue as  reflected in the financial statements revealed that the County   Executive also exceeded  the thirty - five (35%) percent threshold in the previous three (3) financial years (2022   -  49%, 2023   -   52%, 2024   -   55%).  727.2.   Irregular   Engagement of County Employee  The   Special Audit for the financial year 2023/2024 revealed that an employee was  concurrently   engaged by both the County Executive of Elgeyo/Marakwet and   the County  Executive of Turkana. The officer received a gross salary of Kshs.2,315,500 from the two  Count y Executives. This was in breach of   Section   26   of   the   Leadership   and   Integrity   Act,  2012 ,   which prohibits a full - time state officer from engaging in other gainful employment.  727.3.   Irregular Payment of Salary Arrears  Special Audit for the year   2023/2024 revealed that seventy (70) employees were  irregularly paid   an amount of Kshs.15,547,510 monthly gross pay as arrears. The  employees did not meet the eligibility criteria stipulated in Section 6.1 of the Compendium  of Remuneration and Benefits whi ch determines remuneration and benefits for state  officers and other public officers serving in the County Executive.  727.4.   Irregular   Payment of Hardship Allowance  Special Audit for the financial year 2023/2024 revealed that seventeen (17) employees  were overpaid hardship allowance totalling Kshs.632,400. The overpayment was a  financial loss to the County Executive and ineffective use of public resources.  727.5.   Failure   to Withhold and Remit Statutory Deductions  Special Audit revealed that an amount of Kshs.348,000 in respect of PAYE was not  deducted and remitted   to Kenya Revenue Authority. Further, employee and employer  contributions to the National Social Security Fun d (NSSF) amounting to Kshs.656,640  was   not   remitted.   This   was   contrary   to   Section   22(1)(a)   of   the   Public   Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which states that an Accounting  Officer   shall   comply   with   any   tax,   levy,   duty,   pension,   commi tments   and   audit  commitments as may be provided for by legislation.   In addition , there were cases of  delayed remittance of NHIF, PAYE and NSSF deductions.   This exposed the County  Executive to risk of being subjected to penalties and interest.

348  In the circ umstances, Management was in breach of the law.  728.   Non - Compliance with   the Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) records revealed that  the County Executive had a total of 1,542 employees, out of whom 1,461 employees or  approximately 95% were from the dominant community in the County.   This was contrary  to   Section 7(1) and (2) of the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, which  stipulates that all public establishments shall seek to represent the diversity of the people  of Kenya in the employment of staff and that no public establishment shall have mor e  than one - third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In addition, the County Government recruited 15 employees during the year who were all  from the local dominant ethnic community, an indication that Management was not  making any effort to brid ge the existing ethnicity gap.   This contravenes Section 65(1)(e)  of the County Governments Act, 2012, which requires that at least 30% of the vacant  posts at entry level should be filled by candidates who are not from the dominant ethnic  community in the C ounty.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .  729.   Irregularities   in Training Management  Examination of human resource records in relation to trainings expenditure revealed that  Management did not carry out training monitoring and evaluation, employee performance  appraisals and training impact assessments during the year. This was contrary to   Section  H.3(1) of the Public Service Commission Human Resource Manual of May, 2016 which  provides that training in the Public Service shall be based on training needs assessment.  Further, Section H.3(3) requires that selection of trainees for all trainin g programmes will  be based on identified needs and training for performance improvement that address  individual, organizational and national goals. In addition, the criteria of selection of  personnel to attend various trainings could not be established as   the trainings offered  were not linked to employee performance appraisals and identified skills gaps.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  730.   Inefficiencies   in Revenue Management System  Review of contract documents for the Revenue Management System revealed that the  County   Executive   contracted   a   Telcom   Company   for   the   design,   deployment   and  operationalization   of   the   County   Revenue   Management   System   at   a   contract   of  Kshs.27,719,658 payable   in three (3) phases. The supporting documents revealed that  the County Executive paid an amount of Kshs.17,517,718 to the Telcom Company that  included a payment of Kshs.1,296,547 which represents a 4% share of revenue collected  for the period from August,   2024 to May, 2025. However, the system modules for citizen  self - service portal, enforcement and integration with banks and hospital systems were not  operational and integration with the County’s banking systems had not been implemented  and manual reconcil iations continued to be performed by revenue officers.

349  Further, the County Executive had not implemented a Hospital Revenue Management  System for hospitals within the County that is linked to the County Revenue Collection  System. The County was therefore   not in a position to centrally oversee the revenue  collection and reporting process for the health facilities.  In the circumstances, the value for money for the expenditure of Kshs.17,517,718 spent  on the system could not be confirmed.  731.   Long   Outstanding Payables   –   Refundable Deposits and Prepayments  The statement of financial position reflects refundable deposits and prepayments balance  of Kshs.93,654,265 as disclosed in Note 33 to the financial statements. Analysis of ageing  balances reveale d the status as follows; less than one (1) year Kshs.33,499,337; between  1 - 2   years   Kshs.13,763,797;   between   2 - 3   years   Kshs.6,699,967   and   over   3   years  Kshs.39,691,164.   This   was   contrary   to   Regulation   41(2)   of   the   Public   Finance  Management (County Government s) Regulation, 2015, which provides that debt service  payments shall be a first charge on the County Revenue Fund and the Accounting Officer  shall ensure this is done to the extent possible that the county Government does not  default on debt obligations.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  732.   Irregular   Procurement   of Air   Ticketing Services  Included in the use of goods and services amount of Kshs.1,406,917,625 is foreign travel  and subsistence amount totalling   Kshs.5,250,573. However, review of procurement  records revealed the following anomalies:  (i)   The procurement plan for the financial year indicated that air ticketing services  would be sourced through the Request for Quotation (RFQ) method. However, the  servic es were procured through a framework agreement without documented  justification or amendment to the procurement plan.  (ii)   Seven (7) bidders responded to the framework bidding process contrary to Section  114(1)(c) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal A ct 2015 and Regulation  102(1)(b) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, which  mandates inclusion of a minimum of seven alternative vendors for each category.  However, only two (2) firms signed for the framework agreements with the   County  Executive. Further, no contract agreements were provided for the remaining five  (5) bidders, raising concerns over the completeness and competitiveness of the  framework arrangement.  (iii)   Contrary to Regulation 101(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset   Disposal  Regulations, 2020, the use of the framework agreement appeared to restrict fair  competition. All orders were issued to a single supplier, despite the existence of  multiple vendors and the supplier was not among the 12 prequalified firms for air  ti cketing services.

350  (iv)   Pricing terms were not clearly defined in the framework agreement. In addition,  there   was   no   documentary   evidence   of   market   surveys   or   value - for - money  assessments before awarding contracts, contrary to Regulation 101(3)(a) of the  Public   Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, which prohibits awards  where prices exceed indicative market rates.  (v)   There was no evidence that mini - competitions were conducted among framework  contractors as required by Regulation 103(4) of the   Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Regulations, 2020. No written invitations, financial bids, or evaluation  records were presented to confirm that contracts were awarded to the lowest  evaluated tenderers.  (vi)   The framework agreements did not specify essent ial details such as maximum  quantities contrary to Regulations 102(1)(e) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires an estimate of the total volume or  scope of work or quantity of purchases expected to be made for the dur ation of the  framework agreement, as appropriate; and details on ceiling prices contrary to  Regulation 106(5) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations,  2020, which requires that a procuring entity should ensure that the price or  quantities   for all the orders does not exceed any ceiling amount stated in the  contract.  (vii)   Further, the individual LPOs lacked detailed breakdown necessary to establish full  cost as required by Regulation 106(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Regulation s, 2020 which requires that Individual orders shall include all  the details required to establish the full cost or price for the delivery of goods, works  or services.  (viii)   The Head of Procurement did not prepare and submit the required quarterly  reports on fra mework contract usage to the Accounting Officer and Internal Auditor  as required by Regulation 134(3) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal  Regulations, 2020.  In the circumstances,   Management   was in breach of the law.  733.   Conflict   Between   County Act and National Laws  The County   Executive   in a bid to address development disparities through e quality, equity  and non - discrimination envisaged in Article 27 of   the Constitution of Kenya, enacted  specific local legislation to provide a framework for the allocation of funds to ward - based  projects known as the Elgeyo Marakwet Development Act, 2015. However, review of the  Act, revealed that there were sections that c ontradicted National Legislations such as the  Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 and Public Finance Management Act,  2012 and Regulations, 2015.  In addition, there is a risk of voiding projects initiated through a County legislation that is  in conflict with National legislation in accordance with Article 191(1) and (2) of the  Constitution of Kenya, that clarifies on conflicts between National and County legislation

351  in respect of matters falling within the concurrent jurisdiction of both leve ls of Government.  National legislation prevails over County legislation.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  734.   Conflict   of   Interest   by Members of the County Assembly  Members of the County Assembly (MCA) through the provisions of Section 17 of the  Elgeyo / Marakwet   Equitable   Development   Act,   2015   were   also   members   of   Ward  Development Committees in their respective wards. Section 19 of the Elgeyo / Marakwet  Equitable Develo pment Act, 2015 grants the MCAs power to award tenders for ward -  based contracts, monitoring and evaluating projects within the ward, ensuring compliance  with the contract terms. It was therefore evident that the MCAs were involved in the  County Executive f unctions which resulted to conflict of interest. This was contrary to  Section (2)(a) and (b) of the County Governments Act, 2012 which requires that a member  of the County Assembly shall not be directly or indirectly involved in the Executive  functions of   the County Government and its administration; or delivery of services as if  the member were an officer or employee of the County Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  735.   Non - Compliance   with Fiscal Responsibility Principles  The statement of financial performance reflected total receipts of Kshs.5,013,283,841 and  actual   expenditure   of   Kshs.4,748,941,101.   However,   employee   costs   totalled  Kshs.2,635,956,505, representing approximately 53% of total revenue which exceeded  the 35%   ceiling prescribed under Section 15(2)(b) of the Public Finance Management  Act, 2012 by 18%.  Further, the County Executive Committee (CEC) Member for Finance and Economic  Planning did not set a limit on the County Government’s expenditure on wages and  ben efits for its public officers, contrary to Regulation 25(1)(a)) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015.  In addition, the County Executive spent an amount of Kshs.4,748,941,101, out of which  an amount of Kshs.4,516,480,644 (95%) was recurrent expenditure and an amount of  Kshs.232,460,457 (5%) was development expenditure. It was noted that the development  spen ding fell below the 30% minimum threshold required by Section   15(2)(a) of the Public  Finance Management Act, 2012 which   mandates that   at least 30% of National and County  Government budgets must be allocated to development expenditure   over the medium  term,   promoting fiscal responsibility by ensuring funds go to growth, not just recurrent  costs.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  736.   Partial   Funding of Projects  The   County   Executive   initiated   and   awarded   twenty - two   (22)   contracts   totalling  Kshs. 50,627,805   that were not executed to completion. Management explained that the  partial funding was due to inadequate allocation of funds. This was contrary to Section

352  53(8) of the Public Procu rement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which requires that  Accounting Officers shall not commence any procurement proceeding until satisfied that  sufficient funds to meet the obligations of the resulting contract are reflected in its  approved budget estimates . The Act further requires that an Accounting Officer who  knowingly commences any procurement process without ascertaining whether the good,  work or service is budgeted for, commits an offence under this Act.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach   of the law.  737.   Water   Projects   Verification  Physical inspection of sampled water projects during the month of July, 2025 revealed  the following anomalies;  737.1.   Muno Primary and Secondary School Borehole Project  The County Executive initiated a borehole project at Muno Primary and Secondary  Schools at a contract sum of Kshs.3,123,000. However, there was no signage post  installed   at   the   project   site.   Therefore,   Management   did   not   disclose   key   project  information su ch as name, contractor, source of funding, implementation timelines and  cost, undermining transparency and limiting public oversight. In addition, the borehole  area   was   unprotected   since   no   fencing   was   done.   This   exposed   the   borehole  infrastructure to the   risk of environmental degradation, vandalism and posed safety  concerns to school going children.  737.2.   Kapsisi Water Project  The   County   Executive   initiated   Kapsisi   Water   Project   at   a   contract   sum   of  Kshs.3,101,900. However, there was no project signage erecte d at the site. In addition,  the Water Project lacked perimeter fencing, making it vulnerable to tampering or misuse.  Although the water source infrastructure appeared installed, no piping network had been  extended to the targeted beneficiary communities. T his limited access and denied  residents the intended benefits of a clean and reliable water supply, which was the  primary goal of the investment.  737.3.   Cheminya Water Project  The   County   Executive   initiated   Cheminya   Water   Project   at   a   contract   sum   of  Kshs.2,4 97,250. However, it was noted that two (2) solar panels were missing at the  Project   and   the   solar - powered   system   installed   to   support   the   water   project   was  incomplete, yet the panels were vital for powering pumps and ensuring continuous water  flow.  In   the circumstances, the value for money for the expenditure incurred on the water  projects could not be confirmed.  738.   Unsatisfactory Implementation of Works at Kapteren Health Centre  Review of records provided revealed that the County Executive entered into a contract  with a local contractor in May, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.4,589,732 to construct

353  outpatient   block   and   a   septic   tank at   Kapteren   Health   Centre.   However, physical  veri fication carried out in the month of July, 2025 revealed the following anomalies:  (i)   Iron sheets used in roofing was gauge 30 instead of gauge 28 provided for in the  BQs.  (ii)   Ablution block provided for in BQs and connection and piping of septic drainage  were   not done.  (iii)   Leakages were noted on the roof, the contractor was not on site and the building  was not in use.  (iv)   There was no documentary evidence provided by the Project Implementation  Committee on the Contract Management Plan that was to provide for   review  meetings, a risk register maintained to monitor all identified contract risks and their  mitigation plan and a status report that include; executive summary report on  performance of activities and budget; and any other issues relevant to the contract  such as environmental and general   observation on   the performance rating.  (v)   There were two (2) other blocks on the compound which were constructed to  completion in 2013 and was meant to serve as maternity block and laboratory  respectively. However, these tw o blocks had not been put to use.  In the circumstances, the Value for money on the outpatient block and septic tank at  Kapteren Health Centre could not be confirmed.  739.   Unsatisfactory Implementation of Works at Toror Health Centre  Review of contract documents revealed that procurement requisition for the project was  approved on 3 May, 2024. The successful bidders signed a contract agreement with the  County Executive on 3 June, 2024 at a contract sum of Kshs.2,499,900 for a contract  period of ninety (90) days. On 1 August, 2024, the contractor requested for contract  extension covering the period 2 August, 2024 to 30 December, 2024. This request was  granted by the procuring entity on 5 August, 2024. Inspection and acceptance was done  o n 20 December, 2024 and payment certificate for the entire contract sum was raised by  the contractor on 22 January, 2025.  However, physical verification carried out in month of July, 2025 revealed the following  anomalies;  (i)   There was no documentary evidenc e provided by the Project Implementation  Committee on the contract Management Plan that was to provide for review  meetings, a risk register maintained to monitor all identified contract risks and their  mitigation plan and a status report that include execu tive summary report on  performance of activities and budget; and any other issues relevant to the contract  such as environmental and general observation on   the performance rating.

354  (ii)   The Project was delayed by thirty - six (36) weeks based on the initial contract  delivery date and twenty - eight (28) weeks since the lapse of the contract extension  period.  (iii)   Leakages were noted on the roof and the building was not in use.  (iv)   There was no access road to the facility.  (v)   Ownership documents of the land on which the dispensary is located were not  provided for audit review.  (vi)   The Hospital serves less than ten (10) patients daily despite being a primary  healthcare centre where patien ts are attended to at no cost. These low numbers  may be as a result of the inaccessibility of the hospital and raises doubt   if  effectiveness   feasibility was carried out before commencement of the project.  (vii)   The contractor was not on site and there was no ac tivity ongoing at the time of  physical verification.  In the circumstances, the value for money incurred on the expenditure on the   one bed -  roomed staff house constructed at Toror Health Centre   could not be confirmed.  740.   Other Projects   Implementation Follow - Up  The County Executive implemented several projects during the year out of which fourteen  (14)   projects   with   a   total   contract   value   of   Kshs.102,429,488   were   not   properly  implemented.  In the circumstances, the value for money on   the expenditure for the above projects could  not be confirmed.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  741.   Lack   of Fixed Assets Register  Review of records revealed that the County Executive did not   maintain a comprehensive  fixed assets register detailing assets owned, their locations, acquisition dates, values and  custodian’s. This was contrary to Regulation 138(1) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires   each County Government entity  to maintain a register of all its assets in a form approved by the County Treasury.  In the circumstances, effectiveness of internal controls over fixed assets could not be  confirmed.  742.   Weaknesses   in Information Communication Technology Internal Control  Environment  Review of   Information Communication Technology   (ICT) internal control environment  revealed that t he County did not have in place ;   I C T Strategic Committee and a Steering

355  Committee to provide guidance to IT - related decision - making processes ,   I C T Business  Continuity Plan and therefore, in case of a disaster, the County may not recover critical  information resources hence adversely affect   its operations   and   a documented training  program to build I C T capacity.  Further, t he server room ha d a   dysfunctional   air conditioning system   did not have   a  biometric   access   control   system,   environmental   monitoring   system   to   monitor   the  humidity and temperature and a closed - circuit television (CCTV) system to monitor  access to the server room.  In the circumstances, the existence of an effectiveness of the ICT control s could not be  confirmed.  743.   Deficiencies in Audit Committee Operations  Review of the audit committee revealed the following anomalies;  (i)   An   annual   report   on   the   review   of   the   independence,   performance   and  competence of the Internal Audit Unit was not   published contrary to Regulation  159(2) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2015.  (ii)   The Accounting Officer did not develop and submitted to the Chairman of the Audit  Committee   a response and action plan to the   recommendations made in the audit  reports.  (iii)   The Accounting Officer, who was responsible for the implementation of audit  recommendations,   had   not   developed   response   and   action   plan   on  implementation   of   audit   recommendations   and   submitted   the   same   to   the  Cha irperson of the Audit Committee.  (iv)   The Audit Committee did not review and report to the Executive Management on  the significant financial reporting issues and judgements made in connection with  the preparation of the County Executive’s financial statements.  (v)   The Audit Committee did not rev iew the County Executive’s internal financial  controls.  (vi)   The Audit Committee did not perform an independent review of the financial  statements to ensure the integrity and transparency of the financial reporting  process during the period under review.  (vii)   The   Audit Committee did not monitor and review the effectiveness of the Internal  Audit Function.  (viii)   Management did not provide evidence that the Audit Committee had assessed the  performance   of   the   Head   of   Internal   Audit,   monitored   Management’s  responsiveness to   internal audit findings and recommendations, or evaluated the

356  effectiveness of the internal audit function within the County’s risk management  framework during the period under review.  (ix)   One (1) Member of the Committee, who served in the previous committee,   had his  contract extended for a further period of three (3) years. However, no evidence  was provided to show that the performance of the Member had been evaluated  and that was reappointed based on the outcome of his performance appraisal.  (x)   The Audit   Committee did not issue periodic, annual and special/investigative  reports and evidence that the same were made available to stakeholders.  (xi)   The Audit Committee did not produce periodic reports to the Accounting Officer  citing key issues affecting the opera tions of the County Executive during the period  under audit.  (xii)   The Audit Committee did not carry out a self - assessment and submitted to the  Accounting Officer a report on its performance and achievements against its  mandate, roles, duties, responsibilities , its composition, training, meetings, charter  and performance to ensure that the Audit Committee met its objectives efficiently  and effectively.  (xiii)   The Audit Committee did not seek for feedback from the Senior Management on  their effectiveness.  (xiv)   Further, b oth the Internal Audit Unit and the Audit Committee did not have  independent budgets or authority to incur expenditure. Instead, they relied entirely  on   the   Office   of   the   Governor   under   which   they   have   been   placed.   This  arrangement   deprived   the   Audit   Commi ttee   and   Internal   Audit   operational  independence, in contravention of Regulation 155 of Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015. The Regulation requires the Head of  Internal Audit unit in a County Government entity to report admini stratively to the  Accounting Officer and functionally to the Audit Committee.  (xv)   At the time of audit in July, 2025, two (2) Members of the Audit Committee who  were members of the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya (ICPAK)  were not in good pr ofessional standing.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the Audit Committee to provide oversight to the  County could not be confirmed.  744.   Deficiencies in the Internal Audit Function  Review of the Internal Audit Department revealed the   following anomalies;  (i)   The Head of Internal Audit Department did not provide evidence of annual report  of self - assessment of the effectiveness of the Internal Audit Department and  annual review of the performance to County Treasury.  (ii)   The Internal Audit Dep artment did not carry out risk assessments neither did they  have in place a risk register which was essential for effective internal audit.

357  (iii)   The   Internal   Audit   Unit   did   not   undertake   a   professional   assessment   of   its  effectiveness by a professionally recogn ized body or institution in the last three (3)  years.  (iv)   The Head of Internal Audit Department did not submit to the Audit Committee a  progress report summarizing; work performed in comparison with the approved  Annual Work Plan, reports on   consulting engagements undertaken and other  special assignments, risks which Management had accepted to undertake and  were   not   acceptable   according   to   the   Internal   Auditor’s   opinion,   major  disagreements with Management, reports on cooperation between inter nal and  external audit and periodic management accounts.  (v)   There   was   no   Organogram   to   inform   operation   structure   and   reporting  relationships. In addition, it was noted that the Directorate had been placed under  the Chief Officer in the Office of the Governo r, and without a separate budget or  authority to incur expenditure.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the Internal Audit Function could not be  confirmed.  745.   Manual Processing of Salary  The County Executive processed employee salaries totalling Kshs.230,406,186 using  manual payrolls maintained in Excel spreadsheets. The use of manual payroll systems  increases the risk of errors, omissions or manipulation due to lack of automated controls.  In   the   circumstances, the   effectiveness of internal controls and   integrity   of   salary  payments could not be confirmed.

358  Unresolved Prior Year Matters  No .   Audit Issues for 2023/2024  1   Variances Between Financial Statements and IFMIS Records  2   Unsupported Health Facilities Operational Bank Balances  3   Unsupported Pending Bills  4   Unsupported   Expenditure on Legal Services  5   Failure to Establish a County Budget and Economic Forum  6   Excessive Budgetary Allocation to the County Assembly  7   Failure to Operationalize the Office of the County Attorney  8   Failure to Adhere to Ethnic Diversity Requirement in Employment  9   Non - submission of Financial Statements for Level 4 Hospitals  10   Conflict in the Law   -   The Elgeyo Marakwet Equitable Development Act, 2015  11   Conflict of Interest by Members of County Assembly on the   County Executive  Functions  12   Partial   Funding   of Projects  13   Non - Compliance with the 35% Wage Bill  14   Stalled Proposed Maintenance of Chepkerengoi Road in Sengwer Ward  15   Irregular   Funding of National Government Functions  16   Irregular   Payment of College Fees for KMTC Students  17   Implementation of Projects with no Value for   Money  18   Non - Adherence to One Third Pay Policy  19   Irregular Implementation of Income Generating Activity Program (IGA)  20   Understaffing of   Internal   Audit Department  21   Operational   Shortcomings in the Audit Committee  22   Payroll Management for the   County Executive   of   Elgeyo / Marakwet

359  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF NANDI   –   NO.29  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  746.   Inaccuracies in the Financial Statements  746.1.   Unsupported and Long Outstanding Trade and Other Payables  The statement of financial position ref lects trade and other payables opening Nil balance  as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements. However, the ageing analysis for trade  and other payables as disclosed in Note 32 reflects trade and other payables totalling  Kshs.447,408,678 outstandi ng for more than one (1) year resulting in an unreconciled  variance of Kshs.447,408,678.  Further, the statement of financial position reflects trade and other payables closing  balance of Kshs.782,535,628.   However, cash generated from operations at   Note 40 to  the financial statements reflects increase in payables of Kshs.504,314,600   resulting to an  unreconciled variance of Kshs.278,221,028.  In addition, as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements, the ageing analysis  revealed that a total of Kshs.193,227,263, Kshs.145,328,500 and Kshs.108,852,915 had  been outstanding for 1 - 2 years, 2 - 3 years and over 3 years respectively all totalling  Kshs.447,408,678. However, the balance was not supported with creditor’s movement  schedule.  746.2.   Unsupported Refundable Deposits and Prepayments  The statement of financial position reflects Nil balance in respect of refundable deposits  and prepayments as di sclosed in Note 33 to the financial statements. However, the  supporting ledger reflects a balance of Kshs.62,967,159.  Further, Note 21 to the financial statements reflects a deposits and retention bank account  with Nil balance. The account is intended to   hold deposit monies for payments to various  suppliers and contractors. However, the cashbook and bank reconciliation statements for  the account were not provided for audit verification.  746.3.   Inaccuracies   in Transfers from the County Revenue Fund  Note 6 to the financial statements reflects transfers from County Revenue Fund totalling  Kshs.7,599,066,478,   made   up   of   recurrent   account   of   Kshs.6,439,545,543   and  development account of Kshs.1,159,520,935. Howe ver, the financial statements of the  Nandi County Revenue Fund reflect transfers to the County Executive amount of  Kshs.7,733,771,378 resulting in an unreconciled variance of Kshs.134,704,900.

360  746.4.   Variances Between Employee s’   Cost and Payroll Amount  The   stat ement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee s’   costs   amount   of  Kshs.3,372,701,751 as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial statements. However,   re -  casting of payroll records revealed total employee costs of Kshs.2,833,070,772   resulting  in an unreconciled variance of Kshs.539,630,979.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the financial statements could  not be confirmed.  747.   Unsupported Property, Plant and Equipment Balance  The statement of financial position reflects property,   plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.1,168,875,445 as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements.   However, the  assets register in support the reported balance was not provided for verification.  Further, included in the balance is an amount of Kshs.6, 471,120 in respect of purchasing  two (2) parcels of land for amount of Kshs.550,000 and Kshs.5,921,120 respectively.  However, no documentary evidence was provided to show successful registration of the  parcels of land in the name of the County Executive. F urther, the parcels of land  purchased were not demarcated hence it was not possible to differentiate the actual  portion purchased by the County Executive.  In the circumstances, the completeness, accuracy and ownership of property, plant and  equipment bal ance of Kshs.1,168,875,445 could not be confirmed.  748.   Unaccounted for Domestic Travel and Subsistence Expenditure  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services amount of  Kshs.2,635,125,855 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial   statements. Included in the  expenditure   is   amount   of   Kshs.236,588,798   which   relates   to   domestic   travel   and  subsistence   expenses.   However,   supporting   documents   for   expenditure   totalling  Kshs.2,944,230 were not provided for audit.  In the   circumstances, the completeness of the domestic travel and subsistence amount  of Kshs.2,944,230 could not be confirmed.  749.   Unsupported Subsidized Vocational Training Centers Support Grant  The statement of financial performance reflects other grants and sub sidies amount of  Kshs.351,034,826 as disclosed in Note 13 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.13,310,000 in respect of transfers to vocational training  centers. However, supporting documents including acknowledgeme nt for received funds  from the beneficiary institutions were not provided for audit confirmation.  In the circumstances, the regularity and completeness of transfers to vocational training  centers totalling Kshs.13,310,000 could not be confirmed.

361  Emphasis of Matter  750.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final budgeted  receipts   and   actual   receipts   on   a   comparable   basis   of   Kshs.9,186,409,526   and  Kshs.7,813,219,349 respectively, resulting   in underfunding of Kshs.1,373,190,177 or  15%   of   the   budget.   However,   the   County   Executive   spent   an   amount   of  Kshs.7,579,385,582   against   actual   receipts   of   Kshs.7,813,219,349   resulting   to  underutilization of Kshs.233,833,767 or 3% of the actual expenditure.  The underfunding affected the implementation of planned activities and programmes and  may have negatively impacted on the delivery of services to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  751.   Unresolved Prior   Year Matters  In the audit report of the previous year, several issues were raised under report on  Financial Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in the Use of Public  Resources, and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Managemen t and  Governance. Review of the status of implementation of the issues during the audit,  revealed that fifty - seven (57) issues remained unresolved as listed at the end of this  report.  752.   Undisclosed Contingent Liabilities  The statement of financial   position reflects Nil balance for contingent liabilities as  disclosed in Note 44 to the financial statements. However, e xamination of contingent  liabilities records revealed that the County Executive is exposed to substantial potential  obligations and liti gations estimated at Kshs.5,390,422 arising from claims lodged by  contractors and suppliers for works performed, and goods, and services supplied over  the last ten (10) years. Although the claimants assert that the amounts are due and  payable, the County E xecutive disputes the validity of these claims and as a result, did  not recognize and disclose the liabilities in the financial statements for the year ended 30  June, 2025. The absence of disclosure of these long - outstanding and potentially litigious  claim s was inconsistent with the requirements of the applicable financial reporting  framework, which mandates the reporting of material contingent liabilities where the  likelihood of outflow cannot be ruled out. The County remains exposed to significant  financi al and legal risks should the disputed claims be upheld.  Other Information  753.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.

362  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for   Conclusion  754.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility Principles on Wages  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs.3,372,701,751   as   disclosed   in   Note   9   to   the   financial   statements.   This   was  equivalent to 44% of the reported revenue of Kshs.6,439,545,543 which was in excess of  the   threshold   of   35% prescribed under   Regulation 25(1)(b) of the   Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015. Further, there was no evidence  that the County Executive Committee Member for Finance and Economic Planning tabled  a bill in the County Assem bly to control the wage bill.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  755.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of payroll   records revealed that the County Executive had a total of two thousand  nine hundred and seventy (2970) employees out of whom one thousand eight hundred  and fifty - nine (1,859) or approximately 63% were from the dominant ethnic community in  the County. This   was contrary to   Section 7(2) of National Cohesion and Integration Act,  2008 which requires that   no public establishment shall have more than one third of its  staff from the dominant ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the   law.  756.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Pay  Review of the monthly payrolls revealed that two hundred and one (201) employees  received net pay of less than one - third of their basic salar y. This was contrary to the  provisions of Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007, which provides that the total  deductions made by an employer from an employee’s wages shall not exceed two - thirds  of such wages at any one time.  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  757.   Acting Positions Beyond the Stipulated Period  Management paid three (3) members of staff an acting allowance for a duration exceeding  six (6) months totalling Kshs.1,302,641. This was contrary to Sectio n C.14(1) of the Public  Service Commission, Human Resource Policies and Procedures Manual of May, 2016  which requires that when an officer is eligible for appointment to a higher post and is  called upon to act in that post pending advertisement of the post , the officer is eligible for  payment of acting allowance at the rate of twenty percent (20%) of his substantive basic  salary not payable to an officer for more than six (6) months.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

363  758.   Payment   of Sal aries Outside   Human Resource Integrated System  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   employee   costs   amount   of  Kshs.3,372,701,751 as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial statements. However, review  of payroll records revealed that the   County Executive uses both Human Resource  Integrated System (HRIS) and Excel sheets in processing of the payroll. The total  employee costs paid outside the HRIS amounted to Kshs.85,202,776 .   This was contrary  to Section 1.5.1 of The National Treasury Guidel ines through the Financial Accounting  Recording   and   Reporting   Manual   which   requires   that   each   County   Government  Department is responsible for populating the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database  (IPPD) with the information contained in these documents,   issuing each appointee with a  unique payroll number from the system and providing the appointee with a letter of  appointment.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  759.   Unexplained   Redundancies  Review of payroll records revealed a significant reduction in staff numbers from four  thousand eight hundred and eighty - four (4,884) in the month of September, 2024 to two  thousand nine hundred and ninety - nine (2,999) in the month of October, 2024 resultin g  to a decrease of one thousand eight hundred and eighty - five (1,885) staff. Management  attributed the reduction to dismissals and terminations. However, the dismissal records  accounted for one thousand eight hundred and sixty - three (1,863) staff, leaving   an  unexplained variance of twenty - two (22) staff whose employment status could not be  confirmed. In addition, there was no documentary evidence provided to confirm the  reasons for dismissal, compliance with the due process or whether the affected staff wer e  issued with certificates of service as required by applicable laws and Human Resource  Policies.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  760.   Irregular   Payment   to Council of Governors  The statement of financial performance reflects use   of goods and services amount of  Kshs.2,635,125,855 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.210,102,962 in respect of other operating expenses  which includes an amount of Kshs.5,000,000 paid to t he Council of Governors as  contributions. This was contrary to Section 37 of Intergovernmental Relations Act, 2012  which provides that the operational expenses in respect of the Council shall be provided  for in the annual estimates of the revenue and expen diture of the National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  761.   Irregular Engagement of Legal Services  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services expenses  amount of Kshs. 2,635,125,855 as disclosed in   Note 10 to the financial statements.  Included in the expenditure is an amount of Kshs.369,696,231 in respect of specialized  mate rials and services which includes an expenditure of Kshs.41,972,940 relating to legal

364  costs payable to ten (10) Law Firms . Examination of expenditure records revealed that  the engagement of the external legal services was not approved by the County Executi ve  Committee. This was contrary to Section 16(1) of the Office of the County Attorney Act,  2020 which provides that a department or public entity established within a County  Executive shall not engage the services of a consultant to render any legal servic es  relating to the functions of the County Attorney without the approval of the County  Executive Committee.  Further, procurement of the legal consultants was not conducted through a competitive  process since the Law Firms were directly selected from the list of registered prequalified  legal firms without evidence that all listed firms were given an equal opportu nity to  participate. This was contrary to Section 95(3) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015, which provides that a procuring entity shall invite tenders from only  the approved persons who have been pre - qualified.  In the circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  762.   Unutilized   Office Furniture  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.1,168,875,445 as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements. Included in the  balance are   additions during the year amounting to Kshs.1,350,873,095. The additions  include an amount of Kshs.165,416,310 relating to supply of furniture and fittings to the  Governor’s office which had not been put into use one (1) year after the delivery, citing  non - completion of the construction of the County Offices.  Further, the Inspection and Acceptance Committee report was not provided to confirm  the quality and quantity of furniture was delivered.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure f or the procured office  furniture could not be confirmed.  763.   Irregularities in the Procurement of Fuel and Lubricants  The statement of financial performance   reflects use of goods and services amount of  Kshs.2,635,125,855 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.114,554,330 in respect of fuel, oil and lubricants  expenses. Review of payment records rev ealed that t he County Executive entered into a  framework agreement for supply and delivery of fuel and lubricants with seven (7) local  firms. However, only four (4) firms supplied fuel and lubricants to the County Executive  and 90% of the fuel was supplied   by only two (2) of the suppliers. This was contrary to  Regulation 101(2) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which  requires that a procuring entity shall not use a framework agreement in such a way as to  prevent, restrict or dis tort competition .   No justification was provided why only two (2) firms  supplied 90% of total fuel and lubricant supplies out of the seven (7) contracted firms.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

365  764.   Anomalies in Road Maintenance Expenses  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services amount of  Kshs.2,635,125,855 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.651,135,34 4 in respect of routine maintenance of roads  which included an amount of Kshs.10,160,828 incurred on hiring of selected road  maintenance equipment. However,   review of expenditure records revealed the following  anomalies:  (i)   There were no need   assessment reports showing the equipment required for every  road works.  (ii)   Detailed scope of work carried out in each of the roads and their estimated cost  (work plan) was not provided for review.  (iii)   Documents   provided   did   not   indicate   the   kilometers   repaired,   instead,   the  supporting   documents   only   listed   the   specific   roads   where   the   works   were  undertaken without.  (iv)   There were no daily machine utilization sheets showing machine hours worked  and the output achieved.  (v)   There were no measurement sheets to show ho w the billing for road maintenance  work was done in proportion to the number of hours the equipment was hired.  Further, there were no completion certificates.  (vi)   Records of all County Executive machinery and the planned versus actual road  works repaired by t he Department through force account (in - house) including  scope of works planned and achieved were not provided for verification. As a  result, it was not possible to confirm whether the County Executive equipment  performed tasks that were also contracted ou t, resulting in possible duplication of  work.  (vii)   The Department for Roads did not maintain an inventory of public roads under the  County Government specifying the road names and length by surface in kilometres  and their conditions including any records of works done on each road.  In the circumstances, v alue for money for the hire of equipment could not be confirmed.  765.   Irregularities in Drilling of Boreholes  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.1,168,875,445 as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.282,556,506 in respect of infrastructure, which i ncludes  an amount of Kshs.18,993,190 incurred in the construction of boreholes. However, the  expenditure was not supported by detailed design reports, hydro - geological test surveys  and   environmental   impact   assessment   reports   for   drilling   of   boreholes   and   l and  ownership documents where the boreholes were constructed. Further, permit from the  Water Resource Authority (WRA) and water quality testing reports indicating whether the

366  parameters levels were within the recommended water quality standards set by WRA  were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  766.   Delayed Construction of County Aggregation Industrial Park  The statement of financial performance reflects other grants and subsidies amount of  Kshs.351,034,826 as d isclosed in Note 13 to the financial statements. Included in the  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.77,751,287 in respect of County Aggregation Industrial  Park (CAIP). However,   review of contract agreement revealed that the County Executive  contracted a loca l company to construct the Park at a contract sum of Kshs.520,003,128  with effect from 15 August, 2023. The award was made after the first advertised tender  was non - responsive prompting a re - tender where five (5) firms submitted their tenders.  However, the   following anomalies were noted;  (i)   The project was jointly funded by the National Government and the County  Government. However, the level of funding by each Government was not clear  since no agreements or commitment between the two (2) levels of Government  was provided for audit.  (ii)   No documentation was provided indicating that detailed feasibility study was  conducted before commencement of the project including an environmental  impact assessment.  (iii)   The   ownership documents for the land were not provided for review.  (iv)   The performance b ond expired on 26 February, 2024 and had not been  renewed. The absence of a valid bond, exposes the project to possibility of loss  should the contractor fail to deliver the project as per the contract terms.  (v)   The Project Steering Committee was constituted   on 19 May, 2023 for a term of  six (6) months to oversee the Industrial Park project. However, the Committee’s  mandate had not been extended despite the project continuing beyond the  initial six (6) months duration.  (vi)   The contractor requested for variation o f works to the sub -   structure excavation  depth   and   backfill   depth   of   1.2m   to   2.7m   at   an   additional   cost   of  Kshs.39,547,500 or (8%) which was approved through a Professional Opinion  dated   27   October,   2023,   bringing   the   revised   contract   sum   to  Kshs.559,550,6 28. However, the variation was done before the lapse of one  year. This is contrary to Section 139(3) of the Public Procurement and Asset  Disposal Act, 2015 which provides that no contract price shall be varied  upwards within twelve months from the date of   the signing of the contract.  (vii)   The project was scheduled for completion on 15   August, 2025. However,  physical inspection conducted in the month of November, 2025 revealed that

367  work had stalled May, 2025, at only 30% completion level and the contractor  was n ot on site.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the project could not be confirmed and  Management was in breach of the law.  767.   Delayed Completion Works at Kapsengere Hospital  As reported in the previous year, the County Executive entered into contract with a local  contractor for the proposed completion works of Kapsengere Hospital (Phase II) in Terik  Ward at a contract sum of Kshs.9,954,900 on 5 May, 2019. The contract duration   was for  three (3) months, effective from the date of the agreement and was expected to end by  5   July,   2019.   However,   despite   budgetary   allocation   of   Kshs.3,954,900   and  Kshs.9,954,900 having been made in the financial year 2023/2024 and 2024/2025  respecti vely, the project had stalled for six (6) years.  Physical inspection conducted in the month of June, 2025 indicated that the project was  handed over to a new contractor and site handed over on 10 June, 2025. However, the  tender document and contract agreement for the new engagement was not provided for  a udit verification. Demolition of the defective ram was in progress. However, works not  done included the ablution block, outpatient division building and site fencing.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the expenditure for the project could not   be  confirmed.  768.   Delayed Completion Works at Chepterwai Sub - County Hospital  As reported in the previous year, the County Executive entered into a contract with a local  contractor for proposed completion works at Chepterwai Sub - County Hospital Phase II  on 3 1 March, 2022 at a contract sum of Kshs.41,538,221. The contract duration was  twenty - four (24) months and was expected to end by 31 March, 2024. An amount of  Kshs.10,990,472 had been paid in financial year 2023/2024 but the contractor was not  on site. In t he year under review, no budget allocation was made towards the project.  Further, physical inspection carried out in October, 2025 revealed that the contractor was  not on site. The proposed works had not been completed and the project was behind  schedule .  In the circumstances, the value for money on the project could not be confirmed.  769.   Irregularities in the Construction of a Textile Training and Production Plant  As reported in the previous year, the County Executive had entered into a Memorandum  of   Understanding   and   contract   agreement   with   Rivatex   East   Africa   Limited   on  16 January, 2018 and 1 2 February, 2019 respectively for the construction of a textile  training and production plant at Mosoriot Centre. Subsequently, Rivatex East Africa  entered into a contract with a local firm on 24 April, 2019 for the project on behalf of the  County Executiv e. However, the contract agreement with Rivatex East Africa expired on  08 May, 2023 and the County Executive and the same Contractor signed an addendum

368  contract dated on 8 June, 2023 to complete the remaining works at a contract sum of  Kshs.29,111,050.   At   the   time   of   audit,   works   certified   and   paid   for   amounted   to  Kshs.27,116,606 leaving an unpaid balance of Kshs.1,994,444.  Further, the addendum contract included clauses were the County Executive agreed to  settle outstanding amounts due to non - payment by   Rivatex East Africa in certificates No.1  to 3 and contractual claims due to breach of contract amounting to Kshs.2,235,716 and  Kshs.11,203,577 all totalling Kshs.13,439,293. However, payments listing showed that,  on 8 May, 2025 an advocate was paid an amou nt of Kshs.15,894,846 on behalf of the  contractor whose details were not provided for review.  In the circumstances, the value for money on the payment of Kshs.15,894,846 could not  be confirmed.  770.   Procurement Exceeding Threshold for Request for Quotation  Review of procurement records revealed that a supplier was awarded a contract to supply  ten (10) motorcycles at a total cost of Kshs.4,844,735 through the Request for Quotation  method.   The   contract   value   exceeded   the   maximum   allowable   threshold   of  Kshs.3,0 00,000 for use of Request for Quotation method set out in Regulation 106(5) of  the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  771.   Non - Operationalization   of the Nandi Youth Service  The County Executive established   the   Nandi County Youth Service Act,   2019 for the  operationalization of the Nandi Youth Service whose function was to train the youth to  serve the County and employ its members to undertake tasks on the devolved functions.  H owever,   at the time of audit in November, 2025 the Service was not operational and no  explanation was provided for failure to operationalize the Service.  In the circumstance, Management was in breach of law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS,   RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  772.   Training Conducted without Training Needs Assessment  The statement of financial performance reflects use of goods and services amount of  Kshs.2,635,125,855 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. Included in the  balance is Kshs.15,536,702 in   respect of training expenses. However, the amount was  not supported by training needs assessment (TNA), training plans, Departmental skills  inventory   records,   courses   approval   and   selection   criteria   contrary   to   the   Human  Resource Policies and Procedures M anual for the Public Service of May, 2016. Further,  it was not clear how the officers were nominated for the respective trainings without

369  evidence of training projections based on the training needs assessment. In addition,  Management did not prepare quart erly returns on trainings conducted during the year and  evaluation of their effectiveness.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over the management of the  training function could be confirmed.  773.   Weaknesses in Management of Inventories  The statement of financial performance reflects transfer to other Government entities  amount of Kshs.648,434,082 as disclosed in Note 11 to the financial statements. Included  expenditure is an amount of Kshs.444,420,479 in respect of Health Departments’ in   kind  contributions to health facilities for pharmaceuticals and non - pharmaceuticals. However,  physical verification in selected Referral and Sub - County hospitals revealed that the  health facilities lacked proper inventory management systems and relied on   manual  processes for receiving and managing drugs and non - pharmaceutical supplies. Further,  the process flow - from receipts of drugs, transfer to the pharmacy and eventual issuance  to patients was not documented.  Further, physical inspection and review of   store records revealed that the County  Executive did not have an inventory management and control system   capable of providing  real - time information on the location, condition, movement and reorder levels of stores.  Instead, stores records were maintained   manually, making it difficult to confirm the  completeness, accuracy and accountability of inventory transactions.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over inventory management  could not be confirmed.  774.   Failure to Update Imprest Regi ster  Examination of imprest registers revealed that the registers were not consistently updated  with details relating to the date of imprest issuance and surrender.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over the management of  imprest could not be confirmed.  775.   Lack of Staff in the Internal Audit Department  Review of the operations of the County Executive revealed that the Internal Audit Unit  had   an approved staff establishment of ten (10) positions. However, audit examination  noted that no substantive staff had been deployed to carry out the Internal Audit Function.  This was contrary to Section 155(1)(a) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012,  which requires a County Government entity to establish appropriate arrangements for  conducting internal audit in accordance with guidelines issued by the Public Sector  Accounting Standards Board.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of   internal controls over the operations of the  County Executive could not be confirmed.

370  776.   Lack of Approved Internal Audit Plans  Review of the records revealed that there were no approved Internal Audit Plans contrary  to Regulation 163(1)(a) and (b) and (2) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015 which requires that Internal Audit planning shall be  ca rried out on the basis of risk assessment and shall be set out in a three (3) year strategic  plan, on the basis of which an annual internal audit activity plan shall be developed. The  annual   work   plan   developed   should   be   submitted   to   the   Audit   Committee   by  15th February each financial year and approved annual work plan shared with the  Accounting Officer in sufficient time for inclusion in the budget of that entity.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of Internal Audit Function and   risk assessment  could not be confirmed.  777.   Weakness in Management of Fixed Assets  Review of Fixed Assets Management System revealed t he following anomalies:  777.1.   Lack of Assets Register  Review of records revealed that the assets register provided was incomplete and did not  capture all assets owned by the County Executive. Several categories of assets details  in the register were left blan k with no corresponding data. This was contrary to Regulation  136(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015,  which requires the Accounting Officer to maintain an accurate and complete register of  assets under his or her con trol or possession.  777.2.   Failure to Tag Assets  Audit inspection revealed that the County Executive’s assets were not tagged to facilitate  proper identification and tracking. Further, Management had not established policies and  procedures on asset management,   contrary to Regulation 132(2) of the Public   Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires the Accounting  Officer to ensure that both electronic and manual processes and procedures are in place  for the effective, efficient, economical and transparent use of the County Gove rnment  assets.  777.3.   Non - Disposal of Obsolete and Unserviceable Assets  Audit inspection revealed that several defective and unserviceable motor vehicles had  been grounded for a long time. However, Management did not provide satisfactory  explanation for the fa ilure to board and earmark these unserviceable motor vehicles and  transport equipment for disposal. This was contrary to Section 163(1) of the Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which states that an Accounting Officer shall  establish a Disposa l Committee as and when prescribed for the purpose of disposal.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over asset management could  not be confirmed.

371  778.   Lack of a Risk   Management Policy  Review of records revealed that Management had not developed a Risk Management  policy. Further, no risk assessment was carried out during the year unde r review.   This  was   contrary   to   Regulation   158(1)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires the Accounting Officer to ensure that  the County Government entity develops risk management strategies, including fraud  prevention mechanisms and establish a system of risk management and internal control  that supports robust business operations.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of Risk Management System in the County  Executive could not be confirmed.
