390  COUNTY EXECUTIVE   OF   LAIKIPIA   –   NO.31  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  805.   Variances in Transfer to Other Government Entities Amount  The statement of financial performance and Note 9 to the financial statements reflect an  amount of Kshs.418,357,458 in respect of transfers to other Government entities.  Included in the amount are transfers totalling Kshs.20,010,951 to three (3) County  Gov ernment entities which were at variance with the amounts disclosed in the entities’  respective audited financial statements   totalling Kshs.22,460,000   as tabulated below;  County Entity  County Executive’s  Financial Statements  Amount  (Kshs)  Entity’s Financial  Statements  Amount  (Kshs)  Variance  (Kshs)  Rumuruti Municipality   7,000,000   9,500,000   (2,500,000)  Nanyuki Municipality   7,100,000   7,000,000   100,000  Laikipia   County  Development Authority   5,910,951   5,900,000   10,951  Total   20,010,951   22,400,000  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   transfers   to   other  Government entities amount of Kshs.20,010,951 could not be confirmed.  806.   Unsupported Trade   Payables Balance  The statement of financial position and Note 15 to the financial statements reflect trade  and other payables balance of Kshs.1,935,664,585. The balance includes trade payables  totalling   Kshs.1,154,508,149,   which   were   not   supported   by   requisitions,   local  pu rchase/service   orders,   invoices,   delivery   notes,   signed   contract   agreements,  description of the project and/or project locations and supplier reconciliations.  Further, the County Executive did not undertake the mandatory supplier circularization  and recon ciliation exercise as guided under Paragraph 2.3.1 of The National Treasury  and Economic Planning Circular No. 03/2025 of 14 April, 2025, which provided guidelines  on transition from cash to accrual accounting.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and comp leteness of the   trade and other payable  balance of Kshs.1,154,508,149   could not be confirmed.

391  807.   Lack of Asset Ownership Documents  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.35,778,986,723 which as disclosed in Note 14 to the financial statements includes  land and buildings valued at Kshs.32,166,169,389 and Kshs.3,156,256,882 respectivel y.  However, Management did not provide ownership documents such as title deeds,  allotment letters, or lease agreements to support these balances.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness, ownership and existence of land and  buildings   valued   at   Ks hs.32,166,169,839   and   Kshs.3,156,256,882   could   not   be  ascertained.  Emphasis of Matter  808.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   amounts   on   comparable   basis   of   Ks hs.6,911,880,714   and  Kshs.6,103,450,954 respectively, resulting   in underfunding   of Kshs.808,429,760, or 12%  of the budget.   However , the County Executive spent an amount of Kshs.5,722,126,550  against   actual   receipts   of   Kshs.6,103,450,954,   resulting   in   an   un der   utilization   of  Kshs.381,324,404, or 6% of the actual receipts.  The   underfunding   affected the planned activities of the County Executive and may have  impacted negatively on service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  809.   Unresolved Prior Year Audit Issues  In the audit report of   the previous year, several issues were raised under Report on  Financial Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in the Use of Public  Resources, and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance.   However, Managemen t had not resolved eleven (11) issues or given any  explanation for the delay in resolving the issues as at 30 June, 2025 as detailed in the  table below:  No .   Audit Issue s for 2023/2024  1   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility on Wage Bill  2   Non - Compliance with the Third of Basic Salary Rule  3   Non - Compliance to the Law on Ethnic Composition  4   Irregularities in the Procurement and Delivery of Dialysis Equipment  5   Irregular Payment of Allowances to Laikipia County Administration Police  Welf are Account

392  No .   Audit Issue s for 2023/2024  6   Pending Bills Not Paid as First Charge  7   Failure to operate Fully on the E - Procurement Platform  8   Ineffective Internal Audit Department  9   Action on Internal and External Audit Reports by the Audit Committee  10   Failure to Tag Assets  11   Non   - disposal of Obsolete and Unserviceable Assets  Other Information  810.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for   Conclusion  811.   Non - Compliance with Data Protection Requirements  Review of County records revealed that the County Executive had not registered with the  Offi ce of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) as a data controller and data  processor, despite actively collecting, processing and storing personal data of staff,  members of the county executive and service providers during the year under review.  This was   contrary to   Section 18(1) of the Data Protection Act, 2019 which   obligates all  data controllers and processors to register with the ODPC before handling personal data.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  812.   Failure to Construct   the   Official Residences of the Governor and Deputy  Governor  Review of County records revealed that the County Executive had not constructed or  made budgetary provision for the construction of an official residence for the Governor  and   the   Deputy   Governor.   This   was   contrary   to   the   Salaries   and   Remuneration  Commission (SRC) Circular Ref. No. SRC/TS/COG/6/61/48 VOL.II (64) dated 20 May,  2019, which provides guidelines on housing benefits for Governors, Deputy Governors,  and County Assembl y Speakers, and requires that official residences to have   been  commissioned   by 30 June, 2022. In the absence of an official residence, the Governor  and   Deputy   Governor   continued   to   draw   monthly   house   allowance   amount   of  Kshs.300,000 totalling Kshs.3,600,00 0 annually, which was irregular and contrary to the  SRC guidelines.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the   C ircular.

393  813.   Irregularities in the Procurement Processes  The statement of financial performance and Note 8 to the financial   statements reflect use  of   goods   and   services   expenses   amount   of   Kshs.1,377,312,429.   Review   of   the  expenditure revealed the following observations ;  813.1.   Supply and Delivery of Office Cabinet and Stationery  Included in the amount is payment of Kshs.1,456,000   made for the supply and delivery  of   a   lockable   office   cabinet   and   other   stationery   items under the   Department   for  Administration. However, there   were only   two (2) competing bidders who were not in the  procurement category of the procuring entity’s prequali fied suppliers’ list. This was  contrary to Section 106(2)(a) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015,  which requires that requests for quotations be issued only to suppliers registered by the  procuring entity.  813.2.   Supply and Delivery   of Moto r Vehicle Training Equipment  An amount of Kshs.1,159,449 was paid to a local supplier for the supply and delivery of  motor vehicle training equipment for Nanyuki and Salama Vocational Training   Centers,  under   the   Department   for   Education.   However,   the   counter - receipt   voucher   (S13)  indicated that the goods were delivered and taken on charge on 22 June ,   2024, which  was fifty - one (51) days after the expiry of the 30 - day validity period for the purchase order  issued on 2 April, 2024 . This was contrary to Regulation 52(1) of the Public Finance  Management (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which limits the validity of an  order to thirty (30) days from the date of issue.  813.3.   Legal Expenses  Included in the use of goods and services   amount is   other operating expenses totalling  Kshs.60,341,363 which further include legal expenses amounting to Kshs.24,936,096,  made to eight (8) private law firms for provision of legal services to the County Executive.  However, the law firms were directl y procured without written approval of the County  Executive   C ommittee contrary to Section 16(1) of the County Attorney Act, 2020 and  Section 91 of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which establishes  open tendering as the preferred method   of procurement.  Further, the procurement was not supported by Ad - hoc   Evaluation Committee Minutes,  Head   of   P rocurement   professional   opinion   and   serv ice   requisitions   from   the   user  D epartment.  In addition, although the Integrated Payroll Personnel Database   (IPPD)   indicated that the  County   Executive had a Legal Officer and a Legal Advisor, it was not explained why they  could not execute their mandate to represent the Executive on legal matters fo r which the  services were outsourced from external legal firms.  In the circumstances,   the   value for money on the   above   expenditure s   could not be  confirmed .

394  814.   Non - Compliance with the Law   on Staff   Ethnic   Composition  The County Executive had a   workforce of two thousand five hundred and fifty - one (2,551)  staff, out of whom one thousand seven hundred and ninety - five (1,795), or 70% are from  the dominant ethnic community. This was contrary to Section 7(1) and (2) of the National  Cohesion and Integr ation Act, 2008, which requires public establishments to represent  the diversity of the people of Kenya in the employment of staff and not to have more than  one - third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in bre ach of the law.  815.   Non - Compliance with   the Persons   with Disabilities   Act, 2025  The County Executive had a workforce of two thousand five hundred and fifty - one (2,551)  staff, out of whom forty - five (45), or 1.7% are p ersons   with disabilities.   This was contrar y  to Section 5(1)(e) of the People with Disabilities Act, 2025 which states that ‘every county  government shall promote the inclusion of persons with   disabilities   in the county public  service by putting in place measures to ensure that at least five per ce ntum of the  employment positions are filled by persons with   disabilities .  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  816.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility   Principles   on Wage s  The statement of financial performance and Note 7 to the financial statements reflect  employee costs of Kshs.3,284,492,295, which represents 55% of the County total  revenue of Kshs.5,973,584,517.   This was contrary to Regulation 25(1)(b) of the Public  Finan ce Management (County Governments) Regulations,   2015 which states that the  County Government’s expenditure on wages and benefits for its public officers shall not  exceed 35% of the County Government’s total revenue.  In the   circumstances , Management was in   breach of the law.  817.   Non - Compliance with the   One - Third   Rule on Basic Salary  Review of the County Executive payroll revealed that twenty - six (26) employees earned  net salaries of less than a third (1/3) of their basic salary.   This was   contrary to Section  19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which stipulates that without prejudice to a ny right of  recovery of any debt due and notwithstanding the provisions of any other written law, the  total amount of all deductions made by an employer from the wages of his employee at  any one time shall not exceed two - thirds of such wages.  In the circu mstances, Management was in breach of the law.  818.   Failure   to Settle   Long Outstanding Payables  The statement of financial position and Note 15 to the financial statements reflect trade  and other payables balance of Kshs.1,935,664,585, which includes Kshs.1,671,529,901  in respect of trade payables. The ageing analysis for the trade payables indicate   that  payables amounting to Kshs.1,310,222,624 have been outstanding for over three (3)

395  years.   This was contrary to Regulation 41(2) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments)   Regulation, 2015 which provides that debt service payments shall be a  first charge on the County   Revenue Fund and the Accounting Officer shall ensure this is  done to the extent possible that   the county Government does not default on debt  obligations.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFF ECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  819.   Lack   of   Key   Information   Communication   and   Technology   Governance  Structures and Policies  The   County Executive did not have an Information   Communication   Technology (I C T)  strategic committee, an active I C T steering committee and a formally approved I C T  security policy to   ensure data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The absence of  these   critical   governance s tructures and policies indicated   a   significant weakness in the  County’s ICT governance and risk management framework.  In the circumstances , the County's ICT environment wa s exposed to risks of data  breaches, operational disruptions a nd non - compliance with regulatory requirements.  820.   Weak System of Internal Controls over Management of Fixed Assets  The statement of financial position and Note 14 to the financial statements reflect  property, plant, and equipment balance of Kshs.35,778, 986,723. However, review of  records reve aled the following weaknesses:  820.1.   Lack of Land and Buildings   Register  The County Executive did not maintain a register of land and buildings during the year  under review. This exposes County land and   buildings to loss through grabbing or  misappropriation and inefficient land management and planning.  820.2.   Grounded Motor   Vehicles   Not Assessed or Processed for Disposal  Seven (7) defective and unserviceable motor vehicles remained grounded in various  County parking yards, with two (2) under the Department   for   Health, two (2) under the  Department   for   Agriculture and one (1) each under the Department   for   Infrastructure,  Dep artment   for   Water and Environment, and Department of Administration respectively.  However, no justification or documentation was provided to explain why the vehicles had  not been assessed, bonded and marked for disposal. This was contrary to Section 163(1)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015, which requires the Accounting

396  Officer to establish a Disposal Committee to oversee the disposal of unserviceable or  obsolete public assets.  820.3.   Incomplete Asset s   Register  The asset register was no t prepared in accordance with the format prescribed by IPSAS  17 and Appendix 6 of The National Treasury Circular NALM 2/2/(B) dated 14 October,  2020. The register did not meet the minimum required details, including identification or  serial   number,   acquisi tion   date,   description   of   the   asset,   location,   class,   cost   of  acquisition, accumulated depreciation and net book value. As a result, the asset register  was incomplete, undermining the reliability of the asset information presented in the  financial statemen ts.  In the circumstances, the effective ness of   internal controls on management of   County  Executive   assets could not be confirmed.

397  COUNTY EXECUTIVE   OF   NAKURU   –   NO.32  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  821.   Inaccuracies   in the Financial Statements  821.1.   Irregular Transfer to Other Government Agencies  The statement of financial performance reflects transfers to other   Government entities  amount of Kshs.2,122,942,239 as disclosed in Note 11 to the financial statements.  However, review of the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS)  payment details revealed that three hundred and thirty - eight (338) trans fer payments  amounting to Kshs.725,862,918 were irregularly charged to transfers/grants to other  Government   agencies,   instead   of   payments   to   suppliers   or   individuals.   The  transfers/grants to other Government agencies accounts are supposed to transfer funds  from one Government agency to another and not to suppliers or individuals.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and regularity of the transfers to other  Government entities amounting to Kshs.725,862,918 could not be confirmed.  821.2.   Unsupported Adjustments Balance  The   statement   of   changes   in   net   asset   reflects   total   net   assets   balance   of  Kshs.25,079,839,418 which is net off an amount of Kshs.794,430,677 in respect of  adjustments made in the opening balance. However, the adjustment   was not supported  with journal entries and a schedule of the transactions related to the adjustments.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   net   assets   balance   of  Kshs.25,079,839,418 could not be confirmed.  822.   Property , Plant and Equipment   Without Ownership Documents  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.23,168,922,681 as   disclosed in Note 26 to financial statements. However, review of  the property, plant and equipment records revealed th at there were two hundred and  eighteen (218) motor vehicles which did not have log books and eight hundred and  seventy - eight (878) parcels of land without title deeds or allotment letters. No explanation  was provided for the absence of ownership documents   for the motor vehicles and the  parcels of land.  Further, review of the land   register revealed that ten (10) parcels of land had been  encroached by illegal settlers and private developers. However, Management had not  taken any action to reclaim or settle   the matter and acquire the title deed for the  encroached parcels of land.

398  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and ownership of the property, plant  and equipment balance of Kshs.23,168,922,681 could not be confirmed.  823.   Unaccounted   for Disbursements to Another County Fund  The County Executive Receiver of Revenue   -   Revenue Statements under the statement  of revenue and disbursements reflects an   unexplained disbursement   to another County  Fund amount of Kshs.1,960,729,790. However, accountability for the funds was not  provided by way of financial statements of the recipient or the beneficiary Fund. Further,  Management did not provide a detailed schedule indicating the par ticulars of the Fund to  which the funds were disbursed.  In the circumstances, the completeness and regularity of the disbursements to an  unexplained   another County   Fund   amounting   to   Kshs.1,960,729,790   could   not   be  confirmed.  824.   Long Outstanding Receivables   from Exchange Transactions  The statement of financial position reflects receivables from exchange transactions  balance of Kshs.703,353,351 as disclosed in Note 22 to the financial statements.  However, review of the ageing analysis revealed that an amount   of Kshs.602,408,309 or  86% of the total receivables have been outstanding for more than three (3) years making  their recoverability doubtful. Management did not provide any evidence of measures the  County Executive had put in place to ensure recovery of t he long outstanding debts.  Further, Management did not make any provision for bad and doubtful debts in the  financial statements.  In the circumstances, the   accuracy   of receivables from exchange transactions balance of  Kshs.602,408,309 could not be confirm ed.  825.   Inaccuracies   in Trade and Other Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs. 6,486,082,856   as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements. However, review  of   the   supporting   ledger   reflects   a   ba lance   of   Kshs.5,843,012,764   resulting   in   an  unexplained and unreconciled variance of Kshs.643,070,092.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of trade and other payables  balance of Kshs. 6,486,082,856   could not be confirmed.  826.   Unsupported   Intangible Assets  The statement of financial position reflects intangible assets balance of Kshs.221,518,856  as disclosed in Note 27 to the financial statements. However, the intangible assets  balance was not supported with a detailed sched ule indicating the nature and state of the  intangible assets.

399  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the intangible assets balance of  Kshs.221,518,856 could not be confirmed.  827.   Non - Compliance with Facility Improvement Financing Act,   2023  Review of County Executive revenue records for level 4 and 5 hospitals revealed that the  sixteen (16) Facilities in the County collected an amount of Kshs.1,797,785,103 but  transferred Nil amount to the County Revenue Fund. Further, transfer records   indicate  that an amount of Kshs.1,797,785,103 was disbursed to the sixteen (16) Hospitals from  the Facility Improvement Fund (FIF) collection account. However, the Hospitals financial  statements reflected a total amount of Kshs.1,726,121,564 as having been   received from  the FIF account resulting in an unexplained undisbursed amount of Kshs.71,663,539.  Further, the County Government of Nakuru   -   Receiver of Revenue statements reflects  transfers to another County Fund (FIF) amount of Kshs.1,960,729,790 which was at  variance with the County Executive’s records amount of Kshs.1,797,785,103 resulting in  an unexplained variance of Kshs.162,944,687. The inconsistency between the various  reco rds was not explained by Management.  In addition, the Facility Improvement Financing (FIF) revenues were deposited into the  general county revenue accounts instead of the designated Facility bank accounts. This  was contrary to the provisions of Section 20 (1) of the Facilities Improvement Financing  Act, 2023 which requires that all revenues collected by health facilities be retained in  designated FIF accounts and utilized strictly for approved operational and improvement  activities.  In the circumstances, t he accuracy and completeness of County revenue amounting to  Kshs.1,797,785,103 could not be confirmed.  828.   Transactions   Included   in   Integrated   Financial   Management   Information  Systems Payments System but not in the Payment Details Report  Review of the Integr ated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) payments  report processed against the payments made revealed that there were seven hundred  and eight (708) transactions amounting to Kshs.787,431,649 which were paid in IFMIS  but not captured in the IFMI S payment details report as at 30 June, 2025.  In the circumstances, the   accuracy and completeness   of the transactions amounting to  Kshs. 787,431,649 could   not be confirmed.

400  Emphasis of Matter  829.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects total receipts budget  and   actual   on   a   comparable   basis   amount   of   Kshs.23,980,402,312   and  Kshs.19,534,080,837 respectively resulting in under - funding of Kshs.4,446,321,475 or  19% of the budge t. Further, the statement reflects that the County Executive spent an  amount of Kshs.12,116,116,256 against actual receipts of Kshs.19,534,080,837   resulting  in an   under - utilization of Kshs.7,417,964,581 or 38% of the actual receipts.  However, no explanati on was provided for budget utilization difference exceeding 10%  contrary to   Section 164 (2) (a) (iv) of the Public Finance   Management Act , 2012 which  requires a County Government entity to present appropriation accounts showing a  statement explaining any v ariations between actual expenditure and the sums voted.  The under - funding and under - utilization affected the planned activities and may have  impacted negatively on service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of th i s matter.  Other Matter  830.   Unresolved   Prior Year Matters  In the audit report of the previous year, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial   Statements,   Report   on   Lawfulness   and   Effectiveness   in   Use   of   Public  Resources and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governanc e.   Review of the status during audit of the County Executive for the financial  year 2024/2025 revealed that   forty - one (41)   issues remained unresolved as listed at the  end of this report.  831.   Closure   of Nakuru War Memorial Hospital  As reported in the previous year, the Nakuru War Memorial Hospital sits on a parcel of  land measuring approximately 11.25 Hectares and also hosts Nakuru County Referral  and Teaching Hospital, Nakuru Annex Hospital and State House landing field or helipad.  The   land   was   leased   to   War   Memorial   Hospital   for   ninety - nine   (99)   years   from  1 May, 1922 which has since expired.  However, the facility which is a Level 4 Hospital has remained closed for three (3) years  and remained idle after the   expiry of the lease due to ownership wrangles between the  County Executive of Nakuru and War Memorial Hospital Management which is the subject  of an ongoing court case. The Hospital has various installations, equipment, buildings  and other assets which are   worth millions of shillings and which the National and County  Governments have invested over the years. These assets risk becoming obsolete or  unserviceable, being stolen and misappropriated due to the closure of the Hospital.

401  Other Information  832.   There were no material issues relating to   O ther   I nformation.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  833.   Long Outstanding Trade and Other Payables  The   statement   of   financial   position   reflects   trade   and   other   payables   balance   of  Kshs.6,486,082,856 as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements. However, review  of ageing analysis revealed that a balance   of Kshs.1,478,761,394 or 23% of the total  payables have been outstanding for more than one (1) year.   This was contrary to Section  53 (8) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 which states that ‘an  Accounting Officer shall not commence any   procurement proceedings until satisfied  that   sufficient funds to meet the obligations of the resulting contract (s) are reflected in  the approved budget estimates. Further,   failure to clear trade payables in the year to  which they relate distorts the budge t of the following year as they constitute a first charge  on the budget. In addition, the County Executive runs the risk of incurring significant and  unquantified costs of interest and penalties associated with delays in settling the invoiced  bills.  In the   circumstances,   Management was in breach of the law.  834.   Non - Compliance   with   the Law on   Fiscal Responsibility Principle s   on Wage s  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   expenditure   on   employee   costs  amounting to Kshs.6,590,685,950 as disclosed in No te 9 to the financial statements. The  amount constitutes 42% of the total revenue amount of Kshs.15,593,236,618. This was  7% above the limit allowed by Regulation 25 (1) (a) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015 which prov ides that the limit set by the County  Executive Committee Member with the approval of the County Assembly on the County  Government’s expenditure on wages and benefits for its public officers shall not exceed  thirty - five (35) percent of the county governmen t’s total revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  835.   Non - Compliance with   the   One - Third Rule o n   Basic Salary  Review of the Integrated Personnel Payroll Data (IPPD) payroll for the year under review  revealed that a total of one thousand one hundred and sixty - six (1,166) employees earned  net salary lower than a third of their basic salary.   This was   contrary to Sect ion 19(3) of  the Employment Act, 2007 which stipulates that without prejudice to any right of recovery  of any debt due and notwithstanding the provisions of any other written law, the total  amount of all deductions made by an employer from the wages of his   employee at any  one time shall not exceed two - thirds of such wages.

402  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  836.   Payment of Salaries Outside the   Integrated Personnel Payroll Data  Review of the Integrated Personnel Payroll Data (IPPD) pa yroll revealed that salaries and  wages for one thousand four hundred and fifty - seven (1,457) casual employees totalling  Kshs.286,945,211 were paid outside the IPPD system. This was contrary to Treasury  Circular No.13/2019 of 28 August, 2019 which provides   that the allocation of personnel  emoluments must be supported by Integrated Personnel Payroll Data (IPPD) and each  public entity will be required to provide this information to support personnel requirements.  In the circumstances, Management was in breac h of the law.  837.   Avoidable   Costs incurred on Court Decrees  Review of legal records provided for audit   revealed that several legal cases filed in court  against the County Executive were decreed in the interest of the claimants. Further, the  County Executive was instructed by the Court to pay a total amount of Kshs.180,736,467  in respect of the Court decrees   out of which an amount of Kshs.66,472,548 had been  paid leaving balance of Kshs.112,721,131 outstanding. The County Executive lost an  amount of Kshs.180,736,467 arising from court rulings in favor of claimants due to poor  Management decisions.  In   the   cir cumstances,   prudent   management   decisions   in   handling   legal   cases   by  Management could not be confirmed.  838.   Project Implementation Status  Review of the Project Implementation Status report for the year revealed that a total of  three   hundred   and   twenty - five   (325)   projects   with   contract   costs   totalling  Kshs.2,729,019,918 were at various stages of completion as detailed below.  (i)   One   hundred   and   twelve   (112)   projects   with   a   total   contract   sum   of  Kshs.1,854,582,378 had extended beyond the expected dates of completion.  Management did not provide any explanation for the delays in completion and  evidence of action taken against the contractors for del ayed completion of  projects.  (ii)   Three (3) projects with a total contract price of Kshs.17,932,735 had stalled at  different stages of completion. However, Management did not provide the  strategies to have the projects completed or any action taken against th e  contractors for failure to execute the projects to completion within the stipulated  time in the contract agreement.  (iii)   Fifty - seven (57) projects with a total contract cost of Kshs.137,999,172 were  awarded to various contractors during the year under review . However, none

403  of the projects listed in this category had started during the year under review.  Management did not provide explanations why the projects were awarded and  not initiated.  (iv)   One   hundred   and   fifty - three   (153)   projects   with   an   estimated   cost   of  Kshs.718,505,638   were   budgeted   for   the   financial   years   2023/2024   and  2024/2025. However, review of the procurement records revealed that the  projects were still in the early stages of procurement at the time of audit in  October, 2025. Management did not p rovide explanations for the delayed  project implementation which would lead to low budget absorption.  In the circumstances,   the   value for money on resources   spent on the incomplete, stalled  and projects not started could not be confirmed.  839.   Delayed Completion of Projects  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.23,168,922,681 which includes work in progress balance of Kshs.4,177,860,829 in  respect of the on - going, incomplete and delayed pro jects. However, the following issues  were identified in respect of the proje c ts;  839.1.   Delays in Completion of   Inpatient and Outpatient Block at Mai Mahiu Level  4 Hospital   -   Naivasha Sub - County  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a contract with a local company for the proposed construction of an outpatient and  inpatient block at Mai Mahiu Level 4 Hospital in Naivasha Sub - County which was to b e  implemented in two (2) phases. Phase one (1) was awarded at a contract sum of  Kshs.154,528,397. The contract period was forty (40) weeks and the contract agreement  was signed on 28 December, 2020 and was fully paid.  Phase two (2) was awarded to the sam e company at a contract sum of Kshs.68,166,204.  The contract was signed on 28 June, 2024 and the contract period was thirty - two (32)  weeks with the contractor being paid an amount of Kshs.11,941,071 as per the certificate  of payment No.1 dated 16 September , 2024. However, physical inspection carried   in the  month of   June, 2025 revealed that although the contractor was on site, not much progress  had been realized. Review of the acceptance certificate form revealed that the percentage  of work done was at 32% w ith more than 100% of time lapsed.  839.2.   Incomplete Construction of Outpatient Block at Molo Level 4 Hospital  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.23,168,922,681 which includes work in progress amount of Ks hs.4,177,860,829 for  on - going and incomplete projects. Review of the project files and procurement records  revealed that Management entered into a contract with a local company on 26 April, 2021  for the construction of an outpatient block at Molo Level 4 H ospital at a contract sum of  Kshs.150,095,777. Further, two (2) payments of Kshs.12,086,126 and Kshs.12,042,041

404  all totalling Kshs.24,128,167 were made in relation to interim payment certificate Nos.7  and 8 respectively for works done. However, physical in spection of the project carried out  in the month of   June, 2025 revealed that there were no major works done and the  contractor was not on site. In addition, the drainage works were incomplete, landscaping,  clearing of construction and excavation debris was   not done.  839.3.   Stalled Projects Implemented by the Health Department  Review of the Health Department Project Implementation Status report revealed that four  (4) projects started in the previous years with total sum cost of Kshs.159,702,024 had  stalled at different stages of execution. The projects had extended beyond the ex pected  dates of completion. However, Management did not provide documents supporting the  extension of the contract period and explanations for the delays or termination of the  contracts.  839.4.   Stalled   Construction of Outpatient Block at Njoro Level 4 Hospi tal  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a contract with a local company on 28 December, 2020 at a cost of Kshs.148,902,024  and a contract period of forty (40) weeks for the construction of an outpatie nt block at  Njoro Level 4 Hospital. Review of the project file and procurement records revealed that  payments amounting to Kshs.119,944,848 or 80% of the contract sum had been paid.  However, the Project Implementation Status indicated that the contract was   terminated  since the contractor had abandoned the site.  839.5.   Incomplete Construction of Outpatient Department Block at Olenguruone  Sub - County Hospital  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a contract with   a local company for construction of an outpatient department block at  Olenguruone Sub - County Hospital which was implemented in two (2) phases. Phase one  (1) was awarded at a contract sum of Kshs.19,984,065. The contract period was eighteen  (18) weeks and t he contract agreement was signed on 28 February, 2020 and the  contractor was paid the full amount of the contract sum.  Further, phase two (2) was awarded to the same company at a contract sum of  Kshs.19,988,315 for finishing works with the   contractor having been paid the full amount  of the contract price. However, as at the time of the audit in October, 2025 the works were  incomplete and the project was behind schedule.  839.6.   Stalled Construction of High - Altitude Training Facility in Keringet W ard  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a contract with a local company for the construction of the proposed construction of  high attitude training facility in Keringet Ward Nakuru County which was si gned on  10 February, 2021   at a contract sum of Kshs.121,997,573   for a contract period of forty -  two (42) weeks. Review of the project file and procurement records revealed that  payments amounting to Kshs.110,024,225 or 90% of   the contract sum had   been made

405  as at 31 May, 2025 including an amount of Kshs.13,936,277 paid during the year under  review. However, physical inspection of the project revealed that the contractor had not  completed the works   and was not on site. Further no documents were prov ided to support  extension of time that had been granted in form of request for extension of time, approvals  from project engineers and a   letter of no objection.  In addition, the title deed for the land on which the project was constructed was not  provide d for audit to confirm ownership by the County Executive.  839.7.   Stalled Construction of Dormitories, Kitchen, Dining Area and a Shed at the  High - Altitude Training Centre in Keringet  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a contract with a local company for constructi on of two (2) dormitories, kitchen, dining  area and a shed at the high attitude training facility in Keringet Ward. The tender was  awarded on 23 February, 2021   at a contract price of   Kshs.16,999,852   and   payments  amounting to Kshs.13,966,085 or 82% of   the c ontract sum made as at 31 May, 2025.  However, physical inspection of the works revealed that the project was incomplete and  the contractor was not on site.  In the circumstances,   value for money for the expenditure amounting to   Kshs.13,966,085  could not   be confirmed .  839.8.   Incomplete Mechanical Works and Borehole Drilling at The High Attitude  Training Centre in Keringet  The County Executive entered into a contract with a local company for mechanical works  and borehole drilling at the high attitude traini ng center in Keringet Ward   -   Kuresoi South  Sub - County on 22 May, 2023   at a contract price of   Kshs.18,431,860 with expected  completion date of 22 November, 2023.   P ayments amounting to Kshs.15,552,830 or 84%  of   the contract sum had been made as at 31   May, 2025. However, physical inspection of  the works revealed that the project was incomplete as equipping and water treatment,  plumbing and drainage works for ablution block and external water reticulation and lawn  irrigation works were not done.  839.9.   Incompl ete   Construction of Nakuru County Treasury Headquarters  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that Management entered  into a   contract with a local company for   the construction of the Nakuru County Treasury  Headquarters on 2 December, 2020 for a period of ninety - six (96) weeks with expected  completion date of 1 December, 2022 at a contract sum of Kshs.886,630,388. During the  year under review, the contractor was   paid a total amount of Kshs.156,496,439 resulting  in cumulative total payments of Kshs.842,228,974 or 95% of the contract price, as at  30 June, 2025. However, physical inspection carried out on 11 June, 2025 revealed that  the project was about 90% co mplete having nearly taken thirty (30) months after the  original contract period lapsed.

406  839.10.   Incomplete Construction of Naivasha Smart Fish Market  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.23,168,922,681 which includes work in progress balance of Kshs.4,177,860,829 in  respect   of   the   on - going   and   incomplete   projects.   Review   of   the   project   files   and  procurement records revealed that Management entered into a contract with a local  company   for construction of the proposed construction of Naivasha Smart Fish Market at  a cost of Kshs.80,000,000. The project was to be   financed   by stakeholders from East  Africa Grain Council and County Government of Nakuru with both contributing a total  amount of   Kshs.70,000,000 to cater for the works and Kshs.10,000,000 for boundary  walls and external paving respectively. The agreement also included Jomo Kenyatta  University of Agriculture and Technology which was to provide the Bills of Quantities  (BQs). The proj ect commenced on 3 January, 2022. However, physical inspection carried  out   during the month of   June, 2025 revealed that the works were behind schedule,  incomplete and the contractor was not on site. Payment records revealed that the  contractor had been pai d the full amount of Kshs.80,000,000 but the market had not been  completed and was not in use.  In the circumstances,   value for money on expenditure amounting to Kshs.1,392,302,912  spent on stalled, ongoing and incomplete projects could not be confirmed .  840.   Community Boreholes Sunk on Land with Doubtful Ownership  Review of the project files and procurement records revealed that the Department of  Water, Environment, Energy, Climate Change and Natural Resources during the year  awarded tenders to various contractors to supply pipes and fittings and drill boreholes.  As   at 31 May, 2025, the Department had spent   an amount of   Kshs.194,568,159 on the  project’s funds for equipping, drilling and fencing of sixty - four (64) boreholes within the  County in the various sub - counties. However, review of the supporting documents  reve aled that all the boreholes were sunk on land which did not have community  ownership documents. In addition, ten (10) boreholes which had been drilled were not in  use and were lying idle.  In   the   circumstances,   the   value   for   money   on   the   expenditure   amoun ting   to  Kshs.194,568,159 spent on the projects could not be confirmed.  841.   Lack of Value for Money from the Installed Revenue Management System  The County Executive entered into an agreement with a supplier on 1 December, 2020  for the supply, installation,   configuration and commissioning of the Integrated Revenue  Collection Management System at a contract sum of Kshs.34,510,000. According to the  terms   of   reference   (TORs)   the   vendor   was   to   ensure   that   the   County   Executive  maximized the revenue. However, revie w of revenue records revealed that there has  been no much improvement in the revenue collection since its installation. Further, Clause  3.1.2 of the contract agreement states that upon completion of the supply, the client shall  be paid 4.3% of the total re venue processed and collected through the system on a  monthly basis.

407  During the year under review, the vendor was paid a total of Kshs.42,772,154 being 4.3%  of   the   total   revenue   collected   per   month,   for   the   year   under   review.   However,  Management did not d emonstrate that the County Executive’s revenue collection had  improved significantly from the previous year’s collections as was envisaged in the TORs  of the contract yet the Consultant was being paid a fee of 4.3% on total revenue collected  on a monthly b asis.  In the circumstances, the   value for money on the amount of   Kshs.42,772,154   spent on  the Integrated Revenue Collection Management system   could not be confirmed .  842.   Irregularities in the Construction of County Aggregation and Industrial Park  The contract for the construction of Nakuru County Aggregation and Industrial Park was  awarded in the financial year 2023/2024 at a contract sum of   Kshs.464,221,150 and was  to be financed by the County Government and the National Government. However, the  ownership documents for the land on which the aggregation and industrial park had been  constructed were not provided for audit. It was explained that   the County Government  entered into an agreement with Egerton University for the County Government to use the  land, but the agreement was not provided for audit. Further, the   feasibility study reports  and details of the intended works were also not provide d for audit review. This was  contrary to Regulation 75(1) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regulations, 2015 states that, “it shall be the responsibility of the County Treasury to  ensure that any project approved for financing through   grants   -   has been approved by the  Accounting Officer; and   the project feasibility study report has been inspected and  approved by the relevant County Government entity”.  In the circumstances, M anagement was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS O F INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  843.   Lack of Policies and Procedures for Land Management in the Department of  Lands  The Department of Lands did not have in place policies and procedures relating to land  management and guidelines on land acquisition, use, control, protection, maintenance  and disposal.  Further, review of the land register provided for audit revealed tha t the register was  missing key information including parcel numbers for some of the parcels of land, details  of ownership of the parcels of land and their estimated market value.  In the circumstances, existence of effective policies and procedures relatin g to land  management could not be confirmed.

408  844.   Lack of   Annual   Recruitment   Plans  Review of the Integrated Personnel Payroll Data (IPPD) payroll for the year revealed that  one hundred and ninety - six (196) officers were   appointed   and integrated into the  payroll.   However, there were no annual recruitment plans provided by the departments.  Further, no evidence was provided as proof that budgetary availability had been sought  from County Assembly before recruitment process was started. This was contrary to  S ection B.2 (1) of the Human Resources Policies and Procedures Manual fo Public  Service, 2016 which states that public entity shall prepare Human Resource Plans to  support achievement of goals and objectives in their Strategic plans. The plans shall be  base d on comprehensive job analysis and shall be reviewed every year to address  emerging issues and needs.  In the circumstances, effectiveness of internal control mechanisms over human resource  management could not be confirmed.

411  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF NAROK   –   NO.33  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  845.   Non - Compliance with Transitional IPSAS Reporting Requirements  Note 2 to the Financial Statements on Statement of Compliance and Basis of Preparation  of the financial   statements, Management refers to the use of the transitional provisions  under IPSAS 33 but does not specify which elements of the financial statements have not  been recognized and do not outline the steps being taken to achieve full compliance with  IPSAS A ccrual requirements.  In the circumstances, the financial statements as prepared and presented are not in  compliance with IPSAS reporting framework.  846.   Unsupported Expenditure on Rentals of Produce Assets  The statement of financial performance reflects use   of goods and services amount of  Kshs.4,341,684,224 as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements. Included in the  amount is Kshs.249,892,223 in respect of rentals of produced assets which further  includes an expenditure of Kshs.32,651,486 spent on   hiring of motor vehicles and  ambulance services. However, the payment was not supported with local purchase  orders, invoices, daily motor vehicle movement schedules and signed work tickets for the  motor vehicles.  Further,   included   in   the   amount   is   an   exp enditure   of   Kshs.34,760,515   relating   to  expenses incurred during the financial year 2023/2024 which were not disclosed as part  of the outstanding pending bills as at 30 June, 2024. This was contrary to Regulation  97(1) of the Public Finance Management (Cou nty Governments) Regulations, 2015,  which requires the Management of the County to report only transactions which take  place within the financial year up to 30 June. As a result, the rentals of produced assets  expense has been overstated by Kshs.34,760,515 .  In the circumstances, the accuracy, occurrence and completeness of the rentals of  produced assets amounting to Kshs. 67,412,001   could not be confirmed.  847.   Unsupported   Payment   of Fuel, Oil and Lubricants  The statement of financial performance reflects expenditure on use of goods and services  amount of Kshs.4,341,684,224, which as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial statements  includes an amount of Kshs.98,489,800 in respect of fuel, oil and lubricants. H owever,  the contracted supplier details, fuel statements and consumption records for the County  Executive were not provided for audit review. Further, there were no internal control  measures   regarding   the   requisition,   approval   and   receipt   of   fuel   or   eviden ce   of

412  reconciliation of the fuel register, work tickets, total fuel expenses and monthly fuel  expense returns by various   D epartments to the County Headquarters. In addition, the fuel  payment   vouchers   and   supporting   schedules   were   not   provided   for   audit   rev iew.  Therefore, the basis upon which the fuel expense was included in the financial statements  was not clear.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of   fuel, oil and lubricants amounting  to Kshs.98,489,800 expenditure on could not be confirme d.  Emphasis of Matter  848.   Budgetary Control   and   Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts   -   recurrent and development  combined   reflects   final   receipts   budget   and   actual   on   comparable   basis   of  Kshs.17,490,542,593 and   Kshs.14,907,575,149 respectively, resulting in under - funding  of Kshs.2,582,967,444   or 15% of the budget.  The under - funding affected the planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified i n respect of this matter.  Other Matter  849.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the p revious   years’ audit report, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial Statements, Report on Lawfulness and Effectiveness in the Use of Public  Resources, and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance, respectively . Review of the status during audit of the County Executive in  2024/2025 revealed that thirty (30) issues as detailed at the end of this report remained  unresolved.  Other Information  850.   There were no material issues   relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  851.   Irregular Use of Manual Payroll  Review of expenditure on employee compensation for the financial year 2024/2025  revealed that the County Executive operated two parallel payroll systems, excel - based

413  manual   payroll   and   the   Government   approved   Integrated   Payroll   and   Personnel  Database (IPPD ) integrated with the Human Resource Information System (HRIS).  Payroll records indicated that gross payments totalling Kshs. 17,040,129   were processed  through the manual payroll system.  Further, there was no adequate supporting documentation to confirm wh ether the  employees paid   through   the manual system were genuine and the payments were duly  authorized.  This was contrary   to   Section 149(1)   of the   Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which  provides that an Accounting Officer is accountable for ensuring that the resources of the  entity for which the officer is designated are used in a way that is lawful and authorized  and effective, efficient, econom ical and transparent.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  852.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of the County master roll and human resources records revealed that out of five  thousand two hundred   and   eigh ty - six (5,286) employees currently engaged by the County  Executive, three thousand six hundred   and   ninety - four (3,694) or 70% are from the same  dominant   ethnic community.   This was contrary to Section 7(1) and (2) of the National  Cohesion and Integration Ac t, 2008 which stipulates that no public establishment should  employ more than one - third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  853.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Revi ew of the County Executive payroll data revealed that there were several employees  whose salary was less than one third of their basic pay for a number of months during the  year under review.   This was   contrary to Section 19(3) of the Employment Act,   2007 which  stipulates   that   without   prejudice   to   any   right   of   recovery   of   any   debt   due   and  notwithstanding the provisions of any other written law, the total amount of all deductions  made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any one time shall n ot exceed  two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  854.   Delayed Completion of Projects  The County Executive entered into contract agreements with several contractors for the  construction and rehabilitation of ten ( 10) roads to bitumen standards as well as murram  and graveling at a total cost of Kshs. 632,059,513.   Physical inspection of the projects and  review of records revealed that as at the time of the audit in July, 2025 ,   the projects were  either stalled, incompl ete or abandoned. Payment records and vouchers revealed that as

414  the time of the audit, the County Executive had paid a total of Kshs. 470,982,011   to the  respective contractors.  The general conditions of contract require contractors to submit monthly paymen t  applications to the Project Manager giving sufficient details of the work done and  materials on site. However,   this was not done as required.  Further, the following observations were made in respect of the execution of the projects  and payments made: -  854.1.   P roposed Upgrading of Nairagie - Enkare Market Road  During physical verification in July, 2025, it was noted that the market road being  tarmack ed measured approximately 1.4km and not 2km as indicated in the contract  documents. Review of the contract documents revealed that under bill No.1, provisions  were made for a project supervision vehicle, insurance for the project vehicle and project  superv ision   amounting   to   Kshs.8,000,000,   Kshs.500,000   and   Kshs.1,000,000,  respectively. However, no evidence was provided to confirm that the project engineer and  Project Implementation team supervised the works.  Further, review of the bills of quantities reve aled that the item for spreading and  compacting natural gravel for the sub - base was charged twice at Kshs.3,000,000,  resulting in overstatement of the bills of quantities and inflating the project cost.  854.2.   Upgrading of Narok Township Roads to Bitumen Stand ard  Review of the contract documents revealed that the contractor was required to erect three  publicity signboards at a total cost of Kshs.150,000 and allocate Kshs.1,500,000 for  project supervision. However, only two (2) signboards were erected and no ev idence was  provided to confirm how the amount of Kshs.1,500,000 for project supervision was  utilized.  Further,   the   contractor   received   payments   totalling   Kshs.29,887,550   comprised   of  Kshs.3,097,560, Kshs.5,672,070, Kshs.5,545,720, Kshs.13,972,200 and Kshs .1,600,000  for cement and lime treated subgrade and subbase and base, culvert and drainage works,  bituminous surface treatment and surface dressing, bituminous mixes, and road furniture  respectively. However, physical verification of the project in July, 2 025, noted that there  was no evidence of lime treated subgrade as only natural stones were visible on the  surface.  In addition, the drainage works on the roads were not completed to the required standard,  bitumen surface treatment and dressing had not   been carried out as there was no bitumen  on the site and no evidence of bituminous mixes having been used. Similarly, road  furniture had not been installed despite the contractor having been paid for the items. It  was not possible to determine how the paym ents were approved without verification of  completion of actual works.

415  In the circumstances, t here is high risk that the projects will not be delivered within the  contractual period and that   value for money in the implementation of the project may not  be   achieved.  855.   Delayed Commencement of Planned Projects  Review of procurement documents submitted for audit revealed that the County Executive  awarded eleven (11) construction and civil works amounting to Kshs. 238,573,432 , for the  construction of the footbridges and box culverts in various locations. The contra cts were  scheduled to commence on 18 March, 2025 with an implementation period of six (6)  months. However, as at the time of the audit in July, 2025, the signing of the contracts for  the   projects   had   not   been   done   and   the   contractors   were   not   mobilised   to   site.  Management did not provide satisfactory explanations for the delays in executing the  contracts or commencing the projects.  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   for   the   above   projects   amounting   to  Kshs. 238,573,432   could be not be confirmed .  856.   Irregular Funding of National Government Projects  Review of records revealed that included in the construction of roads expenditure is an  amount of Kshs. 303,765,850   incurred on construction and routine maintenance of three  (3) roads which fall under the j urisdiction of National Government Road Agencies as  detailed in the table below:  Road Project   Contract Value  (Kshs)  Agency Responsible  Maasantare Junction  Ololulunga Centre  82,479,886   Kenya Rural Roads Authority  Nairagie Enkare Junction   -  Nairagie Enkare  95,509,809   Kenya Rural Roads Authority  Maasai Mara University Road   125,776,155   Kenya Urban Roads Authority  Total   303,765,850  Management did not provide letters of approval from the relevant agencies and evidence  of written   agreement between the two levels of Government detailing the level of  technical, financial, and capacity building support expected from National Government  agencies as stipulated in Article 187 of the Constitution of Kenya.  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .

416  857.   Non - Compliance with Climate Change Regulations  Review of County Executive’s processes and operations in regard s to   compliance with  the Environment and Climate Change Amendment Act, 2023 revealed that   the County  Executive had not fully implemented the laws, regulations and policies on climate change.  Further, the Departments have not aligned their operations with the Long - Term Low  Emissions Development Strategy (LT - LEDS) 2022 - 2050 as evidenced by lack   of adoption  of the renewable energy(solar) in water supply,   non - adoption of climate - smart agriculture  practices and solar powered street lighting. This was attributed to low levels of awareness  and budgetary constraints that have hampered alignment with t he Low Emissions  Development Strategy.  In addition, Management did not report on the Greenhouse Gas Emissions or carbon  credit projects within the County Executive. Similarly, while stakeholders were engaged  through   various   committees   and   forums,   there   w ere   no   documentation   on   their  contributions. There was also inordinate delay by the County Executive in disbursing  allocated funds for FLLoCA programs which hampered the timely realization of intended  climate finance benefits.  In the circumstances, the Co unty Executive did not fully comply with climate change  regulations, laws and policies.  858.   Failure to Implement e - Procurement System  T he County Executive spent substantial amounts in acquisition of goods, works and  services. However, the County Executive had not implemented the e - Procurement  system hence goods, works and services were procured through manual procurement  system. This was   contrary to Executive Order No.2 of 2018 which directed all public  procuring entities to conduct all procurement processes through the e - procurement  module on the IFMIS system, effective from 1 January, 2019.  Further,   Regulation   49(2)   of   the   Public   Procu rement   and   Asset   Disposal  Regulations, 2020 requires that e - procurement procedures for the supply of goods, works  and services to be carried out by a procuring entity using an e - procurement system which  is integrated to the state porta l.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  859.   Non - Compliance with the Law on Access to Information  T he County Executive did not prepare quarterly reports on   A ccess to   I nformation  I mplementation or Access to Information (ATI) Register   as   it   was not provided for audit  review. Further, the institutional work plan detailing access to information programs and  activities, sensitization, and staff training initiatives on ATI implementation was not  provided.   This was contrary to Section 27 of th e Access to Information Act, 2016 which  requires every Government reporting institution through its Information Access Officer to

417  prepare and   submit an Annual   Access to   Information Report compiled from all quarterly  reports prepared at the end of every fin ancial year.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  860.   Stalled Projects  860.1.   County Aggregation Industrial Park  The contract for the construction of County Aggregation Industrial Park at Limanet, Narok  Town was awarded to a local contractor on 21 July, 2023 at a contract sum of  Kshs.450,017,750.   The   contractor   was   scheduled   to   commence   works   on  24 August, 2023 for a contract period of twenty - eight (28) weeks with the expected  completion date of 10 April, 2024. However, audit inspection conducted in July, 2025  revealed that ninety - six (96) weeks after the lapse of the contract start date, t he project  had stalled. Further, there was no work in progress apart from only a partial perimeter  wall and the contractor was not on site, indicating abandonment of the project. In addition,  the contractor was issued with Certificate No.1 dated 20 March,   2024 by the Department  for   Roads, Public Works and Transport for payment of Kshs.2,034,643 and advance  payment of Kshs.24,000,000.  No explanation was provided for the delay in the completion of the contract and  Management did not provide evidence of   any approved extension of the contract period.  860.2.   Ewaso Ng’iro Barter Market  The contract for the construction of Ewaso Ng’iro barter market and supporting facilities  in Naroosura/Maji/Moto Ward was awarded to a local contractor on   9 August, 2024 at a  con tract sum of Kshs.60,667,501. The contract signed on   12 August, 2024 was to run for  a period of six (6) months with expected completion date of 12 February, 2025 and a  Local Purchase Order was issued on the same date.  Audit inspection of the project in Ju ly 2025, ten (10) months after commencement of the  project, revealed that the project had stalled.   Interview with the site caretaker revealed  that the contractor vacated the site in September, 2024.  In the circumstances,   D elayed completion of projects be yond the contract period may  result in cost escalations and may negatively impact service delivery to the public.  861.   Irregular Transfer of Funds to Mara Operation Account  Review of the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) payment  detai ls for the year under review indicates   that four (4) transactions amounting to  Kshs.11,000,000 were paid from recurrent bank account sub - item under the Mara  Operations account. However, the payments related to transfers made to organizations  that were not   Government agencies or entities. This was contrary to   Section 154 (1) of

418  the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which prohibits an Accounting Officer from  authorizing transfers of an amount that is appropriated   -   for transfer to another County  Government   entity or person; for capital expenditure except to defray other capital  expenditure; or for wages to non - wage expenditures.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  862.   Irregular Transfer of Funds to Narok Kajiado Economic Block  Review of expenditure records for the year revealed that an amount of Kshs.8,000,000  was   transferred to the Narok Kajiado Economic Block (NAKAEB). However, the transfers  were unauthorized since   they were not included in the approved budget for the year.  Further, the transfers were made without any set conditions or formal agreement and no  verifiable documentation was provided in support of the Narok Kajiado Economic Block’s  constitutional manda te. This was contrary to Section 104 (1) of the County Governments  Act, 2012 which prohibits public funds to be appropriated outside a planning framework  developed by the County Executive Committee and approved by the County Assembly.  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  863.   Delay in Completion of Health Facilities  863.1.   Narok County Referral Hospital Block  As previously reported, the completion of the construction of the Narok County Referral  Hospital block has delayed far be yond the expected completion period as detailed in the  table below:  No.   Project Details  Contract  Amount ( Kshs)  Amount Paid  by   30 June,  2025  (Kshs)  Expected  Completion  Date  %  Completion  1   Proposed New Hospital  Block and Mortuary at Narok  County   Referral Hospital.  637,680,794   621,338,949   09 August, 2021   90%  2   Mechanical, Electrical,  Engineering Services and  Associated Works for New  Narok County Referral  Hospital Block  469,614,655   289,797,960   18 July, 2022   65%  Total   1,107,295,449   911,136,909  At the time of audit in July 2025, Management explained that the initial contract had been  terminated. However, no documentary evidence was provided such as request by the  Head of Procurement   U nit for the termination of the contract, an approval by the  A ccounting   O fficer for the termination of the contract, the reasons for the termination and

419  the resultant costs of terminating the contract and a complex and specialized contract  implementation te am recommendation for the contract termination.  Further, the Hospital was not in use three (3) years after the expected completion date  despite the payments amounting to Kshs.911,136,909 having already been made to the  contractor.  863.2.   Lolgorian Level 4 Hos pital  The Sub - County Hospital expansion project commenced on 25 January, 2022 for a  contract period of twelve (12) months at a contract sum of Kshs.89,539,451. The  completion date was to be 24 January, 2023. Review of payments records as at  30 June, 2025 revealed that the contractor had been paid an amount of Kshs.40,000,000  against   the   certificate   raised   for   work   done   of   Kshs.38,236,410   resulting   in   an  overpayment of Kshs.1,763,590.  Further analysis revealed that the second   certificate of works undertaken was signed by  the County Works Officer, the County Engineer and approved the works for payment  despite pending works valued at Kshs.8,730,132 implying that payments were authorized  for incomplete works.  Physical inspection   of the Hospital project in July, 2025,   revealed that   the contractor was  not on site. There was no evidence of contract extension or formal termination despite  the   contract   period   having   expired   more   than   two   and   a   half   years   earlier   in  January , 2023.  In addition, it was observed that although a fully equipped theatre and three (3) fully  furnished   wards   with   a   bed   capacity   of   one   hundred   and   fifty   (150)   beds   were  commissioned in June, 2022, the facilities remained unutilised, as at the time of   the audit  in July, 2025.  In the circumstances, value for money for the expenditure on the Hospital facilities and  equipment   could not be confirmed.  864.   Unremitted Retirement Benefits Contributions  Review of records provided for audit revealed that the County Executive owed an amount  of Kshs.1,911,131,070 to   County Pension Fund, Local Authorities Pension Fund nd LAP  F unds which comprise of principal outstanding contributions and interest balance of  K shs.134,981,919 and Kshs.1,776,149,151 .  However, Management has not made any effort to clear the outstanding balances which  continue to attract penalties. Further, continued non - remittance constitutes a persistent  material breach   and may adversely affect   the ability of pension funds to meet retirement  benefit obligations to the retiring employees.   This was   contrary to Regulation 22(2) (a) of  the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)   Regulations,   2015   which  requires Accounting Officers to comply w ith statutory obligations including taxes, levies,  duties, pensions, commitments and audit commitments as provided for by legislation.

420  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  865.   Grounded Assets Managed   b y   Contracted Service Provider  Du ring physical inspection of machinery in the custody of a contracted service provider,  it   was   observed   that   despite   significant   expenditure   by   the   County   Executive   for  maintenance and servicing, eight (8) equipment were not in use and were grounded.  Manage ment   did   not   provide   mechanical   engineers’   reports   to   confirm   the   current  condition of the machines.  Further, the County Executive had purchased six (6) concrete mixers 400L units and two  (2) reversing drum concrete mixers which were found idle and deteriorating in the yard. It  was not explained why the equipment was acquired if it was not intended for us e.   T he  mixers were   also   not tagged or marked as County Executive property.  In addition, it was observed that the County Executive   was   providing office space to the  service provider within a   county   facility, yet no documentation was provided for the  arrangement.   There was no evidence of rent payments or any benefits to the County  Executive, despite the service provider being paid over Kshs.300,000,000 annually to  manage the equipment.  In the circu mstances, value for money for the expenditure and effective management of  the County Executive’s equipment may not be achieved.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  866.   Lack of an Updated Assets   Register  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and equipment balance of  Kshs.47,478,479,580 as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements. Review of  records revealed that , the County Executive spent an amount of Kshs.4,670,847 ,435 on  acquisition of computers, printers, and other IT equipment. However, an updated asset  register showing all the assets in its possession were not provided for audit review.  Further, the fixed assets register did not disclose the   opening balances and additions for  each asset category including key details such as acquisition dates, acquisition cost,  depreciation rates applied, accumulated depreciation and the net book value.   In addition,  no proper tagging system has been put in pla ce for clear identification of the assets owned  by the County Executive.  In the circumstances, the   effectiveness of   internal controls over assets   management  could not be confirmed.

421  867.   Lack of Fraud and Risk Management Strategies  The County Executive did   not have a Fraud Management Policy in place to assist in  detecting and preventing fraud during the year under review. Further, there was no Risk  Management Policy or strategy in place, leaving the County Executive without approved  processes and guidelines   to mitigate operational, legal and financial risks contrary to  Regulation 158 of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2015.  In addition, the County Executive did not have   D isaster Recovery Plan or Business  Continuity Plan which   outline measures for maintaining operations during unplanned  service disruptions. Management also had not instituted policies and procedures to guide  key financial processes and controls for the management of personnel and related  expenditure. Similarly, M anagement did not perform formal risk assessments during the  financial year.  In the circumstances, Management may not be in a position to evaluate, rank and  prioritize critical risks and channel resources effectively toward mitigating identified   risks.  868.   Ineffective Internal Audit Function and Audit Committee  Review of records provided for audit revealed that the County Executive’s Internal Audit  Department did not have an approved internal audit charter, an approved annual audit  plan and independ ent budget or authority to incur expenditure.  Further, the risk assessment and internal audit reports for the year under review were not  provided including the minutes of the Audit Committee indicating supervisory oversight of  the internal audit function . In addition, the recruitment and operationalization of the Audit  Committee had not been done at the time of the audit in July, 2025.  In the circumstances, there   was   no effective system in place to monitor the County  Executive’s governance and accountabi lity processes and control environment to provide  objective advice on risk management, internal controls, regulatory compliance and  governance matters.  869.   Weak Information and Communication Technology Controls  Review of the County Executive's Information an d Communication Technology (ICT)  Environment revealed lack of an approved ICT Policy. Management had not assessed  the impact of system outage or disruptions to the ICT systems and had not developed  Information Technology Disaster Recovery Plan. Further, IC T Strategic Committee had  not been established to provide governance on ICT matters.  Therefore, in case of a disaster, the County Executive could experience significant delays  or disruptions in activities and may not recover or restore critical infrastr ucture services  and systems, affecting all operations that depend on the Information Communication  Technology.

422  In the circumstances, the integrity, security, and reliability of the County Executive's  financial data and Management Information System could   not be confirmed.  870.   Weak Controls Related to Voided Transactions  Review of the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) records  revealed that various transactions were processed and subsequently voided or cancelled  during the year   under review. However, the transactions were not supported with relevant  documentation such as payment vouchers, authorization or justification for voiding,  journal vouchers for reversing the transactions and records of final payments.  In the   circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls related to recording of financial  transactions could not be confirmed.
