510  COUNTY EXECUTIVE   OF BUSIA   –   NO.40  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  1075.   Inaccuracies in   the   Financial Statements  1075.1.   The Statement of Financial Position  The statement of financial position reflects capital fund balance of Kshs.911,502,580 as  at 30 June, 2025, while the statement of changes in net assets reflects Nil balance.  Further, the statement reflects net assets negative balance of Kshs.151,303,261 as   at  30 June, 2025, while the statement of changes in net assets reflects negative balance of  Kshs.1,062,805,841   resulting in unreconciled   variance of Kshs.911,502,508.  1075.2.   The Statement of Changes in Net Assets  The   statement   of   changes   in   net   assets   refle cts   net   assets   negative   balance   of  Kshs.1,062,805,841   as   at   30   June,   2025.   The   balance   includes   an   amount   of  Kshs.911,502,580 relating to property, plant and equipment which was committed in  Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) and no t purchased.  Further, the net assets balance includes an amount of Kshs.1,837,526,845 described as  unbudgeted pending bills disclosed under accumulated surplus/deficit. However, no  satisfactory explanation was provided by Management on inclusion of these   amounts in  the statement of changes in net assets for the year ended 30 June, 2025 and the analysis  and supporting documents for the amount were not provided for audit review.  1075.3.   Unreconciled   Grants and Transfers to County Funds  Review of the statement of   financial performance and as disclosed in Notes 11(A) and  13(A) to the financial statements revealed transfer to other Government entities amounts  of Kshs.31,000,000 and other grants and subsidies   amounting to   Kshs.918,444,774.  However, confirmation of rec eipts by the respective County Funds revealed variances as  summarized below:  (i)   Note 11(A) to the financial statements indicates transfer to Busia County  Education Support Scheme amount of Kshs.31,000,000, while the financial  statements   of   Busia   County   Education   Support   Scheme   indicated   a  corresponding receipt of Kshs.101,500,000 resulting in unreconciled variance  of Kshs.70,500,000.  (ii)   Note 13(A) to the financial statements indicates grants to small businesses,  cooperatives and self - employed amount of Ksh s.311,129,722, which includes  transfer to Cooperative Enterprise Fund   amount   of Kshs.17,000,000. However,

511  the financial statements of Kakamega County Cooperative Enterprise Fund  reflect ed   corresponding receipt of Kshs.5,500,000 resulting in unreconciled  va riance of Kshs.11,500,000 .  (iii)   Note 13(A) to the financial statements indicates transfer to Climate Change  Fund   amount   of Kshs.243,716,679, while the financial statements of Busia  County   Climate   Change   Fund   reflect ed   a   corresponding   receipt   of  Kshs.216,356,863 resulting in unreconciled variance of Kshs.27,359,816.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   respective   financial  statements’ balances could not be confirmed.  1076.   Unsupported Payment of Staff   Medical Insurance Cover  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements   reflects   expenditure   on   use   of   goods   and   services   amount   of  Kshs.2,497,206,343,   which   includes   insurance   payments   amounting   to  Kshs.341, 910,263.   Included   in   the   insurance   payments   are   two   (2)   amounts   of  Kshs.63,911,807 and Kshs.210,267,470 totalling Kshs.274,179,277 paid to two (2)  insurance companies for provision of medical insurance for staff and dependents for a  period   of   twelve   (12)   m onths.   However,   the   total   insurance   paid   amounting   to  Kshs.274,179,277   exceeded   the   approved   medical   insurance   budget   of  Kshs.254,832,345   resulting in   unauthorized expenditure of Kshs.19,346,932.  Further, the County Executive entered into an agreement wit h an insurance broker for  provision of medical insurance at a contract sum of Kshs.216,855,295. A total of  Kshs.210,267,470 had been paid to the brokerage firm as at 30 June, 2025. However,  Management did not provide details of the staff members, and depen dents covered  including the age, number of children per staff, medical cover for newly recruited staff,  and list of the approved hospitals and medical facilities under the scheme.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and   regularity   of insuranc e payments  for staff medical cover of Kshs.274,179,277 could not be confirmed.  1077.   Unsupported   Legal   Expenses  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 10(A) to the financial  statements   reflects   expenditure   on   use   of   goods   and   services   amount   of  Kshs.2,497,206,343,   which   includes   other   operating   expenses   amounting   to  Kshs.575,667,276. The amount includes legal expenses of Kshs.9,150,232 paid by the  office of the   County Attorney to private   legal   firms representing   the   County   Executive .  However, the payments vouchers were not supported with relevant documentations such  as initial itemized fee notes, amounts paid to date, outstanding balances per case, the  cases being handled and status of those cases, evidence of Court attendan ce, fees as  per Advocates Remuneration Order, 2014, case files showing the value of each case to  authenticate the payments, contract agreements and procurement records.

512  Further, the County Executive did not maintain legal matrix or the legal cases   register and  an ageing analysis of the cases to determine the period in which the cases were  outstanding, amount relating to each case and a request by the Department s   and written  approval of County Executive Committee to engage the services of the consult ants or  legal firms as required by Section 16(1) of the Office of the County Attorney Act, 2020.  The Office of the County Attorney   also   did not prepare and submit annual reports to the  Governor and the County Assembly as required by law.  In addition, it w as observed that the County has a fully - fledged   l itigation Department.  However, it was not clear why the County Executive outsourced the services to external  legal firms in all the cases.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and regularity of   legal expenses  totalling Kshs.9,150,232 could not be confirmed.  1078.   Unsupported Trade and Other Payables  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.3,085,46 4,048.   However, payment  vouchers supporting the entire trade and other payables balance,   ledgers detailing  invoice dates and amounts, payment amounts and outstanding balances, and   ageing  analysis were not provided for audit review.  Further,   Note   32   reflects   two   conflicting   balances   of   Kshs.3,085,464,048   and  Kshs.3,673,835,690 resulting in unreconciled variance of Kshs.588,371,642.  In addition, the balance includes   an amount of   Kshs.1,836,644,923 in respect of prior  year periods accounts payable   relating to financial years 2015/2016 to 2023/2024 which  should have been prioritized as a first charge on the County Revenue Fund. Additionally,  the amount was not included in the budget. This was contrary to Regulation 41(2) of the  Public Finance Managem ent (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires  that debt service payments be treated as a first charge.  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and   regularity   of the trade and other  payables balance of Kshs.3,085,464,048 could not be   confirmed.  1079.   Undisclosed Land Balances  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 26 to the financial statements  reflects property, plant and equipment balance of Kshs.691,827,042 which relates to  assets acquired during the year under review. The balance includes land   amount   o f  Kshs.750,000. However, review of supporting schedules to the financial statements  indicated that an amount of Kshs.18,753,990 was incurred on purchase of twelve (12)  parcels of land for the construction of dispensaries, playgrounds and vocational trainin g  centers. However, the amount was not included in the land balance.

513  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of land balance of Kshs.750,000  could not be confirmed.  1080.   Unexplained   Expenditure on Social Development Programme  The statement of fi nancial performance and as disclosed in Note 13 to the financial  statements reflects other grants and subsidies amount of Kshs.918,444,774. The County  Executive through the Department for Community Development, Youth, Sports, Tourism,  Culture and Social Se rvices incurred expenditure totalling Kshs.38,115,000 as social  development grants. However, review of payment vouchers and supporting documents  revealed the following unsatisfactory matters:  (i)   Committee minutes were not provided to ascertain the number of a pplicant,  application dates, approval dates and details of submission for payment  approval.  (ii)   No acknowledgement forms were provided to ascertain whether indeed the  approved groups actually received the funds .  (iii)   Neither ad - hoc reports nor annual reports were provided for audit detailing the  utilization of funds and a list of beneficiaries.  (iv)   Management did not provide an explanation for the criteria used to allocate  different amounts to various wards or to explain   varying amounts awarded to  successfully vetted groups .  (v)   The grants policy in use has remained in draft form since 2016, although it was  forwarded for approval on 6 June, 2016, no approvals were provided for audit  verification.  In the   circumstances, the regularity of the expenditure amounting to Kshs.38,115,000  could not be confirmed.  1081.   Unsupported Foreign Travel Expenditure  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements reflects an amount   of Kshs.2,497,206,343 in respect of use of goods and  services. This   expenditure   includes   an amount of   Kshs.57,415,943 for foreign travel and  subsistence. Analysis of payment records revealed that six (6) officers were each paid  imprest   totalling   Kshs.3,02 6,856   for   a   foreign   study   tour   in   China   from   20   to  27 October, 2024 on rainwater harvesting and sustainable water management, as per the  invitation letter dated 08 September, 2024 from a Chinese institution in response to a  reques t from the Kenya Water Institute dated 07 September, 2024. However, no evidence  of travel was provided in the form of boarding passes, air tickets   and   attendance  certificates to confirm that the trip took place   and   was attended by the officers. There was  n o documentation on how the knowledge acquired would be applied to improve local  water systems.

514  In the circumstances, the   regularity of the expenditure amount of   Kshs.3,026,856 could  not be confirmed.  1082.   Unsupported Expenditure on   Motor Vehicles Insurance  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 10 to the financial  statements   reflects   expenditure   on   use   of   goods   and   services   amount   of  Kshs.2,497,206,343,   which   includes   insurance   payments   amounting   to  Kshs.341,910,263. Included in th is   expenditure is an   amount   of   Kshs.13,984,046 paid to  an insurance company for provision of motor vehicles and motor cycles insurance cover  for a period of twelve (12) months. Review of documents provided revealed that valuation  and assessment was not con ducted for the insured motor vehicles and motor cycles.  Further, the insurance cover included some motor vehicles without registration numbers  and therefore may not belong to the County Executive. Fifty - nine (59) motor vehicles that  were listed were not op erational and serviceable.  In   addition,   Motor   Vehicle   which   had   been   reported   as   stolen   was   insured   and  m anagement did not provide for audit review key supporting documents including the  police report, internal incident report, insurance claim   documents, Board of Survey  findings, and a statement from the officer responsible for the vehicle.  In the circumstances, the regularity, accuracy and completeness of insurance payments  for motor vehicles cover of Kshs.13,984,046 could not be confirmed.  1083.   A nomalies in the Casuals Payroll  The statement of financial performance as disclosed in Note 9(A) to the financial  statements reflects employee cost totalling Kshs.3,940,068,383 which include basic  wages of temporary employees amount of Kshs.21,884,133. Ho wever, the casual payroll  provided for audit indicates total casual payments of Kshs.131,161,110 for the year ended  30 June, 2025   resulting in   unreconciled variance of Kshs.109,276,977.  Further, Management did not provide supporting documents including m aster payrolls  indicating the number of days worked, daily rate and verification by the human resource  and user departments for audit review. It was also noted that t he requisite documentation,  including departmental requisitions to engage casual staff, ap provals from the County  Public Service Board for their engagement or delegated authority from the County Public  Service Board or delegated authority to the Departmental Accounting Officers and  appointment letters for the casual engagements were not provide d for audit .  In addition, analysis of casual payroll revealed that ten (10) employees appeared  concurrently on the casual payroll, the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD)  payroll and Human Resource Information System (HRIS) system, resulting in duplicate  p ayments amounting to Kshs.1,859,770.

515  In the circumstances, the accuracy, completeness and regularity of casuals’ payment  amounting to Kshs.21,884,133 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  1084.   Budgetary Control and Performance  T h e   s t a t e m en t   o f   c o m pa r i s o n   o f   b ud g e t   an d   a c t u a l   a m o un t s   reflects   f ina l   r e c e ip t s   bu d ge t  a n d   a c t ual   on c o m pa r a bl e   b a s i s   totalling   Ks h s. 9,923,694,532 a n d   Ks h s. 6,949,989,950  r e s pe c t i v e l y,   r e s ul t i n g   i n   un d e r - f und i n g   o f Ks h s. 2,973,704,582 o r   30 %   o f   t h e   bu d ge t .  However ,   t h e   Coun t y   Ex e c u t i ve   s p en t   an amount of   Ks h s. 6,830,609,339   a gain st   a n  actual receipt of   Ks h s. 6,949,989,950   r e s u l t in g   i n   u n de r - utilization   o f   Ks h s. 139,380,611  or 2% of actual income .  The under - funding affected the planned activities and may have   impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public .  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  1085.   Unresolved Prior Year matters  In the audit report of the previous year,   several   issues were raised under the Report on  Financial Statements,   Report   on   Lawfulness   and   Effectiveness in   Use   of   Public  Resources and Report on Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and  Governance.   However, Management had not resolved   forty - two   (42)   issues or given  any explanation for the delay in resolving the issues as listed at the end of this report.  Other Information  1086.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  1087.   Non - Compliance with Law on Supplementary Budget Limits  Review of the budget of County Government for financial year 2024/2025 revealed that,  the supplementary budget amount ed to Kshs.1,541,674,535 representing 16% of the total  approved original budget of Kshs.9,923,694,532. The increase exceeded the statutory  threshold set under Section 135(7) of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 which  provides   that a County Government   may not spend through a supplementary budget  more than ten percent (10%) of the amount appropriated by the County Assembly for that  financial year.

516  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1088.   Non - Remittance of Statutory Deductions  The st atement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 32 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.3,085,464,048. R eview of statutory  deductions   schedules,   payment   vouchers   and   bank   statements   provided   for  audit   reveale d   that   the   County   Executive   failed   to   remit   an   amount   totalling  Kshs.948,816,455 out of which   an amount of   Kshs.679,737,843 related to Pay - As - You -  Earn (PAYE), National Social Security Fund (NSSF), National Health Insurance Fund  (NHIF) and Affordable Housin g Levy (AHL), while   an amount of   Kshs.269,078,612 was  for Laptrust/Lapfund deductions. Further, deductions details for Laptrust and Lapfund   for  the months of December, 2024, January, 2025, February, 2025 and March, 2025 were  not provided for audit review. Failure to settle bills during the year to which they relate  distorts the financial statements for that year and adversely affects the prov isions for the  subsequent year to which they have to be charged.  In the circumstances, Management   was in breach of the law and   exposed to risk of  penalties and interest for late   payment   and non - remittance of statutory dues.  1089.   Project   Implementation   Status   Report  The County Executive had an approved development budget of Kshs.3,863,748,132.  Review of the   P roject   I mplementation   S tatus   R eport revealed that, the projects that were  to be implemented during the year were six hundred and ninety - six (696) with a   budget  of Kshs.2,278,126,826. The Project Implementation Status Report indicated that one  hundred and forty - seven (147) projects   amounting to   Kshs.470,151,152 were completed,  two hundred and seventy - eight (278) projects   amounting to   Kshs.1,264,197,407 wer e  ongoing   and   two   hundred   and   seventy - one   (271)   projects   amounting   to  Kshs.543,778,267 had not been started. This   was   an indication of inadequacy in project  planning and control mechanisms to ensure efficient absorption of available funds.  In the circums tances, value for money   for   the ongoing and   not started projects may not  be realized .  1090.   Delayed Implementation of Infrastructure Projects  T he County   Executive   carried out feasibility studies and procured works for twelve (12)  projects amounting to Kshs.56,533,523. However, audit verification revealed that none of  these projects had commenced and the contract periods had lapsed. Management did  not provide any ju stification for the failure to commence procured works.  In the circumstances, value for money from the delayed projects   may not be realized  1091.   Irregular ities in the   School Feeding Programme  T he County Executive contracted for the supply of 50,651 kilograms   of branded rice at a  contract sum of Kshs.12,270,821 and for the supply of 45,974 kilograms of white milled  rice at a cost of Kshs.9,194,821 through contract agreements signed on 13 September,  2024. However, Management did not provide documents in support   of the procurement

517  process. The rice was intended for distribution to primary schools across five (5)   S ub -  C ounties.   However,   there   were   no   requisitions   or   documented   requests   from   the  beneficiary primary schools indicating the need for the rice supplies   a nd   the County  Executive did not have an approved school feeding policy to guide the implementation of  such programmes.  In the circumstances,   the regularity and value for money for the   expenditure   amounting  to   Kshs.21,465,642   c ould not be confirmed.  1092.   Stall ed   Construction   of   the   Administration   Block   at   Buburi   Vocational  Training College  The County Executive awarded a contract for completion of an administration block at  Buburi   Vocational Training College at a contract cost of Kshs.3,155,040. The contract  period was for four (4) months, with the commencement date being 11 March, 2024.  Physical inspection of the works on 19 June, 2025, revealed that the contractor had  abandoned t he site.  Further, the audit inspection observed deviations from the specifications outlined in the  Bill s   of Quantities (BQs). While the BQs required the use of 200mm thick natural hand -  dressed blocks for walling, the contractor used a mix of small sand b ricks and blocks.  This substitution and change of the specifications approved in the   BQs   was not explained.  In addition, r eview of payment records revealed that an amount of Kshs.2,506,310 or 79%  of the contract sum had been paid to the contractor despit e the incomplete work.  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   for   the   abandoned   project   amounting   to  Kshs.2,506,310 could not be confirmed .  1093.   Unconfirmed Distribution of Fish Fingerlings to Farmers in Agenga Ward  The County Executive awarded a contract for the supply and delivery of   sixty - five  thousand, seven hundred and eighty - nine ( 65,789 )   tilapia fish fingerlings to farmers at a  cost of Kshs.2,499,982. However, there were no requisitions or written requests from   the  respective County Department and/or beneficiary farmers to support the need for the  fingerlings and the criteria used to identify the beneficiaries was not provided for audit.  Further, audit confirmation   from   the listed beneficiaries revealed that the y neither received  the fingerlings nor owned any fish ponds. In addition, the individuals contacted were also  unaware of such fish farming program being implemented in their area.  In the circumstances, value for money   for the expenditure   amounting to   Kshs. 2,499,982  could not be confirmed.  1094.   Stalled   Public Day Care Construction Project  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a public day care – phase  1 in Matayos Sub - County at a contract sum of Kshs.7,984,010, with a contract duration  of ninety (90) days. The contract was awarded on 16 November, 2023, and specified   the

518  scope of work included construction of foundational structures and related the day care  infrastructure. However, review of project records and physical inspection conducted on  1 July, 2025 revealed that no works had been undertaken at the designated si te. The  project site was observed to be a vehicle parking area.   Interviews with officials from the  implementing   Department   indicated   that   uncertainties   regarding   the   suitability   and  availability of the construction site contributed to the delay and eventua l stalling of the  project. It was also established that no feasibility study was conducted and inadequate  community involvement during project identification and design stages.  In the circumstances, value for money in respect of the stalled project could   not be  confirmed.  1095.   Irregularities in Contract Award for the Proposed Renovation of Samia Sub  County Administrator’s Office  The County Executive entered into a contract for renovation of Samia Sub - County  administrator’s office on 27 June, 2024 for a contr act sum of Kshs.2,487,550. The works  had been scheduled to be completed in ninety (90) calendar days after site handover  which   was   dated   5   August,   2024.   However,   the   letter   of   award   was   issued   on  13 June, 2024, the same day that the L ocal Service Order was issued to the contractor.  The acceptance letter by the contractor was dated 14 June, 2024 and the contract  agreement between the Department for Lands and the contractor was signed and  executed on 27 June ,2024. It was not clear how t he Local Service Order was issued  before provision of the acceptance letter by the contractor and before a contract  agreement was signed and executed. During site visit conducted on 2 July, 2025, it was  observed that while most works were executed in acco rdance with the BQs and project  engineer’s instructions, the veranda floor at the back of the building was only partially tiled  with ceramic tiles, leaving the project incomplete.  Further, review of the minutes of the Inspection and Acceptance Committee d ated  13   March,   2025,   revealed   that   the   Committee   had   recommended   the   works   as  satisfactorily completed. This raised serious concerns on the effectiveness and due  diligence   of   the   Committee,   which   appeared   to   have   recommended   payment   for  incomplete works.  In the circumstances, the value for money in respect of the project could not be confirmed.  1096.   Unexplained   Water Pipeline Extensions  The   County   Executive   incurred   expenditure   of   Kshs.22,878,530   for   water   pipeline  extensions in different   areas. However, Management did not provide evidence of public  participation to ascertain the water demand and usage within the said areas warranted  the need for the extension. Further, Management did not provide for audit review the  preliminary engineering   designs, Bill of Quantities, specifications on size and length of  the extension pipes, size of storage tanks (if any), the extent of elevation among other

519  information or technical data to ensure the pipeline extension actually would effectively  deliver wa ter to the intended beneficiaries.  In the circumstances, value for money for the expenditure of Kshs.22,878,530 could not  be confirmed.  1097.   Stalled Projects  1097.1.   Completion of Alupe   Mother and Child Special Hospital Phase III  The County Executive awarded tender for proposed completion of mother and child  specialized hospital at Alupe Sub - County Hospital at a sum of Kshs.24,034,075 on  29 November, 2024 for a   period of four (4) months starting from 29 November, 2024 to  29 March, 2025. Site visit conducted on 04 July, 2025 revealed the works had since  stalled, the contractor was not on site and the contract period had lapsed. Management  did not provide the steps   being taken due to non - performance of the contract.  1097.2.   Construction of Modern Kitchen at Teso North Sub - County Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a modern kitchen at a  sum of Kshs.5,001,210 on 27 December, 2024 for a   period of four (4) months starting  from 27 December, 2024 to 27 April, 2025.Site visit carried out on 4 July, 2025 revealed  that the construction works had stalled at Element Number 1 as per the BQs. Only murram  blinding up to top of hardcore layer had be en completed. Vegetation growth was observed  on the compacted murram surface indicating prolonged delays in concreting works and  may compromise the integrity of the base if not addressed promptly. Further, there was  no evidence of contractor’s presence or   ongoing activity at the site at the time of  inspection.  1097.3.   Proposed   Construction of Incinerator at Port Victoria Sub - County Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for construction of incinerator at Port Victoria  Sub - County Hospital at a contract   sum of Kshs.8,996,920 on 29 November, 2024 for a  period of four (4) months and the contract was to end on 29 March, 2025. Site visit carried  out on 4 July, 2025 revealed the works had stalled, the contractor was not on site and the  contract period had lap sed. As at the time of inspection, the incinerator construction had  advanced to lintel level.  1097.4.   Proposed   Construction   of   Modern   Gender   Sensitive   and   disabilities  Inclusive Sanitary Block at Port Victoria Sub - County Hospital  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a modern gender  sensitive and disabilities inclusive sanitatio n block at Port Victoria Sub - County Hospital  at a contract sum of Kshs.2,488,331 on 29 November, 2024. The contract was to run for  a period of four (4) months up to 29 March, 2025. As at the date of audit inspection on

520  4 July, 2025, the sanitation bloc k construction had progressed to the foundation level but  the contractor was not on site and the contract period had lapsed.  1097.5.   Proposed Construction of Chamasiri Dispensary  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of Chamasiri Dispensary  at a contract sum of Kshs.7,765,193 on 29 November, 2024 for a four (4) months period.  As at the time of audit inspection on 4 July, 2025, work on site had not progressed   beyond  the backfilling stage yet the contract period had lapsed. The contractor was not on site.  Further, the audit could not confirm the ownership of the land where the dispensary   wa s  built.  In the circumstances,   value for money   for the expenditure   spent   on the projects could not  be confirmed.  1098.   Non - Compliance with Fiscal Responsibility Principles on Wage s  The statement of financial performance reflects revenue totalling Kshs. 8,186,028,420 and  employees’ costs totalling Kshs. 3,940,068,383. The employees’ costs constituted fourty -  eight percent or 48% of the total receipts of the County Executive for the year under  review .   This was contrary to Regulation 25(1)(b) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations ,   2015 which   provides   that the County Government’s  expenditure on wages and benefits for its public officers shall not exceed 35% of the  County Government’s total revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1099.   Irregular   Terms of Employment  Review of the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database (IPPD) revealed that the  County   Executive   had a total of three thousand, seven hundred and sixty - two (3,762)  employees as at 30 June, 2025. However, seventeen (17) employees were   serving on  probational terms despite having served for periods ranging from twenty - two (22) months  to one hundred and seventy - nine (179) months.   This was contrary to Section 42(2) of the  Employment Act, 2007 which provides that a probationary period shall   not be more than  six months but it may be extended for a further period of not more than six months with  the agreement of the employee.  1099.1.   Non - Compliance   with the Law on Staff Ethnic Composition  Review of payroll records revealed that out of the total number of staff members of three  thousand seven hundred and sixty - two (3,762), a total of two thousand one hundred and  seventy - five (2,175) or 58% were from one ethnic community. This was contrary to  Section 7(2) of the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008 which   provide s that no  public establishment shall have more than one - third of its staff from the same ethnic  community.

521  1099.2.   Casuals   Engaged Beyond Stipulated Period  Analysis of monthly casual pa yrolls for the period ended 30 June, 2025 revealed that  there were two thousand three hundred and fifty - seven (2,357) casual workers who were  engaged for more than three (3) consecutive months without formal written contracts. The  total amount paid to the   workers amounted to Kshs.41,698,236.   This was contrary to  Section 37(1)(a) and (b) of Employment Act, 2007 which requires that where a casual  employee works for a number of working days amounting in the aggregate to the  equivalent of three months or more,   the contract of service of the casual employee shall  be deemed to be one where wages are paid monthly.  1099.3.   Irregular   Payment of Special House Allowances  Analysis   of   the   County   Executive   payroll   records   revealed   that   thirty - seven   (37)   employees  were paid   special house allowances amounting to Kshs.3,230,132 during the year in  addition to the regular house allowance applicable for their designations.   Management  did not provide approval or advisory from the Salaries and Renumeration Commission for  the payment   of the special house allowance.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1100.   Disputed Ownership   of Amoni Market Land  Records available indicate that the defunct Busia County Council purchased a parcel of  land measuring 2.2   Hectares in Mala b a Town in 1990 at a consideration of Kshs.130,000.  However, the sale has since been disputed and the matter   wa s pending before the Court.  Physical inspection of Amoni Market land on 30 April, 2025 revealed an existing and  operational marke t with a permanent ablution block that was not in use and temporary  incomplete market structure.  In the circumstances, ownership of the land   by the   County   could not be confirmed .  1101.   Irregularities in the   Study Leave   for the Staff  The statement of   financial performance and as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial  statements reflects an amount of Kshs.3,940,068,383 in respect of employee costs.  A nalysis of payroll for the period under review against list of staff on study leave indicated  that there we re seventeen (17) staff members on study leave were paid their full salary  packages without any bonding agreements between the staff and County Executive to  ensure service return or cost recovery.  Further, there was no policy guideline and County Trainin g Committee records indicating  that the staff had been formally approved or released for further studies. The total amount  paid to staff while on study leave was Kshs.44,572,417.

522  In   the   circumstances,   value   for   money   for   the   expenditure   on   study   leave   of  Kshs.44,572,417 could not be confirmed .  1102.   Irregular Payments of Other Grants and Subsidies  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 13(A) to the financial  statements   reflects   expenditure   on   other   grants   and   subsidies   amount   of  Kshs .918,444,774. However, analysis of payment schedules revealed that payments  amounting to Kshs.53,472,228 were irregularly paid to various suppliers and individuals.  This   was   contrary   to   the   provisions   of   Section   138(1)(c)   of   the   Public   Finance  Management A ct, 2012, which defines a grant recipient as the County Government or a  County Government entity authorized to control or spend money, or an incorporated or  unincorporated body not otherwise authorized to control or spend money under this  Act. The d isbursement of funds to entities and individuals who did not meet this definition  raises concerns regarding the appropriateness and legality of the transactions.  In the circumstances,   value for money for the   expenditure of Kshs.53,472,228 could not  be con firmed.  1103.   Unutilized   COVID - 19 Funds in Special Purpose Account  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 21 to the financial statements  reflects cash and cash equivalents balance of Kshs.118,238,299. Review of the list of  bank   accounts maintained by the County Executive revealed that the County had  unutilized funds amounting to Kshs.8,012,540 in a COVID - 19 Special Purpose Account  at the Central Bank of Kenya. No explanation was provided by Management on why the  monies were still   being held in the account or the intended purpose of the funds. Further,  bank reconciliation statements for the account were not provided for audit review.  In the circumstances, the   value for money on the unutilized cash could not be confirmed .  1104.   Failure to Install Hospital Management System at Sub - County Hospitals  The County   Executive   awarded a tender for supply, delivery, installation, customization  and commissioning of an Integrated Revenue Collection and Management System and a  Hospital   Inform ation   Management   System   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.59,885,232.  However, verification of the implementation of the contract agreement revealed that the  Hospital Information Management System was only installed at Busia County Referral  Hospital and not at th e other   S ub - C ounty   H ospitals within the County.  In the circumstances, value for money   for   the expenditure of Kshs.59,885,232 could not  be confirmed.  1105.   Failure to Establish Cash to Accrual Accounting Transition Committee  Review of the implementation of cash basis to accrual basis of accounting roadmap at  the County Executive revealed that the Accounting Officer did not establish a Cash to  Accrual Transition Committee at the entity level and did not appoint a project manage r to  oversee the transition. Further, a detailed roadmap outlining the key milestones at the

523  entity level had not been developed as required by the guidelines issued by The National  Treasury vide Treasury circular No.03/2025 dated   14 April, 2025.  In the c ircumstances, Management was in breach   of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  1106.   Failure to Implement Internal Audit Recommendations  Review of the Internal Audit report dated 21 February, 2025, submitted to the Accounting  Officer, revealed that the audit identified issues across multiple   D epartments. However,  there was no evidence that a response or action plan to the issues highlighted   in the  report was submitted to the Chairperson of the Audit Committee. This was contrary to  Section   165(1)(2)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015, and Gazette Notice No. 2690 Paragraph 6.1(b)(iv) and (c).  Further, the re was no documented effort by the Accounting Officer to implement the audit  recommendations, thereby weakening the effectiveness of both the Internal Audit function  and the broader governance framework.   Also,   the Accounting Officer   did not   publish  periodi c updates on Audit Committee activities on the   County ’s website, as required under  Guideline 6.1(b)(iv) of Gazette Notice No. 2690.  In addition , t he Audit Committee did not provide evidence of conducting an annual self -  assessment   to   evaluate   its   performa nce   against   its   mandate,   roles,   duties   and  responsibilities, as stipulated in Paragraphs 7.2(a – c), 8.1(a – d), and 8.3 of the Gazette  Notice.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the   Internal Audit Function and the Audit  Committee in overseeing the   Co unty Executive’s   operations   could not be confirmed.  1107.   Lack of Approved Staff Establishment and Annual Recruitment Plans  T he County Executive operated without an approved staff establishment. Th erefore , it  was not possible to   d etermine how the cadres and st aff capacity in various   D epartments  were established or whether the County Executive was operating at optimum staffing  levels and what criteria was used during recruitment of new staff.  Further, the County Executive appointed sixty   -   three (63) officers   during the year under  review out of which twenty - three (23) were Directors, thirty - seven (37) Deputy Directors  and three (3) Legal Counsels. However, the   D epartments did not have annual recruitment  plans to guide the appointments. In addition, no evidence was provided of budgetary  availability before appointments were made.

524  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of human resource management could not be  c onfirmed.  1108.   Operational Challenges   in   Department   for   Strategic Partnerships, ICT   and  Digital Economy  Audit review of the operating environment of the Department revealed several critical  issues that had significantly impaired   its   functionality to deliver   services effectively. At the  time of the audit, the entire Department including the offices of the Chief Officer and the  County Executive Committee (CEC) Member w ere   without electricity   which   had been  disconnected for over two (2) months due to unpaid elec tricity bills.   The Department’s  approved budget revealed   that   no allocation had been made under the electricity vote.  Instead,   it   relied on other Departments to settle the bills.   T he Department had been  allocated   an amount of   Kshs.200,000 under the foreign   travel vote. Given its strategic  role in cultivating partnerships and engaging with donors and stakeholders both locally  and internationally, this allocation was insufficient.  Further, the Department ’s   records indicated that a total of twenty - seven (27) individuals  including casual workers, interns, students on attachment and support staff who   were  forced to work in powerless offices leading to significant underutilization of both skills and  manpower   severely disrupted operations .  In addition,   the Strategic Partnerships Unit   was   heavily dependent on ICT infrastructure  to support digital service delivery all of which became largely unachievable without  electricity. As a direct consequence ,   all ICT equ ipment and other electronic devices  remained uninstalled and idle significantly compromising service efficiency and the overall  operational effectiveness of the   D epartment.   Also,   the equipment was stored in the ICT  hub workstations, which were already sque ezed and overcrowded.  In the circumstances, the   effectiveness of the operations at the Department and   service  delivery to the public   could not be confirmed .  1109.   Lack of Risk Management Policy  T he County Executive did not have a Risk Management Policy. As   a result, there were  no formal approved processes and guidelines on how to identify, assess and mitigate  operational, legal and financial risks.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of risk management   in the County   could not be  confirmed.  1110.   Lack   of   Departmental Training Committees and Training Needs Assessment  The County Executive incurred an expenditure of Kshs.192,377,075 on training during  the year under review. Review of the documents provided for audit revealed that  Management had not establis hed departmental training committees and training needs

525  assessment was not undertaken. It was not clear how Management nominated officers  for training.  In the circumstances, the internal controls on trainings management and the impact of  the trainings un dertaken could not be confirmed.  1111.   Ineffective   Management   and Control of Motor Vehicles  Review of the County Executive’s motor vehicle fleet management revealed that the  County ha d   a fleet of   two hundred and seven ( 207 )   vehicles. However, review of records  provided for audit revealed the following unsatisfactory matters:  (i)   Out of the two hundred and seven (207) vehicles, one hundred and twenty -  four (124) were operational, eighteen (18) were unserviceable and immobile  whil e the status and location of sixty - three (63) vehicles was not recorded.  (ii)   The   fleet   register   was   incomplete   and   lacked   critical   motor   vehicles  identification details   such as; registration numbers, chassis numbers, model,  year of manufacturer and locations.   One (1) of the motor vehicles was marked  as written off in the fleet register. However, key supporting documents such as  insurance claim, the insurer’s official write - off notification, proof of settlement,  the accident or incident report and the police re port were not provided for audit  review.  (iii)   The motor vehicles were not equipped with tracking devices or speed limiters  and   n one of the vehicles had their fair value recorded, undermining proper  valuation and accountability.  Further, review of motor vehicles and motorcycles recommended for boarding and  disposal approved by the Chief Officer, Directorate   for   Transport dated 17 June, 2025  revealed that forty - one (41) units were recommended for disposal. Out of these, nine (9)  we re indicated as serviceable in the fleet register, while seventeen (17) could not be  traced or were not listed in the register.  In the circumstances, the   effective , economical, and transparent management of motor  vehicles and motorcycles could not be conf irmed.  1112.   Staff Salary Payment Outside Integrated Payroll and Personnel Database  Review of salary records on employees’ costs revealed that the expenditure included  wages totalling Kshs.105,965,392 which was paid through a manual payroll system   which  is   prone to errors and other forms of misstatement.  Further, analysis of the payment s revealed that three (3) employees were concurrently  listed in the Manual payroll, Human Resource Information System (HRIS) and IPPD  payroll systems, resulting in total payments amounting to Kshs.529,858, while twenty - one  (21) employees appeared in both t he casual and manual payrolls were paid a total of  Kshs.3,978,659.

526  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on management of   payroll and  personnel database   could not   b e confirmed.
