565  COUNTY EXECUTIVE OF MIGORI   –   NO.44  REPORT ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  1200.   Variance in Transfers from County Revenue Fund  The statement of financial performance reflects transfer from County Revenue Fund  balance of   Kshs.8,642,443,185 as disclosed in Note 6 to the financial statements.  However, the County Revenue Fund financial statements reported transfers amounting  to Kshs.8,700,611,436, resulting to an unreconciled variance of Kshs.58,168,251.  In the circumstances , the accuracy and completeness of the transfers from County  Revenue Fund of Kshs.8,642,443,185 could not be confirmed.  1201.   Unsupported Property Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets  The statement of financial position reflects property, plant and   equipment and intangible  assets balances of Kshs.2,490,463,012 and Kshs.8,587,453 as disclosed in Notes 16  and 17 to the financial statements respectively. However, the assets register provided for  audit was incomplete and did not contain all the assets ow ned by the County Executive.  Further, the register did not indicate the individual asset value, date of acquisition and the  projected useful life of the assets   to   aid in   the   computation of the depreciation, unique  identifiers and its location.  In additio n, Management did not have a depreciation policy in place to guide on the rates  of depreciation to be applied on the various categories of assets.  In the circumstances, the existence and valuation, of the property, plant and equipment  balance   and   intangi ble   assets   balance   totalling   Kshs.2,499,050,465   could   not   be  confirmed .  1202.   Unconfirmed Utilization of Early Childhood Development Education Funds  The statement of financial performance as disclosed in Note 9 to the financial statements  reflects an amount of   Kshs.75,042,193 as transfers to other government entities. Included  in the amount is a balance of Kshs.72,151,125 transferred to various primary schools for  the construction of Early Childhood Development Education (ECDE) classrooms and  latrines. However,   the approved policy guiding the transfer of funds to the ECDEs was  not provided for audit verification. Further, the School’s Board of Management did not  submit expenditure returns. Additionally, there was no evidence of advertisements or  quotations to en sure competitive procurement and minutes of the opening and evaluation  committee meetings were not provided for audit.  In   the   circumstances,   the   accuracy   and   completeness   of   the   transfers   to   other  government entities amounting to Kshs.75,042,193 not be c onfirmed.

566  Emphasis of Matter  1203.   Budgetary Control and Performance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects final receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   of   Kshs.9,994,922,213   and   Kshs.8,725,237,886  respectively, resulting in an underfunding of Kshs.1,269,684,327 or 13% of the budget.  However, the statement reflects actual expenditure amount of Kshs.8,663,687,035  against   actual   receipts   of   Kshs.8,725,237,886   resulting   in   an   under - ut ilization   of  Kshs.61,550,851, or 1% of actual receipts.  The underfunding affected the planned activities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  My opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.  Other Matter  1204.   Unresolved Prior Year Matters  In the previous year’s audit reports, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial Statements, Lawfulness and Effectiveness in Use of   Public Resources, and  Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance, respectively.  Review of the status during audit of the County Executive in 2024/2025 revealed that  thirty (30) matters relating to 2023/2024 financial year listed at   the end of this report  remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  Other Information  1205.   There were no material issues relating to Other Information.  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for Conclusion  1206.   N on - Compliance with Facility Improvement Financing Act, 2023  Review of revenue records obtained from Level 4 and Level 5 health facilities in Migori  County revealed that sixteen (16) health facilities collected a   total Kshs.321,376,360  towards the health facilities improvement which was all transferred to Migori County  Health   Services   Fund   Account.   However,   Management   reimbursed   a   total   of  Kshs.175,085,960 to the health facilities resulting in a deficit of Kshs.146 ,290,400. F ailure  to reimburse the total amount transferred by the facilities negatively impacted on service  delivery by the health facilities .   This was contrary to Section 5(1) of the Facilities  Improvement Financing Act, 2023 which requires that all monies raised or received by or  on behalf of all public health facilities be retained in the Hospital Facilities Improvement  Financing account.

567  In   the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1207.   Failure to Settle Accounts Payables as First Charge  The statement of financial position and as disclosed in Note 18 to the financial statements  reflects trade and other payables balance of Kshs.8 66,572,632 which includes payables  totalling Kshs.498,077,436 that had been outstanding for more than one (1) year. This  was   contrary   to   Regulation   41(2)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015, which states that debt servic e payments shall be a first  charge on the County Revenue Fund and the accounting officer shall ensure that the  County Government does not default on debt obligations.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1208.   Non - Compliance with Law on S taff Ethnic Composition  Review of personnel records revealed that the Coun ty Executive had three thousand , one  hundred and   fifty - nine   (3 ,159)   members of staff as at 31 March, 2025 out of whom tow  two thousand, two   hundred and   fifty - four   (2,254)   representing a   71 %   were from the  dominant ethnic community in the County. This was contrary to Section 7(2) of the  National Cohesion and Integration Act , 2008 which provides that no public establishment  shall have more than one third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1209.   Non - Compliance with Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025  Analysis of the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Database (IPPD) records for the month  of March, 2025 revealed that   the   County Executive had a   total   workforce of three  thousand, one hundred and fifty - nine (3 ,159)   out of whom forty - nine (49) or (1.5%) were  persons with disabilities.   This was   contrary to   Section   5(1)(e) of   the   People   with  Disabilities Act, 2025 which states that ‘every county government shall promote the  inclusion of persons with disabilities in the   county public service by putting in place  measures to ensure that at least five per centum of the employment positions are filled  by persons with   disabilities .  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1210.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third   Rule on Basic Salary  Review of the March, 2025 payroll revealed that four hundred and twenty - nine (429)  employees received net salaries which were less than a third (1/3) of their respective  basic salaries. This was contrary to Section 19(3) of the Emplo yment Act, 2007 which  provides that the total amount of all deductions which may be made by an employer from  the wages of his employee at any one time, shall not exceed two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

568  1211.   Retention of Employees Beyond Retirement Age  Review of the IPPD staff register   as at 1 July, 2025   revealed that the County Executive  had three thousand three thousand, one hundred and fifty - three (3 ,159 ) employees out  of whom, twenty - six (26) were over the mandatory retirement age of sixty (60) years  without any justification. No evidence was provided   to show that any of the officerbelong  to the peoples living with disabilities or have special skills. This was contrary to Regulation  70(1)(a), (b) and (c) of the Public Service Commission   Regulations , 2020 which states  that the mandatory retirement age i n the Public Service shall be sixty (60) years and/or  as may be prescribed by the Government from time to time.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1212.   Irregular Engagement of Casual Workers Beyond the Stipulated Period and  Delayed Pa yments  Review of human resource records revealed that the County Executive hired a total of   six  hundred and seventy - seven (677) casual workers for a period exceeding three months,  contrary to Paragraph B.16 of the County Human Resources Manual, 2013   which states  that that county governments can employ casual staff for urgent short - term tasks not  exceeding three months and will be paid in accordance with statutory wages regulations.  Further, the casual workers had not been paid wages for March and Apri l, 2025 as at the  time of the audit. This was contrary to Section 18(2)(a)(b) and (c) of the Employment Act,  2007, which states that wages and salaries shall be deemed due in the case of casual  employees at the end of the day or at the end of the period as   agreed in the engagement.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1213.   Regularity of Procurement and Award of Contracts  Review   of   the   procurement   and   contract   award   processes   revealed   the   following  inconsistencies:  1213.1.   Substandard Fencing Work at Awendo Stadium  Review of project records revealed that an amount of   Kshs.2,495,044 was spent on  fencing the Awendo   Stadium. However, physical inspection conducted on 29 May, 2025  revealed evidence of murram extraction from the field which resulted in some concrete  fencing posts hanging loosely above the ground, posing a safety risk as the fence may  collapse.  In   the   c ircumstances,   the   value   for   money   realized   from   the   expenditure   of  Kshs.2,495,044 on the project could not be confirmed.  1213.2.   Lack of Disposal Plan for   Unserviceable   Motor Vehicles  Review of records revealed that the County Executive had a fleet of one hundred and  ninety - five (195) vehicles, out of which forty - four (44) vehicles were grounded. However,  no disposal plan for the assets was provided for audit review, contrary to Regulat ion  176(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020, which requires

569  the Accounting Officer of a procuring entity to ensure that an annual assets disposal plan  is prepared for items declared as unserviceable, surplus, or obsolete. In a ddition,  Management did not provide measures put in place to either repair or dispose the  grounded vehicles to prevent further losses from wear and tear and the cost of repair of  unserviceable vehicles.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of th e law.  1213.3.   Non - Operational Cold Storages in Migori County  Review of records revealed that the County Executive spent Kshs.9,981,022 on the  construction of fish cold storages at Uriri and Isebania. However, physical inspection  conducted on 4 June, 2025 revealed that the cold storages were neither operational nor  c ommissioned, one year after completion.  In the circumstances, the value for money realized from the expenditure amount of  Kshs.9,981,022 on the project could not be confirmed.  1213.4.   Incomplete   County Aggr egation and Industrial Parks  Review of records revealed that the County Executive entered into a contract for the  construction of the County Aggregation and Industrial   Park at Nyatike at a contract sum  of Kshs.499,380,603 on 30 August, 2023. The contract period was twelve (12) months  commencing on 19 September, 2023 and ending on 12 September, 2024 but was later  extended to 30 August, 2025. As at 30 June, 2025, a total o f Kshs.358,337,493 had been  paid. However, the extension of contract period was not supported by a formal request  from the contractor. Further, physical inspection conducted in April, 2025 revealed that  the project remained incomplete with key works such a s plastering, installation of doors  and windows, painting and steel works, among others, had not been done.  In the circumstances, the value for money that may be realized from the expenditure  amount of Kshs.358,337,493 on the project could not be confirme d.  1213.5.   Incomplete Projects at Department of Public Health  1213.5.1.   Delayed Completion of New Staff House at Taragwiti Dispensary  The County Executive awarded a contract to a local contractor for the construction of a  new staff house at Taragwiti Dispensary at a contract sum of Kshs.2,139,500. The project  was scheduled to commence on 5 April, 2022, with an expected contract period of   120  days. However, physical inspection conducted on 4 June, 2025, revealed that the project  had only progressed up to the lintel level, despite the contract period having lapsed.  1213.5.2.   Delayed Completion of Twin Staff House and Patient Waiting Bay  The Coun ty Executive awarded a contract for the construction of Twin Staff house and  Patient waiting Bay at Komomange Dispensary at a contract sum of Kshs.999,896. The  project was scheduled to commence on 6 May, 2022, with an expected contract period  of 120 days.   However, physical inspection conducted on 4 June, 2025 revealed that the  staff house was incomplete. The outstanding works included branding, ceiling installation,  plumbing, and electrical wiring.

570  1213.5.3.   Delayed Completion of Laboratory  The   County   Executive   aw arded   a   contract   for   the   completion   of   a   laboratory   at  Nyamekongoroto   Dispensary   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.4,138,334.   The   project  commenced on 22 April, 2020 with an expected contract period of 120 days. However,  physical inspection conducted on 4 June, 20 25, revealed that the project was incomplete  with outstanding works including plumbing, construction of a septic tank and door  installation.  In the circumstances, the value for money realized from the expenditure amount of  Kshs.7,277,730 on the   incomplete projects could not be confirmed.  1213.5.4.   Maternity Ward at Nyamotembe Dispensary  The County Executive awarded a contract for the construction of a maternity ward at  Nyamotembe   Dispensary   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.3,862,876.   The   project   was  schedul ed to commence on 22 April, 2020, with an expected completion period of 120  days. However, physical inspection conducted during the audit on 4 June, 2025, revealed  that although the structure was complete, it had not been equipped for use.  1213.5.5.   Laboratory in G etabwanga Health Centre  The County Executive awarded a contract for the refurbishment of the laboratory at  Getabwanga   Health   Centre,   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.1,498,824.   The   project  commenced on 4 April, 2024, with an expected contract period of 120 days.   However,  physical inspection conducted on 4 June, 2025, revealed that the facility was not in use  and had not been branded.  1213.5.6.   Market Shades at Gupimo  Review of records revealed that Kshs.2,730,582 was paid to a local contractor for the  construction of a Market Shade project at Gupimo. However, physical inspection in the  month of May, 2025 revealed that the project was complete but not operational.  1213.5.7.   Land Purchased for the Construction of a Market  Review of records revealed that an amount of Kshs.2,800,000 was spent to purchase of  land   for   the   construction   of   a   market   in   Uriri.   However,   physical   inspection   in  May, 2025 e stablished that the market had not been constructed and the parcel of land  remains idle.  1213.5.8.   Car/Lorry Park at Kehancha Municipality  Review of records revealed that Kshs.4,391,020 was spent in respect of   a contract for the  construction of Car/lorry park at   Kehancha Municipality .   However, p hysical   i inspection  done on 4 May ,   2025 revealed that   although   the project was complete ,   it remained  unutilized .

571  In the circumstances, the value for money realized from the expenditure amount of  Kshs.15,283,302 on the unutilized projects could not be confirmed.  1213.6.   Unsatisfactory Implementation of Water Projects  Note 16 to the financial statements reflects additions to infrastructure assets amount of  Kshs.1,262,759,613. The following unsatisfactory   matters relating to water projects were  noted:  1213.7.   Unequipped Boreholes  Review of records revealed that an amount of Kshs.2,144,820 was spent on drilling a  borehole at Marera. However, physical inspection on 30 May, 2025 revealed that while  the borehole had been drilled it was not equipped, and the County Executive had not  all ocated a budget for equipping the project.  Review of records revealed that Kshs.3,810,146 was spent on drilling and equipping a  borehole   at   Owich   Primary   school   Macalder   Kanyarwanda.   Physical   inspection   in  May, 2025 revealed that although the proj ect was   complete and in use, residents reported  that frequent breakdowns of the pumping system, casting doubt on the quality of  equipping.  1213.8.   Pump Break Down at Oyani Treatment Works  Review of records revealed that Kshs.1,339,800 was utilized to repair the pump at   Oyani  Treatment Works. However, physical inspection in May, 2025 revealed that the repaired  pump had broken down again, casting doubt on the quality of repair works.  1213.9.   Unrelia ble Got Kwach Borehole in Macalder Kanyarwanda  Review of records revealed that Kshs. 3,498,009 was spent on e quipping Got Kwach  Borehole in Macalder Kanyarwanda. Physical inspection in May, 2025 revealed that the  borehole was   complete and in use. However,   residents complained of frequent break  down of the pumping system, casting doubt on the quality of equipping.  1213.9.1.   Unbranded Borehole at Kanyasrega Secondary School  Review of records revealed that Kshs.2,270,148 was spent on drilling of a borehole at  Kanyasrega Secondary School. However, p hysical inspection in May, 2025 revealed that  the borehole was   complete and in use, but was not branded.  1213.9.2.   Incomplete Bongu Raga Wa ter Project  The Department of Water and Energy awarded a contract worth Kshs.24,999,880 for the  construction of main water kiosks and distribution of pipelines under the Bongu Raga  Water Project Phase 4. The contract duration was 120 days, from 13 March,   2024 to

572  12 July, 2024. However, physical inspection on 30 May, 2025 revealed that the project  was incomplete.  1213.9.3.   Dry Borehole at Minyere  Review of records revealed that Kshs.2,145,920 was spent on drilling   Minyere Borehole .  However, physica l inspection on 4 June, 2025 revealed that the boreholes did not yield  adequate water, casting doubt on whether hydrological survey was conducted before  drilling.  1213.9.4.   Vandalized Ngege, Lichota Pipeline  Review of records revealed that Kshs.4,738,267 was paid for the extension of Ngege,  Lichota pipeline. However, verification of documents in May, 2025 revealed that there  was no running water in the extended pipelines due to vandalized pumps and damaged  pip elines.  1213.9.5.   Vandalized Kokuku Water Project  Review of records revealed that an amount of Kshs.3,999,989 was utilized towards the  drilling and equipping of Kokuku Water Project. However, audit inspection revealed that  drilled borehole had no running water due   to vandalized pumps and damaged pipelines.  1213.10.   Non - Operational Public Wi - Fi  Review of records revealed that an amount of Kshs.9,576,000 was spent on the provision  and installation of public Wi - Fi hotspot access points across various locations in Migori  Coun ty. However, physical inspection conducted in October 2025 at sampled points  revealed that the installed Wi - Fi hotspots were not operational due to non - payment of  quarterly internet subscription fees.  In   the   circumstances,   the   value   for   money   realized   fro m   the   expenditure   of  Kshs.9,576,000 on the project could not be confirmed.  1214.   Avoidable Interest on Accrued Legal Expenses  Review of records revealed that the County Executive spent Kshs.3,972,779 in interest  charges on late discharge of legal expenses of Kshs.6,644,247, which included decretal  amounts and judicial review costs. The expenses could have been avoided had timely  settlement of obligations been made.  In   the   circumstances,   the   value   for   money   realized   from   the   expenditure   of  Kshs.3,972,779   could not be confirmed.  1215.   Non - Compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility Principle on Development  Expenditure  The statement of f inancial performance reflects total expenses of Kshs.6,807,826,030  relating to recurrent expenditure while Note 16 to the financial statements reflects

573  additions to property, plant and equipment amounting to Kshs.2,305,015,923, resulting in  total   expenses   for   the   year   of   Kshs.9,112,841,953.   The   development   expenditure  represents 25% of the total expenditure which is below the minimum 30% threshold  required   by   Regulation   25(1)(g)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015.  In t he circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1216.   Failure to Prepare Memorandum for Supplementary Budgets  As disclosed in the statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts, the County  Executive   had   original   approved   budget   of   Kshs.8,596,649,061   for   the   2024/2025  financial year, which was subsequently adjusted by Kshs.1,398,273,152 through a  supplementar y   budget   to   a   final   budget   of   Kshs.9,994,922,213.   However,   the  supplementary budget adjustments were not supported by memoranda from Accounting  Officers to confirm that the changes had been requested and explanations given for either  scaling up or changing   of planned development programmes. This was contrary to  Regulation 39(7) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments) Regulations,  2015 which provides that, the county government entity requesting additional funds  through a supplementary budget p rocess to submit a memorandum to the County  Treasury.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  1217.   Lack of Approved Monitoring and   Evaluation Policy  During the year under review, the County Executive spent Kshs.2,305,015,923 on  additions to property, plant and equipment as disclosed in Note 16 to the financial  statements. However, as at the time of audit in November, 2025 the Monitor ing and  Evaluation Policy prepared by Management remained in draft form and had not been  approved. This was contrary to Regulations 129(1) of the Public Finance Management  (County   Governments)   Regulation,   2015,   which   requires   the   County   Executive  Committee   Member responsible for planning to prescribe a framework for monitoring on  non - financial performance.   The framework should enable accounting officers to evaluate  programmes and projects using financial indicators (expenditure on implementation),  output in dicators (direct deliverables), and outcome indicators (expected effects on  beneficiaries).  In the circumstances, the existence of an effective mechanism to evaluate programmes  and projects could not be confirmed.

574  1218.   Failure to Develop Annual   Recruitment Plans  Review of records revealed that during the period under review, two hundred and eleven  (211) staff were hired by the County Executive. However, no annual recruitment plan was  developed as required by Paragraph B.2(2) of the Human Resourc e Policies and  Procedures Manual for the Public Service May, 2016.  Further, Management failed to prepare human resource plans to support achievement of  goals and objectives in their strategic plans as required by Paragraph B.2(1) of the Human  Resource Po licies and Procedures Manual for the Public Service May, 2016.  In   the   circumstances,   the   effectiveness   of   internal   controls   over   human   resource  management could not be confirmed.  1219.   Non - Compliance with the County Approved Staff Establishment  Review of   the staff establishment   approved and operationalized in 2023   compared to the  employees in position revealed that the County Executive had   a staffing need of 11,023  employees out of which, only 3,509 or 32% were in - post, resulting in understaffing of  7,514   employees.  In the circumstances,   the understaffing may adversely affect the County Executive’s  ability to implement its mandate and offer services to the public.  1220.   Lack of ICT Security Policy and Disaster Recovery Plan  Review of the Information and   Communication Technology (ICT) of the County revealed  that the County Executive did not have an ICT, Data Recovery Plan (DRP) and ICT  Security Policy. In addition, the Management had not installed antivirus programs in its  systems and did not have mechanis ms for ensuring that there was up - to - date security on  the systems software. Further, the County Executive did not have an IT Steering  Committee, a Disaster Recovery Plan, a backup and retention strategy to guarantee  continuity of operations in case of syst em failure. In addition, regular review and risk  assessment of the operational areas were not conducted. As a result, the system users  lack guidance on procedures to minimize risks of errors, data loss and compromise data  integrity and availability.  In th e circumstances, the effectiveness of the County Executive’s IT internal controls, risk  management and governance processes could not be confirmed.  1221.   Failure to Operationalize Risk Management Policy and Framework  The   County Executive had an approved risk m anagement policy. However, there was no  evidence   that   the   policy   was   operational.   Documents   including   risk   registers,   risk  assessment reports, risk mitigation measures taken and mapping future risks, forecasts  and a documented disaster recovery plan were m issing.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the County Executive’s risk management  strategies could not be confirmed.

575  1222.   Weak Internal Controls Over Inventory Management  Review of records revealed that the value of items in stores could not be confir med since  the Management did not carry out quarterly stock take, contrary to Regulation 171(1)(d)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2015 which requires the Head  of the Procurement Function of a procuring entity to conduct quarterly   and annual stock  taking.  Further, there were no records of stores items requested, approved and issued at any  particular time, while the stores ledger had not been updated.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over inventory management  could not be   confirmed.  1223.   Weak Controls over Medical Supplies and Services  During physical inspection conducted in May, 2025, weaknesses in controls over medical  suppliers and services were noted in seven (7) facilities; Migori County Drugs Store,  Rongo Sub - County Hosp ital, Ngere Health Centre, Awendo Sub - County Hospital, Mariwa  Dispensary, Uriri Sub - County Hospital and Lwala Nyarago Dispensary.  At the Migori County Drugs Store, the absence of quarterly stock undermines assurance  on the County’s overall inventory posit ion. Other facilities experienced understaffing in  pharmacy units, lack of appropriate pharmacy infrastructure and reliance on manual bin  cards due to lack of computers and internet connectivity. Further, frequent power outages  affected cold - chain medicine s at Mariwa Dispensary and there was widespread failure by  patients to acknowledge receipt of drugs.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls over medical supplies and  services in health facilities could not be confirmed.

576  List of   Un resolved Prior Year Matters  S/No.   2023/2024 Audit Issue  1   Unsupported Expenditure on Wages  2   Unsupported Legal Expenses  4   Budgetary Control and Performance  5   Late Exchequer Releases  6   County Executive Preparedness to Transition to Accrual   Accounting  7   Non - Compliance   with   Fiscal   Responsibility   Principle   on   Development  Expenditure  8   Pending Accounts Payable  9   Non - Compliance with Fiscal Responsibility Principle on Wage Bill  10   Non - Compliance with Ethnic and Special Needs in the Staff Compo sition  11   Violation of One - Third Rule on Net Pay  12   Failure to Customize Schemes of Service to Suit the County Executive  13   Under Staffing of County Attorney’s Office  14   Non - Compliance   with   Access   to   Government   Procurement   Opportunities  (AGPO)  15   Payments to the Council of Governors  16   Payment to the Lake Region Economic Bloc  17   Inadequate Allocation of Funds for Major Road Works  18   Supply, Installation and Commissioning of Containers Fish Collection Centre  (Cold Rooms)  19   Construction of Kwiriba Market Shed  20   Completion of Masaba Market   Shed  21   Partial Completion of Midoti Market Shed  22   Other Incomplete Markets  23   Un - Utilized Projects  24   Rehabilitation of Kaknene Dam   –   Under FLLoCA Program  25   Proposed Construction of Maternity Block at Olasi Dispensary  26   Unsupported Completion of Project   - Construction of Buembu Dispensary  27   Unsupported Completion of Nyamware Dispensary  28   Projects Not in Use   –   Department of Medical Services  29   Bongu   Raga Water Project  30   Lack of Segregation of Duties in the Processing of Payments of Salary Arrears

577  COUNTY EXECUTIVE   OF KISII   –   NO.45  REPORT ON THE   FINANCIAL STATEMENTS  Basis for Qualified   Opinion  1224.   Non - Compliance with International Public Sector Accounting Standards  Reporting Requirements  Note 2 to Financial Statements on   Statement of Compliance and Basis of Preparation of  the   financial   statements,   Management   having   taken   advantage   of   the   transitional  provisions under IPSAS 33 did not indicate the elements of the financial statements that  were not recognized and the steps b eing taken towards full compliance with Annual  Financial Reporting Template issued by the Public Sector Accounting Standard Board.  In   the   circumstances,   the   presentation   and   disclosure   in   financial   statements   is  not compliant with the IP SAS reporting framework.  1225.   Unexplained Voided Transactions  The   statement   of   financial   performance   reflects   total   expenses   amount   of  Kshs.7,560,021,975.   Review   of   the   Integrated   Financial   Management   Information  System (IFMIS) payments revealed that six hun dred and ninety - three (693) transactions  amounting to Kshs.1,094,702,969 were voided during the year 2024/2025. However, the  supporting documents and reasons for voiding were not provided for audit.  In   the   circumstances,   the   regularity   and   completeness   o f   payments   could   not   be  confirmed  1226.   Use of Goods and Services  The statement of financial performance, and as disclosed in Note 8 to the financial  statements, reflects use of goods and services amount of Kshs.1,373,224,911. However,  the following   unsatisfactory matters were noted:  1226.1.   Unreconciled Fuel, Oil and Lubricants  The balances includes expenditure totalling   Kshs.40,645,666 in respect of fuel, oil and  lubricants. However, the supporting schedules provided for audit reflected fuel, oil and  lubricants amounted to Kshs.37,245,666, resulting in an unreconciled and unexplained  variance of Kshs.3,400,000. Although M anagement explained that the variance relates to  accrued expenditure on fuel, oil and lubricants, supporting documents including the  specific vouchers were not provided for audit.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of use of goods and se rvices  expenditure of Kshs.40,645,666 could not be confirmed.

578  1226.2.   Unsupported Avoidable Legal Expenses  Further, the balance includes an amount of Kshs.347,089,030 in respect of other  operating expenses, which further includes legal fees of Kshs.7,762,065.   However,  documents   provided for audit revealed that a court ruling had been made against the  County Executive on alleged infringement of constitutional rights against a petitioner. The  Environment and Land Court ruling on the case awarded the petitioner Ks hs.5,605,885,  comprising Kshs.5,000,000 damages and Kshs.605,885 being costs of petition borne by  the County Executive. The ruling was made on 31 March, 2023. According to a demand  letter dated 17 February, 2025 by an advocate on behalf of the petitioner,   the County  Executive was supposed to pay the petitioner an accrued amount of Kshs.7,762,065  computed up to December 2024 and which had not yet been settled by the County  Executive. The delay by the County Executive to honour the court ruling resulted in ex tra  costs of Kshs.2,156,180 which could have been avoided had the settlements been made  in full.  In addition, no evidence was provided for audit to confirm whether the County Executive  explored avenues of appeal against the court ruling. The total outsta nding amount in  respect of this petition could not be confirmed as Management did not provide the  breakdown of payments already made to date. Review of pending bills listing as at  30 June, 2024 did not confirm existence of amount payable to the   petitioner.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and disclosure of the Kshs.7,762,065 in respect to  legal expenditure could not be confirmed.  1227.   Cash and Cash Equivalents   -   Failure to Observe Cut - Off Period in Bank  Reconciliation  The   statement   of   financial position,   and as   disclosed   in   Note   12   to   the   financial  statements, reflects a balance of Kshs.309,124,367 in respect of the cash and cash  equivalents. However, review of documents provided for audit revealed that the bank  reconciliation statement s provided for audit revealed reconciling items of unpresented  cheques and receipts in cash book not yet recorded in bank statements which related to  transactions after the end of the financial year on 30 June, 2025 as shown below:  Bank Details  Unpresente d  Cheques  (Kshs)  Receipt in Cash Book  not yet Recorded in the  Bank Statement  (Kshs)  CBK - Kisii County Development Account   751,280,300   305,576,605  CBK - Kisii County Recurrent Account   297,954,624   244,289,655  CBK -   Kisii   County Deposit Account   11,001,687   59,689,238  Total   1,060,236,611   609,555,498  Further, bank confirmation certificates for all the accounts that are operated in the Central  Bank of Kenya (CBK) were also not provided for audit.

579  In the   circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the cash and cash equivalents  balance of Kshs.309,124,367 could not be confirmed.  1228.   Trade and Other Payables  The   statement   of   financial position,   and as   disclosed   in   Note   16   to   the   financial  statements, refle cts trade and other payables balance of Kshs.2,623,281,983. However,  the following unsatisfactory matters were noted:  1228.1.   Unsupported Trade and Other Payables  Review   of   the   supporting   schedules   provided   for   audit   revealed   that   the   balance  comprised   of   eligible   and   ineligible   payables   of   Kshs.1,551,846,299   and  Kshs.1,071,435,684, respectively. However, Management did not confirm why pending  bills totalling Kshs.1 ,071,435,684 were classified as in - eligible. Further, contrary to The  National Treasury Circular No. 03/2025 dated 14 April, 2025, Management did not provide  circularization   results   from   all   suppliers   and   obtain   supplier   statements   as   at  30 June, 2024, and reconcile the payables with their records to ensure completeness of  trade and other payables. The guideline requires that these bills be adequately supported  with all relevant documentation. The bills will form the opening balances   as of 1 July, 2024  and will be subject to audit by the Office of the Auditor - General.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and   completeness of the trade and other payables  balance of Kshs.2,623,281,983 could not be confirmed.  1228.2.   Unconfirmed Legal Liability  The   trade   and   other   payables   balance   includes   legal   payables   balance   of  Kshs.155,831,232. A   detailed listing of forty - five (45) suits revealed some payables dating  as far back as 2015/2016 financial year. No plausible justification was provided on why  th e payables had not been paid in the subsequent years, which could lead to escalation  of penalties and accrued interest. Further, Management provided a listing of accounts  payable as at 30 June, 2025 totalling Kshs.2,623,281,983. However, none of the payabl es  listed by the Legal Department had been incorporated in the balance.  In addition, out of the forty - five (45) suits, twenty - eight (28) suits were indicated as relating  to decretal sum totalling Kshs.132,560,058. However, evidence of certified decree in  respect of outstanding balance was not provided for audit. Review of the suits also  revealed that the forty - five (45) suits were not supported by evidence of formal requisition  from the user department and contract agreements for each of the suits. The ba lance of  Kshs.155,831,232 was not supported by fee notes or any computation of cost.  In the circumstances, the accuracy and completeness of the trade and other payables  balance of Kshs.155,831,232 could not be confirmed.

580  1229.   Unreconciled   Revenue   Collections   and   Revenue   Management   System  Administrative Costs  The statement of financial performance and as disclosed in Note 8 to the financial  statements reflects an amount of Kshs.1,373,224,911 in respect of use of goods and  services. Included in this amount is Kshs.347,089,030 in respect of to other operating  exp enses which includes Kshs.24,902,063 for administrative costs/transaction fees for  the   Revenue   Management   System.   However,   data   migration   a   key   deliverable   in  milestone two had not been achieved at the time of audit in May 2025. Management did  not provide   explanation on challenges impeding full data migration into the System and  action plans towards achieving this milestone.  Review of records for administrative costs for the Revenue Management System revealed  that two (2) invoices dated 7 June, 2024 and 7   July, 2024 of Kshs.8,059,684 and  Kshs.8,598,998, respectively, were paid during the year under review for transaction fees  for revenues collected between 1 April, 2024 to 31 May, 2024. However, the amount of  total revenue collected during the year under re view varied, with the first invoice indicating  Kshs.59,434,341 and the second invoice indicating Kshs.87,611,115 resulting in a  unexplained variance of Kshs.28,176,774.  Further, re - computation of expected transaction fees at 5.4% of revenue collected in   the  invoices revealed that an amount of Kshs.3,209,454 and Kshs.4,731,000 ought to have  been billed for the first and second invoice respectively resulting in overpayments of  Kshs.4,850,230   and   Kshs.3,867,998   for   the   first   and   second   invoice   respectively.  Management did not provide explanations for the inconsistencies in amounts of revenue  collected on the invoices for the same period and the administrative costs paid.  In addition, during the year under review, the Revenue Management System service  provid er was paid an amount of Kshs.4,850,230 as administrative costs for revenues of  Kshs.89,819,066 collected between 26 January, 2024 and 31 March, 2024. However,  review of revenue reports maintained at the County Revenue Department revealed that  no   revenue   w as   collected   through   the   System   during   this   period.   System   review  established that the reporting module in the System had not been fully implemented.  Consequently, system generated reports could not be produced and it was not possible  to perform reconcili ation between the invoiced amount and the amount banked.  In the circumstances the accuracy and completeness of administrative costs for the  Revenue Management System of Kshs.24,902,063 could not be confirmed.  Emphasis of Matter  1230.   Budgetary Control and Per formance  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects total receipts budget  and   actual   on   comparable   basis   of   Kshs.13,953,991,832   and   Kshs.9,320,328,103  respectively, resulting in under - funding of Kshs.4,633,663,729 or   approximately 33% of  the approved budget. The County Executive spent an amount of Kshs.9,011,203,736  against actual receipt of Kshs.9,320,328,103 resulting in difference of Kshs.309,124,367  or 3% of actual receipts.

581  The under - funding affected the planned a ctivities and may have impacted negatively on  service delivery to the public.  1231.   Unresolved   Prior Year Matters  In the previous year’s audit reports, several issues were raised under the Report on  Financial Statements, Lawfulness and   Effectiveness in the Use of Public Resources, and  Effectiveness of Internal Controls, Risk Management and Governance. Review of the  status during audit of the County Executive in 2024/2025 revealed that forty - eight (48)  matters indicated at the end of this   report remained unresolved as at 30 June, 2025.  Other Information  1232.   There were no material issues relating to other information .  .  REPORT   ON   LAWFULNESS   AND   EFFECTIVENESS   IN   THE   USE   OF   PUBLIC  RESOURCES  Basis for   Conclusion  1233.   Failure to Retain Facilities Improvement Funds at the Hospitals  Review of revenue records obtained from Level 4 and Level 5 health facilities in Kisii  County revealed that eighteen (18) health facilities collected a total Kshs.190,435,651  towards the health facilities improvement. Out of the amount, a total of Kshs.173 ,444,017  was transferred to County Health Facilities Improvement Fund Board account. However,  the amount reimbursed by the Board to the facilities could not be confirmed. This was  because the Board made payments on behalf of the health facilities without d isclosing the  expenditures incurred on behalf of specific health facilities. This was contrary to Section  5(1) of the Facilities Improvement Financing Act, 2023, which requires that all monies  raised or received by or on behalf of all public health facilit ies be retained in the Hospital  Facilities Improvement Financing account. In addition, failure to reimburse the total  amount transferred by the facilities negatively impacted on service delivery by the health  facilities.  In the circumstances, Management   was in breach of the law.  1234.   Provision,   Customization,   and   Implementation   of   Hospital   Management  Information System  Hospital Management Information System documents provided for audit revealed that the  County Executive awarded a tender for the   provision, commissioning and implementation  design,   development,   installation   and   commissioning   of   the   Integrated   Hospital  Management Information System (HMIS) at a cost of Kshs.27,878,280 for a contract  period of 2 April, 2024 to 2 April, 2025. Review   of   the   project implementation report  revealed that as at May, 2025, the project was not yet complete. Milestone 4 (receipt of  an acceptable system go live) and milestone 5 (issuing of the certificate of practical  completion) had not been undertaken, because t he infrastructure environment had not

582  been provided.   No explanation was provided why the Hospital Management requested a  system upgrade before assessing the infrastructure environment of the user facilities.  In the circumstances, the value for money   for the amount spent on the project could not  be confirmed.  1235.   Delay in Completion of Reproductive Health Centre in Kisii Mother - Child  Hospital  The County Executive entered into a contract on 20 May, 2024, for the completion of  reproductive health centre at   the Kisii Mother - Child Hospital at a contract sum of  Kshs.100,000,000. The contract period was twenty - four (24) weeks from 4 June, 2024 to  28 November, 2024. However, physical inspection of the project in May 2025, indicated  that the project was estimated   at 65% completion despite the lapse in contract period with  no extension period. The cumulative payments as at the time of audit amounted to  Kshs.55,508,805.  Further,   review   of   the   project   documents   revealed   that   a   contract   variation   of  Kshs.8,529,250 wa s made within two (2) months of the contract period contrary to Section  139(3) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015 that prohibits upward  variation of contract price within twelve months from signing the contract. There was  second variati on of Kshs.1,809,250 and both variations were not reviewed by the  Evaluation Committee or Contract Implementation Team contrary to Regulations 132(2)  of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020.  In addition, the County Executive did not   comply with Regulation 150(1) of the Public  Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations, 2020 which requires prompt payment  within sixty days from date of receipt of invoice since the contractor issued notice of  delayed payments exceeding five months which   affected project cashflows.  In the circumstance management was in breach of law.  1236.   Irregular Payment to Council of Governors  Review of payment records revealed that during the year under review, the County  Executive paid an amount of   Kshs.3,000,000 to the Council of Governors for the purpose  of meeting its operational expenses, contrary to Section 37 of the Intergovernmental  Relations Act, 2012, which states that the operational expenses in respect of the  structures and institutions es tablished in Act shall be provided for in the annual estimates  of revenue and expenditure of T he National Government.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1237.   Projects Status   -   Department of Water, Energy, Environment and Climate  Change  During the year under review, the County Executive implemented various projects in the  Department of Water, Environment and Energy. Physical   inspection   carried out in the  month of May, 2025 revealed the following anomalies:

583  1237.1.   Poor Workmanship in the Reticu lation of Eronge Borehole in Monyerero  Ward  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company on 22 April, 2024 for the  reticulation of Eronge borehole in Monyerero ward at a contract sum of Kshs.1,999,600.  However,   physical   inspection   conducted   did   not   confirm   whether   the   project   was  implemented by the County   Executive   as it had not been branded. In addition,   the pipe  connecting the borehole and the bump chamber had already cracked and, therefore, a  lot of water was lost through leakage.  1237.2.   Underutilization of the Manga Hills Water Project  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company for the construction and  reticulation of Manga Hills Water Project on 20 December, 2024 at a contract sum of  Kshs.9,298,050.   The audit establish ed that   the water produced from the plant was of  good quantity. However, physical inspection revealed that the water was being misused  by the community and was going to waste. it was further noted that Management did not  have a sustainability plan for the   project.  1237.3.   Substandard Works at the Daraja Mbili Secondary School Back Street  Drainage  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company for construction of Daraja  Mbili Secondary School backstreet drainage on 2 January, 2024 at a contract sum o f  Kshs.2,499,684. However, there were no   weep holes   in retaining walls   placed to allow  water to drain from behind the wall to prevent water buildup and potential damage.  1237.4.   Substandard Works in the Installation of Solar System at Nyamache Level  4 Hospital  T he County Executive entered into a contract with a company, for installation of a 6.0KWP  of solar photovoltaic system at Nyamache Level 4 Hospital on 3 July, 2023 at a contract  sum of Kshs.2,948,990. However, the   system was not in use since it could only p roduce  24A but the facility required a system which produces 70A for it to run the machines. It  was not clear whether the proposal arose from the users and whether there was feasibility  study before the inception of the project. Further, the project was no t branded as evidence  that it was implemented by the County Executive.  1237.5.   Under Utilized Riyabu Borehole in Bokimonge Ward  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company for drilling and reticulation  of Riyabu borehole at Bokimonge ward on 22   January, 2024 at a contract sum of  Kshs.4,297,400. However,   the water produced from the borehole was underutilized since  the storage facility provided was only 10,000 litres tank, hence a lot of water was  underutilized . Further, the project was not branded   as evidence that it was implemented  by the County Executive.

584  1237.6.   A Dry Borehole at Nyabera Market in Moticho Ward  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company for drilling and equipping  of a borehole at Nyabera market with hand bump in Moticho ward at a contract sum of  Kshs.2,499,600. However, there   was no evidence of existence of water in the borehole  during the time of physical inspection. Further, the audit established that it had taken more  than four (4) months since the pump broke down. In addition, the project was not branded  as evidence that it was implemented by the County Executive.  In the circumstances value for money realized from the expenditure of Kshs.23,543,324  on the six (6) projects could not be confirmed.  1238.   Delayed Construction of County Aggregation and Industrial Park  The County Executive awarded a contract for the constru ction of County Aggregation and  Industrial   Park   at   a   contract   sum   of   Kshs.477,941,470   which   commenced   on  18   September,   2023. An   advance   payment   of   Kshs.95,588,294   was   made   to   the  contractor   upon   winning   the   tender.   Further,   the   proje ct   was   still   ongoing   and  approximately   50%   complete   despite   the   contract   period   having   expired   on  18 March, 2025. Further, ownership documents for the land on which the construction  was being undertaken was not   provided for   audit to confirm that the land belonged to the  County Executive. In addition, the feasibility study for the project, National Environment  Management Authority (NEMA) approvals, and signed programme of works were not  provided for audit.  In the circumstanc es, value for money realized from the expenditure paid in respect to  the project could not be confirmed.  1239.   Abandoned Project -   Egorofa -   Riotwori - Keboba - Amasago Road Project  The County Executive entered into a contract with a company on 7 December, 2023 for  the construction, repair and maintenance of eighteen (18) Lot 4 roads in Nyaribari Chache  Sub - County for a period of twenty - four (24) weeks at a contract sum of Kshs.53,696,806.  Included   in   this   category   is   repair   and   maintenance   of   Egorofa - Riotwori - keboba -  Amasango road at a cost of Kshs.3,551,746. The contract period lapsed on 10 May, 2024  with no extension and the contract was terminated on 15 November, 2024. Cumulatively,  the contractor had been paid Kshs.11,677,836 as at 30 June, 2025.  Physical inspect ion conducted on 4 June, 2025 revealed that the contractor was not on  site and drainage works and culverts were not done for Riotwori - Egorofa road (0.8km),  gravelling, compaction, drainage works and culverts were not done on Egorofa - Nyamira  River (0.8km) a nd no works were ongoing on the Riotwori - Egorofa and   Egorofa - Nyamira  River sections. Further, no signages had been erected to identify the project with the  County Executive. In addition, review of project documents revealed that the contractor  did not subm it a program of works and monthly progress reports in line with Clauses 8.3.1  and 4.2.1 of the contract   agreement .  In the circumstances, value money spent on the project could not be confirmed.

585  1240.   Irregular Operation of Commercial Bank Accounts  The County   Executive operated a total of seventy - nine (79) bank accounts in both the  Central Bank of Kenya and several commercial banks. Seventeen (17) accounts were  operated in the Central Bank of Kenya, and the remaining sixty - two (62) in commercial  banks. This was   contrary to Regulation 82(1)(b) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires that the County Government  bank accounts be opened and maintained at the Central Bank of Kenya with the  exemption of imprest bank accou nts, such as petty cash and revenue collection bank  accounts.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1241.   Non - Compliance with Fiscal Responsibility Principle on Wages  The statement of financial performance reflects employee costs of Kshs .5,433,906,661  representing   59.7 % of the total revenue of Kshs.9,106,135,362 .   This was contrary to  Regulation 25(1)(a) and (b) of the Public Finance Management (County Governments)  Regul ations, 2015 which requires that the County Executive Committee Member with the  approval of the County Assembly to set a limit on the County Government's expenditure  on wages and benefits for its public officers and the limit not to exceed thirty - five (35% )  of the County Government's total revenue.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1242.   Non - Compliance with the One - Third Rule on Basic Salary  Analysis of the County Executive’s monthly payroll revealed that three hundred and thirty -  fiv e (335) employees received net pay that was below a third (1/3) of their respective  basic salaries.   This was   contrary to Section 19(3) of the Employment Act, 2007 which  stipulates   that   without   prejudice   to   any   right   of   recovery   of   any   debt   due   and  notwiths tanding the provisions of any other written law, the total amount of all deductions  made by an employer from the wages of his employee at any one time shall not exceed  two - thirds of such wages.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1243.   Non - Compliance with the National   Cohesion   and Integration Act, 2008  Review of personnel records revealed that as at 30 June, 2025 the County Executive had  a total of five thousand four hundred and seventy - eight (5478) out of whom five thousand  one hundr ed and sixty - three (5,163) or 94.45% were from the dominant ethnic community  in the County. This was contrary to the provisions of section 7(1) and (2) of the National  Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008   which states that all public establishments shall see k  to represent the diversity of the people of Kenya in the employment of staff and no public  establishment shall have more than one third of its staff from the same ethnic community.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.

586  1244.   Non - Compliance   with   Fiscal   Responsibility   Principle   on   Development  Expenditure  The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts reflects development  expenditure of Kshs.2,243,229,092 or 24% of   total expenditures of Kshs.9,011,203,736.  This was con trary to Regulation 25(1)(g) of the Public Finance Management (County  Governments) Regulations, 2015, which requires that, the county   government actual  expenditure on development shall be at   least thirty percent (30%) of the total County  Government expendi ture.  In the   circumstances, Management was in breach of the law.  1245.   Lack of County Spatial and Valuation Roll  During the year under review, the County Executive did not have the updated and  approved county spatial plan and valuation roll. As a   result, the County Executive may  not be in a position to identify all the revenue collection points leading to under collection  of own generated revenue. This was contrary to Section 30 (1) of the National Rating Act,  2024 which states that “a county gover nment shall cause preparation of a valuation roll  to be undertaken in every five years on the ratable properties within the County”.  In the circumstances, Management was in breach of the law .  REPORT ON EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERNAL CONTROLS, RISK MANAGEMENT  AND GOVERNANCE  Basis for Conclusion  1246.   Ineffective   Internal Controls   in the   Collection and Accounting for Own  Generated Revenue  During the year under review, the County Executive used two   revenue systems for  collection of revenue. However , the point of sale (POS) machines assigned to the various  revenue collectors had no power back up and a proper maintenance plan and, therefore  were likely to affect the operations in case of power failure . Further, two hundred and  eighty (280) point of sale machines were inadequate for the operations of the County  Executive. It was also observed that the super - admin rights were held by the service  provider hence the security and the management of the data   could not be confirmed.  The Local Authorities Integrated Financial Operations Management System (LAIFOM)  was last updated in the year 2010. In addition, it was not clear why the County Executive  had not transferred all the land rates data from the LAIFOM   to Jambo Pay system.  Additionally, the County Executive did not have debt recovery plan for all the outstanding  arrears on the land rates.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on the revenue administration  at the County Executive   could not be confirmed.

587  1247.   Weak Internal Controls on Imprest Management  Review of imprest records revealed that an amount of Kshs.1,750,000 in respect of  various surrender of imprests. The imprests were issued to various personnel within the  Department of   Finance for cash purchases. Review of imprest surrender vouchers  provided for audit revealed that expenditure amounting to Kshs.1,750,000 was not  accounted for in full. The Department had a procurement unit and no justification for  incurring the expenditur e of Kshs.1,750,000 through imprest.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on imprest management could  not be confirmed.  1248.   Understaffing of Climate Change Unit and Oversight Structures  The County Executive had put in place a climate change action plan 2023 - 2027 to guide  in   adaptation   to   the   effects   of   the   climate   change   and   reducing   greenhouse   gas  emissions. Review of climate change documents provided for audit however, revealed  that   the   technical unit had seven (7) staff against the requirement of nine (9) staff as per  the climate action plan which could compromise on the achievement of key objectives of  the Unit. Further, County Executive did not have the capacity to report on the green house  gas emissions as no output had been raised on the same.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the Climate Change Action Plan could not be  confirmed.  1249.   Weak Controls in Information and Communication Technology  During the year under review, the County Executive utilized a number of automated  systems such as the County Electronic Revenue Collection and Management System,  the Integrated Financial Managemen t Information System (IFMIS), the Integrated Payroll  and Personnel Data (IPPD) system, the LAIFOM Land Rate Management System, and  the   Liquor   Management   System   to   manage   its   operations.   However,   the   County  Executive lacked business and IT continuity plans,   a disaster recovery and offsite backup  plan, an ICT capacity building training program, environmental controls policies and  procedures,   an   IT   security/risk   management   policy,   and   an   approved   IT   Steering  Committee   to   ensure   that   the   IT   Department   was   in   ha rmony   with   the   County  Government’s mission and objectives. Further, the County Executive did not have both  the hardware maintenance program and hardware reviews.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of the County Executive’s ICT internal   controls  and IT governance could not be confirmed.  1250.   Lack of an Audit Committee  During the year under review, the County Executive did not have an Audit Committee in  place.   This was contrary to Regulation 167(1) of the Public Finance Management  (County Go vernments) Regulations, 2015 which provides that each County Government  entity shall establish an Audit Committee. As a result, the internal audit reports were

588  discussed only at departmental level. Further, the internal audit did not have a charter  and ope rationalized workplan that was approved by the Audit Committee contrary to  Regulation   163(2)   of   the   Public   Finance   Management   (County   Governments)  Regulations, 2015.  In the circumstances, effective oversight of the internal audit function could not be  co nfirmed.  1250.1.   Dormant Bank Accounts  Included in the cash and cash equivalents balance is an amount of Kshs.309,124,367  held in twelve (12) bank accounts that were dormant and had no operations for more than  one year. Management did not provide   explanation for continuing to operate the dormant  bank accounts. This was contrary to Regulation 88(2) of the Public Finance Management  (County Governments) Regulations, 2015, which provides that the County Executive  Committee Member may suspend the operat ions of any county government bank account  or impose certain conditions, if he or she reasonably believes the purpose of that account  no longer exists.  In the circumstances, the effectiveness of internal controls on cash management could  not be confirmed.
